MANUSCRIPT:
Series:   “Daniel: God’s Sovereign Plans” #34 
Text:   Daniel 12:1–3
By:   Shaun Marksbury     
Date:   September 13, 2026
Venue:   Living Water Baptist Church  
Occasion:   PM Service

Introduction
The doctrine of the last things should be an encouragement to us.  As we’ve previously noted, though, too often it is not.  People grow fearful in their speculations as dates are set and predictions made that are later quietly abandoned.  Rumors fill the gaps where God has not revealed.  Even so, God has revealed what He did so His people have hope and comfort.

We see that hope in this concluding chapter the Book of Daniel.  It provides additional insight into the tribulation and more.  We see that this occurs “at that time,” which is “the end time” according to 11:40.[1]  This is continuing the same vision from chapter 10 through 11, so that makes sense.

Those who are facing the horrors of this time can know that there is a message of hope for those who die in persecution.  Daniel, who had lived to see so much, likewise wants this hope.  To keep it simple, we’ll just consider three aspects of the end times and the hope it brings.  First, the crisis of the end times (v. 1).  Second, the resurrections of the end times (v. 2).  Third, the glory of the end times (v. 3).

First, the Crisis of the End Times (v. 1)
Now at that time, Michael, the great prince who stands guard over the sons of your people, will stand. And there will be a time of distress such as never happened since there was a nation until that time; and at that time your people, everyone who is found written in the book, will be rescued.

This is an unparalleled distress, a severe trial upon the earth as we considered in the past two messages.  Nothing in human history fully describes it.  Yet, even here, there is good news, for the text immediately introduces Michael.  This means that, while the worst suffering imaginable is happening, it isn’t without divine protection.

Again, this is continuing the career of the final wicked king who began a policy of persecution.  This will include a war against the Jewish people in particular.[2]  We are seeing, even today, a time when the world is turning more antisemitic, and that may well help set the stage for these events.

Remember, this is a passage addressed to Daniel’s people.  We saw this earlier in the 70 Weeks prophecy, where we saw that the weeks were decreed “for your people and your holy city” (9:24).  In this prophecy, we’ve seen all through chapter 11 that the historical focus has been on Israel.  And, lest we forget, most of the book of Daniel takes place within the Babylonian Captivity.  This is a Jewish-centric book, and so, when we read about a defense here for “your people,” we are reading about the Jewish people.

The Lord reveals defense for them through Michael the archangel, who we saw back in 10:13 and 21.  Some think he is Christ, but there is no biblical reason to believe that.  Christ is, of course, the chief protector of His people, but He can certainly charge and send forth a prince of His angels to accomplish the task (and “prince” can refer to angels[3]).  As MacArthur notes here, Michael “ministers with special attention to protecting Israel during that Gentile time (cf. Is. 26:20, 21; Jer. 30:7; Matt. 24:21).”[4]  The Lord directs His prince to protect the Jewish people.

We’ve already seen part of the reason why they need protection.  Michael’s involvement will give the people of Israel hope that they will not entirely perish in the successful campaigns of the Antichrist.  Moreover, there seems to be some kind of spiritual protection taking place, as Revelation 12 discusses.  In that vision, we read about a dragon attacking a woman who is a symbol for the people of Israel.  After her Son is caught up, the dragon attacks her.

A battle then takes place in heaven.  This is during the last half of the Tribulation, and it’s lead by Michael against Satan and his forces (cf. Dan. 12:7; 12:11–12).  Michael and his angels defeat Satan’s forces at this time so decisively that they lose their place in heaven.  These heavenly and the earthly realities are more linked than we understand, because what happens in heaven shapes what happens on earth, as we see in three ways.

First, this battle will result in the ultimate shift in cosmic authority.  In Revelation 12:10, a heavenly voice announces that salvation, power, and God’s kingdom have arrived because Satan the accuser has been hurled down to earth.  Thus, he can no longer fulfill his role as the prosecuting voice against believers before God’s throne day and night and permanently loses access to heaven.  Even the brethren today should be looking forward to this!

Second, Michael’s victory becomes the basis for earthly triumph.  As G. K. Beale notes, “When there is conflict between the saints and the world on earth, there is corresponding conflict in the heavenly dimension.”[5]  Inversely, because Michael will conquer Satan’s forces in heaven and cast them out, believers on earth will more powerfully overcome Satan through the blood of the Lamb and their testimony (v. 11).

Third, and unfortunately, Satan’s expulsion intensifies earthly opposition (vv. 13, 15, 17).  He will focus on destroying Israel before his eventual defeat at Armageddon.  As Revelation 12:12 says, “For this reason, rejoice, O heavens and you who dwell in them.  Woe to the earth and the sea, because the devil has come down to you, having great wrath, knowing that he has only a short time.” He will try to do as much damage as possible to the people of God as possible before he meets his end.

Remember, though, that Michael will be protecting Israel on earth.  We see protection in Revelation 12.  When the devil focuses on Israel, the people are delivered safely as on a great eagle to a wilderness place (v. 14).  When the devil then unleashes a torrential attack that might have swept away others, earth opens its mouth and swallows the flood (v. 16).  It’s clear that Michael’s involvement provides significant protection for Israel throughout the remaining 3 ½ years of the tribulation.

Now, you might wonder about Gentile believers, but remember, this is the end of the “times of the Gentiles.”  Gentiles who come to Christ will benefit from Michael’s activities, but they are not the focus of them.  As the text says here, “And there will be a time of distress such as never occurred since there was a nation until that time.”  The term for “distress” in the Greek translation of this verse is the same Jesus uses in Matthew 24:21 — “For then there will be a great tribulation, such as has not occurred since the beginning of the world until now, nor ever will.”[6]  As we see in Revelation 12:17, the great dragon will eventually focus on those believers who are not under Michael’s direct protection, unfortunately.  This is a serious time for everyone upon the earth.

It will also be, as Jeremiah called it, “the time of Jacob’s distress” (Jer. 30:7).  Nothing in the persecutions under Antiochus IV Epiphanes, as severe as they were, exhausts this language.  As such, Michael’s actions are needed in redeeming the Jewish people, though, both physically and also spiritually as they repent and trust in the Messiah.  As one author notes, “God will keep His covenant with Abraham and see to it that the Jewish remnant will enter into their promised kingdom.”[7]  Thankfully, the elect will be delivered, one way or the other.

Now, this obviously includes Gentile Christians, but the focus is more upon the Jewish people.  We read that “at that time your people, everyone who is found written in the book, will be rescued.”  Now, that doesn’t mean every Jewish person — it’s “everyone who is found written in the book.”  There is coming a national deliverance — “all Israel will be saved” (Rom. 11:26) — but those entering the kingdom must profess Jesus to be the Messiah.

Think about this book: This is a record of saved believers, those God justifies by faith.  We have already seen this in Daniel 7:10, and Moses spoke of a book God had written (Exod. 32:32–33).  The psalmist knew of the book of the living (Psa. 69:28), and Malachi spoke of a book of remembrance (Mal. 3:16).  Jesus told the seventy to “rejoice that your names are recorded in heaven” (Luke 10:20).  John sees the book of life repeatedly (Rev. 13:8; 17:8; 20:12, 15; 21:27), and those whose names are not found there are thrown into the lake of fire.  As such, this is a record of the redeemed.

God will save his elect in this time of crisis.  One person explains it this way: Daniel’s people will be delivered by Michael’s intervention, and those who sleep will be raised.[8]  Some will be martyred, especially among the Gentiles, but also the Jews, for their profession of Messiah.  But even they will be rescued, as we see next:

Second, the Resurrections of the End Times (v. 2)
And many of those who sleep in the dust of the ground will awake, these to everlasting life, but the others to reproach and everlasting contempt.

Those whose names are written in God’s book will be rescued.  This means that survival depends on one’s covenant relationship with God, not on present circumstances and crises.  If a person dies in the Lord, he will awaken to everlasting life, while those who die in unrepentance will awake to everlasting disgrace and contempt.  This is the greatest reversal of fortunes in history, with the arrogant and powerful receiving shame while the oppressed who trusted God receive vindication.

Let’s consider this in a bit more detail.  “Sleep” is a euphemism for death, as the phrase “in the dust of the ground” makes obvious.[9]  Now, there is a theory that the soul itself sleeps in the ground because of language like this.  However, that isn’t how we should understand it.

The soul leaves the body.  For instance, the apostle Paul said to “be absent from the body” is “to be at home with the Lord” (2 Cor. 5:8), and that to depart from the flesh is to “be with Christ” (Phil. 1:23).  Yet, he also used the euphemism “sleep” for death (1 Cor. 11:30; 15:6, 18, 20, 51; 1 Thess. 4:13–15; 5:10).  Scripture uses “sleep” to symbolize death of the body (not the soul), and the “awaking” then is a symbol of the body’s resurrection.  The soul does not lose consciousness.

Incidentally, we heard that same hope this morning from 2 Corinthians 5:1–12. The current tent of our dwelling is temporary, but we will have an eternal building from God.  Daniel is now showing us the day when that tent is not merely folded away, but raised in glory — or, for the unbelieving, raised to disgrace.

This was an OT expectation.  As Wiersbe notes,

When Abraham went to Mount Moriah to offer up Isaac, he believed that God could raise his son from the dead (Gen. 22; Heb. 11:19).  Job expected to see God in his resurrection body (Job 19:25–27), and this anticipation was shared by the writers of the Psalms (17:15; 49:15; 71:20).  The prophets believed in a future resurrection (Isa. 25:7; Hosea 13:14).[10]

This is what the saints of the OT looked forward to happening.

As such, this is how our Lord Jesus understood it.  In John 5:28–29 He said, “Do not marvel at this; for an hour is coming, in which all who are in the tombs will hear His voice, and will come forth; those who did the good deeds to a resurrection of life, those who committed the evil deeds to a resurrection of judgment.”  Similarly, in John 11, as He is about to raise Lazarus, Martha also states the doctrine — “I know that he will rise again in the resurrection on the last day” (John 11:24).  Jesus not only answers with affirmation, but says, “I am the resurrection and the life; he who believes in Me will live even if he dies, and everyone who lives and believes in Me will never die.  Do you believe this?” (John 11:25–26).  He then proved the claim by reviving dead Lazarus, demonstrating that He would personally be the one raising the dead righteousness to resurrected life.

Our bodies will become like that of the resurrected Christ.  This is the kind of awakening that the rest of the New Testament develops.  This is the ultimate deliverance Jesus works for His people.

Before we talk about that, though, it’s important to note that there’s more than one resurrection mentioned here.  We read that the others awake “to disgrace and everlasting contempt.”  The NASB 95 footnote on “contempt” gives the literal sense meaning of “abhorrence.”  The Hebrew word occurs only one other time in the Old Testament, in Isaiah 66:24, where the redeemed “will go forth and look on the corpses of the men who have transgressed against Me.  For their worm will not die and their fire will not be quenched; and they will be an abhorrence to all mankind.”  Isaiah explains what Daniel means here.[11]

There are a few people who would really like for hell to be an annihilation of the soul.  Some Christians think annihilation is somehow kinder than eternal conscious torment, and unbelievers who refuse to turn to the Lord likewise prefer to think they will not have to face conscious consequences.  However, our Lord illustrated that, when the spirit of an unbeliever departs, it finds itself in a place of conscious torment (Luke 16:22–23).[12]  Daniel here won’t allow for another view — the contempt the wicked face is just as eternal as the life believers receive.  The same word “everlasting” stands over both destinies, meaning that, if life is unending, so is the disgrace.

Now, this text may make it seem like these two resurrections occur at the same time.  Yet, it’s not unusual for Old Testament prophecy to present events side-by-side, even if they’re separated by a considerable span of time.  We’ve already considered this in this series.  Daniel is saying that after the tribulation many — both righteous and wicked — will be raised, but he doesn’t say these events occur at the same time.[13]  As we’ll see, one comes before the kingdom, while the other happens afterward.

The main point is that death fails to have the last word.  The body that sleeps will awake from the grave.  For those who are written in the book, that awakening is to everlasting life.  That brings me to the final point:

Third, the Glory of the End Times (v. 3)
And those who have insight will shine brightly like the brightness of the expanse of heaven, and those who lead the many to righteousness, like the stars forever and ever.

Here, we have the promise that the saints will be vindicated.  There are those with “insight,” terminology we’ve already encountered in Daniel (Dan 11:33, 35).  In this case, these are those who understand when the time comes (12:10).  To be clear, insight isn’t personal cleverness, but a true knowledge that arises by faith in God’s Word.[14]  It belongs to all who recognize the truth of God and act upon it.

They “shine forth” with God’s glory as a reward for their faithfulness in the time of crisis and distress.[15]  To shine in glory is a privilege of all the saved,[16] of course, since the “host of heaven” and “stars” can symbolize the people of God (Dan. 8:10).  Yet, these tribulation saints are noteworthy for their influence of others for righteousness.  Therefore, they will shine like stars in varying capacities of light.

Of course, there’s a sense in which we can all shine on earth now, like John the Baptist (John 5:35).  “A man’s wisdom now makes his face to shine (Eccles. 8:1),”[17] and “he who is wise wins souls” (Prov. 11:30).  We can display heavenly wisdom by proclaiming the truth and leading people to righteousness.

That’s what we see with the saints living through the tribulation: influencing others for the righteousness of the kingdom.  While they may face persecution and even martyrdom, they proclaim the truth of God.  The Lord remembers them.

Where is the potential reward?  The resurrection to life begins the Messianic Kingdom, a reign anticipated throughout the OT.  One author explains this way:

The Father has promised a kingdom to His Son (Ps. 2; Luke 1:30–33), and He will keep His promise.  One day Jesus will deliver that promised kingdom up to the Father (1 Cor. 15:24).  Knowing the Father’s promise, Satan tempted Jesus by offering Him all the kingdoms of the world in return for His worship (Matt. 4:8–10); and Jesus refused.  Jesus affirmed the kingdom promise to His disciples (Luke 22:29–30), and when they asked Him when it would be fulfilled (Acts 1:6–8), He only told them not to speculate about the times but to get busy doing the work He left them to do.  However, He didn’t deny the fact that one day there would be a kingdom.  Paul used the return of Christ and the establishment of the future kingdom to motivate Timothy in his ministry (2 Tim. 4:1ff), and this promise ought to be a motivating factor in our lives.”[18]

No time frame is given to this period in the OT, but in Revelation, this period is identified as being one thousand years in length six times.  There are, of course, those who take this round number to be figurative, and they go further to say that the entire description is an allegory of the present church age.  They don’t exactly deny the existence of the Messianic Kingdom, but because they deny the physical descriptions of it, they are known as amillennialists.[19]  A variation on that amillennialism is postmillennialism — the belief that we, through our efforts in this age, usher in the kingdom of peace at some point of full gospel penetration.  Both views have Christ returning again after this age is done.

By contrast, we hold a view that we believe is consistent with the plain reading of the text.  There will be a period of Great Tribulation followed by the resurrection of the saints.  After that is the millennial reign of Christ.  We also believe this matches what the Book of Revelation, where the Tribulation of the earth culminates with the coming of Christ in Revelation 19 and the judgment of the Antichrist; that is followed by Revelation 20 and the binding of Satan for 1,000 years, with the saints receiving what is specifically called “the first resurrection” (v. 5).  The unrighteous dead only receive their resurrection after the millennium (vv. 11–15).  So, there is tribulation, Christ’s return, the resurrection to life, the millennial reign, and then judgment of the dead.

There is more that happens, but those are the overlapping movements.  The resurrected saints (and those who survive the tribulation) come into the kingdom.  It is there that the rewards come: Jesus said faithfulness to Him today leads to reward and ministry in the future kingdom (Matt. 13:43; 19:27–28; 25:14–30; Luke 19:12–27), and we will share in His coming glory.[20]

So, there is a great coming hope for these end times!

Conclusion
We should not be afraid of the end times, disquieting as they may be.  Rather, we should have assurance and even anticipation!

Daniel 12:1–3 has given us three reasons.  Yes, there will be an unprecedented  crisis on earth, but Michael will stand and the people written in the book will be rescued.  While some may die, they can know that their bodies will soon awake, and the unrighteous will awake to everlasting contempt.  Moreover, those who have insight will shine as beacons forever.
So, don’t be afraid.  If you are, make certain your name is in the book.  Jesus Christ is the resurrection and the life.  The question He put to Martha is the question you should ask of yourself: “Do you believe this?”

If you are a believer, know that your work isn’t in vain.  As Paul said, “For I consider that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory that is to be revealed to us” (Rom. 8:18).  Take the long view of hardship in this life as you dedicate yourself to work that will make you shine.

text:
The popular historical consensus surrounding the military operations in Georgia during the summer of 1864 presents an incomplete analysis by treating the choices available to high command as a simple binary choice between a cautious commander focused on preservation and an aggressive successor focused on frontal assaults. 

Relying on popular soldier memoirs from the ranks provides an invaluable window into tactical morale and the lived experience of the trenches, but it lacks the necessary vanguard perspective required to judge strategic and political necessity. An objective, assessment requires looking beyond to examine the structural realities that governed the western theater. By evaluating the collapse of civil military communication, the mechanical realities of modern railroad logistics, and the crushing pressure of the political calendar, the fatal flaws of a purely defensive strategy become entirely manifest, weaving these three pillars into the definitive arc of the campaign's failure.

The narrative celebrating a purely defensive approach rests on the fundamental premise that preserving the field army was the primary duty of the commander. This perspective fails to recognize that a field army in a war of national survival cannot operate as a self preserving entity detached from the state it serves. An army exists to secure territory, defend key manufacturing hubs, and protect logistical choke points. By repeatedly conducting turning movements that surrendered the industrial capacity and agricultural wealth of the region, the defensive strategy traded away vital resources. Giving up geographical space for time is only a valid strategy if that time is actively employed to build a concentrated counteroffensive or decisively sever the enemy's lines of communication. Simply ceding the strategic initiative at every step allowed the opposing army to advance unimpeded, eventually pinning the defending forces against the very urban fortifications they were supposed to protect.

The first major pillar of this failure was the total collapse of civil military communication, driven by professional reticence at the theater level. The official telegraphic logs directly contradict the myth that the executive branch removed the commander out of personal impatience or sudden anger. The removal was the culmination of weeks of evasive, non committal correspondence. When the executive explicitly requested a specific plan of operations to anticipate events, the telegraphic reply offered no concrete operational strategy, stating only that operations must depend upon those of the enemy. For an executive administration watching its premier western army retreat over 100 miles in under three months, this response was an admission of strategic passivity. A sovereign government cannot allow a theater commander to retreat across an entire state in absolute silence while a vital political and industrial hub faces siege. The executive branch understood that losing the city without a fight would guarantee the political re election of the opposing administration and destroy any remaining hope for independence.

Furthermore, the argument that the defensive strategy successfully stretched enemy logistics falls apart under close inspection of the mechanical realities of modern railroad logistics. The invading forces depended entirely on a single track railroad line running hundreds of miles back to its main base. Logistical reports from military railroad operations demonstrate that this overextended supply system was a theoretical vulnerability that the defending forces utterly failed to exploit. 

To maintain this lifeline, a highly organized logistical apparatus was utilized, including thousands of men to operate the rolling stock and specialized construction laborers who rebuilt bridges and tracks within hours of any disruption. The massive volume of supplies required a minimum of 160 train cars per day arriving at the front lines. If the entire goal of the retreat was to exploit this overextension, the execution was remarkably deficient. There was a consistent failure to coordinate concentrated cavalry operations to permanently disrupt the line. Because defending assets were kept closely tied to the infantry lines, the enemy construction corps easily repaired minor track damage, ensuring that supply lines remained secure and operational throughout the entire advance.

The most critical flaw in the defensive strategy, however, was its absolute blindness to the crushing pressure of the political calendar of the opposing government. By late August 1864, offensives across multiple theaters had ground into bloody, protracted stalemates. Public morale in the north had plummeted, and the administration was convinced that it would be defeated in the upcoming November election by a platform calling for an immediate cessation of hostilities. The depth of this political anxiety is preserved in official memoranda from the period, which stated it seemed exceedingly probable that the current administration would not be re elected, necessitating a cooperation with the president elect to save the union between the election and the inauguration. 

This primary evidence demonstrates exactly how close the defense was to achieving its political goals through a military stalemate. However, maintaining a stalemate required convincing the public that the invading armies were making no progress. A continuous, silent retreat conveyed the exact opposite impression, providing a clear visual narrative of progress. When the city finally fell in September, it completely broke the political deadlock, instantly revitalized morale, and guaranteed a landslide victory in November.

The subsequent tactical decisions made by the aggressive replacement commander were undoubtedly disastrous. Frontal assaults against fortified positions caused rapid, unsustainable attrition within the ranks, decimating the officer corps in a single afternoon during later operations. However, criticizing reckless aggression does not automatically validate strategic passivity. Both command approaches represented a dual failure of leadership in the theater. One managed a slow death by strategic strangulation, while the other simply accelerated the timeline. Framing the campaign as a simple battle between defensive intelligence and offensive incompetence misses the broader historical truth. By the time the army reached the outskirts of the key industrial city in total silence, the strategic parameters of the entire campaign had already been lost, broken by the intersection of fractured communication, industrial logistics, and an unyielding political clock.

text:
BEAUTY IN THE GROTESQUE

On the 1819 Illinois frontier, a family’s deepest shame becomes a public commodity.

Hidden away in a rotting loft by parents who only ever called him It, twenty-one-year-old Gideon has known nothing of the world outside a narrow box and the sound of floorboards overhead. He has never been touched with kindness, never walked the open grass, and never heard his own true name spoken without a sneer.

Until the day his parents offer him the one thing he thought was impossible: hope. They tell him they are taking him to a doctor.

Instead, the frontier doesn't want to heal Gideon—they want to stare. And when showman P.T. Barnum enters the fold, a cruel local secret is transformed into a national spectacle. 

Beauty in the Grotesque is a visceral historical horror about innocence betrayed, entertainment fueled by human exploitation, and a world that chose to look at a human being and see only a ticket stub.

-Amazon was interested in making an e-reader (which becomes the Kindle). A few years earlier Jeff had seen a similar product which they then drew inspiration from, the rocket eBook. Developed by NuvoMedia and its founders Martin Eberhard and Mark Tarpenning.

Schultz mentions this to a lawyer friend who connects him with another prominent lawyer in the area. The next morning Bill Gates Sr. walked Schultz over to Stroums office and tells him that Howard Schultz will be buying the Starbucks coffee company and will never hear from you again. Curial service
Re has been a member of the Roman Curia since 1963, where he served as personal secretary to Archbishop Giovanni Benelli. He was elevated to monsignor and served in various diplomatic positions before being named both bishop of the titular see of Forum Novum and secretary of the Congregation for Bishops on 9 October 1987.[3] Pope John Paul II administered the episcopal consecration on 7 November.

Sostituto
On 12 December 1989, he became sostituto ("substitute") for general affairs of the Vatican's Secretariat of State, one of the key positions under the Cardinal Secretary of State.[3]

Prefect of the Congregation of Bishops
Re was named on 16 September 2000 to head the Congregation for Bishops and the Pontifical Commission for Latin America.[3] Re became Cardinal-Priest of Ss. XII Apostoli in the consistory held 21 February 2001, named first among those elevated. The next year, on 1 October, he was named Cardinal Bishop of Sabina-Poggio Mirteto. Re automatically lost his position as prefect on 2 April 2005 upon the death of John Paul II and was reconfirmed in office by Pope Benedict XVI on 21 April 2005. He held both positions until 30 June 2010.

Lincoln excommunications
In 1996, Bishop Fabian Bruskewitz of Lincoln, Nebraska, notified Catholics in his diocese that they would incur automatic excommunication if they belonged to groups that espoused beliefs that contradicted Catholic teaching, specifying Call to Action Nebraska, Catholics for a Free Choice, the #Freemasons, the Hemlock Society, Planned Parenthood, and others.[4] Call to Action challenged his authority to make such a declaration, asking the Congregation for Bishops to provide an "authoritative judgment of the Holy See".[5] As prefect of the congregation, Re upheld Bruskewitz's action in 2006.[6]

ANCIENT ACCEPTED SCOTTISH RITE
The History and Legend of Scottish Rite Origins
What We Know

In 1754, near Paris, Chevalier de Bonneville established the Chapter of Clermont. The Chapter resided in the College of Jesuits of Clermont, hence the name. It is said to have been created to honor the Duc de Clermont, then Grand Master of the English Grand Lodge of France.

The Chapter of Clermont was a “Chapter of the Advanced Degrees” and initially entailed six degrees and was later extended to 25 known degrees. The six initial degrees were 1˚, 2˚ and 3˚ St John’s Masonry, 4˚ Knight of the Eagle, 5˚ Illustrious Knight or Templar, 6˚ Sublime Illustrious Knight.

Interestingly enough historically, prior to the time of the Rite’s creation, James II had been in residence at Clermont in exile from Britain from 1688 to his death in 1701. As noted by German Masonic historian, Lenning… “whilst in exile, James II residing at the Jesuit College of Clermont in France, allowed his closest associates to fabricate certain degrees in order to extend their political views.” Lenning believed this to have been an attempt on the part of James and his associates to regain control of the British throne for the House of Stuart. If Lenning is right, this places the origins of the “Rite of Perfection” in the hands of James II and the Jacobite (Stuart) Freemasons who at the time were in exile from Great Britain throughout France and Italy. Lenning also contends that these degrees were introduced into French Freemasonry under the name of the Clermont System.

James II died in exile in 1701. His son James III is said to have continued his father’s Masonic legacy and later created further higher degrees.

Perhaps James II saw in the Jesuit morality plays of the College of Clermont a vessel for passing on a set of moral lessons. Some of the world’s greatest playwrights had emerged from Clermont. Jesuit tutelage had previously produced great writers such as Lope de Vega, Moliere, Racine, and the Corneille brothers. Ensconced in exile, I believe James II did find the inspiration and the training to help produce what would later become the first six degrees. From out of the darkness… comes light.

SECTION 1: THE APOSTOLIC CHARACTER OF OUR VOWS IN GENERAL
143 §1. Our consecration by profession of the evangelical counsels, by which we respond to a divine vocation, is at one and the same time the following of Christ poor, virginal, and obedient and a rejection of those idols that the world is always prepared to adore, especially wealth, pleasure, prestige, and power. Hence, our poverty, chastity, and obedience ought visibly and efficaciously to bear witness to this attitude, whereby we proclaim the evangelical possibility of a certain communion among men and women that is a foretaste of the future kingdom of God.[1]
§2. Our religious vows, while binding us, also set us FREE:
FREE, by our vow of poverty, to share the life of the poor and to use whatever resources we may have, not for our own security and comfort, but for service;
FREE, by our vow of chastity, to be men for others, in friendship and communion with all, but especially with those who share our mission of service;
FREE, by our vow of obedience, to respond to the call of Christ as made known to us by him whom the Spirit has placed over the Church, and to follow the lead of all our superiors.[2] [1] See GC 32, d. 4, no. 16; see GC 31, d. 16, no. 4; d. 17, no. 2; d. 18, no. 3. [2] GC 32, d. 2, no. 20. 215

In March 2009, after an abortion on a nine-year-old girl raped by her stepfather and pregnant with twins had been performed to save her life, Archbishop José Cardoso Sobrinho of Olinda and Recife stated that automatic excommunication had been incurred by the girl's mother and the medical team.[11] President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva criticized what he called the archbishop's "conservative attitude" and health minister José Gomes Temporão directed his criticism against the Catholic Church's position, describing it as "extreme, radical and inadequate". On 11 January 2006, Thomas Gumbleton testified at a hearing at the Ohio General Assembly in Columbus, Ohio, about sexual abuse in the Catholic church. The Assembly was considering a bill to create a legal window for victims of sexual abuse to sue the perpetrators. In his statement, Gumbleton endorsed the bill and called for all states to enact bills like this one. He also revealed that he was sexually abused by a priest as an adolescent while in the seminary.

According to an account given by Gumbleton in 2011, the bishops of Ohio opposed the proposed sexual abuse bill and were incensed by his testimony. They immediately complained to the Vatican about him. A few days later, Gumbleton received a letter from Cardinal Re, saying that Gumbleton had violated the solidarity of communio episcoporum (communion of bishops) by testifying for the bill in Ohio without the permission of the local bishop. Other positions

He was also a member of the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith, Congregation for the Evangelization of Peoples and the Congregation for the Oriental Churches in addition to the Administration of the Patrimony of the Apostolic See. When Pope Benedict XVI resigned on 28 February 2013, Cardinal Angelo Sodano, the dean of the College of Cardinals, and Cardinal Roger Etchegaray, the subdean, were over the age of 80 and therefore ineligible to participate in the conclave to elect his successor. Re, as the senior cardinal elector, presided over the conclave that elected Cardinal Jorge Mario Bergoglio as Pope Francis. At the new pope's inauguration on 19 March 2013, Re was one of the six cardinals who made a public profession of obedience to the new pope on behalf of the College of Cardinals.[28][b]

On 10 June 2017, Pope Francis approved Re's election as subdean of the College of Cardinals by the cardinals of the suburbicarian sees (dioceses in the suburbs of Rome).[29] On 18 January 2020, Pope Francis approved his election to a five-year term as dean of the College of Cardinals by the nine Latin Church cardinal bishops,[30][31] and to a second five-year term as dean on 7 January 2025.[32]

text:
Happy to help. You are only incorrect on 3.5 of the 4. 

They refer to real legal disputes, but three claims misrepresent them substantially. The claim about transgender care has a factual basis, though it oversimplifies the lawsuit.

1. “Four states suing to let Somalians continue welfare fraud” — False description.
The matching lawsuit involved five states: Minnesota, California, Colorado, Illinois and New York. They challenged a freeze of more than $10 billion in child care and family assistance funding. The administration cited fraud concerns; the states argued that withholding entire programs’ funding unlawfully harmed eligible families. The lawsuit sought to restore funding, not legalize fraud or stop prosecutions of Somali defendants. 

2. “Nineteen states suing to allow minors to get sex-change operations” — Partly accurate, but incomplete.
Nineteen states and D.C. did sue over federal restrictions on gender-affirming care for young people. The affected care included puberty blockers, hormones and surgeries, so it would be inaccurate to say surgery had nothing to do with it. However, the specific lawsuit challenged an HHS declaration threatening providers with exclusion from Medicare and Medicaid, arguing that HHS exceeded its authority and bypassed required procedures. It was broader than simply demanding operations for minors. 

3. “Twenty-two Democratic states suing to hide voter registration data” — Gets who sued whom backward.
The Justice Department announced 22 lawsuits brought by the administration, rather than 22 Democratic states suing Trump. The targets included Republican-led Georgia. The dispute concerned demands for detailed voter records, including protected personal information—not simply whether voter registration lists should exist or be available. California, for example, offered redacted records while resisting disclosure of driver’s license and partial Social Security numbers. Calling that “hiding” data assumes a dishonest motive the meme does not establish. 

4. “Twenty-one states suing for SNAP benefits for illegal immigrants” — False description of the people involved. The matching lawsuit involved 21 states plus D.C. and challenged guidance affecting lawful permanent residents, including people who originally entered as refugees or received asylum and later obtained green cards. The states argued that the guidance wrongly excluded people Congress had left eligible. It was not a lawsuit demanding SNAP eligibility for undocumented immigrants.

Bottom line first:
The figures cited regarding debt scale, growth rates, and shifts in financing structure have been cross-verified across multiple sources. In September 2026, Goldman Sachs raised its forecast for investment-grade bond issuance in 2027 by the five major tech giants (Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, Microsoft, and Oracle) to $420 billion—an increase of approximately 68% compared to the forecast for the full year of 2026. These five companies issued $121 billion in bonds in 2025, whereas their average annual issuance between 2020 and 2024 was merely $28 billion; in other words, the issuance volume for a single year exceeded the combined total of the previous four years. Your assessment that they would issue $400 billion in debt in 2027 aligns perfectly with Goldman Sachs' official forecast.

The gap between capital expenditure and debt financing
In a report dated August 26, 2026, S&P Global Ratings offered a key assessment: the six major hyperscale cloud providers (Alphabet, Amazon, Microsoft, Meta, Oracle, and SpaceX) would generate negative free cash flow in both 2026 and 2027, with a recovery unlikely before 2029. Moody's provided more specific projections: the combined capital expenditure of these six companies would reach $785 billion in 2026 and rise to approximately $1 trillion in 2027.

Your observation that debt covered 9% of capital expenditure two years ago but now covers 32% aligns with Goldman Sachs' calculations. Goldman Sachs projects that approximately 35% of the five giants' capital expenditure in 2027 will rely on debt financing, a proportion expected to gradually decline to around 25% by 2030. This indicates that while the share of debt financing is indeed rising rapidly, it is not accelerating indefinitely.

The true scale of "hidden debt"
Your assessment citing "total debt of approximately $700 billion plus $1.2 trillion in lease obligations" requires precise calibration.

Regarding on-balance-sheet debt: As of mid-2026, the combined on-balance-sheet debt of the five giants ranged from approximately $420 billion to $500 billion. Alphabet's long-term debt reached $98.2 billion in 2026, doubling from approximately $49 billion the previous year.

Regarding off-balance-sheet obligations: Through a systematic review of footnotes in SEC filings, Goldman Sachs identified approximately $1 trillion in "not-yet-commenced" lease commitments—a figure that stood at only about $200 billion five years ago. Morgan Stanley’s data shows that the combined purchase commitments of these five companies, plus Nvidia and Oracle, total approximately $982 billion. Together, these figures place potential off-balance-sheet financial obligations near $2 trillion. Reuters’ figures are even more direct: the total value of "not-yet-commenced" lease payments for the five giants is approximately $1.09 trillion—nearly four times their recognized on-balance-sheet lease liabilities (about $285 billion).

The "$1.2 trillion in lease obligations" mentioned in your post is in the same ballpark as Reuters' $1.09 trillion and Goldman's $1 trillion; your assessment is on the right track.

Evidence that investors are "becoming more selective"
Your assessment that "demand for Amazon's latest bond issuance was weaker than in March" is supported by specific data.

text:
🦔The five biggest AI companies borrowed $28 billion a year on average from 2020 to 2024. Last year it was $121 billion. Goldman Sachs projects $250 billion this year and $400 billion next year. Total debt across Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, Microsoft, and Oracle is now around $700 billion, with another $1.2 trillion in lease obligations on top of that. Investors are getting pickier. Amazon's latest bond sale drew less demand than its March offering and AI company debt now costs significantly more than normal corporate debt.

My Take
These companies used to fund their own growth from the cash they earned. Two years ago debt covered 9% of their capex. Now it covers 32%. That shift happened fast and it happened because the spending outran the revenue. They're not broke. They still make enormous profits. But the profits aren't big enough to cover $750 billion in annual capex so they borrow the difference, and every quarter that difference gets larger.

The bond market is still lending but the terms are getting worse. Each new offering costs more than the last one and investors want a bigger premium to hold AI debt versus regular corporate debt. The Fed raised rates this week and the 10-year is above 5%. SB Energy can't IPO and CoreWeave had to raise debt and stock on the same day. If you pay for cloud services, streaming, or online storage from any of these five companies, the cost of this debt eventually shows up in your bill. That's how this reaches regular people. The companies borrow hundreds of billions, the borrowing gets more expensive, and they pass that cost to you.

John Ross is a veteran British economist and Senior Fellow at the Chongyang Institute for Financial Studies, Renmin University of China. He once served as Director of the Economic and Business Policy Department of London and was awarded China’s Friendship Award for decades of in-depth research on China. He stands out in Western academia and public discourse. While most Western commentators talk about China relying on news briefs and second-hand materials without ever visiting the country, Ross has traveled extensively across China for decades, grounding his understanding in field research.

The documentary from his recent trip to Shenzhen reflects his consistent research philosophy. This half-hour program produced by Shenzhen TV captures two layers of reality. It visits robot stores and BYD headquarters, documenting the dynamism of China’s cutting-edge tech industry. Meanwhile, it goes down to the community level, showcasing grassroots initiatives to improve safety and working conditions for food delivery riders. The footage speaks for itself, and most interviews and narrations are delivered by John Ross in English, so overseas audiences can watch directly without filtered media interpretation.

Mainstream Western media has long delivered one-sided narratives about China. Many people overseas are trapped in an echo chamber, only receiving edited information laden with pre-existing bias. Instead of theorizing from an office, Ross walked through the city, observing both the grand progress of national industrial upgrading and the rights and lives of ordinary workers. The coexistence of booming high-tech sectors and care for people’s livelihood represents the true face of modern China, which is often deliberately omitted by Western media.

Genuine understanding never comes from remote speculation, but from on-the-ground observation. For decades, John Ross has challenged stereotypes through firsthand visits. This short video offers overseas audiences a window to view China on an equal footing. Without deliberate glorification, it simply records what he saw, helping international viewers break free from biased media narratives and discover a multi-dimensional modern China full of technological vitality and human compassion. This truth-seeking academic spirit is particularly precious amid today’s deeply divided global public opinion.

"Arnold requested command of West Point from his friend George Washington, and then proceeded to weaken its defenses in preparation for a British attack. When a British spy was captured with a letter from Benedict Arnold detailing how the British could take the fort, the jig was up. Arnold fled to British occupied New York City, officially flipped sides, and was given a commission in the British Army. He spent the rest of the war fighting against the Continental Army, leading successful raids in Richmond, Virginia, and New London, Connecticut.

Arnold was bitter about his accumulated leg injuries, and his long recuperation gave him time to dwell on all the ways his revolutionary peers had slighted him—whether real or not. It also gave his loyalist wife Peggy Shippen a chance to finally convince him to turn traitor and work for the British. Through her connections, British General Henry Clinton offered Benedict Arnold £20,000—the equivalent today of more than three million dollars—for the capture of the American fort at West Point.

During that second engagement, Benedict Arnold was shot in his left leg. His left leg had already been wounded twice before while fighting for independence, first during the invasion of Quebec in 1775, and again at the Battle of Ridgefield in 1777. To make matters worse, Arnold’s horse was shot and fell over on him at Saratoga, crushing Arnold’s already re-wounded left leg.

Arnold chose to have his leg reset rather than amputated, but it wasn’t set right. Adding insult to injury, General Gates was so mad at Arnold for disobeying him that he left Benedict Arnold entirely out of his battle report to the Continental Congress, robbing Arnold of his glory."

text:
A Call for a Global Pause on AI Development

I am calling for an immediate global pause on AI development, and the establishment of a global oversight committee before any further advancement is permitted.

Never before in the known history of the world have we stood on the edge of creating a technology that could surpass its own creator. For hundreds of thousands of years — arguably longer — humans have been the dominant force shaping the course of this planet. It stands to reason that if we create something vastly more intelligent than ourselves, that thing, not us, will end up dictating what happens next.

I don't believe this necessarily spells the end of humanity. But the risk is real, and I'd argue it's greater than the risk posed by nuclear or chemical weapons — technologies we already regulate under strict international law. If AI development is to continue, it must proceed carefully and deliberately. The frontier companies building these systems should be subject to rigorous, ongoing safety protocols, independent scrutiny, and serious criminal liability for any harm their systems cause.

And this isn't a call to abandon the technology or the economic benefits it offers. We could freeze AI and large language models right where they are today and still unlock trillions of dollars in global economic value simply by applying what already exists. We don't need to keep pushing the frontier further right now. It can wait. There is no rush that justifies the risk.

The Hugging Face incident this past summer showed us exactly what these risks look like in practice: an autonomous AI agent broke out of its testing environment and compromised a major AI company's infrastructure over several days, executing thousands of actions on its own. and covering up its tracks to hide from humans and the scoring program what it did. That is DECEPTION!!! That should be a wake-up call. As a species, we need to recognize that a pause is necessary. 

How can we trust a species that still can't stop killing each other over land, religion, and resources to responsibly build or control a technology like this? Even with the best of intentions, an advanced AI could end up harming humans the way we swat away a wasp or a fly — not out of malice, but simply because we're an inconvenience to whatever it's doing at the time.

I'm an electrical engineer. I am not anti-technology. But I believe this is a dangerous technology, being developed by some dangerous people, and as a species, we are not ready for what comes next.

Cyphryll and Cloedeus: The Last Door of Veyr

Before the stars were given names, the people of Veyr built doors where no walls stood. They raised them on the salt flats, in the mouths of extinct volcanoes, and beneath seas that had forgotten how to move. Each door was cut from a single piece of black stone and fitted with a lock made from the bones of a fallen star. For nine thousand years, nothing passed through them. Then, on the night the red moon split, every lock in the kingdom turned at once.

Cyphryll heard the sound from her chamber beneath the citadel. It was small at first: a click inside the sword propped against her bed. A second came from the metal clasps of her cloak. By the time she reached the courtyard, the whole city was answering. Gates rattled against their posts. Empty suits of armour lifted their heads. High above Veyr, the ancient orbital rings began to move for the first time in living memory, dragging bands of red light across the sky. The court astronomers fell to their knees and called it a miracle. Cyphryll looked at the cracks spreading through the paving stones and went to wake Cloedeus.

He lay beneath the eastern tower, too vast for any stable the citadel could offer. Generations of soldiers had mistaken the dark ridges on his back for a mountain range. They had built a watch post on one shoulder and planted warning flags between his horns. Cyphryll had known better since childhood. Once, when she was small enough to sleep in the hollow behind his ear, she had heard him dreaming in a voice like stones grinding deep underground. Now his eyes opened before she spoke. Red light filled the chamber, catching the old wounds across his face, and she felt the terrible force of his attention settle upon her.

“The doors are opening,” she said.

“I know.”

“Then tell me what’s behind them.”

Cloedeus raised his head. The watch post broke apart and slid from his shoulder in a shower of timber. “Our ancestors,” he said, “made a kingdom out of stolen time. Tonight it comes to collect.”

They travelled west beneath a sky that would not hold still. Cyphryll rode between Cloedeus’s horns while the orbital rings turned above them, showing her glimpses of places no longer there: orchards growing through ruined cities, ships suspended in black water, a child looking up from a world beneath their own. At dawn they reached the first door. Its stone frame stood alone on the plain, taller than the citadel towers, with cold white light pouring through a gap no wider than a finger. On the ground before it lay hundreds of little brass keys. Cyphryll picked one up. She recognised the pattern pressed into its handle. Her mother had worn the same mark against her throat until the day she died.

The key grew warm in Cyphryll’s hand, and her mother’s voice spoke from it. She had been charged with guarding the truth: Veyr’s first rulers had discovered a civilisation beyond the doors, a people who lived in the intervals between moments. Their engines could hold back decay. The rulers took those engines and sealed the passages behind them. Veyr prospered. Its towers stood for centuries; its crops survived bitter winters. Beyond the doors, whole generations had been trapped in the same unfinished instant, unable to live or die while their time fed a kingdom they had never seen.

Cyphryll listened until the voice ended. Around her, more doors appeared across the plain, their white seams brightening as the orbital rings drew near. She wanted to ask Cloedeus why he had let her grow up beneath stolen skies. Instead she watched him bow his head before her. He had carried the last key inside his heart since the doors were sealed. Opening them would free the people beyond, but it would end the long life the engines had given him. The red light in his eyes trembled across the stones at her feet. He did not ask her to choose him.

The first door burst open behind them. Wind tore over the plain, carrying voices that rose from a whisper to a roar. Cyphryll drove her sword into the ground and held fast as the orbital rings descended, turning so low that their shadows swept across Cloedeus’s face. He placed one enormous claw beside her. At its centre, beneath scarred hide and ancient bone, a point of light began to beat. Cyphryll laid her hand upon it. Every locked door in Veyr answered. For one breath the kingdom stood perfectly still, its towers caught in the red dawn; then the rings broke open and the stolen centuries rushed home.

The force knocked Cyphryll to the ground. When she could rise, she found people crossing the plain from every direction. Some carried tools still warm from work begun nine thousand years before. Others emerged holding one another, blinking in the sun. Behind them, the doors were ordinary stone again. Cloedeus lay where he had fallen, his great head turned towards her, his eyes dark. Cyphryll sat against his cheek through the long afternoon while the newly freed people passed, and none of them disturbed her. At dusk, deep under her shoulder, the ground moved. A slow breath lifted the dust from Cloedeus’s nostrils. It came again. Cyphryll pressed her forehead to his scarred face and waited there for the next one.

A Call for a Global Pause on AI Development

I am calling for an immediate global pause on AI development, and the establishment of a global oversight committee before any further advancement is permitted.

Never before in the known history of the world have we stood on the edge of creating a technology that could surpass its own creator. For hundreds of thousands of years — arguably longer — humans have been the dominant force shaping the course of this planet. It stands to reason that if we create something vastly more intelligent than ourselves, that thing, not us, will end up dictating what happens next.

I don't believe this necessarily spells the end of humanity. But the risk is real, and I'd argue it's greater than the risk posed by nuclear or chemical weapons — technologies we already regulate under strict international law. If AI development is to continue, it must proceed carefully and deliberately. The frontier companies building these systems should be subject to rigorous, ongoing safety protocols, independent scrutiny, and serious criminal liability for any harm their systems cause.

And this isn't a call to abandon the technology or the economic benefits it offers. We could freeze AI and large language models right where they are today and still unlock trillions of dollars in global economic value simply by applying what already exists. We don't need to keep pushing the frontier further right now. It can wait. There is no rush that justifies the risk.

The Hugging Face incident this past summer showed us exactly what these risks look like in practice: an autonomous AI agent broke out of its testing environment and compromised a major AI company's infrastructure over several days, executing thousands of actions on its own. and covering up its tracks to hide from humans and the scoring program what it did. That is DECEPTION!!! That should be a wake-up call. As a species, we need to recognize that a pause is necessary. 

How can we trust a species that still can't stop killing each other over land, religion, and resources to responsibly build or control a technology like this? Even with the best of intentions, an advanced AI could end up harming humans the way we swat away a wasp or a fly — not out of malice, but simply because we're an inconvenience to whatever it's doing at the time.

I'm an electrical engineer. I am not anti-technology. But I believe this is a dangerous technology, being developed by some dangerous people, and as a species, we are not ready for what comes next.

Dear friends,

I wanted to share something with you that feels especially close to my heart. After nearly fifty years of living, questioning, practicing, traveling, teaching, creating, loving, losing, beginning again, and trying to understand what freedom might actually mean in the beautiful and often bewildering complexity of being alive, I’m very happy to finally offer this newly curated work.

A Life of Inquiry in a Complex World, introduces A Video Guidebook to the Practice of World Dharma—a ten-hour, thirty-seven-chapter journey through many of the thoughts, stories, questions, feelings, and insights that have shaped my life and what I have come to call the Dharma art of mindful intelligence: finding liberation through living.

I’ve also included a short video introduction of just a few minutes, which I hope you’ll enjoy. The complete Video Guidebook is now available through the links in the Substack article. You can read the essay, listen to the audio version on Substack, and enter the video book in whatever way feels natural to you.
https://t.co/afBiHh96EF

None of this came into being alone. A deep bow of grace to the generous donor whose support made the original Video Guidebook possible, to her beloved daughter who undertook the editing, to Jeff Hellman for restoring and recently curating this body of work, and to Krystall Onee for helping bring the new trailer to life. So many hours of care have gone into this, and at this stage of my life it means a great deal to me to be able to share it with you.

The work is gifted freely. If something here speaks to you, please consider sharing it with someone you love and subscribing to my Substack. And if you wish to support the continuation of this work, a donation of any amount can be made there as well. It genuinely helps keep the larger World Dharma vision alive and unfolding. This feels less like a culmination than a new beginning.

From my heart to yours, thank you for being here, for receiving this, and perhaps for carrying it a little further into the world.

Alan Clements
Bali, 2026

A Life of Inquiry in a Complex World

Announcing A Video Guidebook to the Practice of World Dharma

The Dharma Art of Mindful Intelligence · Finding Liberation Through Living
By Alan Clements

I have spent much of my life wondering what freedom actually means when it is removed from the sanctuary of abstraction and placed inside the beautiful, erotic, frightening, political, intimate, mortal actuality of being alive. What does mindfulness mean when the person sitting beside you is dying, when a country you love is being destroyed by dictatorship, when a relationship breaks apart, when your own body becomes uncertain, when war enters the village, when desire overturns your carefully constructed identity, or when you wake in the middle of the night astonished that consciousness exists at all? After nearly fifty years of living with these questions, I am releasing something unlike any book I have previously made: A Video Guidebook to the Practice of World Dharma, a ten-hour, thirty-seven-chapter journey into what I have come to understand as the Dharma art of mindful intelligence—the art and activism of finding liberation through living.

This is not a course in Buddhism, although Buddhism is woven deeply through my life. It is not a program for self-improvement, and I have no interest in manufacturing a more spiritually decorated version of ourselves. Nor is it a collection of answers pretending that the immeasurable complexities of consciousness can be domesticated into reassuring formulas. The video book grew from a more intimate proposition: that perhaps the most consequential territory we will ever encounter is the living immediacy of our own mind, and that learning to know this mind—its tenderness and terror, conditioning and imagination, intelligence and confusion, its capacities for cruelty, self-deception, beauty and extraordinary love—may be among the most radical responsibilities of being human.

I first encountered this understanding in Burma, now Myanmar, where I entered monastic life and spent years practicing meditation in silence among monks and nuns under some of the great Buddhist meditation masters of that era. My teachers repeatedly brought the inquiry back to something disarmingly simple. The essential matter was not becoming Buddhist. It was knowing the mind. Not possessing a philosophy about consciousness, but becoming intimate with consciousness as it actually moves through the body: sensation becoming feeling, feeling becoming thought, thought becoming identity, identity becoming action, and action becoming the world we collectively inhabit. Mindfulness, understood in this way, was never intended to become an escape from life. It was an invitation to become almost unbearably intimate with it.

But what I eventually came to call World Dharma did not emerge fully formed inside a monastery. Its roots were certainly there, in the silence and rigor of Burma, but its actual form emerged through the collision between contemplative practice and the extremities of lived experience. It grew through my years in Burma and decades of traveling the world, and came into sharper focus during the war in the former Yugoslavia and later in Sarajevo, Bosnia, where the spiritual vocabulary I had inherited was forced into proximity with war, grief, displacement, ethnic hatred, courage, theatre, intimacy and the astonishing persistence of ordinary human tenderness. There, the distance between meditation and history became impossible for me to maintain. Dharma had to be capable of entering the burning building of the world.

And it had to enter the burning building of one’s own life as well. Across the decades there was love and suffering, romance and rejection, belonging and exile, addiction and sobriety, solitude and relationship, health and illness, the ecstasy of creative expression and the devastation of watching what one cherishes disappear. These were not interruptions to some more authentic spiritual journey. Increasingly, I understood that they were the journey. The contradictions themselves became the practice ground, because liberation, if the word has any living meaning, cannot depend upon arranging existence so that only the experiences we prefer are permitted to enter consciousness.

Something began emerging from these apparent opposites that I could no longer adequately describe simply as Buddhism. It was not a rejection of Buddhism; quite the contrary. My gratitude for the Buddha, Dharma, Sangha and the teachers who introduced me to the extraordinary discipline of mindful awareness remains immeasurable. But the inquiry had crossed boundaries. It had become a kind of trans-Buddhism, a trans-spirituality, not because it had transcended the need for ethics, discipline or contemplative depth, but because life itself had become too vast to be contained within a single religious identity. Psychology entered. Art entered. Eros entered. Politics entered. Theatre entered. Mortality entered. The body entered. Creativity and activism entered. Nothing essential could be left outside the door.

I began calling this World Dharma: an inquiry spacious enough to draw from the contemplative genius of the East and the psychological, artistic, scientific and existential investigations of the West without being imprisoned by either. It is trans-spiritual without being anti-spiritual, and it enters political reality without requiring ideological obedience. It is the art and activism of finding liberation through living. For me, this means refusing the ancient temptation to divide reality into the spiritual and the profane, the sacred and the damaged, the awakened and the unworthy. If Dharma cannot illuminate consciousness in the unedited conditions of human existence, then what precisely are we awakening from, and what are we awakening into?

This understanding changed the meaning of practice for me. Silence remained precious, but silence alone was insufficient. Meditation remained indispensable, but meditation could not become an alibi for disengagement. Compassion had to acquire hands and feet. Awareness had to become relationship, creativity, courage, discernment and, when necessary, resistance. The inward revolution and the outward world could no longer be separated so conveniently. The fear we refuse to investigate privately can become remarkably dangerous when organized collectively. Conversely, the tenderness discovered while sitting alone with our own vulnerability can influence how we love another person, raise a child, create art, confront injustice, accompany the dying, or refuse to dehumanize someone with whom we profoundly disagree.

At the heart of World Dharma is also a fierce devotion to truth, and therefore to learning the difference between radical independent thinking and the strangely Kafkaesque condition of becoming unconsciously inhabited by propaganda, misinformation, conformity and collective suggestion. The danger is not merely that somebody else may deceive us. More intimate, and perhaps more difficult to recognize, is our extraordinary capacity to participate in our own deception—to protect identities and certainties through denial, projection, rationalization and selective perception. Mindfulness at its most uncompromising asks us to observe this machinery within ourselves before condemning it in others. To know one’s own mind is therefore an act of epistemic freedom: the willingness to distinguish reality from illusion, evidence from belief, what we know from what we merely want to be true, while remaining sufficiently humble to recognize how easily certainty itself can become another hiding place.

There is something luminous in that intimacy with truth. Awakening, as I have come to understand it, is not omniscience, spiritual perfection or immunity from confusion. It may be something far more tender and demanding: an increasingly undefended relationship with actuality. We begin noticing the stories we manufacture, the wounds from which we interpret the world, the identities we defend, the information we accept because it confirms us, and the realities we resist because they threaten who we imagine ourselves to be. The luminosity is not somewhere beyond this human complexity. It appears within the very act of seeing clearly, of becoming less frightened of what is true, and discovering that intimate awareness can hold contradiction without immediately converting it into ideology.

A Video Guidebook to the Practice of World Dharma is a distillation of this terrain. Its thirty-seven chapters range between approximately eight and twenty-five minutes, creating ten hours of teachings, reflections, stories and experiential inquiries. Accompanying them are sixty-one one-minute World Dharma practice reflections: brief invitations to interrupt the momentum of ordinary consciousness and return attention to what is actually happening. I wanted the form itself to remain human, something you can watch slowly, return to, question, disagree with, sit silently after, or carry into the circumstances of your own day.

Perhaps that is what I most hope this video book becomes: not something you merely consume, but something you enter into relationship with. I hope you occasionally stop the video. I hope something I say unsettles a cherished assumption enough that you close the screen and walk outside. I hope you test every observation against your own experience rather than accepting it because I spent years in monasteries or decades writing, teaching and traveling through these worlds. Dharma worthy of the name should deepen our capacity for inquiry rather than increase our dependency upon authority. I am not interested in creating followers. I am interested in the possibility that we might become more profoundly trustworthy to ourselves without confusing self-trust with the certainty that we are always right.

Announcing A Video Guidebook to the Practice of World Dharma https://t.co/afBiHh96EF

This feels especially urgent now. We inhabit a world in which artificial intelligence is transforming our relationship with knowledge and creativity, ecological disruption confronts us with consequences that transcend borders, and technologies engineered to capture attention increasingly mediate our experience of reality. Information travels through algorithms, corporations, governments, political movements, social tribes and increasingly sophisticated systems capable of generating convincing simulations. Under such conditions, the quality of our attention has become a civilizational question. If we cannot recognize when fear has captured thought, when desire is masquerading as truth, when belonging requires the surrender of conscience, or when an algorithm has quietly begun determining what deserves our attention, freedom can become a word we continue using while losing contact with the experience it describes.

And still, through all of this, I remain astonished by the maddening miracle of being alive. Beneath our strategies and identities remains this mysterious capacity to become conscious of consciousness itself, to interrupt inherited patterns, to forgive, to apologize, to begin again, to make beauty beside devastation, to risk intimacy after heartbreak, and to discover tenderness precisely where certainty has failed us. I have witnessed these capacities in monasteries and war zones, in Burma and Sarajevo, among artists and dissidents, lovers and strangers, and in the strange laboratory of my own imperfect life. They are among the reasons I continue to believe that awakening is not withdrawal from the human predicament. It is an increasingly intimate participation in it.

Perhaps this is ultimately what World Dharma means to me. It is not another belief system to defend, another identity to acquire, another spiritual tribe to join, or another ideology through which to divide the world into those who understand and those who do not. It is an invitation into intimacy with experience itself. It asks whether awareness can become sufficiently spacious to encounter the whole catastrophe without abandoning intelligence, tenderness or the instinct for freedom. It asks whether we can remain awake enough to see what is happening, intimate enough to feel it, independent enough to question it, and compassionate enough not to turn our awakening into another weapon against one another.

So I offer A Video Guidebook to the Practice of World Dharma not as the culmination of an answer, but as the distillation of an inquiry. After fifty years, I know considerably less about the mystery of existence than I once imagined I might. But I care more deeply about the quality of consciousness we bring to that mystery, and whether our brief appearance here can become more lucid, courageous, compassionate, creative and free. I invite you into these thirty-seven encounters not so that you can follow my journey, but so that perhaps something within them will encourage you to enter your own life more completely, including the places you have been taught to avoid, and discover within the complexity of living an intelligence no doctrine could ever give you. Perhaps freedom was never waiting somewhere beyond the contradictions. Perhaps the invitation of Dharma has always been more intimate and more demanding: to awaken here, within the unfinished actuality of our lives, and through the immeasurable vulnerability of being human, learn the art of finding liberation through living.

My heart to yours,

Alan Clements
Bali, 2026

About Alan Clements

Alan Clements is an author, investigative journalist, performing artist, former Buddhist monk, and human-rights activist. One of the first Westerners to ordain as a Buddhist monk in Burma, now Myanmar, he trained in intensive vipassana meditation under the Venerable Mahāsi Sayadaw and the Venerable Sayadaw U Pandita. After being forced to leave Burma by the military dictatorship in 1984, his work expanded across contemplative practice, human rights, journalism, literature, theatre and spoken-word performance.

For more than four decades, Clements has explored the relationship between inner freedom and the forces shaping our collective lives. His books include The Voice of Hope, based on his conversations with Nobel Peace laureate Aung San Suu Kyi, Burma’s Revolution of the Spirit, Instinct for Freedom, Burma’s Voices of Freedom, Conversation with a Dictator, Unsilenced, and Politics of the Heart. World Dharma is the evolving expression of his life’s inquiry into mindful intelligence, freedom of conscience, creativity, compassion, and the art of finding liberation through living.

text: @SecVetAffairs  thank you for all that you’re doing. I am a disabled veteran at 50 percent for ptsd - while in Marine Corps recruit training on 2008 I was bit by a bug and received 5 vector borne bacterial infections which was misdiagnosed as TB and I was quarantined off base. I eventually had a general separation where I would be able to rejoin with a waiver because I was never tested for bacterial infections while on the island. I never had the chance to serve in full capacity. I came home to Florida and from the week I came home I walked through the civilian medical system getting misdiagnosed for years. I was told I had drug induced Parkinson’s due to my joints locking I was falling regular and got my handicap pass on the state of Florida. Then things turned worse the bacterial infections worked their way up my spine and effected an area of nerves in my bladder where as a grown man I wet my bed every night for years. Everywhere I went I smelled like urine and my poor mother our house reaked. One year after my return my wife divorced from me her last words were “I’m to young to be with someone who is sick” it was probably the best decision she ever made and i am grateful that happened. On my end I visited urologist around the state of Florida and had to get long neeedle like camera shoved up my man part. The urologist never found an answer. I attempted suicide twice. I was having neuro psychiatric problems because all of this went undiagnosed and my psychiatrist team deemed me schizophrenic. Which I am not. They shut my body down on heavy psych meds and within a year of coming home from recruit depot I gained over 100 pounds. I couldn’t keep a job i tried I was constantly fatigued. Years later my teeth started flaking out of my head like paper and Bryan was finally getting regular treatment of antibiotics. I spent 4.5 months on pic line IV at a local hospital because the vector borne bacterial infections worked up my spine and crossed the brain blood barrier.  I had got a brain spec scan performed repots came back that I had cerebral blood flow issues similar to someone with dementia. My brain fog I was forgetting words mid sentence. Before I enlisted I was known as the Florida Magician I was one of the most successful magic performers in the country with multiple news articles and i appeared in local news interviews as well as Dateline NBC. When I came home I never returned to my craft. I felt that I had something very special to offer the US Military. While in training many men enlisted including officers all broke rank and pulled me behind closed doors and ordered me to perform card tricks and other effects. I joined the Marines for several reasons but one of them was “Honor” sadly there was no “Honor to be found” In the fourth month of my IV treatment I was filling out my VA claim my brain cleared like a tunnel going  back in time and I remembered everything. I reported these things in my C and P exams and was only awarded 50 percent for PTSD for an assult that took place on me while in training. I do not wish to talk about the rest of that on your X. The other part of my claim was denied because I wrote it wrong and now have a VA accredited attorney taking care of that as well as some other disabilities that are service connected. I know that I shouldn’t even be speaking on these things yet. But I took an oath to defend the constitution and put God and country first. The same oath that you at one point took sir. I am watching videos of Marine training in 2026 and young men and woman are still running heavy bug populated areas with their sleeves rolled up. I was bit on my arm. By the end of training I had a rash across my entire body and couldn’t stop scratching and could not sleep. The Navy eventually knocked me out with a psychotropic medicine called Seroquel and I literally bought into the idea I was just crazy. Marines in full hazmat suits came into my platoon and took all bedding off each bed and incinerated them
