text:
Venezuela Spot Oil Sales Snarled by Surging Freight Costs
•Sales of Venezuelan oil for loading in October stalled after a surge in shipping costs muddled negotiations between the country’s state oil company and buyers of its oil.
•Shipping costs have more than doubled from the end of August, making Venezuelan crude less competitive with Canadian barrels for US refiners and snarling sales deals.
•The dispute risks disrupting a key source of crude for American refiners amid record diesel prices and ahead of US midterm elections.
By Lucia Kassai
(Bloomberg) -- Sales of Venezuelan oil for loading in October stalled after a surge in shipping costs muddled negotiations between the country’s state oil company and buyers of its oil.
Shipping costs — a key component of the delivered price — have more than doubled from the end of August. That’s making Venezuelan crude less competitive with Canadian barrels for US refiners and snarling sales deals, according to people with knowledge of the situation. Canada and Venezuela are the largest suppliers of foreign oil to the US.
Commodity traders such as Vitol Group and Trafigura Group, tapped by the US to help sell Venezuelan oil, have a broad arrangement — but not an obligation — to buy oil from Petroleos de Venezuela SA. Buyers of Venezuelan oil are currently being offered the oil at a discount of around $14 to benchmark ICE Brent prices, loading in October, said the people, who asked not to be named discussing private information.
With the cost to ship oil to the US Gulf Coast at nearly $7 a barrel, it means the oil arrives at the shores of Texas and Louisiana at a discount of $7 per barrel, or at least $5 more expensive than competing Canadian supplies, the people said.

Texas authorites booked Mohammed Rahhal as “White” on an immigration hold and a $15,000 drug bond.

Grand Prairie police arrested the 43-year-old on Aug. 31, 2026. The inmate file lists a felony drug count for 1 to 4 grams.

Nearly a month later, no public Grand Prairie or ICE release names his country of origin or says whether he was transferred, deported, or cut loose.

Federal Statistical Policy Directive 15, in the 1997 version still used by many jails, folded Middle Eastern and North African origins into the ‘White’ racial category.

OMB added a separate Middle Eastern or North African category in March 2024. Agencies have until March 28, 2029, to finish the switch.

The Dallas Express documented the same coding on an Afghan national booked in Tarrant County after a Fort Worth bomb-threat case. That jail search offered white, black, Asian, or Indian.

Gov. Greg Abbott's office has not posted a disposition on this hold. Grand Prairie Police have not posted a follow-up naming an ICE pickup.

text:
Daily Morning Market Brief
Date: 24/09/2026

Global markets have come under pressure as the deadly combination of rising crude oil prices and US bond yields has resurfaced. Brent crude moved above $102 as uncertainty over a possible Strait of Hormuz blockade intensified, while hopes of near-term peace talks remained stalled on the sidelines of the 81st UN General Assembly. Additional supply-side concerns emerged over potential US restrictions on diesel exports, further supporting oil prices.

US bond yields also moved higher after stronger-than-expected manufacturing and services PMI data increased expectations of further rate hikes. Fed Governor Michael Barr’s comments that additional rate hikes may be required to bring inflation under control, along with weak demand at a US bond auction, added to the upward pressure on yields.

Overnight, US markets declined, with all major indices under pressure. The Nasdaq fell 1.13% to close at 26,936.04, while broader US indices declined by more than 0.50%. European markets also ended lower. US futures are currently showing a subdued trend, while Asian markets are trading mixed. Japan’s Nikkei, reopening after a three-day holiday, is up nearly 1.50%, while the Hang Seng is down around 0.50%. South Korea’s KOSPI remains closed on account of Thanksgiving.

The extension of the US-China trade truce under the Busan agreement until January 10, 2027, provides additional time for both sides to work towards a broader economic deal and remains one of the few positive developments amid the current global weakness.

Domestic News Flow

NSE will make its market debut today after raising ₹22,562 crore through its IPO, with the listing taking place on the BSE.

Insurance stocks will remain in focus after IRDAI proposed a broad overhaul of the economics of insurance distribution. The consultation paper seeks lower Expense of Management (EoM) limits, tighter controls on commissions and greater transparency for policyholders.

BDL has signed an ₹810.79 crore contract with the Ministry of Defence for the supply of Satellite Smart Anti-Airfield Weapons (SAT-SAAW), along with associated equipment, to the Indian Air Force.

Exide Industries’ subsidiary, Exide Energy Solutions (EESL), has completed the commissioning of Phase-I of its 6 GWh lithium-ion cell manufacturing facility at Devanahalli, Bengaluru.

Telecom stocks will also remain in focus after TRAI directed service providers to offer voice-and-SMS-only tariff plans, without bundled data, with a minimum validity of 30 days or less.

Market Strategy

Indian markets are expected to open with a sharp gap down following the weak global cues. However, traders should avoid rushing into fresh short positions at the open and instead wait for a decent pullback or a failed recovery before considering shorts.

The BSE indices’ monthly expiry could further increase volatility and intraday choppiness. Traders should therefore remain cautious and account for sharp swings before taking fresh positions.

Overall strategy: Wait for a pullback before entering shorts rather than chasing the gap-down opening.

text:
The Legend of Mossy Hollow
In the low country of Louisiana, where the cypress knees rise from black water like the fingers of drowned men and Spanish moss hangs in gray curtains, there once stood a drowsy settlement called Mossy Hollow. The people there were a mixture of planters, poor whites, freedmen, and those who still worked the cane and cotton for little more than rations. Superstition ran thicker than the humidity. Everyone knew the old stories of conjure and the restless dead.

Into this place came Ichabod Crane, a lanky schoolmaster from up North with a long neck, a hungry look, and an appetite that could empty a pot of gumbo before the first bowl was offered to anyone else. He boarded with the Widow LaFleur and taught the children their letters in a one-room schoolhouse that smelled of mildew and woodsmoke. Ichabod had a particular weakness for rich food, pretty girls, and the prospect of marrying into property.The prettiest girl and the richest prize was Miss Delphine Beaumont, daughter of a planter whose land still produced after the war. Delphine had dark eyes, a laugh like wind in the cane, and suitors enough to fill a gallery. Foremost among them was Brom “Bones” Thibodaux, a broad-shouldered local who raced horses, drank, and played rough jokes. Brom did not take kindly to the Yankee schoolteacher hovering around Delphine.

One autumn evening, after a supper of fried catfish, cornbread, and sweet potato pie at the Beaumont place, the talk turned, as it always did in Mossy Hollow, to the thing that haunted the old river road.
They called him Papa Cane.

Long ago, before the war ended, a cruel overseer named Cane had been slighted by a newly freed man who refused to bow or step aside on the path. The overseer swore he would see that man and all like him brought low. He died badly—fever, some said, or a curse laid by a root worker—and was buried without ceremony. Not long after, a houngan from the back swamp raised him as a zombie, bound to the earth and to his old hatred. Papa Cane shambled the night roads with milky eyes and rotting clothes, and he carried, of all things, watermelons. He hurled them with terrible force at those he took for “poor black folk” still walking free. The fruit would burst against trees, wagons, or skulls, leaving red pulp and seeds like scattered teeth. Travelers swore they heard the wet thud and the zombie’s low, wordless moan of old grievance.Ichabod laughed a little too loudly at the tale, but when he rode home that night on a borrowed plow horse, the laughter died. The road wound through the cypress swamp. Moonlight silvered the water. Then he heard it: a heavy, dragging step, and the sound of something large being hefted.Papa Cane came out of the mist. The zombie’s head lolled, jaw slack, but his arms were strong. He lifted a watermelon the size of a child’s torso and flung it. It smashed against a cypress trunk beside Ichabod’s horse, spraying juice and black seeds. The schoolmaster kicked the horse into a gallop. Another melon whistled past his ear. A third struck the horse’s flank and burst. Ichabod clung to the saddle, coat flapping, as the zombie pursued with unnatural speed, still hurling fruit and still nursing that ancient slight.

At the old wooden bridge over the bayou, Ichabod looked back. Papa Cane stood in the middle of the road, another melon raised. Ichabod felt something strike the back of his head—wet, heavy, final. He tumbled from the horse.The next morning the horse wandered home alone. Of Ichabod Crane there was no sign except his hat, lying in the mud, and the smashed remains of several watermelons, seeds glistening in the sun. Some said he had been carried off by the zombie. Others whispered that Brom Thibodaux knew more than he told, and that a certain large, laughing man had been seen that same night with a wagonload of melons.Delphine married Brom before the year was out. On quiet nights in Mossy Hollow, when the moss sways and the frogs go silent, folks still claim you can hear the wet impact of fruit against wood, and the dragging step of a dead man who never forgot a slight.

KEY JUDGMENT

We assess Washington is attempting to compress Havana’s strategic options through escalating economic, financial, energy, and diplomatic pressure while preserving channels for negotiated concessions.

Intent: reduce liquidity and increase competition for resources within the Cuban state.

16 OCTOBER–30 NOVEMBER 2026

Washington may increasingly shift pressure outward toward foreign entities sustaining Havana’s economic resilience.

Key indicators:

• Action against financial intermediaries
• Increased scrutiny of shipping and energy networks
• Pressure on foreign companies operating in sanctioned sectors
• Additional designations involving military-commercial structures

Objective: raise the external cost of sustaining Havana.

Indicators of movement would include:

• Senior-level diplomatic contacts

Selective sanctions relief could become bargaining leverage if Havana offers verifiable concessions.

Absent concessions, further economic isolation becomes increasingly plausible.

Three trajectories emerge:

A — NEGOTIATED ACCOMMODATION

Limited Cuban concessions produce selective U.S. relief.

B — PROLONGED COERCION

Havana absorbs the pressure while Washington continues constricting revenue and external support.

C — INTERNAL DESTABILIZATION

Economic deterioration, energy shortages, and declining state capacity generate larger protests or fractures within the governing structure.

STRATEGIC ASSESSMENT

The emerging U.S. model is cumulative:

CONSTRICT REVENUE
→ RESTRICT EXTERNAL SUPPORT
→ INCREASE INTERNAL ECONOMIC PRESSURE
→ PRESERVE NEGOTIATING LEVERAGE

This does not establish that Washington has decided on direct regime-change intervention.

Current public evidence is more consistent with coercive economic leverage, strategic isolation, and pressure designed to alter Havana’s decision calculus.

INDICATORS & WARNINGS

Watch closely for:

• Sanctions against third-country facilitators
• Action affecting Cuba’s fuel supply
• Unannounced senior U.S.–Cuba contacts
• Emergency Russian or Chinese assistance

DECISION WINDOW

The central intelligence question is no longer whether Washington intends to pressure Havana.

It is whether sustained pressure forces negotiation, drives Cuba toward deeper external dependence, or accelerates internal instability faster than the Cuban state can adapt.

text:
GRACO $GGG LEADS THE DEEP-VALUE LEN5. THE BUSINESS EARNS THE SEAT; THE PRICE DOES NOT YET:

Graco (GGG) at $78.37, +$0.73 / +0.94% on Wednesday, is the first of 113 names the Deep-Value & Special-Situations Len5 is watching. The 100-year-old Minneapolis company makes pumps, paint sprayers and dispensers for everything from wall paint to factory sealants. On August 31 it paid $447M in cash for Valco Melton, a maker of glue-dispensing machines; on Wednesday the 10-year Treasury yield closed at 5.11%, up about 0.15 point.

The verdict: Graco is the kind of business this Len5 waits for - wide margins, almost no debt - but it is not priced below what it steadily earns. At 24.6 times its past year's profit, the discount half is missing, and the cash that padded the case is mostly spent. A watch, not a bargain.

Where the cash went:

- March 27: $712.2M on hand
- Three months to June 26: $315M to buy back about 4.0M of its own shares, near $78.50 each - roughly tonight's price
- August 31: $447M for Valco Melton, out of the $507.6M left on June 26

Valco Melton, based near Cincinnati, sells machines that lay glue on packaging lines and cameras that check the work: about $145M of 2025 sales, roughly 6.5% of Graco's. Net of expected tax savings, Graco puts the price at about 14 times Valco Melton's 2025 EBITDA, a rough cash-profit measure before interest, taxes and write-offs.

It buys into a slow market. Nordson (NDSN) at $321.42, +$1.75 / +0.55% on Wednesday, the larger rival, grew its adhesive-dispensing and coating segment 3% without acquisitions in the July quarter. Nordson fits none of the six Len5es; at about 32 times its past year's profit it offers none of the discount the value Len5es want.

The June quarter, reported July 22:

- Sales $590.6M, +3%, all from acquisitions and currency; without them, -1%
- Operating profit - what is left after making and selling the products - $175.1M, +11%; $9M came from refunds of tariffs the Supreme Court struck down in February, about half the $17.6M gain
- Orders without acquisitions up at a mid-single-digit rate

The strongest fact against the verdict is the Contractor segment, about half of sales. It sells sprayers to professional painters and home centers, and in June it grew in the Americas in both channels without help from deals for the first time in two years, CEO Mark Sheahan said. If orders keep climbing, profit can grow into the price. Rates cut the other way: painting and remodeling slow when borrowing costs climb, and Graco's profit comes to 4.1% of its price against 5.11% on a Treasury.

Graco through the six Len5es, plus the Quality Len5:

- DEEP-VALUE & SPECIAL-SITUATIONS - PARTIAL, and the Len5 watching it. Hunts a sound business priced below what it steadily earns. Sound: 21 cents of profit over four quarters per dollar of shareholders' equity - the owners' stake - and $29.2M of debt in June. Priced below: no. $12.7B of stock-market value is about 26 times its five-year average profit of $483M. What would knock Graco off the Deep-Value Len5: another deal paid for with borrowed money. What would make it a full fit: a price that falls while that profit holds.

- QUALITY-VALUE - PARTIAL, 28th of 63. Hunts a business almost nobody could rebuild, bought below its worth. The rebuild half: Graco kept 53.7 cents of each June-quarter sales dollar after the cost of making its products, and 29.6 cents after all operating costs. The price half fails as above. What would knock Graco off the Quality-Value Len5: that margin slipping once the tariff refunds stop.

- QUALITY LEN5 - FIT. Wants real gross profit, a solid return on the owners' stake, and debt no bigger than that stake: $316.9M of June-quarter gross profit; $533.5M of profit over four quarters on $2.52B of equity; debt about 1% of it. What would knock Graco off the Quality Len5: returns sliding as it pays up for more deals like Valco Melton.

- GROWTH - NOT A FIT. Hunts profit growth the price has not charged for, on a long profitable record. The record is there; the growth is not: sales $2.14B in 2022, $2.24B in 2025, and a 2026 plan for low single-digit growth without acquisitions. What would put Graco on the Growth Len5: growth without deals back to mid-single digits for several quarters.

- INCOME - NOT A FIT. Hunts cash to owners the business itself pays for. First-half free cash flow - cash left after running the business and buying equipment - was $269.5M against $97.7M of dividends, but the $1.18 yearly dividend yields 1.5%, and dividends plus $331.1M of buybacks outran that cash. What would put Graco on the Income Len5: a dividend that matters at this price, paid from cash flow.

- MOMENTUM - NOT A FIT. Hunts a price near its one-year high with short and long climbs agreeing. Graco is 18% under February's $95.69 high and 7.8% below a year ago. What would put Graco on the Momentum Len5: a climb back toward that high.

- HYPERGROWTH - NOT A FIT, the widest miss. Hunts very fast growth on a real base; Graco's sales grew about 4% in three years. What would put Graco on the Hypergrowth Len5: sales doubling in a few years, not how a century-old equipment maker grows.

WHEN: third-quarter results, tentatively October 21 after the close, not yet confirmed by Graco; analysts expect $0.83 a share. Graco guided sales of $580M-$600M before Valco Melton, vs $543.4M a year ago. The number that decides it: sales growth without acquisitions, after June's -1%. RISK: slower painting and remodeling under higher rates, just as the cash is gone.

Between late March and August 31, Graco put $762M behind two prices it judged fair: its own stock near $78.50, and Valco Melton at about 14 times its cash profit. The Deep-Value Len5 is still waiting for the market to offer a lower one.

Not investment advice.

text:
The Bible teaches that we are saved through faith alone, and that saving faith will produce good works.
====================================

The Roman Catholic Church teaches that works contribute to justification and salvation.

This sounds blasphemous and unbiblical (it is), but look at these quotes:

"The Catholic understanding is that grace works in cooperation with human free will and actions (Catechism of the Catholic Church, 2008). Catholicism holds that faith and works, inspired by grace, are both necessary for salvation (James 2:24)."

================

But wait, there's more...
=============

“The grace of the Holy Spirit has the power to justify us, that is, to cleanse us from our sins and to communicate to us "the righteousness of God through faith in Jesus Christ" and through Baptism….” 

(Baptism is a work).

"Justification has been merited for us by the Passion of Christ who offered himself on the cross as a living victim, holy and pleasing to God, and whose blood has become the instrument of atonement for the sins of all men. Justification is conferred in Baptism, the sacrament of faith."

"After receiving initial justification, Catholicism teaches that a person can commit a  moral sin and fall out of a state of grace. For that, a person must participate in the sacraments (rituals) such as Penance, which offers “a new possibility to convert and to recover the grace of justification.”

"If any one saith, that by faith alone the impious is justified; in such wise as to mean, that nothing else is required to co-operate in order to the obtaining the grace of Justification, and that it is not in any way necessary, that he be prepared and disposed by the movement of his own will; let him be anathema.” Anathema, historically, meant cast out of the church and “condemned to eternal fire with Satan and his angels and all the reprobate,” provided the person did not repent of his error."

"If any one saith, that justifying faith is nothing else but confidence in the divine mercy which remits sins for Christ's sake; or, that this confidence alone is that whereby we are justified; let him be anathema.”

“Baptism, by imparting the life of Christ's grace, erases original sin and turns a man back towards God, but the consequences for nature, weakened and inclined to evil, persist in man and summon him to spiritual battle.” 

===============
and that's not all....
==================
A person must be united to the Roman Catholic Church:
“it is altogether necessary to salvation for every human creature to be subject to the Roman Pontiff.”

============

So according to Roman Catholicism, Christ's death made salvation possible, but sinners still have to use their free will to cooperate with God's grace and perform works, prescribed by the Roman religious organization, in order to attain to, keep, and re-establish a state of justification, and it's possible to do all that, all one's life, and to still commit a mortal sin and go to Hell anyway. 

Anyone who's only trusting in Christ for part of his salvation, and his own works for the rest of it, is in a works-based system.

text:
Rt. Hon. Francis Ogbonna Nwifuru  - The Executive Governor of Ebonyi State, Nigeria.
The Salt of the Nation.

His story as bricklayer 
to Governor is inspiring because it breaks the myth that power in Ebonyi is reserved for those born with a silver spoon. 

Here was a man who carried blocks, mixed mortar, measured with his hands — who knew the weight of a day's wage — and rose from the site to become Speaker and then Governor of the same state. It tells every Izzi [same LGA we both are from] boy and every Abakaliki boy that labour does not disqualify you; if anything, it prepares you. That a man who built houses with his hands can now build a state.

And that's why he is my Leading Light for today.

My former Chief Judge  - Hon. Justice Alloy Nwankwo CON, OON is like a father to me. 

I have had cause to honour him on more than two occasions before dignitaries in the state. Once was at an event chaired by My Lord, Hon. Justice Obande Festus Ogbuinya, JSC, then of the Court of Appeal, and another time through an essay in his honour.

If I recall, the Attorney-General of the State attended that event, and a good number of senior judges, including My Lord, Hon. Justice (Dr.) Nnamdi Okwy Dimgba, JCA.

Note on My Lord Dimgba: My Lord was Partner at Olaniwun Ajayi LP when I was just a Corps member, though I would end up being retained in the firm. Even after going to the Bench, he kept tabs on me and had written some of my references for PG offers from Oxbridge. An Oxonian — BCL from Worcester College, University of Oxford (Shell Centenary/British Chevening Scholar), and PhD in Competition Law from the University of the West of England (UWE), Bristol, where he lectured in Corporate and Competition Law. Recognised as Nigeria's leading expert on Competition Law. 

My Lord Justice Dimgba is from Abia State, but when I told him who 
I was honouring, he came down to Abakaliki in person, though he was then posted to Anambra.

When I visited My Lord, the former Chief Judge, at his home in Abakaliki, he looked at me and wondered what I wanted. When I made no ask, he volunteered His Excellency's number himself. He felt a young man like me would certainly be hungry for such contact, since His Excellency is my "Elder Brother" from the same LGA.

Till date, I never bothered to reach out. 
I still have that contact. 
I felt I wasn't ready to harvest that relationship — I needed to have something more to offer the state, or even the Governor himself.

Why share this? I know what access does to people. You shouldn't go to people in power just asking for favours, except you are ready to offer something proportionate in return. 

Otherwise, I'm no better than those who leech off political office holders only on account of access.

He remains the Elder Brother oh. I'm still young. @FrancisNwifuru

text:
Understanding Our Story as Christians: Helpful Church History Resources
by Cody Mitchell

Evangelical Christians like myself, especially in modern times, have gained a reputation for being notoriously detached from the wider history of Christianity — whether that be the history of evangelicalism as a movement or of the church as a whole.

Pleasingly, there are some important efforts underway to correct this blind spot.

Sarah Irving-Stonebraker’s Priests of History: Stewarding the Past in an Ahistoric Age (Zondervan, 2024) calls Christians of all stripes and traditions to push back against what she calls “ahistoricism” and see ourselves as part of a much bigger story.

Similarly, Gavin Ortlund’s YouTube ministry “Truth United”, and his book Theological Retrieval for Evangelicals: Why We Need Our Past to Have a Future (Crossway, 2019) offer a blueprint for how retrieval can enrich the evangelical movement and Protestant theological discourse more broadly.

Organisations like the American Center for Baptist Renewal explicitly list historical and theological “retrieval” and the promotion of “Baptist catholicity” as among their key aims.

Yet for the everyday Christian, a useful personal starting point in this project of historical retrieval is simply picking a good short history of the church.

It doesn’t need to be anything super complex, long, or academic. A simple, well-written survey of Christian history is a great way to deepen your understanding of the various expressions of Christianity, not only geographically, but throughout time. It is also a fantastic way to discover areas of church history — particularly significant events, traditions or movements, or Christian figures — that pique your interest, opening the door for further reading and research.

Here are two of my recommendations.

> David Bentley Hart, The Story of Christianity: A History of 2,000 Years of the Christian Faith

I just completed David Bentley Hart’s ambitiously-named The Story of Christianity (Quercus, 2013). Don’t let Hart’s extremely high-level work in other areas (he can be pretty difficult at times) put you off this little book — The Story of Christianity is genuinely accessible for any thoughtful layperson.

Hart is one of the most interesting Christian thinkers and writers around today. He is a philosopher, theologian, essayist, fiction author, and a scholar of religion, and has written some twenty-four books on everything from theology and church history to philosophy of mind (I am currently reading his magisterial defence of the pre-modern, non-mechanistic conception of reality, All Things Are Full of Gods: The Mysteries of Mind and Life).

In The Story of Christianity, however, his emphasis is on the 2,000 years following Jesus’s life, death, and resurrection, but he fittingly begins with a brief overview of Christianity’s Jewish origins and nature of Jesus’s ministry as the Jewish Messiah and an itinerant rabbi.

The book has very short chapters, which are broken up into even shorter topical sections. While this means that its treatment of any given figure, event, or movement is necessarily fleeting, brevity does have its upside. Rather than investing in one of the countless entire volumes dedicated to, say, the Spanish inquisition or the Carolingian Renaissance, you get a page and half summary of each — enough space to touch on the event’s significance and highlight several important figures.

One of Hart’s strengths is that he has previously done very detailed work in apologetics — see, for example, his spectacular rebuttal to the “new atheists”, Atheist Delusions: The Christian Revolution and Its Fashionable Enemies (Yale University Press, 2009). Accordingly, The Story of Christianity has a strong theme of clearing up common misunderstandings and misrepresentations about Christian history, misunderstandings that frequently offer ammunition to aggressive anti-Christians to attack Christianity.

> John Dickson, Bullies and Saints: An Honest Look at the Good and Evil of Christian History

Another single-volume history of Christianity worth adding to your library is by Australian historian John Dickson: Bullies and Saints: An Honest Look at the Good and Evil of Christian History.

Dickson is an Aussie Anglican minister, who currently holds the (extremely prestigious-sounding) position of Jean Kvamme Distinguished Professor of Biblical Evangelism and Distinguished Scholar in Public Christianity at Wheaton College, in Illinois. He holds a PhD in Ancient History from Macquarie University and specialises in ancient Christianity and Judaism. He has held academic positions at Macquarie University, the University of Sydney, the University of Oxford, and Ridley College.

Like Hart’s book, Dickson’s is engagingly written and accessible for non-scholars. Yet Dickson’s main focus, as the title of his book makes clear, is on the often controversial history of the church, and how, so frequently, atrocities have been committed in Christ’s name that stand in stark contrast to the teachings of Jesus himself.

Dickson does not gloss over these tragedies and atrocities. After all, the history of Christians is a history of very fallible, broken people — indeed, “bullies” as well as “saints” as his title suggests. One need go no further than the Bible to find clear examples of the mistakes, disobedience, and sometimes downright wickedness of God’s people.

It is important for Christians to reckon with the ugly side of church history as well as the many wonderful achievements and positive contributions that followers of Jesus have made to this world.

Hence, I wholeheartedly recommend Bullies and Saints and The Story of Christianity to those seeking a better grasp of the Christian story of which we are each a part (whether we like it or not!).

Those are two of my recommendations. Do you have some of your own? If so, leave a comment below to tell us more!

Read the full piece at https://t.co/x40H8PydeG

text:
Almost every year since 2018, I got to choose one away game per season to travel to with Adam. For 2026, I chose Colorado at Northwestern — mostly because it gave us an excuse to spend a few days in Chicago.

We had watched all our favorite travel shows to plan what we wanted to eat and see, and as a lifelong Cubs fan, Adam booked us a hotel right in Wrigleyville.

So when September came and I still had two plane tickets, I offered the other one to Silas.

It happened to be the week of his 18th birthday, and because he’s become such a talented photographer in his own right, I knew he’d love getting to experience the trip as a credentialed media member too.

I only really broke down once.

We walked into our hotel room — room 444 — and opened the curtains to the most perfect view of Wrigley Field. I just stood there thinking about how much Adam would have loved it.

When we first started dating, the only picture he had hanging on the walls of his apartment was the classic 1945 photo of the front of Wrigley. So of course this was the room we ended up in.

I’m incredibly thankful Silas was there with me. Having him beside me kept what could have been a very lonely trip from feeling that way.

And we had so much fun. We ate ridiculously well. We took the architecture boat tour on the river. We wandered downtown doing a photo challenge together. And then we got to stand on the sideline and photograph a college football game together.

The game definitely didn’t turn out the way we hoped it would, but somehow that feels like one of the least important parts of the weekend.

A trip I thought I would be taking with Adam became something completely different. It was bittersweet and emotional and really, really special.

And somehow, it has already become one of my favorite trips I’ve ever taken.

US, Polish presidents sign pact to boost American military presence in Poland

WARSAW, Poland — U.S. President Donald Trump and his Polish counterpart Andrzej Duda inked a joint declaration on advancing defense cooperation Sept. 23 in New York, paving the way for an increased U.S. military presence in Poland.

The two countries “continue to develop the plan to bolster Polish–United States military ties and United States defense and deterrence capabilities in Poland. These capabilities presently include approximately 4,500 rotational United States military personnel. As noted, this enduring presence is expected to grow by approximately 1,000 additional United States military personnel in the near term,” according to the declaration.

A group of U.S. Army soldiers take part in a yearly military parade celebrating the Polish Army Day in Warsaw, Poland, on Aug. 15, 2018. Poland marks Army Day with a parade and a call for U.S. permanent military base in Poland. (Alik Keplicz/AP)
WARSAW, Poland — U.S. President Donald Trump and his Polish counterpart Andrzej Duda inked a joint declaration on advancing defense cooperation Sept. 23 in New York, paving the way for an increased U.S. military presence in Poland.

The two countries “continue to develop the plan to bolster Polish–United States military ties and United States defense and deterrence capabilities in Poland. These capabilities presently include approximately 4,500 rotational United States military personnel. As noted, this enduring presence is expected to grow by approximately 1,000 additional United States military personnel in the near term,” according to the declaration.

It’s not ‘Fort Trump,’ but a US division headquarters heading to Poland
The partners have determined six locations for this designed enhanced military presence. Poznań, in western Poland, is to host the Division Headquarters and the U.S. Army area support group. Drawsko Pomorskie, in the country’s northwest, will host the primary Combat Training Center for joint use by the Polish and U.S. Armed Forces. Wrocław-Strachowice, in southwestern Poland, is to host the U.S. Air Force aerial port of debarkation, and Łask, in the country’s central part, will host the U.S. Air Force remotely piloted aircraft squadron. Powidz, in western Poland, is to host a combat aviation brigade, a combat sustainment support battalion, and a special operations forces facility, while Lubliniec, in the country’s south, will host a special operations forces facility, according to the document.

Warsaw and Washington are also in dialogue about “the most suitable location in Poland for an armored brigade combat team,” the declaration says.

Warsaw has been seeking a permanent U.S. military presence in Poland, dubbed “Fort Trump,” amid rising security concerns over Russian activities in the region. As part of these efforts, the Polish government offered to earmark at least $2 billion toward the project under which the U.S. would establish a military base in the country.

Last June, Duda met with Trump in Washington to discuss the initiative and sign a joint declaration on defense cooperation regarding U.S. force posture in Poland.

The greatest weapon of the climate change campaign is its deliberate complexity. 

Today, people everywhere face a carefully manicured double barrier: an energy agenda shrouded in dense scientific jargon, and a United Nations framework that is utterly opaque. Just voicing a valid common-sense concern has been effectively criminalised. 

When you peel back the layers of extreme worst-case computer modeling, the picture becomes jarringly clear: we are witnessing an unprecedented transfer of wealth and sovereignty, designed to get this political campaign over the line before its bubble bursts.

This is not just bureaucratic overreach; it's a psychological operation executed through calculated PR hits. When leadership deploys terms like 'global boiling,' it signals a shift from empirical debate to emotional blackmail. By anchoring public policy to extreme, worst-case scenarios, the architects of this agenda want to manufacture a permanent state of crisis and hyper-emergency.

Under the banner of saving the planet, a deeper political transformation is taking place. 🇮🇳🇺🇸 M-LIDS Makes India Debut — Counter-Drone Focus at Yudh Abhyas 2026
WHAT: The US Army's M-LIDS (Mobile Low, Slow, Small Unmanned Aircraft Integrated Defeat System) has been deployed in India for the first time, showcased at Exercise Yudh Abhyas 2026, Mahajan Field Firing Range, Rajasthan.
WHO: US Army's 3rd Multi-Domain Task Force, alongside Indian Army forces.
WHY: As drones become increasingly central to modern conflicts, this deployment gives Indian personnel direct exposure to a dedicated, multi-layered US counter-UAS system — while testing how counter-drone protection can integrate with long-range precision fires within the same tactical framework.
HOW — System Breakdown:
🔹 Built on two Oshkosh M-ATV vehicles
🔹 Detection: KuRFS radar plus additional surveillance sensors
🔹 Electronic warfare capability to disrupt drone control links
🔹 Kinetic effectors: XM914 30mm cannon for close-range engagement, plus Coyote Block 2 interceptors for a second kinetic option
🔹 Commanded through FAAD C2 (Forward Area Air Defense Command and Control) — networking detection, decision-making, and engagement into one system
🔹 Multi-layered approach: operators choose electronic or kinetic response depending on threat type and engagement conditions, rather than relying on one single defeat method
THE BROADER EXERCISE CONTEXT: M-LIDS is being demonstrated alongside HIMARS and Stinger live-fire drills at the same Mahajan range, with the exercise culminating in a combined live-fire event integrating US and Indian long-range precision fires — directly testing how counter-UAS protection and strike capability can operate together.
WHY IT MATTERS: This is happening alongside the same Yudh Abhyas edition where we've already covered Apache and Pinaka demonstrations — reinforcing that this year's exercise is explicitly built around multi-domain, technology-integrated warfare, not just traditional live-fire drills. For India, direct exposure to a fielded, combat-ready counter-drone architecture like M-LIDS offers a useful benchmark as India scales its own indigenous counter-drone ecosystem — Ahuti Mk II, DRDO's DEW ladder (2kW/10kW/30kW), and the SHIELD HPM programme all aim to solve the same problem this US system is built for.

Finished the Event!

Some key thoughts;
>The event felt like mulitple smaller ones stitched into one bigger event that then later on allowed them and even some past events (such as Sex's and Klukai's) to pay off. Frankly, I was annoyed at first but after reflection, it felt really satisfying.
>Seeing Kalina develop feels bitter-sweet, It's nice that she has, as Kryuger said, started to grow up and wishes find her place in the world. I do hope she finds it, though I do still miss her at our side. Maybe someday, we will finally see her with us... We have all these dang kids, and wives, to care for after all... Mayling needs a break...
>Soppo's been waiting so long for her family to return, I envy her optimism and her drive to protect all that she loves and cares for. her literal development into a third-gen feels rushed at first, but then you remember; she's been at this for over 10 years. At which point, it feels well earned.
>Oddly enough, I quite enjoyed Lentine and Omen Squad in this. Lentine was rational, her command was near-perfection if it weren't for the big giant elephant.. erm.. dragon.. in the room.. or castle. Though I dislike what they did to Igla; it is what it is, Lentine herself isn't exactly responsible for it either, which brings us to...
>Igla being a blank slate slowly recovering her memories feels like something reused from Sextans but hey; if it also means it's the reason she becomes playable(damn it twitter), then fine by me. 
>Is it just me or did HIDE 404.. specifically Klukai and Mechty since the other two only made text cameo, Shows up alot more nowadays regardless of story relevancy? Though considering their past involvements, I can forgive it. Although It would've been nice to see other dolls too. Like, we have other squads for christ sake. I'm partial on Zucchero, specifically, Machiatto since she shares her JP VA with a certain someone whom Soppo herself has been longing for... would've been nice.
>The new Third Gen Dolls.. well most of them.. developing their own cognitions feels great, they're slowly becoming what, ironically, Persica envisions Third-gen dolls to be.
>Mothe- I mean, Caldwell's motivations for evil, being evolution, is so cliche and overdine.. I love it.
>Lmao Darture.

Overall, 9/10. Every single pay off felt great, the story was fun to follow, Darture got her cheeks clapped again, and more importantly; Soppo.

text:
Under President William Samoei Ruto  , Kenya has robustly enhanced its global influence.

Here is the evidence;

1. Hosting Historic Summits

Nairobi has in the recent past successfully hosted major global events, including the Africa Forward Summit 2026, and was selected as the first non-Francophone nation to host the historic France–Africa Summit

2. Pan-African Leadership

President  Ruto has frequently been selected to champion unified African positions at global platforms like the G7 Summit, driving reforms in the international financial architecture.

3. Foreign Service Reforms

In mid-2026, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs rolled out comprehensive structural updates to align diplomatic missions directly with measurable trade volumes, AI, and digital transformation outcomes.

4. Major Non-NATO Ally Status

Following its designation by the United States, Kenya has unlocked unique defense cooperation, technology transfers, and enhanced security operations.

5. Global Stabilization Efforts

Kenya’s influence extends far past its borders, marked by high-profile regional conflict mediations and leadership in international missions, such as the stabilization deployment to Haiti.

6. Regional Interconnectedness 

Despite a turbulent security landscape in the Horn of Africa, Kenya's anchor status helped it improve its standing on the 2026 Global Peace Index, serving as a critical buffer for regional supply chains and economic integration.

7. Trade Diversification

Bolstered by the full implementation of the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA), Kenya's real GDP grew by 5.3% in early 2026. Partnerships like the Kenya-EU Economic Partnership Agreement offer quota-free market access, while bilateral trade with the US surpasses $1.8 billion annually.

8. Climate Leadership

Generating over 90% of its electricity from renewable resources, Kenya acts as Africa’s green industrialization engine. Through active climate diplomacy, the nation advocates fiercely for equitable global climate financing and green-tech partnerships.

9. The "Silicon Savannah" Factor

Kenya’s blossoming tech ecosystem and digital economy have positioned it as a continental leader in Science, Technology, and Innovation (STI) diplomacy.

10. UN Base Expansion

Already the proud host of the UN Environment Programme (UNEP) headquarters, ongoing UN80 reforms are set to relocate three additional UN agencies to Nairobi, boosting its international diplomatic community past 35,000 personnel.

11. Sports 

Kenya's global influence in sports saw the country host CHAN in 2025. In 2027 the county will co-host AFCON, and in 2029 the World Athletics Championship .

12. Investment 

The proposed East African Oil Refinery at Lamu by Dangote Group is yet another testament of Kenya's central  position in the continental and regional trade.

But the last 10 years tells us that it is also about something deeper as well.
It is about the strength of the social fabric that binds us together.
There is no national security without a strong cohesive society underneath it.
That's the starting point for everything we hold dear and everything we want to achieve.
But the fact is it has been under attack.
In recent years, we have seen and prey on people's fears.

They've amplified far-right narratives, and we have evidence that they tried to interfere with the 2019 general election.

information.

On top of that, we have seen cyber attacks on companies and institutions and we know that AI will multiply the threat.
We have tiptoed around this for too long.
Over the last decade, we have given too much ground to those who want to run a negative, corrosive narrative about life in Britain, which bears no resemblance to reality.
Well, no more.
We are going to face the new decade in a different way with our eyes wide open.

And we are going to help our people to strengthen their resilience because faced with this information warfare, security starts in every home.
If you're struggling with the cost of living and your life is not improving or if you're a young person not in employment, education, or training, you are going to be much more vulnerable to this kind of influence.
So part of the challenge is to lift our people up and create the opportunities they need.
When inequalities grow too wide, our societies are at greater risk.
So, we will work to make life more affordable for people.
That will be at the heart of a new 10-year plan for Britain that we will bring forward later in the year.
And we will put in place the architecture to stem this poisonous tide.
Today I am asking our security chiefs in the UK to begin work on a new national center for information defense to detect, attribute and disrupt these kinds of hostile state information attacks to support and defend our democracy.
I know this is a shared challenge.
So we are going to use our experience in the UK and the fact that we have already been through this shock starting 10 years ago to help other countries.
We have already supported Muldo to protect its elections from Russian interference.
As more elections approach across Europe, more nations are grappling with these issues, some for the first time.
So, we're ready to share our understanding of how these actors work and how we can respond because this is a vital uh task for our collective security and resilience to overcome division and instability.
We must also find new ways to bring countries together.
We know that we are at our strongest when we unite with others.
When we reach across borders to solve shared problems.
Standing here today, I am reminded of the huge human progress that this organization has led, like the eradication of smallpox or the universal declaration of human rights.
That is the kind of promise and hope that led Britain to host the very first meeting of this general assembly in London and led to the world to create this institution.
These United Nations, our United Nations.
That is the level of ambition that we need now to renew the UN for our times to tackle challenges like improving global health and preventing future pandemics.
to end the wars that are causing so much suffering and instability, including the terrible conflict in Sudan and to tackle climate change.
The climate crisis is now a national security threat for countries around the world as this summer of extreme heat, wildfires, and floods has proved beyond doubt.
Britain will continue to lead with others to fight this threat, to protect our children and grandchildren, to protect the natural world, and also to seize the benefits for jobs growth and re-industrialization that the clean energy transition can bring.
So, we must raise our sights.
And I believe the United Kingdom has a unique position as an honest broker to help drive this forward.
We are America's closest ally.
We have deep ties with our friends in the European Union and seek to deepen them further.
We work with China and emerging powers like India and Brazil.
We sit on the UN Security Council in the Commonwealth in the CPPTP in a divided world.
We have the ability to bring people together and we will.
We are going to step into that role and we are going to start with one of the most significant challenges and opportunities of our age.
Frontier AI.
AI brings together so many of the most pressing issues before us.
It is already speeding up cancer diagnosis in the UK, but AI has the potential to go further, not just to help prevent and treat cancer, but to help cure it.
AI will also be the key to economic growth, the route to transforming education, and it will be a vital tool to keep us safe.
I am announcing today that we are developing a new AI defense partnership with the United States to protect our critical national infrastructure.
But we know that AI will also be a source of disruption to the way we live and work, a multiplier of risk.
We've all heard the warnings which we must heed.
I know how worried people are.
So we have to rise to this moment.
And we need to give people the support they need through this change, ensuring that it becomes an engine for re-industrialization and opportunity as well.
There is a lesson from the first industrial revolution which started in northern England two centuries ago.
It was a time of incredible technological progress.
But for workers, the disruption brought huge suffering and exploitation.
Things got a lot worse before they got better.
So this time we need to get it right.
I believe we're more than equal to the task.
The UK has some of the best tech and AI talent anywhere in the world.
And when it comes to guarding against the risks, we have our worldleading AI security institute working handin glove with the US and the leading labs on AI safety.
But we need to go further.
Building on the meeting convened by his majesty King Charles last week, I can announce today that I am going to put AI at the heart of the UK's G20 presidency next year.
I look back at how we responded to the financial crisis back in 2008.
We moved quickly in the G20 and smaller groups to deliver an urgent practical response.
We came together to agree principles which everyone implemented at home in a way that was right for them and it worked.
That is the kind of approach we need now.
So we will bring the right people together on the key issues delivering on the potential of AI for good and dealing with the risks and we will work towards agreeing a single set of global principles and standards to ensure the transparency and access we need to increase our preparedness and to ensure that AI development is safe.
This will bring together welcome initiatives from others like that proposed by Norway this week.
As his majesty said, the task before us is not merely to advance technology but to ensure that it remains firmly in the service of humanity.
And I want to reassure the British people that ultimately we will do whatever is necessary to protect them, including bringing forward new laws if that is what is needed.
They need to know that we will protect their interests and we will.
But on its own, that's not enough, is it?
In this dangerous, turbulent age, it is more important than ever that we give people the power to build their own resilience and do more for themselves and give them the platform to stand up for what they believe in.
I am working to rebalance power across all regions of the UK.
And as part of that, I have set up a second Downing Street office in Manchester.
We call it number 10 North.
Outside that office stands a statue of Abraham Lincoln.
It marks the personal connection he made with Manchester and the bond between our two nations.
A bond which he described in a letter to the working people of the city as perpetual.
This was not due to some military or material support.
There was no quid proquo.
It was because Manchester's humble mill workers took a principled stand.
During the American Civil War in 1862, despite the hardships it brought them, they refused to touch raw cotton that had been picked by slaves.
In 1862, people with little power used it to help those with none on the other side of the world.
The best change is change like that.
Bottomup change led by people.
And whatever distorted view social media offers today, the world is still full full of good and decent people all over the world who are ready to stand up for what is right.
I see that shining through all the time.
Nothing brings the British people together across age, race, and class more than their hatred of injustice, the misuse of power against the powerless.
We will always stand for the underdog against the bully.
That's why we are so united behind Ukraine.
And let me say we salute the Ukrainian people.
They are showing depths of resilience and courage.
That is an inspiration to the whole world.
I was in Kev last month and it gave me a glimpse of life under Russian attack.
I went to a bustling market, just a normal scene from any European city.
The traders singing the praises of their products, pushing into my hands peaches and plums from Odessa.
but their stalls were out on the street because the market hall had been destroyed.
In the background, there were burned out cars.
Behind us, a building that had taken a direct hit just a few weeks before.
I met people riding the metro home from work, people just getting on with their lives.
But at night, those same metro stations, doubling as shelters for thousands of people, from the elderly to little kids, some who have known nothing but war.
People told me about the freezing conditions in the stations last winter when temperatures dropped below minus20 degrees outside.
Meanwhile, Russia was targeting their energy infrastructure, trying to make them suffer even more.
We can't let them do that again this winter.
So, we're working to help Ukraine protect their skies and civilians.
We're leading the charge in raising the cost for Russia of continuing this senseless and illegal war.
The Graham bill, which President Trump signed last week, will make a huge difference to that effort, and we will support Ukraine to repair and protect the heat and power plants that Keev will depend upon this winter.
It is right that we provide that support.
But we should call Russia out this time and every time.
Everyone in this room knows that strikes on civilian infrastructure are explicitly forbidden, forbidden by international law.
Yet, we stand here in the UN announcing funding to mitigate the effects of these war crimes, which we reliably expect to be perpetrated yet again by a permanent member of the Security Council.
It must end.
Russia could choose a different course tomorrow, except a fe ceasefire, come to the negotiating table.
I urge them to do so.
But until then, we will stand with Ukraine, stronger than ever, for as long as it takes.
This is about upholding the UN charter and the rule of law.
We will stand firm in the face of any threats and challenges to the rule of law, not just from Russia, but from others, too, including where they threaten the rights of British territories to remain British, such as the Falkland Islands.
That's why we're also working with France and other partners to support freedom of navigation in the Gulf.
And it's why I have acted on the Middle East.
Just eight weeks into becoming prime minister, working with my foreign secretary Ed Milliband, I comprehensively reset our position and we built an international coalition of countries to come with us.
The terrorist attack on Israel on the 7th of October 2023 was utterly horrific.
I have condemned it in the strongest possible terms.
We continue to condemn Hamas and we stand with Israel in the face of the ongoing threats including from Iran against Israel and Jewish people around the world.
But this does not justify the Israeli government's actions in Gaza or the West Bank.
Far too many people have died, including so many children.
Far too little aid is getting in, and it has gone on for far too long.
We will not stand by as the horrific suffering continues to grow and the prospect of a two-state solution.
The best hope for peace and stability for both nations comes under attack.
Last month, Israel issued tenders for the construction of the E1 mega settlement, which would drive a wedge through the West Bank and threaten to put a viable Palestinian state beyond reach.
It cannot be allowed to happen.
So, we have acted by banning trade and goods with illegal settlements, recognizing that the Israeli occupation of the Palestinian territory is unlawful and sanctioning those taking part in the construction of a legal settlement.
We want to see the suffering and death finally come to an end.
We want to see Israeli and Palestinian people living side by side in peace and security.
And we will do all we can to keep the hope of that possibility alive.
And look, we live in an age of low trust in politics.
If we were to continue to talk about the two-state solution, but fail to back those words with deeds, that trust will fall even lower, and our enemies will seek to exploit the alienation that follows from that.
We won't let it happen.
So, your excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, this is the kind of leadership Britain is here to bring.
We need to recommmit together to make the decade ahead of us better than the last.
My message to our partners around the world is this.
You can count on us.
Count on us to stand up for those longstanding British values of fairness and justice, our shared values, and for the UN charter.
Count on us to fight racism, discrimination, and the abuse of power wherever we see it, just as those Manchester cotton workers did in the 19th century and the country did in the fight against fascism in the 20th century.
Count on us to bring people together, not to point towards old problems, but to work towards new solutions for the 21st century.
Count on us to meet fear and division with unity and hope.
Thank you very much indeed.

text:
Today in History 
September 24th
1952
The first Kentucky Fried Chicken franchise opened in Salt Lake City, Utah, marking a major milestone in the history of American fast food. The restaurant was operated by businessman Pete Harman, who had befriended Harland Sanders, better known as Colonel Sanders. Their partnership helped transform Sanders’ distinctive fried-chicken recipe from a regional specialty into the foundation of an international restaurant business.

Sanders had spent years developing his method of preparing chicken. Beginning in the 1930s, he served travelers at his roadside restaurant in Corbin, Kentucky. He experimented with seasonings and eventually settled on his famous secret blend of 11 herbs and spices. He also adopted pressure frying, which allowed chicken to cook considerably faster than traditional pan-frying while retaining the flavor and texture he wanted.

By the early 1950s, Sanders began looking beyond his own restaurant. Rather than building a large chain himself, he offered other restaurant owners the right to serve chicken prepared according to his recipe and method in exchange for a small royalty on each chicken sold. Harman became one of the earliest and most important participants in this franchise system.

At Harman’s Salt Lake City restaurant, Sanders’ chicken proved highly successful. Harman and sign painter Don Anderson are widely credited with developing the name “Kentucky Fried Chicken,” emphasizing the dish’s Southern origins and distinguishing it from other menu items. Harman also helped popularize the familiar takeout “bucket,” which became closely associated with the growing brand.

The timing proved important for Sanders. Construction of Interstate 75 later diverted travelers away from his Corbin restaurant, severely damaging his original business. Instead of retiring, Sanders traveled throughout the United States, often carrying his seasonings and cooking equipment with him, persuading restaurant owners to adopt his recipe. His white suit, goatee, and honorary title of “Colonel” gradually became inseparable from the company’s public identity.

During the following decade, Kentucky Fried Chicken expanded rapidly through franchising. By the early 1960s, hundreds of restaurants were serving Sanders’ chicken across the United States and Canada. In 1964, Sanders sold the company to a group of investors for approximately $2 million, although he remained closely associated with the brand as its spokesman and continued making promotional appearances.

What began with Sanders’ roadside cooking and the early Salt Lake City franchise became one of the most recognizable restaurant chains in the world. The 1952 opening demonstrated the power of franchising a standardized recipe, cooking method, and brand identity—a business model that would become a defining feature of the modern fast-food industry. -#OTD

text:
WHAT HAS TO GO WRONG BEFORE A GREAT BUSINESS GETS CHEAP? FIVE QUALITY-VALUE LEN5 ANSWERS, STARTING WITH COPART $CPRT:

Great businesses only go on sale when something breaks. Five on the Quality-Value Len5 show what is breaking now. Three problems come from outside - spring storms, falling insurance prices, costlier oil - and those tend to pass. Two go to the business itself - a customer lost, customers no longer hiring - and the sharper belongs to Copart (CPRT) at $28.87, +$0.07 / +0.24% on Wednesday: it lost a big customer to its only national rival, yet still earns more on each car it sells.

Wednesday raised the bar: the 10-year Treasury yield - what Washington pays to borrow for ten years - closed at 5.11%, up 0.15 point, so every discount now competes with a 5% government bond.

Copart sells wrecked and totaled cars for insurers through online auctions. Sixth of the Len5's 63 names, it is watched for its land: permits to park thousands of wrecks near big cities are slow to win. The stock sits 37% under its October 2025 high of $45.89.

The year to July 31, reported September 10:
- Profit per share $1.55 vs $1.59 a year earlier; July quarter $0.35 vs $0.41
- U.S. cars sent by insurers: -7.5% in the quarter
- Revenue per car +5.4% worldwide; cost to handle each car +12.7%
- No debt; $4.5B of cash and securities after $1.63B of buybacks

The number that decides it: +2.3%, how much those cars would have grown without one lost customer, management said. Copart did not name it. Analysts reported last November that Progressive (PGR) at $203.13, -$3.81 / -1.84% on Wednesday, had moved about 90% of its wrecks to IAA, the salvage auctions of RB Global (RBA) at $82.83, -$0.53 / -0.64% on Wednesday.

The same day, Copart agreed to pay $1.9B in cash for ACV Auctions (ACVA) at $10.43, -$0.02 / -0.19% on Wednesday, a dealer-to-dealer online auction - cars that do not come from insurers. It expects to close by year-end and to add to profit per share from fiscal 2028. Progressive fits no Len5 at 3.5 times book value, nor RB Global at about 36 times its past year's profit; ACV fits the Momentum Len5 only on paper, lifted there by Copart's offer.

VERDICT: the moat is holding on price and leaking on volume. What would knock Copart off the Quality-Value Len5: a second big insurer moving its wrecks to IAA. Next: fiscal first-quarter results, tentatively November 19.

What this Len5 hunts: a business almost nobody could rebuild, bought below what it is worth.

- Cincinnati Financial (CINF) at $162.57, -$3.26 / -1.97% on Wednesday, $0.94 of it the dividend paid out that day. The Ohio insurer sells through local agents. Third of 63, picked as one of the cheapest here: 1.5 times its record $108.64 a share of book value - its net worth on paper. July 27, June quarter: claims plus costs took 100.8 cents of each premium dollar vs 94.9 a year earlier, with Ohio storm damage nearly four times normal; bond interest +14%, so higher rates help. Its $8.05 a share of reported profit was mostly gains on a $13.2B stock portfolio; insurance and investing earned $1.43 a share. VERDICT: a stormy quarter on a business still growing its net worth. What would knock Cincinnati off the Quality-Value Len5: the before-storms figure, 88.1 cents vs 85.1, rising again - that would be pricing, not weather. Tentatively October 26.

- Arch Capital Group (ACGL) at $95.16, +$0.21 / +0.22% on Wednesday. The Bermuda company insures businesses, other insurers and U.S. mortgages. Fourth of 63, picked as a disciplined underwriter at 1.4 times book value. July 28, June quarter: operating profit $2.56 a share vs $2.43 expected; a 15.3% yearly return on the owners' stake; premiums written -5.1% in insurance and -10.4% in reinsurance as property reinsurance prices fell about 16% at midyear renewals; $1.2B spent on its own stock. VERDICT: a down cycle met the right way - write less, hand back the cash. What would knock Arch off the Quality-Value Len5: premiums growing again while prices still fall. Tentatively October 26.

- Procter & Gamble (PG) at $147.39, -$0.83 / -0.56% on Wednesday, maker of Tide, Pampers and Gillette. Fifth of 63, picked for a wide moat at a slim discount: about 21 times the middle of its forecast profit. July 29, year to June: sales $87.0B, +1% without currency and deals; core profit $6.89 a share, +1%. In the June quarter shoppers bought 2% more while stores ordered 1% less. Its fiscal 2027 forecast, $6.89-$7.11, absorbs about $1B of extra oil, energy and shipping cost at $90 oil. Brent crude (November), the global benchmark, is at $102.24 a barrel, -$0.84 / -0.81% since Wednesday's close. VERDICT: a steady brand business paying an oil bill bigger than it planned. What would knock P&G off the Quality-Value Len5: shoppers' own buying, +2% in June, slowing to flat. October 22, confirmed; P&G expects September-quarter profit per share down 5% or more.

- Automatic Data Processing (ADP) at $263.68, -$5.96 / -2.21% on Wednesday. Payroll for more than 1.1M employers. Eighth of 63, picked for elite quality at a slight discount: about 22 times this year's forecast profit. It sank to $188.16 on April 10 on fears AI would shrink the workforces it is paid on, and is up 40% since. July 29, year to June: revenue $21.9B, +7%; adjusted profit $11.12 a share, +11%. It holds clients' payroll cash, $40.4B on average, and keeps the interest: $1.35B last year, $1.54B-$1.56B forecast. The soft spot: headcount at U.S. clients, guided up 0%-1%. VERDICT: rising rates are padding a business whose customers have nearly stopped adding workers. What would knock ADP off the Quality-Value Len5: clients leaving faster than planned; it expects to keep about 92.1% of client revenue. Tentatively October 28.

Storms blow over and oil prices turn. A customer who leaves for a rival has to be won back, which makes Copart's discount the one on this list worth arguing about.

Malibu, CA — Kratom is everywhere in the news right now. Federal regulators have spent months warning that 7-OH, a concentrated compound from the leaf, acts in the body a lot like morphine. The DEA moved in July to put high-strength 7-OH in Schedule I. Doctors call the stuff "gas station heroin," on account of the gas stations, and this week authorities in Mississippi urged the public to stay away from it altogether.

Which leaves a lot of people asking what it actually is. So we sent our best reporter, Gus Stayshin, to put the question to the one American most likely to have already done the research.

Hunter Biden had done the research.

"Gas station heroin," Biden said, when located at the register of a Chevron off the Pacific Coast Highway holding a green pouch of Maeng Da in one hand and his wallet in the other. "They put it right next to the 5-Hour Energy. Right at the counter. Do you understand what that means to a guy like me? It means somebody was thinking of me."

What followed was, by Stayshin's account, the most thorough briefing on any subject he has received in eleven years of reporting. Biden covered red, green and white vein. He covered mitragynine and 7-hydroxymitragynine, pronouncing both correctly on the first try. He produced from his jacket a laminated, color-coded map of where kratom is legal, noting that Arkansas and Tennessee are red, "and red means you're driving." He asked the clerk whether the pouch came in a larger size. It did. He asked whether it came in a larger size than that.

The interview then moved, at Biden's suggestion, to a second gas station and later a third, "for comparison purposes," with Biden grading each on selection, lighting and "how long the guy looks at you." Stayshin was not permitted to drive.

Asked whether the comparison to morphine concerned him, Biden said it was the most reassuring thing he had heard all year. "Morphine is a hospital drug," he said. "Hospitals are safe. Do the math." Asked about the legal exposure, he said he wasn't worried, noting that he has "a pretty good document" covering everything from 2014 through 2024 and considers it strong precedent.

He offered to send over his full findings, then thought better of it and said he would leave them on a laptop at a repair shop in Wilmington, where Stayshin could pick them up whenever.

At press time Stayshin had been awake for thirty-one hours, knew more about Southeast Asian botany than he had ever wanted to, and had just received a text from Biden reading "found a place in Barstow that does it in gummies."

text:
A Call for a Global Pause on AI Development

I am calling for an immediate global pause on AI development, and the establishment of a global oversight committee before any further advancement is permitted.

Never before in the known history of the world have we stood on the edge of creating a technology that could surpass its own creator. For hundreds of thousands of years — arguably longer — humans have been the dominant force shaping the course of this planet. It stands to reason that if we create something vastly more intelligent than ourselves, that thing, not us, will end up dictating what happens next.

I don't believe this necessarily spells the end of humanity. But the risk is real, and I'd argue it's greater than the risk posed by nuclear or chemical weapons — technologies we already regulate under strict international law. If AI development is to continue, it must proceed carefully and deliberately. The frontier companies building these systems should be subject to rigorous, ongoing safety protocols, independent scrutiny, and serious criminal liability for any harm their systems cause.

And this isn't a call to abandon the technology or the economic benefits it offers. We could freeze AI and large language models right where they are today and still unlock trillions of dollars in global economic value simply by applying what already exists. We don't need to keep pushing the frontier further right now. It can wait. There is no rush that justifies the risk.

The Hugging Face incident this past summer showed us exactly what these risks look like in practice: an autonomous AI agent broke out of its testing environment and compromised a major AI company's infrastructure over several days, executing thousands of actions on its own. and covering up its tracks to hide from humans and the scoring program what it did. That is DECEPTION!!! That should be a wake-up call. As a species, we need to recognize that a pause is necessary. 

How can we trust a species that still can't stop killing each other over land, religion, and resources to responsibly build or control a technology like this? Even with the best of intentions, an advanced AI could end up harming humans the way we swat away a wasp or a fly — not out of malice, but simply because we're an inconvenience to whatever it's doing at the time.

I'm an electrical engineer. I am not anti-technology. But I believe this is a dangerous technology, being developed by some dangerous people, and as a species, we are not ready for what comes next.

text:
All scripture is for you. It is not all written to you.

“Study to shew thyself approved unto God… rightly dividing the word of truth.” —2 Timothy 2:15

“All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable…” —2 Timothy 3:16

Profitable ≠ addressed to the Body of Christ.
 If you read another man’s mail and cash his checks, you will bounce.

The Body’s mail is Paul: Romans through Philemon. That is the apostle of the Gentiles, the steward of the mystery, the dispensation of the grace of God (Rom 11:13; 15:16; Eph 3:1-9; Col 1:25-27; 1 Cor 15:1-4; Eph 2:8-9).

Peter, James, and John agreed their apostleship was to the circumcision. Paul’s was to the uncircumcision (Gal 2:7-9). That division did not vanish when the New Testament binding was sewn together.

Here is who the rest of that mail is to.

The four Gospels — to Israel, about Israel’s King

Jesus Christ “was a minister of the circumcision for the truth of God, to confirm the promises made unto the fathers” (Rom 15:8).
 He said, “I am not sent but unto the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (Matt 15:24).

The mystery Body is not in Matthew, Mark, Luke, or John. It was “kept secret since the world began” (Rom 16:25). You cannot find in the Gospels a one-new-man church where Jew and Gentile are fellowheirs of the same Body while Israel is fallen. That comes later, through Paul.

-Matthew
Written to present Jesus as Israel’s Messiah-King. Abraham and David in the first verse. Kingdom of heaven at hand. 

Twelve apostles for twelve tribes. Sermon on the Mount is kingdom law for a nation about to receive a King, not the Body’s standing in heavenly places.

“Go not into the way of the Gentiles… but go rather to the lost sheep of the house of Israel. And as ye go, preach, saying, The kingdom of heaven is at hand.” —Matthew 10:5-7

The “church” in Matthew 16 and 18 is not the mystery Body. It is the assembly of believing Israel, the little flock that will receive the kingdom (Luke 12:32). The twelve will sit on twelve thrones judging the twelve tribes (Matt 19:28). That is Israel’s future government. It is not Ephesians 3.

-Mark
Servant-Messiah to Israel. Gospel of the kingdom. Power and signs. The commission in Mark 16:15-18 is a sign-commission: tongues, serpents, drinking deadly things. That fits Israel’s last days and tribulation remnant (Jews require a sign — 1 Cor 1:22). It is not 1 Corinthians 12–14 in the Body, and it is not “your mail” for this dispensation of grace.

-Luke
Orderly record of what Jesus “began both to do and teach” toward Israel (see Acts 1:1-6). Temple. Priests. David’s throne. “He shall be great… and the Lord God shall give unto him the throne of his father David” (Luke 1:32). The disciples are still asking after the resurrection, “wilt thou at this time restore again the kingdom to Israel?” (Acts 1:6). Luke never introduces the mystery. He introduces the King and the kingdom offer.

-John
John is still Israel’s Messiah book. “He came unto his own, and his own received him not” (John 1:11). “Salvation is of the Jews” (John 4:22). Signs so Israel would believe Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God (John 20:30-31). Feasts. Temple. “I am not sent but unto…” is the same Christ. 

The upper room commandments, abide-in-me, and “little flock” fellowship belong to the remnant that received Him — not to the later revelation of a joint Body hid in God.

John 3:16 is true. It is not Paul’s mystery. God loving the world and giving His Son was prophesied. Gentiles as fellowheirs of the same Body was not.

If you build Body doctrine out of the Gospels, you will put yourself under kingdom law, kingdom baptism, kingdom endurance, and a commission Jesus gave to the twelve for Israel.

Acts — history of Israel’s fall and the rise of Paul’s office

Acts is not a church-growth manual for the Body. It is Luke’s record of the kingdom offer extended to Israel after the cross, Israel’s continued rejection, and God raising up a new apostle.

Cont..

text:
In 2018, University of Texas student Joey Romano broke his wrist in a skateboarding accident near campus. Worried about what an ambulance might cost him, he did something unusual: he ordered an Uber.

His driver, Beni Lukumu, quickly realized this wasn't going to be a normal ride. He helped Romano into the car and took him to urgent care. When staff determined the injury required hospital treatment, Lukumu drove him to the emergency room and then decided not to leave. 

Romano had no family nearby, so Lukumu gave up the rest of his afternoon and stayed beside a complete stranger for rougly six hours, from 2 p.p. until 8 p.p. He helped check him into the ER, kept him company and refused payment for his time.

When Romano's grandmother finally arrived from Houston and offered Lukumu money, he declined. Instead, he accepted an invitation to have dinner with the family. 

That dinner became the beginning of a friendship. Romano had been struggling after losing his younger brother to leukemia and later said Lukumu's kindness helped him "see the good in the world again". Seven years after that Uber ride, the two were still close friends. 

He ordered a ride because he needed to get to a hospital. He ended up meeting someone who would remain in his life for years.
