Nine Things You May Not Know About the Warren Commission

Find out more about this much-maligned investigation into the murder of America’s 35th president.

1. Some members of the Commission were reluctant to serve on it.
Lyndon Johnson initially resisted the idea of forming a federal commission to investigate John F. Kennedy’s assassination, preferring to allow the state of Texas to review what he called a “local killing.” But after learning that both the U.S. Senate and the House of Representatives were considering launching their own inquiries, the newly installed President assembled the Warren Commission in the hope of avoiding multiple and possibly conflicting reports on the shooting.

Johnson wanted the Commission to include members from each of the different branches of government, but many of his preferred choices were hesitant to participate. Wary of the possible legal entanglements of serving, Chief Justice Earl Warren turned down the opportunity to chair the commission multiple times, and only agreed after Johnson argued that an inadequate report could incite a public panic and even spark a nuclear war. Meanwhile, conservative Senator Richard Russell flatly refused to serve because he disliked Warren’s liberal judicial record. Johnson waived off Russell’s protests and publicly named him to the Commission anyway, saying his participation was necessary “for the good of America.”

2. Gerald Ford secretly provided information on the Commission to the FBI
While serving as a leading member of the Warren Commission, future U.S. President Gerald Ford also acted as an inside informant for J. Edgar Hoover and the FBI. Several months after his death in 2006, a cache of declassified documents revealed that Ford, then a U.S. congressman, had approached FBI Assistant Director Cartha DeLoach and offered to confidentially keep the Bureau informed on the Commission’s deliberations. 

Among Ford’s many leaks was the revelation that two unnamed members of the Commission—most likely Richard Russell and Hale Boggs—remained unconvinced by FBI evidence that the kill shot had been fired from the Texas School Book Depository.

3. Earl Warren suppressed key evidence from the Commission.
Warren was a close friend of the Kennedy family, and his personal attachment may have interfered with his duties to the Commission. In one of the most infamous episodes of the investigation, Warren denied his fellow Commission members access to Kennedy’s autopsy photos because he deemed them too disturbing. He later refused to allow the Commission to interview certain witnesses whom Lee Harvey Oswald may have known in Mexico, and even tried to block an interview with first lady Jackie Kennedy because he didn’t want to invade her privacy.

4. The Commission secretly interviewed Fidel Castro.
Many believed that Fidel Castro might have conspired in Kennedy’s murder, and it turns out that the Cuban dictator personally proclaimed his innocence in an off-the-record interview with the Warren Commission. 

According to journalist Philip Shenon, at one point in the investigation, Commission lawyer William Coleman met face to face with Castro on a fishing boat off the coast of Cuba. During a three-hour exchange, Castro repeatedly denied having any involvement in the assassination. No notes were taken during the secret rendezvous, and only Earl Warren and one other investigator were ever made aware of it.

5. The FBI and the CIA intentionally misled the Commission.
The FBI and the CIA had monitored Lee Harvey Oswald in the months before the assassination, but both agencies later tried to downplay their knowledge of him to the Warren Commission. Oswald had once even left a threatening note for an FBI agent at the Bureau’s office in Dallas. Fearful of catching blame for not preventing the assassination, the FBI later destroyed the note and even removed the agent’s name from a typewritten transcript of Oswald’s address book provided to the Warren Commission. Congressman Hale Boggs would later say that FBI Director J. Edgar Hoover “lied his eyes out” to the Commission’s investigators.

Evidence also suggests that the CIA had Oswald under surveillance when he made a trip to Mexico in September 1963 and visited the Cuban and Soviet embassies, but the agency repeatedly denied any connection to the alleged shooter. The CIA also neglected to inform the Commission about its many covert operations in Cuba—including several schemes to assassinate Fidel Castro—even though those revelations might have helped shape the investigation.

6. The Commission offered no clear explanation of Oswald’s motives.
While the 888-page Warren report went into great detail outlining how Lee Harvey Oswald could have killed Kennedy, it gave little explanation of why he did it. 

In its findings, the Commission stated that Oswald’s actions could not be explained if “judged by the standards of reasonable men,” saying only that he was an isolated individual plagued by a life of failure and disappointment. The report would later conclude that, “the Commission does not believe that it can ascribe to him any one motive or group of motives.”

7. Both Lyndon Johnson and members of the Kennedy family privately disagreed with the Commission’s report.
Although they praised the Warren Commission report in the media, many government leaders had serious misgivings about its findings. Commission member Richard Russell reluctantly signed the Warren Report even though he could not rule out the possibility of a conspiracy, and he later admitted to having “lingering dissatisfaction” with many of its conclusions. Congressman Hale Boggs had similar doubts about the report, in particular the “single bullet theory”—the argument that one shot had stuck both President Kennedy and Texas Governor John Connally.

Lyndon Johnson remained in lock step with the Warren Commission’s findings for most of his career, but he privately disagreed with the single bullet theory and reportedly believed that the Cubans had engineered the assassination. Likewise, President Kennedy’s brother, Attorney General Robert Kennedy, publicly commended the Warren Report even though he suspected a conspiracy had taken place.

8. Public trust in the report plummeted after only a few years.
When the Warren Report was first released to the public in September 1964, polls showed that only 56 percent of Americans agreed with its “lone gunman theory.” But within months, critics began to poke holes in its conclusions and methodology, and conspiracy theories cropped up alleging the involvement of everyone from the Mafia to Lyndon Johnson himself. 

By 1966, a second poll would show that only a meager 36 percent of people still had confidence in the report. Today, studies show that around two-thirds of Americans believe in some form of conspiracy surrounding the assassination.

9. A second government investigation came to a different conclusion.
After the public release of new information including the Zapruder film—an amateur recording showing the Kennedy assassination in shocking detail—the U.S. House of Representatives formed the United States House Select Committee on Assassinations and reopened the investigation on the president’s murder. 

In 1979, the HSCA stated that acoustic evidence from a Dallas police officer’s radio showed it was likely that two shooters had fired on Kennedy’s limousine, and it concluded that the assassination “probably” involved a conspiracy. Although subsequent investigations have cast doubt on the radio evidence, the HSCA’s report helped fuel public dissatisfaction with the efforts of the Warren Commission.

U.S. District Judge Timothy J. Kelly, a Trump appointee from 2017 and the same judge who forced the White House to give CNN’s Jim Acosta his pass back in 2018, signed a Temporary Restraining Order in the early hours of Thursday morning.

A lawyer for the outlets accused the Trump Administration of banning the news organizations “completely out of the blue” and urged the judge to immediately restore their access.

🇿🇦 A Memorial Once Criticised for Exclusion Has Opened Its List ~ 🌈✝️ The Crosses Stayed White. The Story Didn’t 🌈 When the Names Change the Meaning of the Crosses.
On a hillside in Limpopo nearly three thousand white metal crosses have stood for more than twenty years. Each one marks a life taken in a farm attack. For a long time the memorial carried a quiet accusation: that only certain names were being remembered. 

Then, in August 2026, Lex Libertas published a preliminary list of more than 2,200 names of people murdered in farm attacks and invited the public to correct it. The organisation stated that the list follows the South African Police Service definition of a farm attack and is not limited by race. 

Black farmers, farmworkers and dwellers are included. The white crosses are no longer accurately described as a single-colour memorial. 

They have become, in the most practical sense, rainbow crosses. That adaptation is the news. Everything else follows from it.

1. The List That Changed the Colour of the Crosses

The Witkruis Monument began in 2004 as a local act of remembrance organised by farmers and a University of Limpopo criminologist. Critics fairly observed that its public face centred almost exclusively on white victims. 

The 2026 White Cross Project answers that criticism with a document rather than a press statement. Lex Libertas released the names, opened them to verification by relatives and researchers, and prepared to plant them on the National Mall in Washington on 26 September. 

Each cross will carry a verified name. The visual language remains white timber; the human content is multi-racial.

This is not a rhetorical claim. It is a published list subject to public correction. In a country that has spent three decades arguing about whose pain counts, the decision to subject the names to open scrutiny is itself an act of enlargement. 

The project does not ask South Africans to forget rural violence. It asks them to remember it without the old racial filter.

The institutional significance is easy to miss. Civil-society organisations that collect victim data often face accusations of selective memory. By placing the list in the public domain and inviting correction, Lex Libertas transferred a measure of ownership from the organisation to the wider society. 

That transfer changes the burden of proof. 

Those who continue to describe the memorial as racially exclusive must now engage the published names rather than the colour of the timber.

Sjoe!
A memorial that once looked like a closed book has become an open spreadsheet. In South Africa that is almost a revolutionary act.

Stirring Questions:
If a memorial once criticised for exclusion publishes a multi-racial list and invites the country to check it, what further evidence would be required to accept the adaptation as genuine?
When the dead of every background are named in the same place, does the visual of white crosses still function as exclusion, or does the content override the colour?
Why does the act of opening a list to public correction matter more than any press statement about inclusion?

These questions matter because they move the argument from symbolism to verifiable practice. A democracy that cannot test claims about memory will eventually lose the ability to trust any memorial at all.

2. The Day That Learned to Enlarge Itself

Heritage Day did not begin as a rainbow. It began as Shaka Day. When the first democratic parliament drafted the public-holiday calendar and omitted 24 September, the Inkatha Freedom Party objected. The compromise that followed transformed a specific Zulu commemoration into a national day for every culture’s contribution. 

Nelson Mandela later described the decision as recognising that the country’s rich and varied cultural heritage has power to help build the new nation (Mandela, 1996).

That historical enlargement is the precedent. 

South Africa has already practised the exact logic now required. A single-community memory was not erased; it was held inside a larger frame. The White Cross Project, having moved toward a multi-racial list, occupies the same logical space. 

It is a particular memorial of rural violence that need not cancel the broader heritage. The national calendar once learned to enlarge itself. The question is whether the country still remembers how.

Political scientists who study transitional justice note that successful post-conflict societies rarely abolish difficult commemorations. They absorb them. The South African compromise of 1995 is a textbook example of absorption rather than erasure. 

The same method remains available. Refusing to apply it to the rural dead of every race would not protect the rainbow; it would prove that the rainbow was a temporary political arrangement rather than a reusable civic skill.

Sjoe!
A calendar that once made room for a Zulu king can, in principle, make room for a multi-racial list of rural dead. The only question is whether the country still has the muscle memory.

Stirring Questions:
If the nation could once turn Shaka Day into Heritage Day without diminishing Zulu memory, why would the same method fail when applied to the rural dead of every race?
What is lost if the capacity for enlargement is treated as a once-off political deal rather than a reusable civic skill?
When a holiday exists precisely because one community’s date was expanded, what does it mean to refuse expansion for another form of difficult memory?

These questions matter because they test whether the founding compromise of Heritage Day was a living method or a closed historical event. The answer determines whether the rainbow remains a practice or becomes a museum piece.

3. The Test of Difficult Memory

Heritage is not only language, food and dance. It is also the hard inheritance of violence, loss and contested land. When one community’s dead are named, the instinct to minimise that naming risks teaching every other community that its own future losses may also be erased. 

The adapted White Cross Project, by placing verified names of every background on a high-visibility international stage, tests whether the inclusive method that created Heritage Day is still operational.

Showing more love, not less, means creating room for the crosses without requiring them to dominate every other narrative. 

That generosity is the opposite of selective amnesia. Suppressing difficult memory does not produce unity; it produces a hierarchy of whose dead may be seen. Allowing space for the rural dead of every race strengthens the multi-cultural compact precisely because it refuses to rank suffering by identity.

Legal scholars who study the right to truth note that societies which systematically under-remember certain categories of victims eventually face legitimacy problems that no amount of official narrative can repair. 

The cumulative evidence from transitional societies is consistent: public naming, even when uncomfortable, is stabilising. Silence is not.

Sjoe!
Memory is not a scarce resource. Treating it as one is the surest way to make every community poorer.

Stirring Questions:
If difficult memory is treated as a zero-sum threat, which community’s future losses will be the next to be minimised?
What civic muscle is strengthened when a society practises the harder form of inclusion—the inclusion of pain that does not flatter the national story?
Why does the refusal to erase one set of names protect the future visibility of every other set?

These questions matter because memory is not a private luxury. It is the raw material from which trust is either built or permanently rationed.

4. The Ethic of Non-Collective Care

In mid-September 2026 the United States announced visa restrictions aimed at foreign nationals responsible for or complicit in specific policies: uncompensated land seizures, race-based discrimination, and incitement of imminent violence against minorities. 

The measure was deliberately individualised. Lex Libertas welcomed its targeted character. At the same moment the White Cross Project was preparing its multi-racial list. 

Both moves reject collective punishment.

On a Heritage Day marked by water-infrastructure strain and a strengthening El Niño, the convergence is practical. A country already under climate and service pressure cannot afford broad sanctions or broad erasure. 

Protecting ordinary citizens from additional hardship while refusing to let patterns of extreme rural violence disappear from public view is not a contradiction. It is the operational form of unity without uniformity.

Economists who study the costs of collective sanctions note that the burden falls disproportionately on those least able to influence policy. Targeted measures, by contrast, preserve the possibility of reform without compounding existing vulnerabilities. 

The same logic applies to memory. Collective forgetting and collective blame are mirror images of the same failure: the inability to distinguish responsibility from identity.

Sjoe!
In a country where the dams are watching the sky and the municipalities are watching the leaks, the last thing anyone needs is another blunt instrument.

Stirring Questions:
If both international pressure and domestic memorialisation can be drawn to affect responsibility rather than identity, what prevents that ethic from becoming normal practice?
When water systems and food security are already under stress, why does collective punishment become more, not less, reckless?
What does a society gain by distinguishing decision-makers from citizens in both policy and memory?

These questions matter because the alternative—collective blame or collective forgetting—has already been tried. The results are visible in the tiles that still need scrubbing of blood and the dams that still need careful management.

5. The Practised Capacity

Every culture that helped make Heritage Day brought both pride and pain. Zulu kingship traditions, Afrikaner language struggles, Xhosa oral histories, Indian indenture memory, Khoisan land connection—all of them. 

Erasing any strand weakens the fabric. 

The White Cross Project, now framed as inclusive of all races, offers one more strand: the rural dead of every background.

When South Africans can stand on Heritage Day and affirm both that these crosses matter and that every other heritage matters equally, the rainbow ceases to be a slogan and becomes a practised capacity. 

That capacity is what allows the dream to endure beyond any single memorial or any single crisis. Honest remembrance does not fracture the nation. Selective forgetting does.

Constitutional scholars have long noted that Section 235 of the 1996 Constitution, which recognises the possibility of cultural self-determination within the national framework, remains unused. The section was never a promise of secession; it was an acknowledgement that the rainbow could contain distinct threads without unravelling. 

The inclusive memorialisation of rural violence is a small, practical expression of the same idea: particular loss need not threaten the whole.

Sjoe!
A nation that can hold more than one truth at a time is not confused. It is simply adult.

Stirring Questions:
What becomes possible when a nation treats enlargement as a reusable skill rather than a historical accident?
If the rural dead of every race are named without cancelling any other heritage, what new forms of shared responsibility become thinkable?
Why does the practised capacity to hold multiple truths matter more than any single correct narrative?

These questions matter because the rainbow nation was never a finished painting. It was a method. Methods that are not practised eventually become myths.

Synthesis

The evidentiary records weave together. A published multi-racial list open to public correction establishes that the White Cross Project has adapted. The origin of Heritage Day establishes that South Africa has already practised the exact enlarging logic now required. The test of difficult memory establishes that suppression teaches every community that its pain may be next. 

The ethic of non-collective care establishes that both international pressure and domestic memorialisation can reject collective punishment. The practised capacity establishes that the rainbow endures only when it is used.

The evidence is falsifiable. A closed, racially exclusive list would falsify the adaptation claim. A refusal to apply the Heritage Day method to any difficult memory would falsify the claim that the method remains available. The stakes are not abstract. They concern whether a country that once enlarged a single-community day can still enlarge its circle of care when the memory is rural, violent, and multi-racial.

Independent lines of evidence—civil-society documentation, constitutional history, transitional-justice patterns, and the design of the recent visa measure—converge on the same practical conclusion. 

Enlargement is possible. Erasure is optional. The choice remains open.

Objections

Some will argue that any focus on farm attacks risks inflating a small statistical category at the expense of the far larger national murder toll. The objection is serious. Farm murders remain a fraction of total murders. Yet the patterns of extreme brutality documented by independent crime-scene professionals, and the multi-racial character of the published victim list, justify specific remembrance without denying the wider crisis.

Others will argue that the visual of white crosses, regardless of the names, remains racially coded. Colour carries history. Yet content can revise meaning. A list that includes every verified victim and is open to public correction is the strongest available evidence that the project has moved beyond the earlier limitation.

A third objection holds that international memorialisation damages the country’s image. Image is not the primary good. Accurate memory and non-collective care are. A nation that can hold its own difficult truths is stronger, not weaker, in the long run.

Conclusion

On this Heritage Day the choice is practical. The White Cross Project has published a multi-racial list and invited the country to check it. Heritage Day itself was born from the decision to enlarge rather than erase. 

Targeted accountability and inclusive memorialisation together model a form of care that refuses both collective punishment and selective amnesia.

South Africans can meet the named crosses with the same generosity that once turned Shaka Day into a national day, or they can treat difficult memory as a zero-sum threat. 

The rainbow dream endures only when it is practised—when particular loss is held inside a frame wide enough for every colour, including the colour of the crosses that now carry every verified name.

Sjoe. 
The tiles still need scrubbing. The calendar still knows how to enlarge itself. The rest is practice.

Can Trump and Xi turn a high-profile Washington summit into a new trade deal?

US President Donald Trump is hosting Chinese President Xi Jinping at the White House on Thursday for a state summit focused on stabilizing ties and seeking progress on trade, despite persistent disputes over Taiwan, technology and artificial intelligence.

♦️ What happened?

📌 #Trump welcomed #Xi to #Washington on Wednesday evening ahead of their second meeting this year and Xi’s first visit to the US capital in more than a decade. The two leaders are expected to emphasize the stability of US-#China relations, while seeking limited agreements rather than a major diplomatic breakthrough.

 📌 Xi said upon arrival that #Beijing and Washington should be “partners, not rivals” and that the historical logic of peaceful coexistence between the two countries had not changed.

♦️ Why does it matter?

📌 The summit comes as the world’s two largest economies remain locked in competition over trade, technology, #Taiwan and critical minerals. Both governments have an interest in keeping relations stable, even as disagreements continue to pose a risk of renewed tensions.

📌 Trade is expected to be the most promising area for progress, with the two sides considering an extension of their existing trade truce and possible agreements on tariffs, agriculture and non-tariff barriers.

♦️ What are the details?

📌 US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Washington and Beijing had agreed to extend until January 10 an agreement that paused a trade war in which mutual tariffs had exceeded 100%.

📌 The talks could also produce agreements to lower some tariffs, combat drug trafficking and expand military-to-military communication. Trump is also expected to seek the release of Americans and other people detained in China.

📌 US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said the two countries are expected to make announcements on agriculture and non-tariff barriers. China is also making progress on a commitment to purchase 200 Boeing aircraft, although no additional orders have been confirmed.

📌 Artificial intelligence could provide another area for cooperation. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said there was early thinking about creating a communications mechanism similar to a Cold War-era hotline to prevent dangerous incidents, while US officials are expected to maintain export controls on advanced US technology sought by #China.

♦️ How did we get here?

📌 The summit follows months of efforts by Washington and Beijing to prevent their trade conflict from escalating. The previous meeting between Trump and Xi took place in May, when Trump received a major welcome in China and later described a proposed $14 billion US arms package for Taiwan as a negotiating tool.

📌 Since then, China has strengthened its trade position and maintained significant control over global supplies of rare earth minerals, while the two governments have continued to disagree over Taiwan, export controls and technology.

♦️ What does it mean?

📌 The immediate focus is on maintaining the trade truce and producing limited agreements that can demonstrate progress without resolving the deeper US-China rivalry. Taiwan remains one of the most sensitive issues, with Xi expected to press Trump to halt US arms sales to Taipei.

📌 The two leaders are also expected to discuss the Iran war. Reuters reports that China has offered to help put pressure on Iran, although there has been little indication that Beijing is prepared to exert pressure on its ally in line with US demands.

♦️ What’s next?

📌 Trump and Xi will hold their summit in Washington on Thursday, followed by a state dinner attended by senior figures from the technology and business sectors, including Tim Cook, Jeff Bezos, Sundar Pichai, Sam Altman, Elon Musk and Jensen Huang.

📌 The key issues to watch are whether the trade truce is formally extended, whether the two sides announce agreements on tariffs and agriculture, and whether they make progress on AI communication, Taiwan or other areas of strategic tension.

Washington has proposed an AI crisis channel with Beijing. What would make either government use it?

In “Hold the Line,” the Forum on Preventive Defense’s first policy brief, I draw on nuclear risk reduction and conversations with American and Chinese officials and experts, including during several visits to China this year and last, to offer five reciprocal commitments.

Measures that seem reassuring to one side can look threatening to the other. Some Chinese officials and experts worry that hotlines could convey threats, help manipulate crises, or encourage greater risk-taking by making escalation appear easier to control.

Those concerns deserve attention as AI diplomacy develops. So do Chinese proposals for practical cooperation. Shared danger creates reasons to talk, but it does not automatically produce agreement about whose security a channel would serve.

The five commitments:

1️⃣ Warn before attribution.
2️⃣ Answer without conceding.
3️⃣ Protect disclosures without granting immunity.
4️⃣ Make domestic reporting work.
5️⃣ Test the entire response.

A connection between senior officials can provide political backing. An emergency system also needs continuously staffed contacts, standing authority, and routes to the companies and technical responders able to contain the harm.

The brief builds on work on dialogue and incident notification by @cpruhl @Scott_R_Singer, Xiao Qian, Tianjiao Jiang, @Clarissa_Koh7 @SarahJGodek @kelmgren at @iapsAI, and others. It also draws on @ZilanQian’s analysis of Chinese risk perceptions, @mattsheehan88’s work on institutions, and @JulianGewirtz’s argument about domestic governance.

Daily Journal, the publisher he chaired, owned legal newspapers in California and Arizona.

Trustees were required to advertise each sale through them. As defaults surged, those ads generated excess cash while the same crisis pushed financial shares lower.

"We were like an undertaker who suddenly got prosperous in a plague year."

During fiscal 2009, Daily Journal invested $20.4M in marketable securities. By September, the portfolio was valued at $54.1M.

Munger had already studied the financial institutions he wanted to own. When the opportunity appeared, he bought in one day and used no leverage.

text:
In November 2002, a short paper appeared on the preprint server @arXiv. Its author was a 36-year-old mathematician in Saint Petersburg, Russia, who had largely withdrawn from the mathematical mainstream and had published relatively little since his celebrated work of the mid-1990s. He was working as a researcher at the Steklov Institute, but had turned down academic positions at several leading universities. Within four years, mathematicians around the world had reached consensus that the paper and two that followed had achieved something no one had managed in a century: they had solved the Poincaré conjecture. It was the first of the seven Millennium Prize Problems to be resolved, and it remains the only one officially recognized as solved. Its author, Grigori Perelman, would then decline almost every major honor and financial award offered to him for the achievement.

The conjecture is often described as a question about the "shape" of three-dimensional space. That captures the basic idea, but not quite the mathematics. Henri Poincaré posed the problem in 1904 as a question in topology: if every loop in a closed three-dimensional manifold can be continuously shrunk to a point, must that manifold be topologically equivalent to the three-sphere, (S^3)? In modern terminology, the question asks whether every closed, simply connected 3-manifold is homeomorphic to (S^3). The corresponding higher-dimensional problems were solved in stages. Stephen Smale proved the generalized conjecture in dimensions five and higher in 1961, while Michael Freedman solved the topological four-dimensional case in 1982. The three-dimensional case remained open and became one of the most famous unsolved problems in mathematics.

Beginning in the 1970s, William Thurston transformed the subject with his geometrization program, proposing that three-dimensional manifolds could be decomposed into pieces carrying one of eight standard geometric structures. The Poincaré conjecture would follow as a special case of this much broader statement. In 1982, Richard Hamilton introduced Ricci flow, a geometric evolution equation that changes a manifold's metric according to its Ricci curvature. The basic idea can be compared, loosely, to the way heat spreads through an object: irregularities tend to smooth out over time. Hamilton hoped that Ricci flow could transform complicated three-dimensional spaces into geometrically understandable ones and thereby prove Thurston's conjecture. But there was a major obstacle. As Ricci flow evolved, curvature could become arbitrarily large in finite time, producing singularities that Hamilton could not completely control.

Grigori Perelman had been immersed in mathematics from an early age. Born in Leningrad in 1966, he attended Sergei Rukshin's famous mathematics circle and, at sixteen, represented the Soviet Union at the 1982 International Mathematical Olympiad in Budapest. He received a perfect score of 42 out of 42 and won a gold medal. Perelman went on to study at Leningrad State University and completed his doctorate in 1990 before joining the Steklov Institute. In 1993, he received a Miller Research Fellowship at the University of California, Berkeley. In 1994, he published a remarkably short proof of the soul conjecture of Cheeger and Gromoll, a significant result in Riemannian geometry. Several leading American universities subsequently offered him positions, but Perelman declined them and returned to Saint Petersburg in 1995. In 1996, he wrote to Richard Hamilton explaining that he believed he had found a way around the difficulties in the Ricci-flow program and offering to collaborate. The collaboration did not materialize, and Perelman continued working largely on his own.

His breakthrough finally appeared on arXiv. On 11 November 2002, Perelman posted "The Entropy Formula for the Ricci Flow and Its Geometric Applications". The paper did not contain a conventional announcement that the Poincaré conjecture had been solved. Instead, in Perelman's extremely compressed style, it developed new tools for Ricci flow and included a sketch of how they could be used to prove Thurston's geometrization conjecture. Two more papers followed, in March and July 2003. Together, they supplied the mathematical framework that completed Hamilton's program and established the geometrization conjecture in the form needed to settle the Poincaré problem.

Among the crucial ingredients were Perelman's no-local-collapsing theorem and his analysis of canonical neighborhoods. These results gave mathematicians the control they needed over the shapes that appear near singularities of three-dimensional Ricci flows. When a singularity developed in a controlled cylindrical region, the problematic neck could be cut out and replaced with suitable caps, after which the Ricci flow could continue. This process, known as surgery, provided the mechanism needed to carry the flow through singularities. Perelman's papers were remarkably terse, often stating sophisticated arguments with far fewer intermediate details than a conventional mathematical exposition would normally provide. Several groups therefore undertook detailed examinations of the work, including Bruce Kleiner and John Lott, Huai-Dong Cao and Xi-Ping Zhu, and John Morgan and Gang Tian. Their extensive expositions, together with the scrutiny of many other mathematicians, helped establish the consensus reached by 2006 that Perelman's arguments were correct.

The recognition that followed was extraordinary. In May 2006, the Fields Medal committee voted to award Perelman mathematics' highest distinction. Sir John Ball, then president of the International Mathematical Union, traveled to Saint Petersburg that June and spent roughly ten hours over two days trying to persuade Perelman to accept the medal. Perelman had already made up his mind. At the International Congress of Mathematicians in Madrid in August 2006, he was announced as one of the Fields Medalists, but he did not attend the ceremony and declined the medal, becoming the first person to refuse a Fields Medal. Perelman explained that he was not interested in money or fame and expressed deep dissatisfaction with aspects of the mathematical community and its standards of recognition. His rejection of major honors was not new: in 1996, he had also declined the European Mathematical Society Prize awarded to him. Later in 2006, Science magazine named the proof of the Poincaré conjecture its Breakthrough of the Year, the first time the distinction had gone to a mathematical achievement.

That same year, another controversy surrounding the proof became highly public. In August 2006, The New Yorker published Sylvia Nasar and David Gruber's article "Manifold Destiny," which described tensions surrounding the recognition of Perelman's work and the detailed proof written by Huai-Dong Cao and Xi-Ping Zhu. The article portrayed Fields Medalist Shing-Tung Yau as attempting to give greater prominence to the work of Cao and Zhu in a way that diminished Perelman's contribution. Yau strongly disputed the article's characterization and threatened legal action, although no lawsuit followed. The details and interpretations surrounding that episode remain contested. Perelman had, however, already resigned from the Steklov Institute in December 2005 and had expressed serious concerns about ethical standards and what he regarded as tolerated dishonesty within parts of the mathematical community.

The Poincaré conjecture was not immediately eligible for the Millennium Prize. The Clay Mathematics Institute's rules require a proposed solution to be published in an appropriate outlet, to have at least two years pass after publication, and to receive general acceptance from the mathematical community. On 18 March 2010, Clay formally awarded Perelman the $1 million Millennium Prize for the solution of the Poincaré conjecture. He declined it. Perelman did not attend the June 2010 Paris conference organized to celebrate the solution, and on 1 July the Russian news agency Interfax reported that he had confirmed his decision to reject the money. His explanation was more specific than simply saying that he disliked publicity: Perelman said that he considered his contribution to the solution no greater than Richard Hamilton's and that he was dissatisfied with the way the mathematical community had treated him and Hamilton. The Clay Mathematics Institute subsequently used the funds associated with the declined prize to establish the Poincaré Chair at the Institut Henri Poincaré in Paris, intended to support promising young mathematicians.

Since then, Perelman has largely disappeared from public mathematical life. He has given very few interviews and has avoided the public spotlight. Reports over the years have described him as living privately in Saint Petersburg, but his current circumstances are not publicly documented. One reported anecdote captures his attitude toward publicity particularly well: a journalist who reached him by telephone was reportedly told that Perelman could not talk because he was out picking mushrooms. There have also been occasional Russian media reports about his activities, including a 2014 report claiming that he had taken a position connected with nanotechnology in Sweden, but such reports have not been independently confirmed by Perelman.

The Poincaré conjecture remains the only one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems that the Clay Mathematics Institute has officially recognized as solved. That status is particularly relevant in September 2026, following recent attention surrounding an OpenAI research result on the Navier–Stokes problem. OpenAI has reported a result concerning a forced version of the equations and has explicitly said that it does not intend to claim the Millennium Prize for that result. The Clay Mathematics Institute has described the Navier–Stokes problem as apparently settled while emphasizing that its evaluation process is deliberately slow and that mathematical scrutiny remains necessary before the problem can be formally recognized as solved.

Perelman's story illustrates why extraordinary mathematical claims are not settled by announcements alone. They become accepted through sustained scrutiny, reconstruction, verification, and the willingness of other mathematicians to spend years trying to determine whether an argument actually works. In the end, Perelman's achievement was not simply that he solved a problem that had resisted mathematicians for a century. He completed a program begun by Hamilton, established the much broader geometrization theorem, and then walked away from the fame, medals, and million-dollar prize that followed.

[References: Grigori Perelman, Manifold Destiny, and Millennium Prize Problems (Wikipedia); Clay Mathematics Institute; Science, "Breakthrough of the Year" (Dec 2006); The New Yorker, "Manifold Destiny" by Sylvia Nasar and David Gruber (Aug 2006); Masha Gessen, Perfect Rigor (2009).]

(Photo: Grigori Perelman at Berkeley, 1993. George M. Bergman / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.)

"The San Francisco Standard obtained subpoenas issued in early September that focus on the funding of Newsom’s international travel via a nonprofit, the California State Protocol Foundation. In recent years, the nonprofit has been bankrolled by corporations, including companies with business interests in California, as well as by charities controlled by the wealthy and powerful. Many of these donations were officially reported as being made at Newsom’s request. One of the subpoenas states that the records are being requested “for use in a criminal investigation pending in the Eastern District of California.” (RELATED: Why Newsom Is More Terrified of the DOJ Investigation Than He Wants to Admit)

It’s unlikely these corporations — or even some of these nonprofits — were being charitable out of the goodness of their hearts. They obviously thought they would get something out of the arrangement. The question is whether there was an explicit offer on the table for what they would get in return for donating to Newsom’s international travel fund. If so, that would be an illegal quid pro quo. The feds are subpoenaing six years of records surrounding the California State Protocol Foundation to find out.

Funds distributed by the California State Protocol Foundation have paid for Newsom’s trips to Rome, Brazil, China, Germany, and Switzerland, all of which he used to prop up his image on the national stage in service of his future presidential campaign. (RELATED: Gavin Newsom Is Getting Desperate Over California’s ‘Image Problem’)

Many of the companies that have donated to the California State Protocol Foundation have done so at Newsom’s specific request, including Zoox (Amazon’s autonomous vehicle company), LSN Partners (a consulting firm), Blue Cross Blue Shield, Realize CPA, Centene Corporation (a major health care company), and CVS Pharmacy, according to government records."

text:
Block-Level Orientation on Reintegration of Out-of-School Children Held at Khamdong,#sikkim.

Gangtok, 23 September 2026: A Block-level “Orientation on Operational Guidelines for Reintegration of Out-of-School Children in Sikkim” for the Block Information Team, Panchayat Members, Ward Councillors, Heads of Institutions (HOIs) and School Management Committee (SMC) Chairpersons of Government and Private Schools under Khamdong Block was held at the Auditorium Hall of PM SHRI Singtam Senior Secondary School on 22 September 2026.

The programme was organised under the aegis of Samagra Shiksha, State Project Office, Education Department, Government of Sikkim, in collaboration with the District Education Office, Gangtok District.

The programme was attended by Mrs. Asha Khatri, Additional Director, Samagra Shiksha, Education Department; Mrs. Chimi Denzongpa, Chief Education Officer, Gangtok District; Joint Director, Skill Development Department; Block Development Officer, Khamdong BAC; Panchayat President and Ward Panchayats of various wards under KhamdongBlock; and Ward Councillors from Singtam Nagar Nigam.

The programme also witnessed the participation of Block Education officials, BRCs, CRCs, School Heads and teachers representing 27 Government and Private Schools under Khamdong Block, along with members of the School Management Committees.

School dropouts and Out-of-School Children (OoSC) continue to remain an important challenge despite sustained efforts to improve access to and retention in education. Children who remain outside the education system are more vulnerable to risks such as child labour, early marriage, substance abuse, exploitation and long-term social exclusion, which can adversely affect human capital development and the socio-economic progress of the State.

Taking cognizance of the issue, the Education Department, Government of Sikkim, has developed the “Operational Guidelines for Reintegration of Out-of-School Children in Sikkim”, aimed at ensuring zero dropout and universal retention of children in the age group of 6–18 years. The Guidelines seek to rehabilitate, reintegrate and reskill OoSCthrough flexible, dignified and sustainable pathways, while also establishing mechanisms for the early identification and prevention of children at risk of dropping out.

The Guidelines were officially launched as a State policy on 15 August 2026 by the Hon’ble Chief Minister of Sikkim, Shri Prem Singh Tamang.

As part of the implementation process, the Khamdong Block of Gangtok District has been selected as a pilot area to systematically operationalise and test the mechanisms for identifying children at risk of dropping out, identification and tracking of OoSC, provision of special training, reintegration and universal retention before scaling up the initiative across the State.

The opening session and introduction to the programme were presented by Mr. Sushil Tamang, Deputy Director, Samagra Shiksha, Education Department, followed by a keynote address by Mrs. Chimi Denzongpa, Chief Education Officer, Gangtok District.

Subsequently, Mrs. Asha Khatri, Additional Director, Samagra Shiksha, delivered a detailed PowerPoint presentation on the various provisions, modalities and implementation mechanisms under the Operational Guidelines for Reintegration of Out-of-School Children in Sikkim.

A key focus of the presentation was on the roles and responsibilities of the Block Implementation Team (BIT) in developing and maintaining the Dropout Registry, as well as the role of schools in developing and maintaining the At-Risk Register. The importance of timely identification, tracking, follow-up and coordinated intervention for children at risk of dropping out was also highlighted.

Mr. Amrit Sharma Social Worker from District Child Protection Unit under Women, Child & Senior Citizen & Divyangjan Welfare Department made a presentation on the mechanism for conducting the Social Investigation Report (SIR) of Out-of-School Children, highlighting the importance of understanding the individual, family, social and economic circumstances of children for appropriate intervention and reintegration.

Mr. K.C. Rai, Joint Director, Skill Development Department, also briefed the participants on various training and skill-development programmes being offered by the Department and highlighted the opportunities available for skill development and alternative pathways for eligible children and youth.

An open interactive session was subsequently conducted, providing participants with an opportunity to raise queries, share feedback and offer suggestions regarding the implementation of the Operational Guidelines at the grassroots level.

The orientation marked an important step towards strengthening school-community convergence, early identification of children at risk of dropping out, systematic tracking of OoSC, inter-departmental coordination and effective reintegration and retention of children in education and appropriate skill-development pathways.

The programme concluded with detailed discussions and deliberations on the ward-wise assignment of areas/councils to the Block Implementation Team functionaries for systematic identification and development of the Dropout Registry.

First Lady Melania Trump Releases Details on the State Dinner with His Excellency Xi Jinping, President of The People’s Republic of China, and Madame Peng Liyuan:

President Donald J. Trump and First Lady Melania Trump will welcome His Excellency Xi Jinping, President of The People’s Republic of China, and Madame Peng Liyuan for a State Dinner in the East Room of the White House this evening. The First Lady led the preparations for the dinner, which will be attended by the official delegations as well as business leaders and government officials.

MENU
The menu showcases American ingredients with subtle Chinese influence, bringing the culinary traditions of both nations together. The meal begins with a toast of Schramsberg "Blanc De Noir," honoring the historic “Toast to Peace” shared by President Nixon and Premier Zhou Enlai in Beijing in 1972. The same American sparkling wine served at that historic gathering continues to be enjoyed at White House functions today.

First Course Yellow Squash Velouté Wild Mushroom Fricassée Crispy Pancetta Scallion Oil
The first course offers a refined and silky-smooth velouté made of sweet yellow squash. This course is gently blended to highlight its delicate seasonal flavors of earthy wild mushrooms, sautéed with fresh herbs. Together, these ingredients create a rich fricassee, complemented by crispy pancetta for a savory and smoky contrast. A finishing drizzle of scallion oil adds vibrance and a subtle allium brightness to the dish.

Second Course Sesame Crusted Sea Bass Braised Baby Bok Choy Roasted Garden Eggplant Sauce Verte
The second course is prepared delicately with fresh seabass and coated in toasted sesame seeds. This combination creates a fragrant nutty crust while keeping the fish tender. The fish is served with crisp baby bok choy and roasted garden eggplant, creating lightly caramelized flavors. The dish is finished with a vibrant sauce verte of fresh herbs, which add brightness, acidity, and a garden character.

Dessert Vanilla Crémeux & White House Honey Ice Cream Walnut Frangipane Sour Cherry Confit
The dessert course is a smooth vanilla crémeux with a vibrant sour cherry confit center, set a top a rich walnut frangipane. The dessert’s fruit shaped form is complimented by a delicate ice cream made with harvested White House honey.

ENTERTAINMENT
There will be several performances during the formal dinner, which will be headlined by Mr. Christopher Macchio, a classically trained tenor who performed at the 2025 Presidential Inauguration. The evening’s entertainment will feature performances by military musicians from the United States Marines Corps and the United States Army, including “The President’s Own” United States Marine Band, “The Commandant’s Own” United States Marine Drum and Bugle Corps, the United States Army Chorus, and the United States Army Strings.

FLORAL & DÉCOR
The décor for the evening is an expression of warmth and celebration and draws on the color red’s longstanding cultural significance throughout Chinese history. Urns showcase overflowing red blossoms. Tables are dressed in rich red linens and adorned with dahlias and ranunculus. Among the seasonal blooms, the tables feature vermeil from the White House collection. The Reagan State Service is featured on the tables. These details blend Chinese artistry and American tradition together, showcased within the timeless elegance of the White House.

text:
The Other Partition

The British were leaving.

After generations of colonial rule, they were preparing to divide a territory whose competing national movements could no longer agree on a common political future. One community demanded a state of its own. Another feared what partition would mean for its people, its homes, and its future.

A border would be drawn. New countries would be born. And millions of ordinary people would discover that the world they had known was about to disappear.

Muslims who had lived in their towns and villages for generations suddenly faced an impossible decision. Stay in a country where they feared becoming a vulnerable minority, or leave everything behind for a new Muslim homeland.

Some left because they believed in the promise of that homeland. Others fled because the violence made remaining impossible.

Families abandoned houses, shops, businesses, and farmland. Entire neighborhoods emptied. Refugees traveled by train, truck, and foot, carrying whatever they could salvage. Some never reached their destinations.

And the migration ran both ways. As Muslims moved toward their new homeland, millions of people from other communities traveled in the opposite direction. They, too, abandoned homes that had belonged to their families for generations.

The violence was horrific. Communities turned on one another. Trains carrying refugees became targets of massacres. Women were abducted. Families were separated. People who had been neighbors became enemies almost overnight.

By the time the upheaval subsided, millions had been displaced, hundreds of thousands were dead, and two new countries were struggling to establish themselves amid the wreckage.

The refugees carried their memories with them. They remembered the streets where they had grown up, the houses their grandparents had built, and the graves of relatives they could no longer visit.

For many, there would be no going back.

You know this story, don't you?

You know about the British withdrawal, the partition, the Muslim refugees, the abandoned homes, and the violence surrounding the birth of a new state.

You probably have a name for it.

Except I haven't been talking about Palestine.

I've been talking about India.

And the year is 1947.

-The Partition You Probably Didn't Have in Mind-

On August 14, 1947, Pakistan celebrated its independence. India followed on August 15.

British India had been divided into two independent dominions: India and Pakistan. Pakistan itself consisted of two geographically separated territories, one to the west of India and the other to the east. The eastern territory would eventually become independent Bangladesh in 1971.

The resulting population movement was staggering.

More than 14 million people crossed the new borders. Millions of Muslims moved into Pakistan, while millions of Hindus and Sikhs moved in the opposite direction.

The worst violence occurred in Punjab, where the border cut through communities that had lived alongside one another for generations.

Pakistan did not emerge from a peaceful exchange of territory. Neither did India. Both countries were born amid a catastrophe that remains embedded in the memories of those who experienced it.

But the catastrophe did not make either country disappear.

The new states took responsibility for enormous displaced populations. India and Pakistan established relief and rehabilitation programs, provided routes to citizenship, and attempted to incorporate refugees into their national life.

The borders did not resolve every dispute, either. Kashmir remains an example of how unfinished that history is.

Yet the unresolved status of Kashmir does not mean India and Pakistan have been waiting since 1947 to become countries.

Their founding and the catastrophe of partition are both historical facts.

Neither erases the other.

And that brings us to another British territory, another partition proposal, and another war that began within months of these events.

-Now We Can Talk About Palestine-

On November 29, 1947, the United Nations voted to recommend dividing British Mandatory Palestine into Jewish and Arab states.

The Jewish Agency accepted the proposal, despite its reservations about the proposed borders and Jerusalem.

The Arab Higher Committee rejected it.

The disagreement was not merely about where the boundary should run. The Arab Higher Committee advocated an independent Arab-majority state encompassing all of Palestine. It rejected the establishment of a sovereign Jewish state in any part of it.

That rejection had consequences.

Fighting began almost immediately after the UN vote. Palestinian Arab militias and irregular forces attacked Jewish communities and transportation routes. The violence escalated into civil war as British authority collapsed.

On May 14, 1948, Israel declared independence. The following day, armies from neighboring Arab countries entered the war.

The proposed partition had offered two states. Instead, a war was fought over whether the Jewish state would survive.

During the conflict, approximately 700,000 Palestinian Arabs became refugees.

People left for more than one reason: combat, fear, the collapse of local authority, orders from Arab commanders, and, in some places, expulsion by Jewish or Israeli forces.

Haifa provides an important example.

During the April 1948 battle for the city, local Arab leaders called for evacuation, while Jewish officials appealed to Arab residents to remain. The fighting itself, fear, and the collapse of local Arab leadership also contributed to the exodus.

Haifa cannot explain every departure across the country. But it establishes that Arab political and military decisions were part of the history, not merely background to it.

There was no single documented order that explains every departure. The causes varied by place. That variation does not reverse the sequence of the war.

The war was not a refugee operation that created a state. It was a war over the establishment of a state, and that war produced refugees.

By the time the fighting ended in 1949, Israel had survived. Jordan controlled Judea and Samaria (the West Bank), and Egypt administered Gaza.

The Palestinian Arab state proposed in 1947 had not been established.

For the next nineteen years, neither Jordan nor Egypt created a sovereign Palestinian state in the territories under its control. Jordan formally annexed the West Bank in 1950, while Egypt retained control of Gaza without annexing it.

Those years are part of the history of Palestinian statelessness. They are also part of the history of the Arab governments that controlled the territory.

The proposed partition never produced the two states envisioned by the United Nations.

But Israel had been established.

And while the consequences of the 1948 war continued to unfold, another population was being uprooted across the Middle East.

-The Jewish Refugees Nobody Should Forget-

Between 1947 and 1972, approximately 856,000 Jews were uprooted from Arab countries, according to the Israeli Knesset.

That is a larger population than the approximately 700,000 Palestinian Arabs displaced in 1948, although the two figures cover different periods.

These Jews were not Europeans who had recently arrived in the Middle East.

Many belonged to communities that had existed in Iraq, Yemen, Egypt, Libya, Syria, and elsewhere for centuries, sometimes for more than two thousand years.

Jewish Baghdad was not a recent invention. Neither was Jewish Sana'a, Jewish Cairo, or Jewish Tripoli.

These communities had their own histories, languages, religious traditions, institutions, businesses, and property.

And across much of the Arab world, they were disappearing.

Anti-Jewish violence, discriminatory legislation, arbitrary arrests, restrictions on employment, confiscation of property, and outright expulsions drove or pressured Jews to leave. Conditions differed by country, and some emigrants were also motivated by Zionism and the prospect of building lives in Israel.

In Iraq, an ancient Jewish community was virtually emptied following the introduction of a denaturalization law in 1950 and the freezing of emigrants' assets in 1951.

In Egypt, Jews faced arrests, expulsions, and property sequestration, particularly during the Suez Crisis in 1956.

Jewish communities elsewhere experienced their own upheavals.

Within a generation, much of the Jewish presence across the Arab world had disappeared.

Many of these Jews went to Israel. Others settled in Europe, the United States, and elsewhere.

Israel received Jewish immigrants as people eligible for citizenship. It housed many of them in transit camps, known as ma'abarot. Conditions were often poor, but the camps were temporary. They were eventually dismantled or developed into permanent communities.

The new arrivals and their descendants became part of Israel's population.

They did not stop remembering Baghdad, Cairo, Tripoli, or Sana'a.

But their history became part of Israel's history.

Consider what this means when discussing 1948.

The Palestinian Arab refugee crisis is routinely treated as the defining consequence of Israel's establishment. Yet the same historical period also saw the destruction or near-disappearance of ancient Jewish communities across much of the Arab world.

A history of Middle Eastern refugees that remembers only one population is an incomplete history.

And the differences in what happened to these refugee populations afterward are substantial.

The partition of India led to vast population movements in both directions. India and Pakistan developed policies to absorb and integrate those populations.

Israel likewise absorbed hundreds of thousands of displaced Jews.

The Palestinian Arab refugees followed a different political and institutional path.

Jordan granted citizenship to large numbers of Palestinians. Other host countries imposed varying restrictions on citizenship, employment, property ownership, and integration.

UNRWA, established to assist Palestinian refugees, also registers eligible descendants of the original refugees. Its registered population has therefore grown across generations, including among people who have acquired citizenship.

That is an institutional fact, not a demographic mystery.

Palestinian leaders have treated return to Israel not only as a remedy for displacement, but as a claim against the Jewish state itself. Compensation and resettlement close a partition. A demand that the descendants of 1948 return en masse to Israel is a demand that the partition be reopened inside the country that survived the war.

That is why this file never became history.

The contrast with Jewish immigration to Israel is therefore about more than numbers.

Israel incorporated the Jewish refugees into its national population. The Palestinian refugee question remained unresolved, even where refugees acquired citizenship.

Citizenship does not erase memory.

It changes the political relationship between memory and the state.

-The Partition That Never Stops Being Debated-

The late 1940s were a period of enormous political transformation. Empires were retreating. Borders were being redrawn. New states were emerging from wars, partitions, and population movements that left millions of people displaced.

India and Pakistan were part of that history.

So was Israel.

The conflicts were different, but the historical setting matters.

Nobody has to pretend the partition of India was peaceful to recognize that India and Pakistan became independent countries.

Nobody has to pretend that Kashmir was resolved to recognize that their statehood did not remain suspended until every territorial dispute was settled.

And nobody has to erase the history of the Jewish refugees from Arab countries to understand that Israel incorporated those refugees into its national life.

Yet arguments about Israel's establishment frequently return to a different question: whether the consequences of 1948 invalidate the Jewish state's legitimacy.

That is not simply a disagreement about the number of refugees, the circumstances in which a particular village was emptied, or the borders proposed by the United Nations.

It concerns whether Jewish sovereignty is accepted at all.

The Arab Higher Committee rejected the proposed Jewish state in 1947. That rejection preceded Israel's declaration of independence, the invasion by neighboring Arab armies, and much of the displacement that followed.

The proposed Arab state was not established. The Jewish state was.

Those events cannot be understood by beginning the story with the refugees and working backward, as though everything preceding their displacement were irrelevant.

Nor does the existence of unresolved refugee claims, by itself, undo a state's existence.

That is the distinction the India comparison brings into view.

I began with India for a reason.

If I had opened with Palestine, many readers would have arrived carrying their conclusions. They would have recognized the story immediately and started sorting every fact into a familiar argument.

Instead, for a few paragraphs, the people were simply people. The refugees were simply refugees. The partition was simply a catastrophe unfolding at the end of British rule.

Then I gave you the name.

India.

Nothing changed in the facts when I named the country. What changed was the history you associated with them.

India and Pakistan emerged from a partition marked by extraordinary violence and displacement. Their independence did not require the past to become painless, their borders to become uncontested, or every refugee claim to be settled.

Israel was established after a partition proposal accepted by the Jewish Agency and rejected by the Arab Higher Committee, after a war fought over Jewish statehood, and amid two refugee crises whose histories deserve to be remembered.

A country born amid catastrophe is still a country.

The history remains.

So does the country.

First Lady Melania Trump Releases Details on the State Dinner with His Excellency Xi Jinping and Madame Peng Liyuan

FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE

President Donald J. Trump and First Lady Melania Trump will welcome His Excellency Xi Jinping, President of The People’s Republic of China, and Madame Peng Liyuan for a State Dinner in the East Room of the White House this evening. The First Lady led the preparations for the dinner, which will be attended by the official delegations as well as business leaders and government officials.

MENU

The menu showcases American ingredients with subtle Chinese influence, bringing the culinary traditions of both nations together. The meal begins with a toast of Schramsberg "Blanc De Noir," honoring the historic “Toast to Peace” shared by President Nixon and Premier Zhou Enlai in Beijing in 1972. The same American sparkling wine served at that historic gathering continues to be enjoyed at White House functions today.

First Course
Yellow Squash Velouté
Wild Mushroom Fricassée
Crispy Pancetta
Scallion Oil

The first course offers a refined and silky-smooth velouté made of sweet yellow squash. This course is gently blended to highlight its delicate seasonal flavors of earthy wild mushrooms, sautéed with fresh herbs. Together, these ingredients create a rich fricassee, complemented by crispy pancetta for a savory and smoky contrast. A finishing drizzle of scallion oil adds vibrance and a subtle allium brightness to the dish.

Second Course
Sesame Crusted Sea Bass
Braised Baby Bok Choy
Roasted Garden Eggplant
Sauce Verte

The second course is prepared delicately with fresh seabass and coated in toasted sesame seeds. This combination creates a fragrant nutty crust while keeping the fish tender. The fish is served with crisp baby bok choy and roasted garden eggplant, creating lightly caramelized flavors. The dish is finished with a vibrant sauce verte of fresh herbs, which add brightness, acidity, and a garden character.

Dessert
Vanilla Crémeux & White House Honey Ice Cream
Walnut Frangipane
Sour Cherry Confit

The dessert course is a smooth vanilla crémeux with a vibrant sour cherry confit center, set a top a rich walnut frangipane. The dessert’s fruit shaped form is complimented by a delicate ice cream made with harvested White House honey.

ENTERTAINMENT

There will be several performances during the formal dinner, which will be headlined by Mr. Christopher Macchio, a classically trained tenor who performed at the 2025 Presidential Inauguration. The evening’s entertainment will feature performances by military musicians from the United States Marines Corps and the United States Army, including “The President’s Own” United States Marine Band, “The Commandant’s Own” United States Marine Drum and Bugle Corps, the United States Army Chorus, and the United States Army Strings.

FLORAL & DÉCOR

The décor for the evening is an expression of warmth and celebration and draws on the color red’s longstanding cultural significance throughout Chinese history. Urns showcase overflowing red blossoms. Tables are dressed in rich red linens and adorned with dahlias and ranunculus. Among the seasonal blooms, the tables feature vermeil from the White House collection. The Reagan State Service is featured on the tables. These details blend Chinese artistry and American tradition together, showcased within the timeless elegance of the White House.

Distributed on September 24th, 2026.

This will be a very fruitful environment for business owners as they pay lower taxes, have more freedom, get support from the state and pay lower salaries as part of them will be paid by the state guaranteeing the unconditional basic income. We will all win with this system so please support it and do something good for you and your future generations.

Jesus wants that everyone can profit, the poorest and the richest on Earth. There shall be equality.

🚨🇨🇳 PENTAGON IN SHOCK: CHINA’S J-10C PILOTS DEVELOP TACTICS TO DEFEAT MORE ADVANCED FIGHTERS

China’s J-10C pilots are developing new tactics to take on more advanced aircraft, as the People’s Liberation Army Air Force focuses on training, coordination and tactical innovation instead of relying on aircraft specifications alone.

The single-engine J-10C is the least advanced fighter currently being procured by the Chinese Air Force. Larger and newer aircraft such as the J-16, J-20 and J-35 offer significant hardware advantages. However, Chinese officers argue that well-trained pilots can still extract considerable combat value from a mature aircraft through smarter tactics and cooperation with other platforms.

J-10 flight group commander Bu Jiawen said the aircraft remains in its prime and continues to serve as a versatile fighter capable of air-superiority, ground-attack and other missions.

🔸 Chinese pilots are training against aircraft with a clear hardware advantage. According to Bu, his unit initially suffered decisive defeats when facing more advanced opponents in exercises. Rather than continuing to fight on their opponents’ terms, the pilots spent roughly one to two years analyzing the encounters and developing unconventional tactics for specific combat scenarios.

🔸 The focus is shifting from individual fighters to coordinated operations. Chinese Air Force officers increasingly emphasize cooperation between aircraft with complementary capabilities. In such a force, a lighter J-10C can operate alongside heavier aircraft such as the J-16 and stealth fighters, allowing each platform to contribute according to its strengths.

🔸 Pilot proficiency can narrow a technological gap. Bu argued that an aircraft’s effectiveness depends heavily on how much of its potential its crew can exploit. His unit has focused on studying opposing tactics, identifying weaknesses and developing solutions tailored to particular situations rather than attempting to overcome every technical disadvantage directly.

🔸 The export J-10CE has already gained combat experience. The Pakistan Air Force used the fighter during the 2025 India–Pakistan clashes. Pakistani officials credited it with air-to-air victories against Indian fighters, although individual loss claims remain disputed. Bangladeshi officials later cited its reported combat performance while pursuing a possible acquisition of the aircraft.

🔸 The J-10C remains a frontline Chinese fighter. Although it lacks the stealth capabilities of China’s fifth-generation aircraft, its modern sensors, long-range weapons and ability to operate alongside other platforms allow it to remain relevant in high-end missions.

China is building an air force in which several generations of fighters can operate together. The J-10C’s role is not to replace stealth aircraft, but to remain useful as a lighter, mature platform while more advanced jets handle the missions that depend most heavily on stealth, range and payload.

For the Pentagon, the problem is scale and flexibility. China does not need every aircraft in its fleet to be a fifth- or sixth-generation fighter if its less advanced jets can still create serious problems through better tactics, coordination and pilot proficiency.

Can better tactics enable older fighters to compete with newer, more advanced aircraft?

$RJET: One of the major U.S. regional airlines, operating a fleet of approximately 310 Embraer E170/175 aircraft under Capacity Purchase Agreements (CPAs) with American Airlines, Delta, and United Airlines. It operates over 1,250 daily flights, serving around 130 cities across the U.S., Canada, the Caribbean, and Mexico. The company will expand in scale following the acquisition of Mesa Air Group (expected completion in November 2025) and owns its own pilot training school, LIFT Academy. Headquartered in Carmel, Indiana, with approximately 8,400 employees.

Macro Context: Domestic U.S. air travel demand remains robust; mainline carriers prefer outsourcing regional routes to specialized regional operators to control costs and maintain fleet flexibility. A persistent pilot shortage makes in-house training academies scarce, valuable assets. Post-acquisition economies of scale help dilute fixed costs and enhance bargaining power with partners. Rising fuel prices and interest rates present short-term headwinds, though CPA contracts typically include cost pass-through mechanisms.
Core assets consist of the long-term CPA fleet serving the "Big Three" carriers (approx. 275 aircraft currently flying under CPA, plus some leased to partners and a small number unallocated). LIFT Academy provides pilot and maintenance technician training, helping to alleviate industry-wide talent bottlenecks. Post-acquisition fleet size will be approximately 314 aircraft, predominantly E175s. Unlike biotech firms, there is no traditional drug pipeline; growth is driven by increased utilization, integration synergies, and new aircraft deliveries.

Q3/Q4 2026 and 2027: Progression of Mesa integration (subject to FAA Safety Management System revision cycles; merger of operating certificates expected by early 2028) — realization of synergies.
Upward revision of full-year 2026 guidance has already been realized; subsequent quarterly performance and block-hour execution will directly determine valuation re-rating.
Around November 8, 2026: Next quarterly earnings report.
From 2028 onwards: Delivery of the remaining 26 Embraer aircraft slots (next delivery expected around April 2028) — long-term capacity growth.
Ongoing rollout of the 10-year contract with United Airlines for 60 additional E175 aircraft. Bullish Thesis: Revenue surged following the M&A (Q2 revenue of $571.1 million, a significant year-over-year increase), and guidance was raised to over $2.1 billion in full-year revenue with adjusted EBITDAR of $395–$405 million, signaling better-than-expected demand and execution. Valuation is low (low P/S and P/B ratios); if integration proceeds smoothly, completion rates recover, and key partners continue outsourcing, there is room for profitability and valuation multiples to rebound. The pilot training business offers additional optionality value.

Target Price: $22–$**

Renowned Bollywood music composer and singer Salim Merchant paid an emotional tribute to the Late Assamese music legend, Zubeen Garg, during his visit to Assam this week, coinciding with the observance of Zubeen Divas across the state.

Merchant visited Zubeen Kshetra in Sonapur, where he paid floral tributes and reflected on Zubeen Garg’s lasting contribution to Indian music.

As part of his visit, Merchant also toured Zubeen Garg’s residence and personal recording studio, where he was received by the singer’s wife, Garima Saikia Garg. He interacted with several prominent Assamese musicians, including Rahul Gautam Sharma, Shyamantak Gautam, and Dikshu Sharma.

Merchant also offered prayers at the Kamakhya Temple in Guwahati, seeking blessings during his visit. Later, he shared photographs from his visit on social media and wrote, “Love Assam. This trip will always have a special place in my heart.”
