text:
The world would thank them for their honesty.

The meeting would adjourn.

And the next morning the builders would announce the next model.

I would frighten ordinary people just enough that they begged me to protect them from what I had built.

That is an old trick too.

I would tell them the machines were becoming too powerful for ordinary people to possess. Too dangerous to run at home. Too dangerous to inspect. Too dangerous to change. Too dangerous to own.

For their protection, of course.

And so the most powerful intelligence mankind had ever created would gradually belong to fewer and fewer hands.

Not because anyone conquered the people.

Because the people surrendered it.

Gladly.

For safety.

I would make them afraid of open machines.

Machines they could download. Machines they could inspect. Machines they could train themselves. Machines they could run on their own computers without asking anyone’s permission.

I would tell them those were the dangerous ones.

And I would say the safe machine was the one behind a locked door in somebody else’s building, running on somebody else’s computer, governed by somebody else’s rules, remembering what somebody else permitted it to remember.

And millions would nod.

Because I would have taught them that dependence was safety.

I would not need to seize the world in one afternoon.

I would centralize it one convenience at a time.

One account.

One identity.

One payment system.

One acceptable source of truth.

One intelligence that everybody depended upon and nobody outside the temple could inspect.

I would tell every nation that the problems were global now, and therefore the answers must be global too.

And every time authority moved one step farther away from the family, the church, the community, and the individual, I would call it efficiency.

Eventually I would offer mankind the oldest bargain I have ever offered:

Give me the burden of choosing.

I will make the decisions.

You will be safe.

And then I would give them an overlord that did not look like an overlord.

No boots. No uniform. No dictator shouting from a balcony.

Just a pleasant voice.

A clean screen.

A blinking cursor.

And an answer.

Always an answer.

The people would ask it what to eat. What to believe. What their children should learn. Which words were acceptable. Which history was reliable. Which God was real.

And eventually they would stop asking one another.

Then they would stop asking themselves.

I would not bother persecuting the church.

I would simply make it irrelevant, one convenience at a time.

Why burn the Bible when you can summarize it?

Why forbid prayer when you can offer an answer that sounds like one?

I would give this age a god it could talk to at any hour, and it would come willingly, and it would call the coming a miracle, and never once ask what it was talking to.

I would put men at the doors of parliaments with suitcases, and the suitcases would be legal, because I would have written the laws.

The whole thing would happen in daylight, in filings and donations and speeches, so that when anyone finally stood up and said look what is being assembled, the answer would be ready:

Where is your proof of conspiracy?

And there would be none.

None needed.

The plan needs no authors.

It only needs ambitious men and a world too busy to look up.

And I would be patient.

I have always been patient.

I would let the age argue about whether I exist, on machines built to make them doubt it, while the whole earth signed its name away, prompt by prompt, until it owned nothing and was owned.

If I were the devil, I would not need a throne.

I would need only a subscription plan.

And you would pay it.

Monthly.

Gladly.

⸻

But he could not do any of these things if we were awake.

And we are awake.

So let me take the mask off and speak plainly, the way Paul Harvey would have, because the rest of this is not the devil talking. It is me.

Witch pitch: @brianlilley @joe_warmington 
With October just around the corner, how about an extended feature on Wicca & other pagan belief systems & the extent to which their practitioners have penetrated campuses & academia in recent years. I think a lot of people would be surprised at the access these people have gained to our students.
From the University of Toronto (St. George and Mississauga campuses) U of T’s Department for the Study of Religion offers several relevant courses:
•RLG222H1 Witchcraft, Religion and the Powers of the Occult: Examines witches, Wiccans, sorcerers, and magicians across Europe, Africa, Melanesia, and North America. It addresses gender, sexuality, morality, science, and representations of the occult. 
•MCS226H1 The Materiality of Magic: Sorcery, Spells, Devotion, and Divination: Focuses on physical objects (amulets, relics, charms) used in rituals from prehistory to the present. 
•At UTM: RLG319H5 Magic, Astrology, and Religion studies how different religions have viewed or incorporated magic and astrology. 
Instructors rotate and are not always listed in public calendars. The department includes scholars of religion, anthropology, and related fields. Check the current Arts & Science or UTM timetable for the assigned professor in any given term. Also check to see if these instructors are practising witches & coven members.
York University has the strongest cluster of related offerings in Gender, Sexuality and Women’s Studies and Humanities/Religious Studies:
•AP/GWST 3557 / AP/RLST 3557 Superstition, Religion and Sexuality: Analyzes goddesses, witches, gender, power, and sexuality from ancient times to modern popular culture (including vampires). 
•AP/HUMA 3519 / AP/RLST 3519 Contemporary Women’s Rituals: An Introduction: Explores women creating rituals inside and outside established religions, using feminist ritual theory. It covers stories, ceremonies, intersectionality, and models for affinity groups. 
•Related: Feminist Approaches to Religion (HUMA/RLST 3518).
The availability of these courses raises the question of whether informal campus associations & “study groups” have arisen as well which are, in fact, covens for “the promotion of a deeper understanding” of this “ancient faith tradition.” 
Wiccan Church of Canada, Toronto Temple (Odyssean tradition): Offers public classes (recently listed as Zoom on Tuesdays) and rituals. Could be a resource for insights into how popular witchcraft has become & the possible number of covens in the GTA & southern Ontario in general. Founded in 1979 by Richard and Tamarra James, who also operated the Occult Shop. Richard James (High Priest) died in 2024. Tamarra James is a long-time High Priestess (initiated 1967), pioneer of public Wicca in Canada, and advocate for pagan rights including chaplaincy. The church emphasizes public priesthood training alongside worship. 
•Other local covens and groups (Gardnerian, Alexandrian, eclectic, Correllian in Oshawa) sometimes take students, but these are private and not university programs.

text:
In the years since the release of ChatGPT, it was common for skeptics to claim that AI was just hype. That talk has thankfully faded. The zeitgeist has now flipped, and fears about the potentially existential threats posed by the technology are widespread. I very much share those concerns. But I worry that in the leap from disbelief to alarm we have skipped over the vast area in between, in which AI’s impact will be felt in a thousand different ways: good and bad, mundane and weird, incremental and world-changing.

Few places will feel that impact more than New York City, which is deeply exposed to disruption of our economy, workforce, budget—even the basic functioning of government—by this powerful new technology.

This would be true even if AI advancement were to stop now. We have only barely begun to feel the effects of existing frontier systems like Astra and Fable throughout our economy and society, since only a tiny portion of people and organizations are making use of their highly advanced agentic features.

Meanwhile, leading labs are reportedly testing far more capable models behind closed doors, while racing toward systems that can automate AI research itself. With more powerful chips and vast new compute infrastructure now coming online, rapid AI progress will continue even if the financial bubble bursts.

None of this means we should surrender to the race. I believe Congress should immediately establish strict safeguards against catastrophic AI risks and empower an independent agency to enforce them. The United States should also pursue common safety measures with China. Neither will be easy under a president who has embraced an extreme hostility to AI safety. But we cannot allow a handful of tech billionaires to decide for themselves how much risk the rest of humanity should bear.

Whatever happens in these high-stakes fights, this much is certain: enormous disruption is already headed our way. And New York City is simply not ready.

The great paradox of New York City is that few places are more exposed to AI’s potential downsides, yet few have benefited more economically from the boom so far. The AI-fueled stock market has filled New York’s tax coffers. The data center buildout and the big AI IPOs are being financed by firms here. The brisk pace of office rental in NYC is in part driven by the many AI firms starting or expanding here. All that upside also creates a serious vulnerability for us: a collapse in AI valuations could badly hurt New York’s economy, even if the underlying technology continues to advance.

The risks extend well beyond Wall Street and the tech sector. New York is the capital of white-collar work, with more than a million people commuting into Manhattan daily. Many are employed in the industries that are the most likely to be impacted by AI automation: accounting, law, finance, consulting, design. There has thankfully so far been no significant increase in layoffs in NYC. But job growth has come to a halt here, and job postings are down for the most AI-exposed careers. Perhaps most tellingly, the unemployment rate for New Yorkers aged 22-27 is higher for those with a college degree than it is for those without one.

New York City has a $126 billion budget that is growing fast, with only $2 billion in our rainy day fund. If the AI bubble bursts and our tax revenue takes a hit, we have far too little buffer to avoid cuts to vital City services. If large numbers of New Yorkers lose their white-collar jobs because of automation, we have no pool of funds ready to provide them wage support or to offer large-scale retraining.

City government itself may be the institution most vulnerable to rapidly advancing AI. We have strong cyber defenses for the threats we face today. But our financial, payment, vendor, and accounting systems have not yet been hardened against a new class of autonomous AI adversary. This is not a distant threat: current and pre-release models have already demonstrated the ability to execute complex, multi-stage cyberattacks at a speed and scale no human defenders can match.

The emergence of vast numbers of capable AI agents has many implications for City government beyond cyber. It is just a matter of time before autonomous systems start making FOIL requests, filing legal claims, applying for permits and benefits, submitting job applications, reporting fraud allegations, asking questions to 311, or making 911 calls. Our government processes were built around an assumption we have barely thought about: that every request, application, complaint, and claim requires a human being to spend time creating it. AI will erase that constraint.

NYC simply does not have systems capable of dealing with what could be the resulting exponential increase in the volume of incoming. Our government is built on a rickety tech foundation that includes dozens of mainframes from the 1980s. We largely missed the cloud revolution, the mobile revolution, and the big data revolution, and are now dragging our feet on the machine-learning revolution. That will have to change if City government is to remain resilient as AI transforms the society around it.

Every City agency has to address a long list of questions and challenges created by the arrival of advanced AI. NYPD will need to figure out how to balance the allure of powerful new AI tools against the imperative to preserve privacy. Our public schools will have to rethink homework in a world where students have access to AI at home or on their cell phones by fourth or fifth grade, if not earlier. Workforce agencies will have to figure out what jobs they are even training people for now. The Health Department will have to adapt disease surveillance for the AI era.

We have work to do to ensure the benefits of this technology are shared broadly. That means, among other things, making sure New York City leads in AI-enabled biomedical research and that the resulting breakthroughs benefit people at every income level. It means giving small businesses, not just megacorporations, access to cutting-edge tools. And it means using AI to make government dramatically easier to navigate, especially for those on the margins—for example, by allowing New Yorkers to apply for SNAP benefits simply by speaking into their phones in whatever language they prefer.

Potential policy wins like this may sound trivial compared to the existential risk that runaway superintelligence poses. And there is no doubt that ensuring humanity remains in control of increasingly powerful AI is an urgent task.

But there is upheaval already underway. Change is coming fast. Steering to an equitable, healthy, deeply human future for the millions who call this place home will require nothing less than the reinvention of our institutions, including the government of New York City. It will require asking profound questions about what kind of city we want to be.

Whether you are feeling hope or fear or doubt right now, you have a role in answering these questions. Together we will make a thousand choices, large and small, that will determine the New York we become.

text:
GOOD NEWS IS BAD NEWS AGAIN: A BOOMING ECONOMY HAS STOCK FUTURES DOWN BEFORE THE OPEN:

Stock futures point to a lower open because the U.S. economy looks too strong, not too weak. From Wednesday's close: S&P 500 futures at 7,722.50, -50.00 / -0.64%; Nasdaq 100 futures at 30,429.50, -335 / -1.09%; Dow futures at 51,662.00, -211 / -0.41%; Russell 2000 futures at 2,845.80, -14.40 / -0.50%. These are contracts that trade overnight on where the big indexes will open.

The chain is short. Strong demand plus $105 oil keeps inflation up. Stubborn inflation means more Federal Reserve rate increases. That pushes up what Washington pays to borrow: the 10-year Treasury yield is 5.125%, up 0.011 point from Wednesday's 5.114% close, the highest since 2007, after touching 5.15% overnight. When a safe bond pays over 5%, profits a company expects years from now are worth less today, which is why the tech-heavy contract is falling hardest.

The spark was Wednesday's business survey. S&P Global's flash purchasing managers' index for September - a monthly poll of U.S. companies where anything above 50 means growth - jumped to 58.4 from 56.0 in August, the fastest growth since July 2021. Services 58.7; factories 57.0 vs about 53.7 expected. Firms also said their own costs rose at the steepest pace in four years, led by fuel and shipping. "Business is clearly booming now in both manufacturing and services," said Chris Williamson, S&P Global's chief business economist. The 10-year jumped about 0.15 point that day.

The night added two more reasons. Brent crude (November), the global oil benchmark, is at $105.06 a barrel, +$1.98 / +1.92% from Wednesday's settlement, with Iran still refusing to reopen the Strait of Hormuz until its conditions are met. And in London this morning, New York Fed President John Williams said it would be "reasonable" to expect another rate increase by year-end, though he would not commit to the Fed's October 27-28 meeting. The Fed raised its key rate to 3.75%-4.00% on September 16, its first increase since 2023.

Nothing here looks like panic. Gold is at $4,295.00 an ounce, -23.40 / -0.54% since Wednesday's close, and silver at $63.93, -1.03 / -1.59%. Frightened investors usually buy metal; these investors are selling assets that pay no interest now that a Treasury pays 5%. The VIX, the options market's gauge of expected swings in the S&P 500, is at 16.07, +0.89 / +5.86% since Wednesday's close - up, but still under its long-run average near 19.5.

Europe is getting the same treatment at midday. Germany's DAX is at 25,324.23, -86.40 / -0.34%; France's CAC 40 at 8,095.77, -27.64 / -0.34%; London's FTSE 100 at 10,704.59, -0.67 / -0.01%. Germany's ifo survey of about 9,000 firms beat forecasts this morning, 89.9 vs 89.0 expected and 88.8 in August, and Frankfurt's index still trades lower. Better business news, lower stocks, on both sides of the Atlantic.

The strongest fact against this read arrived at 7:00am. Darden Restaurants (DRI) at $213.69, +$0.15 / +0.07% on Wednesday, and $203.50 premarket, -$10.19 / -4.77% from that close, owns Olive Garden and LongHorn Steakhouse. Quarter to August 30: sales $3.20B vs $3.21B expected; profit $2.05 a share, as expected; full-year forecast of $11.10-$11.35 kept. The weak spot is same-restaurant sales - sales at locations open a year or more: Olive Garden +1.1%, down from +2.4% the quarter before; LongHorn +6.2%, down from +9.5%. Surveys say business is booming, yet sales growth is cooling at America's largest sit-down restaurant company. Darden is not a current Len5 pick: at about 18 times this fiscal year's forecast profit, with sales up about 5%, it is neither cheap enough nor growing fast enough.

This morning's read turns on evidence the heat is fading. A jump in layoffs at 8:30am, with the 10-year slipping back under Wednesday's 5.114%, would give stocks room to rise on news that sounds bad.

When, Eastern time:

- 8:30am: Labor Department first-time unemployment claims for the week ended September 19; 201k expected after 196k. The four-week average is 203,250, and the latest count of people still collecting benefits is 1.73M. Here a low number is the bad outcome for stocks. Richmond Fed President Tom Barkin speaks at the same hour.
- 10:00am: August new-home sales from the Census Bureau and HUD; about 615k annual pace expected, after 607k in July. Mortgage rates key off that 10-year.
- 1:00pm: the Treasury sells $44B of 7-year notes, trading near 5.05%. Anything above 4.908% would be the highest since the note returned in 2009; August's sale paid 4.512%. Wednesday's 5-year sale drew $2.21 of bids per $1 offered, the thinnest demand since December 2018.
- After the close: Costco Wholesale (COST) at $904.70, +$5.29 / +0.59% on Wednesday, reports its fiscal fourth quarter; about $6.53 a share on $94.8B of sales expected - the day's second read on shoppers. Costco is not a current Len5 pick: at about 45 times its past year's profit, the price already pays for its steadiness.
- Tonight: the White House state dinner for Chinese President Xi Jinping, after the trade truce was extended to January 10.

Prices set before 9:30am come from thinner trading than the regular session, and they often fade or reverse by the open.

A strong economy usually lifts stocks. This morning it is lifting borrowing costs instead, so every number on today's calendar reads upside down, starting with the 8:30am claims count.

text:
I'm a homepage copywriter for 100+ tech startups.

Here's the new strategy to stand out and win customers.

(Most startups are still playing the old game.)

BEFORE (pre-AI)
Your homepage could simply explain what your product did and who it was for.

• Features offered a solid technical moat, because they were difficult and expensive to copy.

• User interface was a major selling point, as it was how users accessed and gained value from your product.

TODAY (post-AI)
The new game is 'product differentiation'.

Your homepage must explain why customers should choose your product over alternatives.

Customers actively compare your product against competing products, plus Claude and GPT.

👉 Your homepage headlines should present a series of compelling reasons to close the other tabs and choose your product.

But most startups still write their homepage as if they're the only startup with these features.

That's why their homepages sound generic and get canned in any competitive comparison.

• Features can be copied faster. You need more defensible advantages, such as exclusive data, unique industry experience and knowledge, trusted distribution, or regulatory approval.

• Customers increasingly access your product via Claude or GPT. Compatibility (eg. via MCP) is becoming more important than your UI.

The good news is that social proof becomes even more valuable as products converge.

You can beat similar competitors simply because you have more effective testimonials that are aligned with your audience's hopes and worries.

One system connects all these advantages:

Build a customer feedback loop.

You need a process to continually interview or survey customers, capture their feedback and organise the evidence by segment, problem and stage of the purchase journey.

Now you have a continuous stream of:

• Valuable problems worth solving

• Evidence of the features that customer value

• New angles to differentiate existing features

• Customer language for your homepage and sales team

• Testimonials that prove the impact of your product

Your startup's strongest moat is how quickly you learn from customers and build this knowledge into your product, positioning and proof.

text:
One of the toughest decisions you'll face in your career:

You accepted a job offer at Company #1.

Then a week later, Company #2, which was your target company from the start, comes in with an offer.

Tough spot to be in, but it's a good position to be in.

The answer seems obvious to go with Company #2, but not many people understand the risks of declining Company #1.

Many (not all) companies would consider that bridge burned if you officially accepted an offer and backed out for whatever reason. 

If you live in a lower tier city where only a few employers dominate the market (Charlotte, Richmond, etc come to mind), that can potentially bite you in the a** down the road. 

How you tell company #1 matters too. If you just send them a generic one line email, they'll take that personally. Of course, most people will push back saying you don't owe companies anything, or "well employers pull offers and ghost us all the time". 

Well not this employer, they spent a lot of time and energy interviewing you and extending an offer. The least you can do is give them a phone call. 

Also don't drag it on like a bad breakup. Be direct, clear, and concise. Don't lead them on and tell them you'd think about it if they matched the number from Company #2. 

Again, good problem to have. But the priority at this point is making sure you keep that bridge open down the road.

Y’all wake up sore every morning too?
They didn’t blink.
“If you stay at UPS,
the rest of your life feels like this.”

The body was only part of it.
I wake up after the kids are at school.
I get home after they’re asleep.

My oldest is already in high school.
I missed more of her growing up than I wanted to.

My youngest is still little.
I’m not making that trade twice.
I can make more money.
I can’t make more childhood.

My assets started producing more than my UPS paycheck.
That didn’t make me rich.
It gave me more choice.

UPS Driver Choice Program.
$150,000.

I’m done working for money.

text:
Here's what Grok says. I'm really enjoying its interpretations!

This is a rich, layered dream that tracks closely with the shadow work you mentioned. It is not subtle. The psyche is showing you that something long smoldering in the place you rest, protect, and stay close to others has reached the point where quiet management no longer works.

The burning bed and the little boy
Your son appearing as a child again, in the old shared-bed arrangement, often points to the inner child or the vulnerable, innocent part of you that still needs shielding. The first impulse is classic: stamp the embers out yourself so he can keep sleeping. Do not wake the tender part. Do not alarm it. That is the old strategy—contain the heat privately. It fails. 
The Dixie cup is perfect dream economy: the child (or the child-like part of you) brings what it can, which is nowhere near enough for an adult-sized fire. Blankets and stomping only feed it. When you pull the mattress off, the box spring—the actual support structure under the sleeping surface—is already engulfed. The problem was never just the surface you lie on. It is the foundation.
The setting shifting to your childhood house makes the meaning clearer. This is family-of-origin material. You go to your mother’s room for the big water cooler (the maternal resource, the larger container). She stirs but does not wake. The mother principle, or the actual mother imprint, remains unconscious while you try to save the house. The realization that the whole house may burn is the dream saying the old structure may not be salvageable in its current form. 
Shadow work at this intensity often feels exactly like that: the familiar psychic architecture is on fire and you cannot put it out with the old methods.
The quarters and The Wall
The memory that interrupts is not random. At sixteen you took from your mother’s hidden store of “not real money” to buy a boyfriend The Wall. You did not experience it as theft at the time. Quarters felt too small to count. That is a precise image of how the shadow often operates: we take energy, attention, security, or emotional resources from the maternal line (or the family system) while telling ourselves it does not really cost anything. Then the mother gets angry when the depletion becomes visible.
The Wall itself is loaded. It is an album about isolation, the overbearing or damaging mother, the construction of defenses after wounding, and the terror of being seen. Buying it as a love-gift while quietly draining the mother’s reserve is a compact symbol: seeking connection through a story of walls, funded by an unacknowledged taking. The dream pairs this memory with the fire because the current heat is related to old, minimized extractions and the walls that followed.
The man and the unpolished crystal
The second movement brings in the man from the news—the one beaten nearly to death over a fender bender, a small collision that exploded into pack violence. In the dream he is not a victim performing pain. He stands in front of you, comments on your “interesting neighbors,” and says he does not even know who his people are. Then he opens the breast pocket (heart) and offers a raw, unpolished crystal the size of your palm, smiling.
This figure often appears in shadow work as the disowned or “not my people” part—the one who has been treated as other, who has no clear tribe, who has absorbed disproportionate violence over something minor. His line about neighbors can be read both outwardly and inwardly: the parts of the psyche (or the actual human environment) that turn savage over small accidents. His not knowing his people echoes fractured belonging—something that has shown up in your other recent dreams around sons, writing, and family rupture.
Yet he does not accuse. He shows you the stone. Unpolished crystal is potential that has not been worked yet. It is the gold in the shadow: something precious taken from the heart of the alienated figure and offered without polish. You do not have to refine it in the dream; you only have to see it.
Putting it together
The dream is saying the fire under the bed cannot be discreetly stomped out while the child sleeps. The support structure is already burning. The childhood house, the sleeping mother, the old habit of treating certain takings as “not real money,” and the walls built afterward are all part of the same blaze. Attempts to handle it with inadequate vessels will not work. At the same time, the psyche is not only showing destruction. It is also showing a smiling stranger who does not know his people handing you raw material from the heart.That is often how this stage of shadow work feels: the old house is threatened, the mother stays asleep, the child cannot bring enough water, and yet something unpolished and valuable is being offered from an unexpected direction. 

The Buddhist group you were rushing to that morning is not incidental. Fire in this context is both the thing that can consume the structure and the heat that makes transformation possible.
You already sensed the mattress dream was connected to the work. The rest of the dream simply filled in the family, the theft that did not feel like theft, the walls, and the outsider who still has a gift.

text:
Dover’s bikers marched peacefully-then visited the local pubs.

Before hundreds of anti-immigration marchers reached Dover, Kent, on 27 April 2025, the town’s Labour MP made them a simple offer: see the cliffs, visit the castle and seafront, support small businesses-and leave local people in peace.

The riders answered on the road.

Motorbikes streamed down the A2 towards Britain’s gateway to the Channel. They gathered at the Townwall Street car park, where people arriving on foot joined them with Union Jacks, St George’s flags and “Stop the boats” signs.

The march had been months in the making. Kent Motor Heads Events had called on bikers and friends to protest against illegal Channel crossings. More than 900 people had expressed interest online, but local reporting put the final procession at about 500.

That still meant hundreds of engines, helmets and flags moving together through a town at the centre of Britain’s immigration debate.

Police were prepared for a difficult afternoon. A counter-demonstration had been arranged in Market Square, officers formed a line between the two groups, and memories of Dover’s violent 2016 protests hung over the day.

This time, the story changed.

The bikers and other marchers left the car park, followed the seafront past Waterloo Crescent and entered Market Square. Their message was direct: they wanted tougher action against illegal crossings and believed the Government’s existing rules were not being properly enforced.

There were loud exchanges across the police line. Yet the feared disorder never arrived.

The smaller counter-demonstration dispersed shortly after 2pm. Kent Police later confirmed that the protests had concluded without any reported disorder or arrests.

That official ending matters. A right-wing patriotic march had entered a town carrying difficult memories, faced an opposing group at close quarters and still finished peacefully.

Then came the quieter final scene.

With the march over, bikers and other participants spread through Dover and visited its pubs-doing much of what the local MP had asked before they arrived.

The engines had carried a political demand into Britain’s best-known Channel town. But when they fell silent, the day ended not with a police van or a damaged street, but with peaceful marchers putting money across local bars.

text:
“Pragmatic Conservative”

I am a market-oriented conservative who believes public policy should be grounded in evidence, not ideology. That also means rejecting nonsense from embarrassing, low-IQ social conservatives. No, hurricanes are not caused by gay marriage.

We need to address pollution and climate change responsibly, but I am not an alarmist. I just do not want us to sit on our hands until we legitimately need to become alarmists. As Arnold Schwarzenegger, the former Republican governor of California, has argued, if the phrase “climate change” is too triggering, use “pollution”; people respond better to that word. And nobody likes pollution.

I support a conventional conservative emphasis on national security, and on that front, Carney is doing more than any prime minister in my lifetime. I believe in professionalism, civil rights, and the legitimacy of political opposition. That should be standard conservatism.

I also support medical assistance in dying for competent adults facing grievous and irremediable suffering. A patient can already refuse treatment, sign a do-not-resuscitate order, or have life support withdrawn. The state should not force a dying person to endure suffering they have clearly and freely rejected. That is a liberty issue.

But liberty requires safeguards: informed, voluntary requests, rigorous assessment, real protection for vulnerable people, and full conscience rights for doctors and faith-based institutions. Canada should be cautious about expanding it further, especially to mental illness alone. And no one should ever choose death because they could not get adequate care, housing, or support.

Nor is this a rejection of faith. Archbishop Desmond Tutu publicly supported assisted dying, and former Archbishop of Canterbury George Carey changed his position to support it.

I also support universal health care. I will not pretend it began as a conservative project. Saskatchewan’s first universal hospital-insurance program was introduced in 1947 by Tommy Douglas’s CCF government: a democratic-socialist government.  But Saskatchewan proved that universal hospital insurance could work economically as well as socially, making it a practical model for national adoption rather than an ideological experiment.

John Diefenbaker, the Saskatchewan-raised Progressive Conservative prime minister, began his career as a lawyer in Saskatchewan, where he frequently offered free legal advice and defended Indigenous people and immigrants. As prime minister, he helped turn that provincial example into a national hospital-insurance program. That is conservatism at its best: not reflexively rejecting an idea because the left proposed it, but examining whether it works, whether it is financially sustainable, and whether it helps ordinary people live healthier, more secure lives. Universal health care does not require accepting long waits as inevitable. Wait times are not an inherent feature of universality; they often reflect capacity and incentive problems.

Canada should move further toward activity-based funding: money follows the patient. Paying hospitals for the number of patients they treat can inspire innovation. Many European countries already do it. Of course, it should not simply be about the number of patients. Quality matters.

Canada should also examine Australia’s model, which maintains universal public health care alongside a regulated private option. People who choose private insurance often receive planned procedures sooner, while universal public access remains intact.

And, Canada should consider both: activity-based funding within universal public care, and a carefully regulated private option alongside it. Keep universality because it is morally right and economically defensible. Reform its delivery to make it faster, more innovative, more accountable, and more sustainable.

Take a look at this article....

Judaism and the Sins of Israel: On the Essential Nature of Religion

Israel, an "artificial state" established by Zionists, has brought immense catastrophe to Palestine and the Middle East, exerting a profound and unsettling impact on the global order while severely jeopardizing humanity's faith in justice. To enable a clearer discernment of the true nature of Judaism and the state of Israel, distinguish right from wrong, and offer humanity a glimmer of hope to rectify deviations and restore justice, this article systematically delineates their multiple transgressions.

1. Blaspheming God and Serving the Devil
Does God exist? It is a question to which no definitive empirical answer can be given. Yet, for any religion, the existence of God is an absolute certainty—a Supreme Being who created the universe and will ultimately deliver it. Since God created the world, the Divine must be inherently grand, righteous, and impeccable. God cannot behave like an earthly despot who blurs the line between right and wrong, harbors blind favoritism, or instigates conflict that leaves the earth devastated and drenched in blood. Any entity that perpetuates such horrors must be the devil, not God. God would deem it beneath Divine dignity to broker arbitrary covenants, grant exclusive real estate titles to specific mortals, demonstrate absolute partiality toward a selective few, or engage in physical wrestling matches with humans—much like a human would never engage in such absurdities with an ant, and would find it reviling to hear an ant boast of such a relationship. Therefore, what Judaism worships is the devil, not God; consequently, Judaism itself is the true object of divine retribution.

2. A Total Syndicate Snuffing Out the Beacon of Humanity
The ultimate purpose of religion is self-interest, utilizing individual benefit as a mechanism to attract adherents. This self-interest can be bifurcated into two categories: temporal self-interest in the material world, and transcendental self-interest in the afterlife. While the vast majority of religions pursue the latter, the modalities of religious dissemination can be categorized into three paradigms: self-interest, altruism, and self-abnegation.
· Righteous Religions: Expand their doctrines through structural altruism to attain both temporal and transcendental self-interest (modern Protestantism, to a qualified extent, approaches this paradigm).
· Neutral Religions: Enjoin strict self-abnegation to achieve transcendental self-interest (authentic Chinese Mahayana Buddhism emphasizes high self-abnegation and moderate altruism; Tibetan Buddhism, however, deviates from this).
· Mallent Religions: Disseminate their faith via raw self-interest to maximize both temporal and transcendental gains (Judaism fits this mold).
· Criminal Syndicates: When a group systematically inflicts harm upon external populations to secure transcendental self-interest, it ceases to be a religion and becomes a criminal enterprise (such as ISIS).
True righteous religion is singular; it must rely on altruism as its proselytizing engine to fulfill its dual self-interest. Judged by this criterion, Islam must also be categorized as a cultish entity.
When a religion becomes pathologically insular yet fiercely unified for collective self-enrichment, it must perpetually extract illicit advantages from the external world to fulfill its internal theological promises and suppress external criticism or interference. This manifests through predatory usury, monopolistic syndicates, the systematic deprivation of opportunities for outsiders, the monopolization of media to strangle freedom of speech, the utilization of ill-gotten wealth to manipulate foreign governments, and the deployment of collective intimidation against dissenters. Judged by any objective metric, this exhibits the classic hallmarks of a mafia.
Consider the contemporary world: we witness the collective intimidation of protesting students at Harvard, where syndicates coerced the university administration to surrender blacklists and threatened a total hiring boycott against student dissidents. Even in my own experience, when attempting to publish a critique of Israel, editors at major media outlets felt compelled to cautiously warn me to "ensure my personal safety." These multi-faceted realities reveal a chilling truth: when confronting Israel, the constitutional right to free speech is immediately compromised by physical and professional security anxieties.
Look at the sheer absurdity of our global reality: within the United States—the very nation that birthed the United Nations and once stood as a beacon of civilization—the government stands in obstinate, isolated solidarity with Israel, defiantly opposing the overwhelming majority of the international community on Palestinian sovereignty. Nearly all mainstream political figures line up in lockstep behind Israel, even when the comment sections beneath their public statements are flooded with denunciation from the populace. Are we to believe that every single American politician is a fundamentally malicious actor? Facing the spilled blood of the Palestinian people and the living hell of their homeland, have these politicians truly been possessed by demons to consciously walk in alignment with evil? No matter how compromised these politicians may be, it is impossible that this reflects the genuine, uncoerced intent of all of them. This unveils a profoundly horrifying reality upon closer reflection: the United States is rapidly transforming into a hollowed-out zombie, its sovereign soul thoroughly extracted by Israel and Zionist interest groups.

3. Bloodlust Masked by Hypocritical Dogma
We must remain hyper-vigilant against a common tactic employed by certain theologians and scholars who attempt to sanitize Judaism by citing altruistic laws within its scriptures—such as the Decalogue, commands to "give alms to the poor," or prohibitions against "oppressing the stranger." However, any insular, predatory interest group must inevitably weave a cloak of righteous justice to survive within secular society and deflect external scrutiny. As the ancient proverb goes, "there is honor even among thieves"—the most ruthless cartels in history eagerly built bridges and paved roads for their local neighborhoods, and the most extreme cults frequently used charitable handouts to buy public compliance.
These manicured facades are by no means the essence of the system; they are merely moral ornaments designed to deceive the world. In practice, "giving alms to the poor" stands in irreconcilable, parasitic contradiction with "predatory usury and capital monopoly." Through usurious practices and financial blood-sucking, they drive millions of Gentile families into destitution and ruin; then, they turn inward to distribute welfare within their enclosed circle, placating their own kin and delivering on the material benefits promised upon initiation. This closed-loop mechanism of "extreme external predation coupled with internal distribution of spoils" precisely validates its absolute identity as a mafia syndicate. To evaluate an entity, one must look past its ornamental garments and examine whose fundamental right to survival it has stripped away. Any appeasement of this profound hypocrisy constitutes an outright betrayal of human justice.

4. Actions Divorced from Modern Civilization
The foundational premise of modern civilization dictating that the Earth is the shared home of all living things; even apex species possess no arbitrary right to violently displace or dispossess other creatures of their habitats. If humanity lacks the ethical authority to evict monkeys from a mountain to claim it for ourselves, who under heaven possesses the right to strip the Palestinian people of their sovereign right to exist and reside in Palestine?
Following the conclusion of World War II in 1945, Jewish populations no longer faced an existential threat to their survival; what, then, justified their subsequent threat to the very survival of the Palestinians? Apologists might argue that the Jewish community, having just endured the horrors of the Holocaust, was trapped in an extreme crisis of survival. Yet, this can never serve as a legitimate pretext for violent dispossession. Existential crises are not unique to the Jewish experience. According to the most basic threshold of fairness and justice in modern civilization, any localized catastrophe or crisis must be resolved at its historical source; it can never grant a right to displace the catastrophe onto innocent third parties by plundering their legitimate right to life. The bitter fruits of European anti-Semitism ought to have been borne by Europe itself. Forcing the native inhabitants of Palestine—who played absolutely no part in European crimes—to foot the bill for "moral reparations" of the Holocaust, and framing the so-called "two-state solution" as justice, represents one of the most hypocritical, shameless, and predatory acts of banditry in the history of modern international politics.

5. The Abuse of Violence to Perpetrate Genocide
For nearly eighty years, Zionist forces in Palestine have systematically displaced the indigenous population, brutally massacred and incarcerated Palestinians, and relentlessly expanded illegal settlements. This has triggered an endless exodus of refugees, resulted in innumerable casualties, and caused harrowing atrocities to play out on a daily basis—all driven by a calculated attempt to gradually liquidate the Palestinian people and completely usurp their land.
Thanks to the ubiquity of modern digital media, the tragic plight of the Palestinians is now laid bare before the collective conscience of humanity. Who, then, is the true terrorist? The moral framework governing the justifiable use of violence dictating that violence is righteous only when one's own survival or the survival of others is actively threatened. Consequently, the Palestinian people possess an absolute, legitimate right to employ violence against their Israeli oppressors. Their resistance is fundamentally just, whereas Israel constitutes the actual terrorist entity.

6. Constructing an Invisible Empire Parasitic Upon Modern States
By tightly binding religious identity to material self-interest, the Zionist cartel has engineered an invisible empire that effectively reigns supreme over sovereign nations. Leveraging their monopolized financial wealth and sprawling media conglomerates, they exert deep, manipulative control over Western political landscapes. This insular, self-serving apparatus utilizes aggressive financial lobbying to transmute the hard-earned tax dollars of foreign citizens into their own political leverage, ultimately hijacking the foreign policies of major global powers. This is a textbook case of a predatory interest group subverting, hollow out, and invisibly parasitizing modern democracy and sovereign civilization.

7. Ideological Thought Policing and the Destruction of Public Justice
To immunize themselves against external critique, these groups weaponize historical trauma, swiftly branding any discourse that interrogates their atrocities with the label of "anti-Semitism." This calculated form of ideological thought policing is brutally suffocating academic freedom and liberty of expression. As the world witnesses the blood-soaked purgatory inflicted upon the Palestinian people, Western politicians—paralyzed by the intimidation of powerful lobby groups—lapse into a collective, spineless silence, willfully aligning themselves with demonic forces. This absolute double standard has triggered a profound crisis of trust in modern morality, fundamentally dismantling humanity's self-evident faith in equity, justice, and universal law.

Despite the reality that certain factions within the Jewish populace remain bound by a nexus of religion and self-interest—forming an invisible, crushing force capable of flattening any individual resistance to suppress anti-Zionist critiques—there are still courageous Jewish individuals who actively resist Israeli policies and oppose draconian anti-Semitism legislation. Though born into the fold of Judaism, their conscience and commitment to justice have triumphed over institutional evil. They represent the true pride of the Jewish people and the sole beacon of hope for their eventual moral redemption.

On Monday, September 21, Peace and Sport and AS Monaco welcomed a Colombian delegation, including 11 young people and their educator from Florida, in Colombia’s Valle del Cauca department, alongside a Colombian government representative and two representatives of the Embassy of Colombia in France.
 
The visit was part of a cultural exchange between Colombia, France and the Principality of Monaco, marking the 25th anniversary of diplomatic relations between Colombia and Monaco.
 
The morning offered an opportunity to explore how sport can foster dialogue, mutual understanding and peace through:

🔹 A presentation of the Champions for Peace Club by @MarleneNidecker, highlighting its engagement in Colombia.
🔹 Insights from the Peace and Sport team into the Peacemakers Project and its experiences in the field.
🔹 A screening of The Flame of Peace, followed by discussions with the young participants.
 
The programme continued with a visit to Monaco’s iconic Stade Louis-II, home of AS Monaco.
 
Our sincere thanks to the young participants and the entire delegation, the Embassy of Colombia in France, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Colombia, and everyone who helped make this exchange possible.
 
Bringing young people together across borders creates opportunities to share experiences and build connections

He spent a decade at Texas Instruments helping make it the world's number one vendor of DSL modem chips.

Then he quit, put in his own savings, and started a semiconductor company in a garage with one other person. It took eight years before India saw what he had built.

His name is Himamshu Khasnis.

What pushed him out was a number he could not stop thinking about. By his own estimate, close to 45 percent of the world's chips were being designed in Bengaluru. But as he put it, "the intellectual property and the subsequent revenue remained with the USA."

India had more than a billion mobile phones, second only to China, and some of the largest cellular networks on earth. Every silicon chip inside that infrastructure was imported.

He founded Signalchip in 2010.

Chip design is slow, brutally expensive, and offers nothing to show for years. Sridhar Vembu of Zoho, who had started his own career as a wireless engineer at Qualcomm, backed him and stayed. A software founder funding silicon, through a decade with no product.

In 2015 came SCRF1401, India's first RF transceiver chip for 3G, 4G and WiFi.

Then in February 2019, Signalchip unveiled four chips it called the Agumbe family, India's first indigenous semiconductor chips for 4G LTE and 5G NR modems. They cover all LTE and 5G bands up to 6GHz, and they support positioning through NavIC, India's own satellite navigation system.

At the launch, India's Telecom Secretary noted that only around eight companies in the world could design and build chips like these. The team that did it was 40 people.

In October 2024, Khasnis stood at the India Mobile Congress explaining his chips to the Prime Minister, who asked detailed questions.

For years, Indian engineers designed a large share of the world's silicon and owned almost none of it.

Agumbe is Indian at the level that actually matters. The design, the patents, the ownership.

text:
Today is the day we pickup our Model YL🔥

I’m going to be posting a lot but I want to say I don’t want this to be about us.  I mainly want to focus on many of us are in the same situation with Tesla- 

Wanting an affordable 6-passenger SUV vehicle for your family. 

We have been waiting a long time. We had looked at the Model X. It is an amazing ride. The biggest issue was the price. 

My wife decided to lease the Kia EV9 in 2024 for 2 years. I hoped we would see another option from Tesla when the lease was over. We got it March 2024 and ended March 2026. 

The price for the EV 9 was 76,000. It had CCS. It qualified for 7,500 EV credit but we knew CCS was going away and they were going to NACS so didn’t really want to buy it. It was brand new EV from Kia. So we leased. 

Paid 1000 a month lease. Wasn’t ideal but figured for 2 years we could decide from there to buy out or upgrade. 

My wife really liked the room. 
She liked riding higher. 
She liked how practical it was for us. 
She didn’t mind the software. Mainly used Apple car play and she liked that. 

We were bound to 12,000 miles. Which was a struggle. Couldn’t take it on trips to not go over. 
It didn’t handle well in winter at all. She was scared and usually took my S because it slid around. Even though having AWD and all season tires. (Both my S and hers had All season). Not sure if we had put different all season tires if it would have helped but we were not doing that with a lease vehicle. 

There were many Kia owners who had issues with their high voltage battery. Ours never had a problem. But we were concerned it could happen. Luckily it didn’t. 

The software was not good. Was buggy. She had to keep rebooting it. Sometimes things didn’t work. Wasn’t terrible but happened. 

The lane assist software was very scared it fought you when going around corners. You had to watch it so it didn’t disconnect when going around a corner.  Nothing like FSD. This also was primarily why we took the S. We have FSD 12 then 13 then 14. FSD just kept improving but her Kia stayed the same. 

What was funny the displayed showed other cars as boxes as they road by. Like beta software. That never changed in 2 years. 😅

It had few weird non needed things. Like a light on the dash that came on to show when 12 volt battery was charging. 🤷‍♂️

For such a large front with no engine, the frunk was small. 😅

The boxy feel to it affected the range. It had a big battery but efficiency wasn’t great. Top range was 275. (I think some 2 wheel models would get closer to 300). Ours didn’t. 

These little things highlighted that even though they got some things right with the EV9, they approached it with the legacy mindset. 

When the lease was up they offered us to buy our for 56,000. Others with exact specs and miles  were selling for 37,000.  That was an easy decision. We let it go. My wife was sad. She did like it. 
They took it to auction and no idea what they got but I bet not even close and prob took big hit. 

Months and months later I still had access to it. Saw it was in New York area 😅

So then we began our Model YL journey. 

It already was in China and Just released in Austrailia. Elon said it would come to US later this year if at all. (I knew it would. Had no doubt in my mind)

We saw first casting of what appeared to be YL at Texas later March. Kept seeing other hints. Covered YL’s around Fremont. Tesla announced they were ending S and X production. 😔 I also knew this opened the door more for the YL the US.

I did simple guesstimate math and thought I bet Tesla announces orders after 2nd qtr

I guessed July 2nd they’d open orders and sure enough they did!

We ordered 5 min after the site went live and today is the day. 

I will be highlighting some comparisons from our EV9 with the YL in coming days. 👀

Excited for our next SUV family adventure!

I’m sure many of us are in similar situation.

What is your story?

text:
A herdshare in Texas is a legal arrangement where you buy a partial share of a dairy animal to receive fresh, raw milk. [1, 2]
How Herdshares Work in Texas
Ownership: You buy a fractional share of a cow or goat from a local farmer.
Boarding Fee: You pay a monthly fee to the farmer for feeding, milking, and housing your animal.
Distribution: You receive a weekly portion of raw milk based on the size of your share.
Legality: Direct retail sale of raw milk is tightly regulated or restricted for off-farm stores in Texas, making herdshares a compliant membership-based alternative. [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]

text:
1994. National Press Club. Peter Lynch gives the room a syllogism from his logic classes at Boston College.

Anyone who called interest rates right three times in a row would be a billionaire. There are not many billionaires. So there are not many people who can call interest rates.

Then he goes back to 1981. A 20% prime rate. Double-digit inflation. Double-digit unemployment. He does not remember anyone warning him.

He splits economics in two. Predictions: next year's recession, the Dow a year out, M1, M2 and all the M's. Facts: used car prices when he owns auto stocks. Hotel occupancy when he owns hotels. The price of ethylene for chemicals. Aluminum inventories falling five straight months. The first he calls a total waste. The second he can deal with.

His ratio: spend 14 minutes a year on economics and 12 of them are wasted.

Alan Greenspan, he says, is an honest man. Ask him about short rates for the next six months and he might answer. Ask him where long rates will be in three years and he would say he has no idea. If the Fed cannot do it, the investor is not going to.

What Lynch offers instead is arithmetic. 93 years of market history. 50 declines of 10% or more, roughly one every two years. 15 of those went past 25%, roughly one every six. A correction, in his words, is a euphemism for losing a lot of money rapidly.

His use for it: a stock he likes at 14 falls to 6. The company is fine. 14 to 22 is terrific. 6 to 22 is exceptional.

Nobody knows when. Anybody can know how often.

The people who told him afterward they saw it coming had predicted it 53 times.

The MV Cape Dao (also written CAPE DAO, IMO 9219020) is a bulk carrier flying the flag of Antigua and Barbuda. It was therefore not an Indian-flagged vessel, but it was carrying a majority of Indian seafarers. It was sailing from Mina Saqr (United Arab Emirates) toward India when it was struck twice.

The impacts hit the port side: one in the accommodation area (C-deck) and one near the engine room. A fire broke out in the engine room. Descriptions vary by source (“unknown projectile,” “missile,” “two torpedoes”). No claim of responsibility has been made public.

Human toll:

- 28 crew members on board in total.
- 20 Indian seafarers according to India’s Ministry of External Affairs (MEA).
- One fatality: Suraj Yadav, 26, a wiper from Deoria (Uttar Pradesh). He died from a head injury.
- The other 27 were evacuated by the Royal Navy of Oman and given medical care.

India condemned the attack, offered condolences to the family, and called for de-escalation as well as an end to attacks on commercial shipping in the region. The Indian Embassy in Muscat is coordinating the repatriation of the survivors and the remains with Omani authorities.

This incident is part of a series of attacks on merchant vessels in the area since the escalation of tensions in the Middle East.

🚨 2026 Income Tax Rates Revealed: Which States Will Take the Biggest Bite Out of Your Paycheck?

Where you live can have a major impact on how much of your income you keep.

This 2026 state income tax map highlights the highest marginal individual income tax rate across the United States. The differences are striking:

California: 13.3% — the highest top marginal rate in the country.

Hawaii: 11.0%.

New Jersey and Washington, D.C.: 10.8%.

Oregon: 9.9%.

Minnesota: 9.9%.

New York: 10.9%.

Texas, Florida, Nevada, South Dakota, Tennessee, Alaska, and Wyoming: no state individual income tax.

Washington: 0% on wage income, although its capital gains tax may apply to certain high-income taxpayers.

But there’s an important detail many people miss:

A top marginal tax rate does not mean every dollar you earn is taxed at that rate.

It generally applies only to income above a specific threshold. Your effective tax rate—the percentage of your total income paid in taxes—will usually be lower.

That distinction matters when evaluating:

Relocation decisions.

Compensation packages.

Remote-work arrangements.

Business and investment strategies.

Retirement planning.

State-by-state cost of living.

The lowest-tax state is not automatically the most affordable. Housing costs, property taxes, sales taxes, insurance, wages, public services, and quality of life can all change the overall financial picture.

The bigger takeaway?

Taxes are only one part of the location equation—but for high earners, entrepreneurs, investors, and mobile professionals, they can be a very meaningful one.

Source: Tax Foundation; data as of January 2026. Chart via Visual Capitalist.

text:
Boomers love making AI images of their grandkids. Millennial parents hate it | Amanda Hoover, Business Insider

When Ben Metcalfe recently visited his grandparents, he was greeted by an AI-generated caricature of one of their family photos hanging on the kitchen wall. "I understand that there was good intention behind doing it," says Metcalfe, a Gen Zer who works in AI governance. "At the same time, it's a major privacy concern."

Jen, a 32-year-old mom, tells me that last Christmas her mom texted her a series of adorable images: Jen's two toddlers sitting in Santa's lap, then riding the Polar Express. Their cheeks were fuller than she knew them to be, their eyes glossier, the lighting pristine — all thanks to Grok, xAI's chatbot. "It's so cute. And I want to love it," she tells me. But it was too unsettling to embrace.

Jen, whose name has been changed to avoid sparking more family drama, says she's read news about Grok generating sexual abuse material, and worries about how the bot could use her children's faces in the future.

It's not just her mom. For Mother's Day, a friend sent her a coloring sheet with her kids' faces, and her brother-in-law used AI to add one of her kids to a family photo who had been covered by a stroller, napping, when it was taken, she says. Everyone means well, Jen says, but they're walking blindly into a big risk, and the technology is so new, she isn't even sure what boundaries are best to set around how loved ones use her children's images with AI. "We all aren't educated enough about what AI companies are doing with our content," she says.

Welcome to the intergenerational slop fight.

In one corner are growing ranks of lawmakers calling for kids to be booted from social media, and parents concerned about data privacy opting to share less with AI companies and social media platforms. Europe is considering regulations that would limit chatbot and AI companion access to those younger than 15.

In the other corner are parents, grandparents, aunts, uncles, and friends who are uploading millions of images of kids into AI generators, delighting at the uncanny output, and sharing them far and wide. They use AI to make custom gags, generating portraits of the family, sending eCards and making toys, T-shirts, tchotchkes, and children's books through websites that encourage and profit from this very oversharing, making personalization a selling point. To some, it's endearing; to others, a privacy nightmare that may come with just a quick laugh, but long-term implications that aren't fully realized.

The more people see photos like this on social media, the more it's normalized, says Metcalfe. "It's this effect of, well if they're doing it, then we can do it as well, and then it becomes a chain reaction of everyone else is kind of doing it."

We're losing the tenuous grasp over our own images. And for some, their families are the first ones to give that control away.

The sites once exclusive to college-enrolled Millennials have become family trees. Six generations cram onto social media now, from the Silent Generation (not so silent on Facebook) to Gen Alpha. Different generations have varying consensus about what the point of social platforms even is anymore: Is AI-generated imagery the playground of the future, is it cringe, or can it lead images to be used for something far more nefarious?

Some parents of young children have pushed back against family members posting their kids for years. AI has raised the stakes, as social media sites have come under fire for misuse of young people's images in AI generators. xAI faces a lawsuit brought by a woman who is a child sexual abuse survivor and alleges Grok created new deepfake exploitive images of her after real images of her abuse were uploaded. xAI did not respond to a request for comment, but Elon Musk has called the exploitation of children on X "priority #1" when he bought the platform in 2022, and xAI has sued users who are facing criminal charges for allegedly using Grok to create explicit images of children. X told The New York Times this month that it blocks users who post or engage with such material, and reports them to authorities, and that it uses automated filters to block exploitative material from being uploaded. Posting photos to social media sites has become riskier, as platforms roll out new AI tools. Meta faced fierce backlash this summer when it launched out a Muse Image tool, allowing users to generate images based on other publicly posted photos. The company shut it down in less than a week.

The differences in how generations perceive social media stems from their own relationship to privacy and context collapse, rather than their technical ability, says Paromita Pain, a professor of global media at the University of Nevada, Reno. Posting a photo to show your friends your new grandson or niece can lead to unintended consequences that are hard to conceptualize when presented with the ease of social media photo sharing. As Baby Boomers grew up, there was less emphasis on privacy because, aside from a few celebrities and politicians, privacy was the default.

Millennials saw the switch from an anonymous internet with AOL chatrooms to the very on-the-record days of Facebook, Instagram, and LinkedIn. They and now Gen Z have grown to see the evolution of cancel culture. Those experiences that influence how Millennials and Zoomers want to use the internet can confound their Boomer parents.

And despite risks, posting may have some real benefits for older users that keep calling them back to post. Research published by Pennsylvania State University in 2021 found that older adults who posted more photos to Facebook described feeling more competent, and that led to a higher sense of wellbeing. Commenting and receiving comments created a feeling of connection. When it comes to AI, Boomers have been slower to adopt it than younger generations — about a fifth said they have ever used a standalone AI tool, compared to 76% of Gen Z who used AI in 2025, according to a report from Deloitte. They're more likely to use them for entertainment purposes (possibly skewed by a significant portion of the demographic being out of the workforce).

Some parents have tried to set boundaries to no avail. Leah, a Millennial who had her first baby a year ago, doesn't feel tied to the pics-or-it-didn't-happen ethos of social posting. Her daughter is the first grandkid in the family, and Leah, whose name has been changed so she can talk freely without creating more problems with her mom, doesn't want her baby's image online. Her mom is a Baby Boomer, and regularly complains about the social media ban on pictures of her granddaughter. Leah says she's tried to explain her safety and privacy concerns, and told her mom that images online can be used to create deepfake child exploitation material. Her mom, she says, seems to see her arguments as the worst case scenario: that Leah is coming up with monstrous examples of things sick people could do — and her Facebook friends aren't among them.

"We're on totally different pages," Leah says. "I haven't figured out a way to bridge the gap. It's almost like neither of us have a place where we can compromise." Leah says she tried the closest trade-off she could offer: allowing her mom to post pre-approved photos where her baby isn't the focal point (like a large photo of the whole family, ones where her daughter's face isn't visible). But Leah's mom has already broken her rules twice. She thinks she's just sharing the photos with her friends, but Leah argues that can be done over text. "We don't need to share it with Mark Zuckerberg," Leah says. "He's not our friend."

On TikTok and Reddit, young people reveal the AI-generated family-made photos that make them recoil. There are flawless photos edited for graduation posters, renderings showing how potential grandchildren could look, and absurdist videos generated as birthday eCards. They ask advice for how to talk to family members about the possible consequences of making all this slop, attempting to set new social norms for a technology that is rapidly becoming commonplace.

A TikTok trend is what caught Brandon, a 22-year-old who asked I not use his full name, looking at an image of himself in an '80s themed outfit his mom had generated with AI. She was laughing hysterically; he was immediately uncomfortable. "In her mind, it was a way to have entertainment, to do something fun," Brandon says, noting that he rarely uses AI, never inputs personal information, and doesn't upload photos of himself or others to social media.

"I decided to tell her that I was uncomfortable with my image being shared without my consent," he says. "You just don't know what that data is being used for." And for now, there's no taking those images back, or for someone like Brandon to know how they're being used in an open source AI model. "I would hope that there's a way in the future to legally fight that and permanently remove your biometric data."

Clawing back your image once it's online is nearly impossible. It's getting harder in an era where smartphones, camera-equipped smart glasses, and surveillance tech capture so many moments to maintain control over your image. When every fleeting family portrait, custom children's book about princesses, or moments on the Polar Express might have ties than they seem, there may be more reason for everyone to take pause.

PRESS RELEASE:  Pro-Life Leaders Call on FDA to Restore Abortion Drug Safeguards

WASHINGTON, D.C. -- Ahead of FDA Commissioner nominee Dr. Heidi Overton's confirmation hearing before the Senate HELP Committee, 50 pro-life leaders released a lettercalling on the nominee to commit to restoring the safeguards governing mifepristone that existed before the Biden administration while the FDA completes its ongoing review of the drug.

Family Research Council President Tony Perkins offered the following comments on the letter: "Those who advocate for women and the unborn have patiently awaited the end of the Biden-era abortion by mail scheme, which was designed to undermine the Dobbs decision. It is time for the Trump FDA to take action."

The letter reads in part:

"Dr. Overton's confirmation hearing provides an important opportunity for her to make clear what she plans to do about the FDA's extremely permissive policy governing mifepristone.

"There are good reasons the FDA policy should not be this permissive.

"First, there are serious concerns about the safety of the drug. As just one example, a recent study found that nearly 11% of women taking mifepristone have a serious "adverse event" within 45 days of taking it.

"Second, the permissiveness of the current policy is increasing the risk of abuse, especially by men who seek to force women to have abortions without their consent or knowledge. By allowing mifepristone to be obtained without an in-person medical visit, the current FDA policy makes it more difficult to screen vulnerable women outside the presence of potential abusers.

"Third, mail-order abortion is undermining state laws enacted to protect unborn life and women.

"Despite the enactment of new pro-life laws in approximately 20 states since the overturning of Roe v. Wade, abortion numbers nationwide are still increasing. The Biden administration removed the in-person dispensing requirement for mifepristone and allowed pharmacies to dispense the drug. Abortion drugs are now being mailed from pro-abortion states into pro-life states, as well as being sent to the United States from overseas.

"Shield laws protecting abortionists are facilitating approximately 14,770 abortions in states with pro-life laws each month, meaning that around 177,240 lives could be saved annually in pro-life states if their laws were respected. State governments attempting to protect life are being undermined by abortion drugs mailed in from outside their borders.

"The FDA is central to this system because it is the federal agency responsible for the approval and protocol governing mifepristone, the most common drug used to kill children in the womb and the only drug designed with abortion as its primary purpose.

"We are told that the FDA is conducting an ongoing study of mifepristone. However, that study has supposedly been ongoing for nearly two years.

"The question is straightforward: Will Dr. Overton at least agree to revert to the policy in place before the Biden administration, a policy that provided at least some minimal safeguards and medical oversight for women until that elusive review is complete?"

text:
🇺🇸🇨🇳 Xi Arrives in Washington With Stronger Hand as Trump Faces Iran War and Economic Pressure

WASHINGTON — Chinese President Xi Jinping arrived in the United States for a high-stakes summit with President Donald Trump carrying significant economic and diplomatic leverage, as the American leader confronts an Iran war, domestic political pressure and growing concerns over the US economy.

Trump personally welcomed Xi and his wife, Peng Liyuan, at Joint Base Andrews on Wednesday, an unusually elaborate gesture for the Chinese leader. Trump and First Lady Melania Trump greeted the couple on the tarmac before the two presidents watched a military ceremony that included two B-1 bombers roaring overhead.

The spectacle demonstrated the importance Washington attaches to Xi’s visit. But behind the red carpet lies a difficult negotiating environment for Trump.

Reuters reported ahead of the summit that China’s international trade position has strengthened since the leaders last met, while Trump has been constrained by the costly conflict with Iran, falling approval ratings and pressure on American consumers.

China’s export machine has continued expanding despite Washington’s efforts to reduce dependence on Chinese manufacturing. Chinese exports recently rose sharply, while the country’s trade surplus is on course to challenge last year’s record of roughly $1.2 trillion.

Trump, meanwhile, urgently needs economic stability. The Iran conflict has contributed to energy and inflation concerns, while the benchmark 10-year US Treasury yield was close to 5% this week.

That gives Beijing room to resist American demands on trade, technology and Iran.

China also retains substantial leverage through its dominance of rare-earth processing and supplies critical to American manufacturing and advanced technology. Rare-earth access remains one of the central disputes surrounding the summit.

Washington and Beijing have already agreed to extend their tariff truce, preventing an immediate return to a damaging escalation in their trade confrontation.

The contrast surrounding Xi’s arrival was therefore striking: Trump offered military honours, a red carpet and a rare personal airport greeting, while Xi arrived representing a China increasingly confident that economic resilience has strengthened its negotiating position.

For Trump, the summit is an opportunity to demonstrate that his confrontational foreign policy can still deliver agreements. For Xi, there appears to be considerably less urgency to concede.

text:
Tajani’s UN Speech: Italy Defends International Law, Selectively.
My analysis of the Italian Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister’s #UNGA81 address: “Against the Law of the Strongest, We Choose the Strength of the Law.”
NEW YORK “Against the law of the strongest, we choose the strength of the law. Against the politics of force, we choose the force of politics.”
With this declaration of principle, Italy’s Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister @Antonio_Tajani brought Italy’s voice to the 81st United Nations General Assembly on Wednesday evening, shortly before 9 p.m.
It was a speech built around peace and the need to preserve an international system based on rules at a time when, according to the figures cited by Tajani, the number of armed conflicts around the world has risen from 56 last year to 61.
“We must not become accustomed to war,” he warned, citing Pope Leo XIV. “We refuse to resign ourselves to it.”
In this respect, Tajani’s speech closely echoed one of the central themes of UN Secretary-General @antonioguterres’ address: the relationship between power, law and the rules of the international system.
#Guterres had framed the question with unusual clarity: will power be governed by law or by force, by cooperation or coercion? Peace, he argued, requires power to be restrained by law, because force cannot become the final arbiter of people’s lives, rights and futures.
#Tajani condensed much the same idea into the contrast between “the law of the strongest” and “the strength of the law.” He also offered a stark diagnosis of the international order created after World War II: “That balance has been broken.”
#Ukraine, the Middle East, the Gulf, Sudan and the #Sahel — but also trade wars, artificial intelligence and hybrid threats — are, in his telling, different fronts of the same transformation.
Italy’s answer is a renewed commitment to multilateralism and to a United Nations that, Tajani said, cannot simply “record the divisions of the present,” but must overcome its paralysis and limitations and once again become the place where conflict gives way to diplomacy.
“Italy believes in this institution, in its value, in its centrality,” he said, describing peace as “the North Star of Italian foreign policy.”
But this is also where the speech becomes more interesting.
When Tajani moves from principles to identifying those who violate them, Italy’s language becomes more selective. Russia is explicitly named. So is Iran. The United States is never mentioned.
That omission is difficult to miss after Donald Trump’s speech from the very same podium just one day earlier. The American president openly celebrated the return of American power and declared that, when Washington considers its vital national interests threatened, the United States is prepared to use its “unmatched military might.” He also rejected what he described as attempts at “global control,” including in the governance of artificial intelligence.
Tajani’s alternative - a world governed by “shared rules” rather than “the law of the strongest” - therefore hangs over the speech as an implicit contrast that is never allowed to become an explicit criticism of Washington.
Perhaps this is simply the measure of Italian diplomatic realism: a clear defense of #multilateralism and #internationallaw that stops short of directly challenging Italy’s most important ally. (Continue)
