text:
When AI Decides If My Patient Gets Their Medication | Cynthia Chen-Joea DO & MPH & FAAFP & DABOM, Psychology Today

AI driven insurance denials are hurting patients and burning out physicians.

Key points

- AI models used by insurers have been shown to deny care at rates up to 16 times higher than typical review.

- Patients often don't realize a denial can be appealed, and the delay can result in poorer patient health.

- Physicians and staff spend an average of 13 hours a week on prior authorizations, fueling burnout.

- California now bars insurers from denying care using AI alone, but most states still lack that protection.

---

As a physician, one of my most exhausting challenges isn't diagnosing illness or building treatment plans. It's fighting insurance companies. I've lost count of the hours my team and I spend battling insurers on behalf of our patients.

Take Patient A, who has uncontrolled diabetes and needs a GLP-1 medication, now widely recognized as a first line treatment for diabetes and weight loss, right behind metformin. There was no contraindication, no missing documentation, and no clinical reasoning for denial. The claim was rejected anyway, likely due to the algorithm driven tools insurance companies increasingly rely on now. These AI models have been shown to deny care at rates as much as 16 times higher than typical review.

Using AI to automatically deny claims create major barriers between patients and their much needed and sometimes lifesaving medications. Patients don't always come back right away. Sometimes it's two or three months later, after they got a rejection letter, assuming that was the final word. They move on with their busy lives, never knowing they could appeal or that we could help them do so.

Only about one in ten denials ever gets appealed, and it's not because the other nine in ten were correct. It's because appealing takes time, paperwork, and persistence that a sick or busy patient often doesn't have. By the time we see the patient again, some have ended up in the ED with the exact complication the medication was supposed to prevent.

When we are notified of the denial or do catch it in time, the work falls on us to appeal, submit prior authorizations, write letters, sit on hold for hours on the phone, resubmit paperwork, and escalate claims. Physicians and our staff spend an average of 13 hours a week on prior authorizations alone, and nearly nine in 10 of us say the process itself is contributing to burnout. Sometimes we win, sometimes we don't, but either way, every step drains time, energy, and emotional bandwidth from physicians like myself, our staff, and our patients. This process erodes the trust between medicine and the people it's supposed to serve.

These practices have become an unethical pattern that impedes patient health. They are now the subject of major lawsuits against large insurance companies. The claims allege that insurers deployed flawed AI tools that produce batch denials with very high error rates, overriding treating physicians' decisions without human clinical review. One claim suggested that insurance companies did this and banked on patient fatigue to avoid paying out. In one legal case, the AI tool used by the insurance company was found to have a 90 percent error rate, with more than 80 percent of its denials reversed on appeal. That means the algorithm was getting it wrong almost nine times out of 10, and it is still deciding whether a patient should get their medication.

There are some regulatory shifts already underway, and they offer real reason for hope. State and federal regulators are pushing to ban automated, sole AI health insurance denials, requiring a licensed physician to sign off and a human clinician involved throughout the review process. A California law, effective January 2026, already prohibits payers from making coverage decisions based solely on AI, and CMS has similarly clarified that Medicare Advantage plans cannot base coverage determinations purely on algorithmic decisions. Before a Medicare Advantage plan can issue a denial, a physician or other qualified healthcare professional must review whether it is appropriate. This is important because it puts a real person, someone trained to weigh a patient's full history, back at the center of a decision that can mean the difference between a patient getting their medication or ending up in the ED.

Physicians and patients need a faster, more transparent insurance review process, one where clinical judgment is not treated as an afterthought to an algorithm's verdict. This systemic failure doesn't just affect individual patient health. It contributes to physician burnout and erodes trust in our entire healthcare system, and it's a problem we can no longer afford to leave unregulated. We need insurers to remember that behind every denied claim is a real person, a patient waiting for a medication that could save their life.

I didn't go into medicine to spend my afternoons on hold with an insurance company. I went into it to take care of people, and it's time our healthcare system let physicians do exactly that.

text:
In 1928, Walt Disney traveled to New York expecting more money. He returned without his most successful character, most of his animators, or the legal right to continue the series keeping his studio alive.

Disney had produced 26 cartoons featuring Oswald the Lucky Rabbit. But one detail buried inside the contract changed everything: Disney did not own Oswald.

When he requested a larger budget, distributor Charles Mintz offered less and revealed that he had already recruited most of Disney’s animation team. Disney could accept the deal or walk away from his own creation.

He walked.

On the train back to California, Disney began developing a replacement with Ub Iwerks. Months later, Mickey Mouse appeared in Steamboat Willie and became the foundation of an entertainment empire.

Disney learned that creating something valuable means little if someone else owns it.

Decades later, standing in front of the camera, he reduced that entire lesson to one sentence:

“I only hope that we never lose sight of one thing, that it was all started by a mouse.”

In 2006, Disney finally recovered Oswald by trading sportscaster Al Michaels’ NBC contract for the character’s rights.

The character Disney lost created the rule.

The character he owned created the empire.

text:
Herbert Marcuse – The Man Who Gave the Student Riots Their Philosophy.

Not a politician and not a street organizer. A 70 year old German born professor with a thick accent was teaching at the University of California San Diego during the height of the Vietnam War. While his Frankfurt School colleagues wrote obscure and dense philosophy in quiet libraries, Marcuse wrote the explosive handbook that turned bored Western college students into a militant ideological army. In 1968, the three ultimate symbols of student revolution were named 3Ms Marx Mao and Marcuse.

1. His central crisis was simple. Marx's working class had failed to revolt. By the 1960s, Western factory workers had cars, televisions and suburban homes. They were not angry because they were comfortable. Marcuse argued in One Dimensional Man in 1964 that modern capitalism had bribed the working class into passive submission with consumer goods. If the traditional working class was integrated into the system, the revolution needed a brand new driver.

2. He identified the new revolutionary agent as marginal groups and students. Since the working class was corrupted by prosperity, Marcuse pointed to university students, racial minorities, radical intellectuals and outcasts, which were groups still alienated by mainstream society. He realized that the university campus, and not the factory floor, was the true pressure cooker for the modern left.

3. His most controversial contribution was a 1965 essay titled Repressive Tolerance. He argued that traditional Western tolerance of allowing all viewpoints equal freedom of speech was actually a trick that maintained the status quo. His solution was radical, because to achieve a truly just society one must practice discriminatory tolerance. That meant suppressing conservative, right wing or traditionalist ideas while giving total freedom to revolutionary left wing ideas. It was the original theoretical blueprint for what we call modern cancel culture and speech codes.

4. The CIA had unwittingly helped build his career. During World War II, Marcuse worked for the OSS, which was the predecessor to the CIA, as an analyst analyzing intelligence on Nazi Germany. The US government paid a neo Marxist philosopher to study state power, and Marcuse took those insights into the mechanical vulnerabilities of Western institutions straight back into academia.

5. When the student uprisings of May 1968 paralyzed Paris, and street protests rocked West Berlin and Berkeley, the rioters carried banners reading Marx Mao Marcuse. He became an instant media celebrity, and a target of intense hatred from the American Right. California Governor Ronald Reagan openly demanded Marcuse be fired from the University of California, and local veterans groups offered a 20000 dollar bounty to buy out his teaching contract just to get him off campus.

6. Marcuse refused to bow out. He received death threats, and had to go into hiding under armed protection, but he continued lecturing to thousands of cheering students. He died in Germany in 1979 at the age of 81, having successfully mentored students like Angela Davis, who would go on to lead the next generation of activist movements.

7. Look at today's university campuses, modern corporate sensitivity training and the debates over what speech should be tolerated or canceled. The idea that speech itself can be violence and that opposing views must be denied a platform, is not a modern internet invention. It is Herbert Marcuse's 1965 essay running on a 60 year loop.

DOJ: UC San Francisco Medical School Discriminates Against Whites and Asians | Alana Mastrangelo, Breitbart

The University of California, San Francisco (UCSF), an elite medical school, illegally discriminated against white and Asian applicants according to the DOJ. As a result, millions of dollars in federal funds could be at risk.

The DOJ is accusing officials at the top medical school of illegally discriminating against white and Asian applicants, giving black candidates almost 13 times better odds of admission than white students with similar qualifications in 2025, according to a report by the California Post.

“Unfortunately, at UCSF Medical School, MCAT scores and undergraduate GPAs have taken a backseat to race,” Harmeet K. Dhillon, assistant attorney general in charge of the DOJ’s Civil Rights Division, told the newspaper.

“Aspiring doctors should be admitted based on their qualifications,” Dhillon added. “The Supreme Court has spoken clearly — federally funded medical schools may not admit students based on misguided and illegal notions of diversity.”

Dhillon reportedly sent a blistering nine-page letter to UCSF Chancellor Sam Hawgood on Tuesday, warning the medical school to reach a resolution or face a lawsuit and other enforcement actions.

On average, black and and Hispanic students admitted from 2023 to 2025 posted lower scores and undergraduate GPAs than the typical white and Asian applicants UCSF rejected, the DOJ found.

Last year, the university admitted seven percent of black applicants and 4.8 percent of hispanic applicants, while accepting a mere 1.7 percent of white applicants and two percent of asian applicants, federal officials say.

Meanwhile, admitted white students that year averaged a 519 MCAT — the 96th percentile — and had a 3.95 GPA, while Asian students averaged a 518 — the 95th percentile — with a 3.93 GPA. Admitted black students averaged a 514 and a 3.86 GPA, with Hispanic students averaging a 513 and a 3.88 GPA.

“In other words, the average admitted black and Hispanic student academically underperformed the average rejected white and Asian student,” Dhillon wrote.

The Justice Department determined that UCSF “deliberately discriminated” based on race in its admissions process for the incoming classes of 2023, 2024 and 2025, in violation of Title VI of the Civil Rights Act.

The letter also noted that the university receives nearly $1 billion in federal funding annually, including a $5 million grant from the DOJ.

UCSF officials pushed back on Tuesday, maintaining that they “disagree” with the Justice Department’s findings.

“Admission to the UCSF School of Medicine is among the most selective in the country,” university officials reportedly said. “Every applicant is evaluated through a rigorous, individualized review process that prioritizes academic excellence.”

“Academic achievement is fundamental to that review. Grades, prior coursework, and MCAT scores are important measures of an applicant’s readiness for a UCSF medical education,” they added.

Officials with the elite medical school went on to claim that other factors such as “clinical experience, research, service,” and “leadership” are used to identify future physicians.

But federal officials say UCSF used application essays, hardship questions, interviews, and other supposedly race-neutral criteria as stand-ins for race, allowing the school to identify and favor applicants from groups it considers underrepresented in medicine.

The DOJ pointed to two pipeline programs that offer specialized admission tracks, scholarships, and other assistance.

Black, Hispanic and other designated students made up 89 percent of enrollment in one of the programs during the 2024-25 academic year, the Justice Department added.

UCSF reportedly turned over admissions data to the DOJ — which started its investigation in March — after receiving multiple extensions. However, federal officials said most of the documents the university sent in were unresponsive.

The Justice Department also noted that the school did not explain the racial gaps in grades and MCAT scores among admitted students.

Dhillon invited UCSF to negotiate changes to its admissions practices and pipeline programs, and gave the university ten days to respond. If no agreement is reached by October 2, federal officials could sue to force compliance, the California Post reported.

UCSF officials asserted, “Academic excellence has always been central to our admissions process,” adding, “We will continue to engage constructively with the department and look forward to resolving this matter.”

text:
Restitution Sentence Affirmed

Psychiatrist Who Was Convicted of Fraud Asked the First Circuit to Reduce his Punishment
Post 4851
Posted on September 24, 2026 by Barry Zalma

Fraud to Private and Public Health Insurers Doesn’t Pay

In United States v. Gustavo Kinrys, Nos. 24-1592, 24-1716, United States Court of Appeals, First Circuit (September 21, 2026) Gustavo Kinrys, a Massachusetts psychiatrist, submitted fraudulent claims to private and public health insurers from 2015 through 2018, including bills for more than 1,000 sessions when he or the purported patient was outside the country. When insurers requested supporting records, he delayed through a fictitious office manager and created false documentation.

A jury convicted Kinrys on fourteen counts. The district court imposed a 99-month sentence, calculated intended loss at slightly more than $19 million based on billed amounts, ordered $6,537,309.59 in restitution, and ordered $6,527,391.19 in forfeiture.

At sentencing, the district court calculated Kinrys’s base offense level to be seven and then added twenty-eight levels-worth of enhancements, including a twenty-level enhancement for the loss amount. This yielded a recommended guideline range of 168 to 210 months for the first seven counts of conviction, and sixty months for the remaining counts. The district court sentenced Kinrys to ninety-nine months in prison on the first seven counts and sixty concurrent months in prison on the remaining counts. It also required Kinrys to pay $6,537,309.59 in restitution and $6,527,391.19 in criminal forfeiture.

LAW:

Under U.S.S.G. § 2B1.1(b)(1), loss is the greater of actual or intended loss. When a scheme is rife with fraud, the billed amount is prima facie evidence of intended loss; the defendant may rebut it with evidence that he intended to obtain less, but the government retains the ultimate burden to prove the enhancement by a preponderance of the evidence. Subjective intent is reviewed for clear error.

Under the Mandatory Victims Restitution Act, restitution compensates victims for actual losses caused by fraud and may not produce a windfall; distinct civil claims against victims are not adjudicated at a criminal restitution hearing.

DISCUSSION:

Kinrys argued that intended loss should equal the roughly $8.3 million he expected under negotiated in-network reimbursement rates rather than the more than $19 million billed, reducing the enhancement from twenty to eighteen levels. He relied on his provider contracts and failure to collect co-pays. He also argued that restitution should be reduced by allegedly legitimate claims for which insurers had not paid him.

ANALYSIS:

The First Circuit held that the district court did not clearly err in using billed amounts. Although Kinrys’s in-network status supported his position, other evidence supported an intent to obtain as much as possible: he sued insurers for billed charges and greater damages, sometimes received full billed amounts, retained payments exceeding contract rates, and offered no contrary evidence at sentencing beyond counsel’s argument.

His failure to collect co-pays was not persuasive because collection could have exposed the scheme or discouraged patients. The restitution offset also failed because the order included only fraudulent claims, while the unpaid claims were separate, disputed reimbursement requests affected by unmet preauthorization or documentation requirements. Any entitlement to those payments belonged in a civil or administrative proceeding, not the restitution hearing.

CONCLUSION:

The First Circuit affirmed both the intended-loss calculation and the restitution order.

A criminal restitution hearing, where distinct, unrelated, and contested billing is not before the court, is not the proper venue to resolve such claims. Accordingly, the First Circuit affirmed the district court’s decision to decline offsetting the restitution order based on Kinrys’s allegedly legitimate claims.

ZALMA OPINION

Psychiatrist convicted of insurance fraud and ordered to make restitution tried to reduce the order or eliminate it unsuccessfully to the First Circuit Court of Appeal. His crime was obvious, the amount he obtained from defrauded insurers and the government was proved by the DOJ and the trial court’s decision was affirmed.

Every child should be able to play alongside their peers. 

We’re highlighting Hicks Park Inclusive Playground in West Memphis, a space intentionally designed to create a safe, and accessible place for children of all abilities. The playground offers ground-level play and mobility-friendly features, giving children with disabilities more opportunities to explore and play alongside their peers.

What makes this space especially meaningful is that West Memphis didn’t simply add an accessible feature to an existing playground. The city created a purpose-built inclusive playground with the goal of making sure children with disabilities have a place to enjoy the outdoors and be part of their community.

Hicks Park is a reminder that inclusive recreation doesn’t have to be complicated. It starts with making sure children and families have a place where they can show up, play, connect, and feel welcome.

We’re grateful to the City of West Memphis for investing in a playground where every child gets to be part of the fun.

text:
Gov. Braun Announces 300 High-Wage Jobs at New Amazon Manufacturing Facility

GREENWOOD, Ind. – Indiana Governor Mike Braun announced today that Amazon will invest more than $100 million to establish a new manufacturing facility in central Indiana, creating 300 skilled manufacturing and engineering jobs by the end of 2028.

"Amazon's decision to locate this facility in Indiana is a powerful testament to the strength of our manufacturing workforce, our world-class infrastructure, and our commitment to creating an environment where businesses of all sizes can grow and thrive," said Gov. Braun. "This $100 million investment will bring 300 high-paying, skilled jobs to the community that offer Hoosier families real careers in advanced manufacturing. Indiana has always been a state that builds things, and Amazon's investment reinforces our position as the nation's leader in manufacturing."

Amazon will purchase and equip a 585,000-square-foot facility at 1175 Collins Road in Greenwood to produce products that power the company’s fulfillment and robotics network across North America. The facility, which is expected to launch in 2028, will integrate advanced fabrication, robotic welding, automated powder coating and assembly capabilities under one roof – supported by AWS and AI-powered smart manufacturing systems and robotics.

New roles coming to the facility include Computer Numerical Control (CNC) operators, welders, powder coating technicians, assemblers, manufacturing engineers, quality assurance specialists, controls engineers and program managers. The positions will offer average salaries of nearly $100,000 annually.

“We're thrilled to bring 300 advanced manufacturing jobs to Greenwood, Indiana, and to continue investing in growth and opportunities across the state," said Holly Sullivan, Vice President of Economic Development at Amazon. "This facility represents a significant investment in the Indianapolis community that will create jobs with a median salary well above the regional average. Indiana has a world-class manufacturing workforce and business-friendly environment, and we’re excited to continue creating opportunities for people across the state and helping them learn the new skills they need to take advantage of those opportunities.”

Amazon selected the Greenwood site based on Indiana’s unmatched manufacturing workforce, competitive cost structure, world-class logistics infrastructure and business-friendly environment. The central Indiana region also offers exceptional access to manufacturing talent, including a pipeline of more than 2,500 industrial engineering graduates annually from institutions across the state, including Purdue University, Rose-Hulman Institute of Technology and Ivy Tech Community College.

The state’s central location and logistics infrastructure – ranked 13th nationally for transportation – provide direct access to Amazon’s fulfillment network across North America, enabling efficient distribution of manufactured products to facilities nationwide.

“Indiana’s commitment to creating a pro-growth business climate with an unmatched workforce continues to pay dividends for Hoosiers, attracting new investments and most importantly, high-paying career opportunities for Hoosiers,” said Indiana Secretary of Commerce Chuck Goodrich. “Amazon’s new facility will support our state’s future-focused advanced manufacturing sector, which supports more than 518,000 jobs, putting Hoosiers at the center of making the products that power the world.”

Amazon has invested more than $40 billion in Indiana and created more than 27,000 Hoosier jobs since first launching operations in the state in 2008. What started with a single fulfillment center has grown into one of the company’s most significant operational footprints in the country – spanning fulfillment and sortation centers, robotic facilities, delivery stations, same-day delivery sites, data centers, wind and solar farms, and carbon-free energy projects.

The company is also a partner in the state’s workforce training and development initiatives. Since 2019, more than 4,200 Amazon employees in Indiana have participated in the company’s free education and skills training programs through Amazon’s Career Choice program, opening new pathways to higher-paying careers and fulfilling opportunities. Thirty-two education partners across Indiana participate in the program, which pre-pays tuition for employees pursuing in-demand certifications and degrees – from cloud computing to nursing to skilled trades. In addition, Amazon offers training for members of communities throughout state, including Amazon Future Engineer for K-12 students and AWS Educate for early-career talent - part of the company's Future Ready 2030 initiative to prepare 50 million people with the skills needed to succeed in the future of work.

“We want projects that bring real, long-term value to our community, and 300 skilled jobs with average salaries of nearly $100,000 a year is exactly the kind of opportunity we want to see,” said Greenwood Mayor Mark W. Myers. “Amazon’s investment reflects the kind of high-quality development that strengthens our economy, creates meaningful careers and adds to Greenwood’s future. We are proud that Amazon has chosen Greenwood for this major investment and look forward to welcoming this new advanced manufacturing operation to our city.”

Amazon’s Greenwood facility represents the next evolution of that commitment: bringing advanced manufacturing capabilities in-house to strengthen Amazon's supply chain, create high-paying skilled jobs, and invest in the communities that have supported the company's growth.

The legal fight over the White House media ban just got thornier. Worldwide News Network's Stacy Lyn is in Washington with the latest.: “While a federal judge ordered the Trump administration to restore White House access to journalists from CNN, MSN, and Politico, some still remained barred this morning. A Politico reporter had his press pass confiscated by the Secret Service while trying to get in. And CNN says some of its journalists were also denied entry. Judge Timothy Kelly put the ban on hold for 14 days while the outlets challenge it, ordering the White House to restore their press credentials. Stacy Lynn, Worldwide News Network, Washington. ”

The White House is about to hold a state welcoming ceremony for Chinese President Xi Jinping this morning. After meeting with the Chinese Vice Premier, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced the U.S. and China have agreed to extend their bilateral trade truce by two months. Bessent told Fox News what the U.S. would like to see next.: “There are some deliverables that have not been perfect on the Chinese side, so we also want to see now that we've sat down and told them our expectations to see if over the coming months they can be a bit more fulsome in enacting the agreement. ”

Attorney General Todd Blanche posted on social media this morning that the Trump administration will appeal to the Supreme Court, after a lower court rejected a policy that allowed the quick deportation of migrants to countries other than their own. The group Human Rights First says the administration has sent more than 25 thousand migrants to at least 29 third countries, in many cases Mexico.

From North Carolina to Maine, coastal communities are getting ready for a rare September nor'easter. This public works employee is in Seaside Heights, New Jersey.: “We're out in the streets cleaning all the storm sewers so that if we do get tidal flooding, the water has someplace to go. ”
Waves out in the open Atlantic could swell to 25 feet.

President Trump is rethinking his plan to ban diesel exports as a way to lower record high diesel prices.
NewsNation's Alicia Nieves reports there are several ideas on the table.: “We're now hearing also louder calls from Congress to take action. Iowa Republican Ashley Hinson is calling for the House to return to Washington immediately, posting on next that she wants Congress to still consider pausing diesel exports, suspending the gas tax, expanding E-15 and biodiesel, and even creating a diesel relief program for truckers and farmers. There's a lot of talk about options here, but not necessarily seeing a ton of action in terms of bringing prices down. ”
Diesel is averaging 6.51 a gallon this morning, a penny below the record it set yesterday.

The FDA has approved Eli Lilly's once-weekly insulin injection "Onswik" for adults with type 2 diabetes. it could offer an alternative to daily shots.

The Navy now says eight sailors in the U.S.S. Lincoln Strike Group attempted suicide during its record-long deployment to the Middle East earlier this year. One of them jumped off the aircraft carrier in August, but was rescued. Another tried to jump off in March, but was stopped by his shipmates.

text:
SAF Files Reply Brief in Case Challenging Maryland's Glock Ban

The Second Amendment Foundation (SAF) and its partners have filed a reply in support of their motion for preliminary injunction in Bathras v. Moore, SAF's challenge to the Maryland Glock ban signed into law by Gov. Wes Moore earlier this year.

SAF filed the lawsuit in May immediately after Gov. Moore signed Senate Bill 334 into law. The new law states that a person "…may not manufacture, sell, offer for sale, purchase, receive, or transfer a machine gun convertible pistol." It further defines a "machine gun convertible pistol" as a firearm that contains a cruciform trigger bar. Unique to Glock and Glock-style handguns, a cruciform trigger bar is a pivotal component to the overall design of the handgun. SB 334 purports to ban these popular and completely legal handguns in an effort to prevent their already-illegal conversion into machineguns. The ban goes into effect on Jan. 1, 2027.

"Handguns are protected by the Second Amendment, and Glock-style handguns are overwhelmingly popular for everyday civilians, police and military users." said SAF Senior Director of Legal Operations Bill Sack. "The contrived premise of this bill is that Glocks must be banned because criminals can alter them into machineguns. But that conversion is already illegal and so is the possession of the parts necessary to do it – upon threat of stiff federal incarceration. But Maryland lawmakers passed a bill, not aimed at the tiny fraction of Glock owners who illegally alter their firearms, but rather at everyone who would choose one of the most popular brands of handguns on the market with which to exercise their rights."

As noted in the brief, "…the State's argument is not that 'machinegun convertible pistols' are 'excessively dangerous' as sold. Rather, the State's argument is that machinegun converted pistols are. But it has no support for the principle that an ordinary handgun, which the Supreme Court has already held is protected in Heller, can be considered 'dangerous and unusual' because it could be turned into a different kind of weapon by adding an illegal part or making other criminal alterations to the handgun." SAF is joined in Bathras v. Moore by Atlantic Guns, the National Rifle Association, Firearms Policy Coalition and two private citizens.

"Maryland is known as the Free State, yet Marylanders are being told that a major chunk of the commercially available handgun market is off limits for them," said SAF founder and Executive Vice President Alan M. Gottlieb. "If residents in Maryland were truly free, then this absurd law would never have made it past the inception stage. Instead, it's taken the filing of a lawsuit to ensure the Second Amendment rights of those living in Maryland are defended from idealogue lawmakers who think they can decide which constitutional rights citizens in the state can freely exercise."

For more information visit https://t.co/vK9m9gMfR1.

First Lady Melania Trump Releases Details on the State Dinner with His Excellency Xi Jinping, President of The People’s Republic of China, and Madame Peng Liyuan:

President Donald J. Trump and First Lady Melania Trump will welcome His Excellency Xi Jinping, President of The People’s Republic of China, and Madame Peng Liyuan for a State Dinner in the East Room of the White House this evening. The First Lady led the preparations for the dinner, which will be attended by the official delegations as well as business leaders and government officials.

MENU
The menu showcases American ingredients with subtle Chinese influence, bringing the culinary traditions of both nations together. The meal begins with a toast of Schramsberg "Blanc De Noir," honoring the historic “Toast to Peace” shared by President Nixon and Premier Zhou Enlai in Beijing in 1972. The same American sparkling wine served at that historic gathering continues to be enjoyed at White House functions today.

First Course Yellow Squash Velouté Wild Mushroom Fricassée Crispy Pancetta Scallion Oil
The first course offers a refined and silky-smooth velouté made of sweet yellow squash. This course is gently blended to highlight its delicate seasonal flavors of earthy wild mushrooms, sautéed with fresh herbs. Together, these ingredients create a rich fricassee, complemented by crispy pancetta for a savory and smoky contrast. A finishing drizzle of scallion oil adds vibrance and a subtle allium brightness to the dish.

Second Course Sesame Crusted Sea Bass Braised Baby Bok Choy Roasted Garden Eggplant Sauce Verte
The second course is prepared delicately with fresh seabass and coated in toasted sesame seeds. This combination creates a fragrant nutty crust while keeping the fish tender. The fish is served with crisp baby bok choy and roasted garden eggplant, creating lightly caramelized flavors. The dish is finished with a vibrant sauce verte of fresh herbs, which add brightness, acidity, and a garden character.

Dessert Vanilla Crémeux & White House Honey Ice Cream Walnut Frangipane Sour Cherry Confit
The dessert course is a smooth vanilla crémeux with a vibrant sour cherry confit center, set a top a rich walnut frangipane. The dessert’s fruit shaped form is complimented by a delicate ice cream made with harvested White House honey.

ENTERTAINMENT
There will be several performances during the formal dinner, which will be headlined by Mr. Christopher Macchio, a classically trained tenor who performed at the 2025 Presidential Inauguration. The evening’s entertainment will feature performances by military musicians from the United States Marines Corps and the United States Army, including “The President’s Own” United States Marine Band, “The Commandant’s Own” United States Marine Drum and Bugle Corps, the United States Army Chorus, and the United States Army Strings.

FLORAL & DÉCOR
The décor for the evening is an expression of warmth and celebration and draws on the color red’s longstanding cultural significance throughout Chinese history. Urns showcase overflowing red blossoms. Tables are dressed in rich red linens and adorned with dahlias and ranunculus. Among the seasonal blooms, the tables feature vermeil from the White House collection. The Reagan State Service is featured on the tables. These details blend Chinese artistry and American tradition together, showcased within the timeless elegance of the White House.

text:
SECTION THREE — What Biden Owns (3/3)
On January 20, 2021, Joe Biden inherited a force of roughly 2,500 U.S. troops in Afghanistan and a withdrawal deadline written into the Doha agreement the previous administration had signed with the Taliban. He did not inherit an order he was required to execute on those exact terms. He inherited options. As sitting president he had the constitutional authority to keep a residual force, to condition any further drawdown on facts on the ground, to change the timeline, or to go to zero. Every one of those choices remained his. The Doha text set a road. It did not drive the vehicle.
General Kenneth F. McKenzie Jr., then commander of U.S. Central Command, testified under oath before the Senate Armed Services Committee on September 28, 2021, that he had recommended maintaining 2,500 troops. He stated the assessment that shaped that recommendation in plain language: “the withdrawal of those forces would lead inevitably to the collapse of the Afghan military forces and, eventually, the Afghan government.” He also told Congress he had recommended a larger residual force — about 4,500 troops — in the fall of 2020, while Donald Trump was still president. The advice was not invented in April 2021 to obstruct an incoming Democratic administration. It was the same operational judgment, offered to two presidents.
Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff General Mark Milley gave substantively the same account under oath. His assessment, he said, had been consistent from the fall of 2020 through the spring of 2021: keep a steady-state force of about 2,500, with room to bounce as high as 3,500, in service of a negotiated, conditions-based outcome rather than a calendar-based exit. Defense Secretary Lloyd Austin would not recite his private recommendation to the president in open session, but he testified that the military’s input “was received” and considered. McKenzie added that he had been present when General Scott Miller, the commander of U.S. Forces–Afghanistan, made the same case directly, and that he was “confident that the president heard all the recommendations and listened to them very thoughtfully.”
Four days after Kabul fell, on August 19, 2021, Biden sat for an interview with George Stephanopoulos. Stephanopoulos put the published reporting to him: top military advisers had wanted about 2,500 troops left in place. Biden first said that was not true, that the advice “was split.” Pressed again on whether anyone had told him to keep 2,500, he answered: “No. No one said that to me that I can recall.” The men who ran the operation later said, under oath, that they had said exactly that, and that he had heard it. An unsworn recollection on television does not outweigh sworn testimony to Congress from the commander of Central Command, the chairman of the Joint Chiefs, and the secretary of defense. Biden went to zero against direct military advice. The public record of what he was told does not support his own account of what he was told.
The April 2021 guidance did not merely set an end date. It capped the force that would remain to protect the diplomatic mission. McKenzie testified that the guidance he received was to complete the withdrawal of U.S. combat forces and plan for a diplomatic security force of “absolutely no more than 650” service members. That number was a civilian policy decision, not a battlefield discovery. It made it militarily impossible to hold three things at once: the embassy in Kabul, Hamid Karzai International Airport, and Bagram Airfield. Austin told Congress that retaining Bagram alone would have required putting as many as 5,000 U.S. troops in harm’s way just to operate and defend it. Once the cap was 650, McKenzie said, “the Bagram option went away.” That is how a twenty-year logistics and air hub, with twin runways and an adjacent detention complex, became expendable on a spreadsheet.
U.S. forces vacated Bagram overnight on July 1–2, 2021. There was no public ceremony. Afghan officers later said they were not told in time. The new Afghan commander of the base, Gen. Mir Asadullah Kohistani, said he confirmed the Americans were gone only around seven o’clock the next morning. In the gap, looters came through the gates. The prison next to the airfield — the Detention Facility in Parwan — held on the order of 5,000 prisoners, including Taliban, al-Qaeda, and Islamic State–Khorasan inmates. The United States had transferred the facility to Afghan control years earlier, in 2013, but the base around it was the reason the prison remained a controlled site rather than an unlocked warehouse of militants. When the United States left the base in the dark, it left the prison’s future to an Afghan force that was already losing districts by the week, with no public handoff plan adequate to what would happen if that force failed. Six weeks later the Taliban walked in and emptied it.
Twenty-three career diplomats at Embassy Kabul used the State Department’s protected Dissent Channel on July 13, 2021 — a full month before the capital fell — to warn that the Afghan military was collapsing faster than official assessments held and to urge immediate acceleration of evacuation planning, including an airlift for at-risk Afghans. Dissent cables are rare by design. They exist so that officers on the ground can tell Washington it is wrong without being punished for saying so. Reporting at the time, later confirmed in congressional inquiry, established that the cable reached Secretary of State Antony Blinken. The administration announced Operation Allies Refuge the next day. Evacuation flights did not become an urgent, scaled operation until the Taliban were already at the gates of Kabul. National Security Adviser Jake Sullivan, according to contemporaneous reporting, learned of the cable’s existence from the press a month after it was sent. A National Security Council Deputies process that should have treated evacuation parameters as an emergency did not convene at the level the moment required until August.
The Non-Combatant Evacuation Operation was not authorized until August 14, 2021 — one day before the government it was meant to extract people from ceased to exist. McKenzie later told Congress the decision to conduct a NEO “rested with the Department of State and they made that decision on 14 August.” An Axios report on the NSC Deputies Small Group meeting that afternoon — 3:30 to 4:30 p.m. Washington time, while Taliban columns were closing on the capital — showed senior officials still assigning basic tasks: identify transit countries, notify local Afghan staff to register interest in relocation, work out who had priority. Hours later President Ashraf Ghani fled. The embassy burned documents. Helicopters lifted staff to the civilian airport that was now the only way out of the country, because Bagram was already gone. McKenzie’s later judgment was not ambiguous: the events of mid- and late August were “the direct result of delaying the initiation of the NEO for several months, in fact, until we were in extremis, and the Taliban had overrun the country.”
On August 26, 2021, a suicide bomber detonated at Abbey Gate, the single crowded point of access that the 650-troop cap and the Bagram withdrawal had left available. Thirteen U.S. service members were killed — eleven Marines, one soldier, and one sailor — along with roughly 160 Afghan civilians. More than forty other Americans were wounded. The attacker was later identified by the Defense Department, after a supplemental review of the original investigation, as Abdul Rahman al-Logari, an Islamic State–Khorasan member since 2016. U.S. officials and subsequent reporting established that he was among the thousands released when the Taliban seized Parwan and Pul-e-Charkhi in mid-August, after the United States had already vacated the air base that sat beside Parwan. He had been in custody for years, including over a foiled plot in New Delhi. Eleven days after that prison emptied, he walked a vest to the one gate America still held. A later Army review concluded ISIS-K had other bombers available and that the attack was not preventable at the tactical level by the Marines standing the gate. That finding, if accepted, does not erase the prior policy choice that put thirteen Americans on a single choke point next to a released prison population, with Bagram already surrendered and no second airfield to spread the risk.
What Was Left Behind, and Why
The Department of Defense estimated that approximately $7.12 billion in U.S.-funded Afghan military equipment was still in Afghan government inventories when the government collapsed — aircraft, tactical vehicles, weapons, munitions, communications gear, and night-vision equipment among it. That figure was not a journalist’s guess. It appeared in a congressionally mandated Pentagon accounting and was repeated by the Defense Department Inspector General and, later, by the Special Inspector General for Afghanistan Reconstruction. Of the $18.6 billion in equipment the United States had provided the Afghan National Defense and Security Forces from 2005 to August 2021, $7.12 billion remained in the country when U.S. forces completed their withdrawal on August 30. The operational condition of a large share of that inventory was unknown then and is unknown now. The Pentagon reported more than 40,000 of some 96,000 provided vehicles still in country, including about 12,000 Humvees, with their condition listed as unknown. More than 300,000 of 427,300 provided weapons remained. Aircraft worth $923.3 million remained; some at Hamid Karzai International Airport were demilitarized before the last U.S. aircraft left. Night-vision devices, radios, and biometric kits were left in volumes the department could describe by category and could not then retrieve. SIGAR later wrote that this taxpayer-funded stock, together with the facilities built to house it, formed “the core of the Taliban security apparatus.”
That was the Afghan army’s kit. Separately, the State Department’s own inspector general examined what Embassy Kabul did with the sensitive security assets that belonged to the United States government rather than to Kabul’s doomed ministries. Audit Report AUD-GEER-25-01, issued in October 2024, found that Embassy Kabul abandoned 26 percent of its firearms and 63 percent of its armored-vehicle fleet during the evacuation. Many of those assets were left intact. Some were disabled only by ad hoc, improvised methods — sand in fuel tanks, dirt in engines — that the OIG judged insufficient to prevent capture. The post had shipped out a sliver of its firearms in the spring of 2021, on the order of 4 percent, and had destroyed or shipped 37 percent of its armored vehicles in advance of a possible drawdown. It did not draw the inventory down to what a collapse would require. When the collapse arrived, the surplus was still there.
The OIG did not treat this as the unavoidable fog of a bad week. It named institutional failures inside the Biden State Department that preceded the fall of Kabul and made the outcome more likely no matter how fast the Taliban moved in August. Embassy Kabul held a volume of sensitive security equipment that significantly exceeded daily operational need. The OIG called the pattern “retention bias”: the tendency of a high-threat post, scored that way under the Department’s Vehicle Allocation Methodology, to accumulate armored vehicles and protective gear beyond what usage justified, without a plan for what happens to the surplus if the post has to leave in hours rather than months. Ammunition stocks sat at more than twice Defensive Equipment and Armored Vehicle Division guidelines. A 2020 management estimate had already flagged roughly half the armored-vehicle fleet as excess. The scoring system rewarded keeping the vehicles. Nobody built the off-ramp.
The post had no adequate, pre-formulated disposition or emergency-destruction plan built for a rapid-collapse scenario. Existing emergency language did not specify tools, timelines, or alternatives. There was no excavator on hand to crush vehicles. Concrete for denial was not sitting ready. Security personnel received inadequate guidance and insufficient training in the emergency destruction procedures that did exist. That is why, when the moment came, they were reduced to improvising. An inspector general does not write that sentence about a post that was ready.
The OIG drew a direct contrast with Embassy Kyiv six months later. When Kyiv suspended operations in February 2022, staff removed all sensitive security assets before the post closed. Special protective equipment was shipped. Armored vehicles were driven out. A senior Kyiv security official acknowledged that Kyiv’s smaller baseline inventory was part of that success, and that a Kabul-speed collapse might have forced abandonment there too. The OIG did not let that caveat swallow the finding. The training failures, the missing written disposition plans, the absence of tripwires for when to stop shipping and start destroying, and the retention-bias scoring that stuffed Kabul with surplus kit were institutional. They were not a function of Kabul’s evacuation being larger. An embassy that had done the planning got its equipment out. An embassy that had hoarded the equipment then abandoned much of it intact.
The failure did not end when the last aircraft left. The Defensive Equipment and Armored Vehicle Division, inside the Bureau of Diplomatic Security, failed to fully and accurately account for the sensitive security assets that were exfiltrated from Kabul. During reconciliation it prematurely declared certain assets abandoned that were later found and recovered — in some cases more than a year later, into 2023. Local records at Kabul were lost when servers were destroyed. The Department’s inventory system was not editable by post security officers, so accountability depended on spreadsheets that no longer existed. The result was a records failure severe enough that the Department could not say with confidence, in the aftermath, which equipment had been lost, which had been stolen, and which had simply been misplaced in its own system. The OIG traced part of this to a hole in the Foreign Affairs Manual: there was no formal requirement that the Department conduct a comprehensive post-suspension asset reconciliation at all. Policy required reporting missing property within fifteen days under ordinary circumstances. It did not contemplate a post that had been emptied by helicopter while hostile forces took the city.
The OIG issued twelve recommendations. They are not atmospheric. They are a punch list of what did not exist in usable form on August 15, 2021.
One: reevaluate the Vehicle Allocation Methodology and rewrite the criticality scoring system to eliminate the retention bias toward armored vehicles at high-threat posts, including by requiring justifications for keeping low-usage, high-criticality vehicles.
Two: require overseas posts to assess, periodically, whether their holdings of special protective equipment and hazardous materials match actual usage and operational need, and to cut the surplus when they do not.
Three: put into the Foreign Affairs Handbook a requirement that posts maintain written disposition plans, including emergency destruction plans, for special protective equipment, hazardous materials, and armored vehicles.
Four: issue detailed guidance on how to write those plans — which stakeholders to involve, how to plan for more than one evacuation scenario, how long shipping actually takes, how long destruction actually takes, what tools and vendors must be on hand, where every asset sits, and what tripwire ends the effort to ship and starts the effort to destroy.
Five: require each post’s Emergency Action Committee to review and approve those plans on a schedule, and to update them when the facts change.
Six: revise emergency destruction procedures for special protective equipment so they describe methods that can actually be executed inside a compressed timeline, with the equipment and the minutes each step requires, and send that guidance to every overseas post.
Seven: write the same kind of usable emergency guidance for hazardous materials.
Eight: revise armored-vehicle disposal procedures for an exigent evacuation — estimated times, priority of steps, which steps may be skipped when there is no time, and visual aids for every model the Department maintains worldwide.
Nine: train post security personnel on those practices before the crisis, not during it.
Ten: write into the Foreign Affairs Manual a requirement that, after any suspension of operations, the Department conduct a comprehensive reconciliation of special protective equipment and armored vehicles, with a named responsible official and a deadline, and with a duty to follow every lead on where the property went.
Eleven: require a report to the Department’s Accountable Property Officer stating the final status of the post’s assets after that reconciliation.
Twelve: close the remaining gap in how the Department records, tracks, and returns property after a post is emptied, so that “abandoned,” “recovered,” and “never left” are not three different stories told about the same rifle a year apart.
The Department concurred. Concurrence after the fact is not preparation before the fact. Twelve recommendations to invent the machinery of a competent withdrawal, issued in October 2024, are an official admission that the machinery was not there in August 2021.
Defense and reconstruction oversight confirm the Taliban seized substantial stockpiles of the military equipment provided to the Afghan forces — small arms, vehicles, and night-vision devices among them. Taliban officials have since had to issue their own controls on captured material, which is an admission from the group that benefited from the abandonment that the windfall created a problem past their command. United Nations reporting and subsequent investigations have described a thriving secondary market: local commanders allowed to keep a share, weapons moving to affiliated militants, and at least some NATO-caliber arms assessed as reaching groups the Taliban does not fully control. Claims that the entire stockpile has been handed in bulk to ISIS-K have often outrun the evidence. The more careful finding is narrower and worse enough: ISIS-K still operates in the same territory where the equipment was left; night-vision and small arms are the items most useful to any militant who can buy or steal them; and the United States has no realistic way to retrieve what it funded. The risk is not that every rifle is now in an ISIS-K cache. The risk is that the United States lost the ability to know.
None of this happened because a war that had already gone on for twenty years finally ended. Wars end in many ways. This one ended in the particular way a president chose after he was told, under the advice of the men who would have to live with the choice, what going to zero would do. Doha built a deadline and a political trap. It did not require a 650-person cap that made Bagram indefensible. It did not require leaving Bagram in the dark in early July with a prison of five thousand next door and no serious public plan for the inmates if the Afghan units folded. It did not require sitting on a dissent cable from twenty-three officers in the embassy for a month while the provinces fell. It did not require authorizing the evacuation the day before the government vanished. It did not require thirteen Americans to die on a single gate because the second airfield had already been given away. It did not require an embassy to hoard armored cars it had no plan to destroy. Those were choices made in 2021 by the administration that held the office.
Biden held every option Doha had left open. He chose the fastest and least-defended version of an exit that his own military leadership told Congress, under oath, would collapse the government he was leaving behind. When asked about that warning under far less pressure than the men who gave it, he said he did not remember getting it. Thirteen Americans died covering a gate that existed because of a troop cap he set. Billions of dollars in equipment sat abandoned not simply because events moved fast, but because the departments under his administration had spent years accumulating kit they never planned to deny to an enemy, trained no one to destroy it properly when the moment came, and then could not account afterward for what had actually been lost. Kyiv, six months later, under the same administration, with Kabul already in the after-action file, is the control case. Planning produced a different result. The absence of planning produced this one.
This is not a shared failure split evenly across two administrations. Trump signed Doha and drew the force down to the 2,500 Biden inherited; that is on the record and it is not nothing. McKenzie gave Trump the same warning and recommended 4,500 rather than zero. The inherited ceiling was a problem. The decision to go through the floor, against the advice of Central Command and the Joint Chiefs, on a timeline that discarded Bagram, delayed the NEO, and left the accounting to an inspector general three years later, is a different act. Doha built the road. Biden drove off the end of it, at speed, with the headlights off. The deaths, the abandoned equipment, and the sloppy books afterward are what was on the road when he did.
A president who cannot account for a direct warning from his own commanding general — a warning that general later gave to Congress under oath — has either a memory problem or a candor problem. Neither is a small thing in the man who decided how thirteen American families would spend every August 26 for the rest of their lives. An administration whose own inspector general later has to write twelve recommendations explaining how to plan for a fast withdrawal, after the fast withdrawal already happened and people died in it, was not simply unlucky. It was unprepared at every level someone was actually responsible for preparing. Unprepared is a policy word. The plainer word is neglected. The neglect had a date, a force cap, a vacant airfield, a late cable, a later NEO, a gate, and a list of names.
Questions about who was actually making these decisions in the summer of 2021 — whether Biden himself, or others around him — are addressed directly in the next chapter, which takes up his documented mental state during this period and the record of what those closest to him did or did not disclose about it.

text:
Thanks to Radio Castor for reviewing WILD WEST: AMERICAN STORIES. The review is in French (see link), but here is an English version:

WILD WEST: AMERICAN STORIES by Grant Maloy Smith
RC Editorial Team • 9/21/2026

Summary of this article:

1. Presentation of the artist: Grant Maloy Smith
2. Presentation of the album: Wild West: American Stories
3. Exclusive Interview: Meet with Grant Maloy Smith
4. Track by Track: Analysis of the 18 titles of the album

1. Presentation of the artist: Grant Maloy Smith
An American composer, interpreter, and multi-instrumentalist from Florida, Grant Maloy Smith is an impressive voice in roots and contemporary American music. Often compared to seminal figures such as John Prine, Willie Nelson, and Jimmie Dale Gilmore for the nuance of his storytelling, he has made a specialty of chronicling American history and culture through deeply profound thematic albums.

His work exploring collective memory – whether focusing on the Great Depression with “Dust Bowl: American Stories” (which topped the Billboard charts) or Appalachian traditions – has earned him international acclaim. This success includes over 11 weeks in the Billboard Top 10, two Grammy® Award certificates, and notable performances at legendary venues such as Carnegie Hall and Lincoln Center in New York.

Before dedicating himself fully to music, Grant Maloy Smith enjoyed a thriving career in the technology and scientific instrumentation sectors, where NASA used his innovations. An accomplished and versatile artist, he also writes children's books, composes for independent film, and actively champions causes such as veterans' welfare, the elderly, and Indigenous rights. He is also the co-founder of the Indie Collaborative, a world-class organization dedicated to independent music.

2. Presentation of the Album: Wild West: American Stories
With “Wild West: American Stories,” Grant Maloy Smith delivers his most ambitious work to date: a double album featuring 18 tracks and a 90-page illustrated book written entirely by his own hand. This multimedia epic chronicles the unfolding and complexities of the conquest of the American West during the 19th century.

From the Lewis and Clark expedition to the Gold Rush – taking in the Pony Express, the birth of cowboy culture, and the construction of the transcontinental railroad – the album paints a striking historical portrait. Grant Maloy Smith highlights iconic figures – such as Sacagawea and the legendary Deputy U.S. Marshal Bass Reeves – without ever shying away from the conquest's darker chapters, including the tragedy of the "Trail of Tears" endured by Native American nations.

To bring this colossal project to life – which he wrote and produced entirely – Grant assembled an elite collective of Grammy® and IBMA Award-winning musicians: Rob Ickes on dobro, Scott Vestal on banjo, Michael Cleveland and Matt Combs on fiddle, Jeff Taylor on accordion, and Mike Johnson on pedal steel guitar.

A true work of art, the accompanying hardcover book details each song's historical context, offers a behind-the-scenes look at the creative process, and features period photographs alongside original illustrations. *Wild West: American Stories* stands as a masterful tribute to the people and landscapes of the American West.

3. Exclusive Interview: Meeting Grant Maloy Smith

RadioCastor: Where does your passion for that era – the Wild West, cowboys, and the founding of America – come from?

Grant Maloy Smith: When I was very young, American television was teeming with Western series like “Gunsmoke,” “Bonanza,” “The Rifleman, and “Wagon Train.” All my friends had cowboy hats and boots. There’s even a photo of me wearing a cowboy hat at age two! It all started very early for me. But it goes beyond mere pop culture: the westward expansion of the United States in the 19th century was a pivotal era in our history. Our young nation transformed from a former colony into a continental power, tripling its size from the Pacific to the Atlantic. Wagon trains that took months to traverse rugged landscapes gave way to the transcontinental railroad, and the telegraph made communication instantaneous. It was a dangerous, captivating, and decisive century.

RadioCastor: From the rodeo cowboys and the Tex-Mex energy of "El Paso Señorita" to the lyricism of "Colorado," the album presents a diverse gallery of portraits. How did you choose the characters for these 18 stories?

Grant Maloy Smith: It was a difficult choice, given the sheer number of extraordinary figures. I could have written about a hundred people, but I had to select a representative cross-section. "Teddy O Teddy" is about Theodore Roosevelt – a frail New York aristocrat who became an outdoorsman in the wild Dakota Territory, then a war hero and President. Bass Reeves was a young runaway slave who learned hunting and tracking skills from Native Americans before becoming the first Black Deputy U.S. Marshal west of the Mississippi. "Doc" Holliday was a dentist with tuberculosis who headed West for the dry climate, became Wyatt Earp’s friend, and became a hero of the O.K. Corral shootout. I mixed these real-life figures with fictional characters created to embody the spirit of the times.

RadioCastor: Several tracks, such as "Tear Trail" or "Voices on the Wind," address the tragedy of Native American nations and the "Trail of Tears" with great emotion. Was it important to put this history at the heart of the album?

Grant Maloy Smith: Absolutely. The western frontier wasn't empty; millions of Indigenous people had lived there for millennia. As I sing in "Westward Dreams": "The land is ancient... but new to us." Expansion led to the forced displacement of entire nations. On this album, the story of the Trail of Tears is told through the eyes of a U.S. Army soldier ordered to march his Cherokee friends over 1,600 kilometers. It was also essential to pay tribute to Sacagawea, the 16-year-old Shoshone woman who guided the Lewis and Clark expedition with her baby on her back. To embody her voice and tell the story from her perspective, I enlisted the sublime Nashville singer Abbie Parker.

RadioCastor: A 90-page book and an 18-track album – that’s a massive undertaking! If you had to sum it all up in a single sentence, what would you say?

Grant Maloy Smith: Aside from the actual founding of the United States in the late 18th century, the 19th century brought the most profound and dramatic transformations to our territory and our national culture.

RadioCastor: Wouldn’t you like to put your talent to work on the events we are living through today by becoming a direct witness to current affairs?

Grant Maloy Smith: Not really, because we don’t yet have the necessary perspective on current events. Time allows us to understand causes, effects, and patterns. True objectivity is only possible once events belong to the past. When you read books about Abraham Lincoln, you realize just how much half the country hated him while he was alive. 160 years later, he is revered as the liberator of the slaves and one of our greatest presidents. In his day, no positive consensus existed because people lacked a historical perspective.

RadioCastor: When you aren’t writing or making music, what do you do?

Grant Maloy Smith: I like to go cycling every day when I can. Beyond the fresh air and exercise, it helps me clear my mind and reflect on life, family, and friends – things beyond just music.

RadioCastor: What are your plans, and what surprises do you have in store for us?

Grant Maloy Smith: I’m working on several albums simultaneously. You might have noticed that I deliberately left out the purchase of Alaska from Russia on this album: that’s because Alaska deserves an entire album in my *American Stories* series! I’m also preparing a record dedicated to America’s "blue roads" – the back roads – and the rural places that reveal our national character. I’m also more than halfway through a collaborative album with Kevin Lucas, a marimba and percussion virtuoso. I wish I could do it all at once!

4. Track by Track: Analysis of the album’s 18 tracks

1. Go West, Boys
Driven by a lively, infectious country-bluegrass rhythm and underpinned by acoustic guitar arpeggios, a bouncing banjo, and virtuosic fiddle playing, this opening track lays the foundation for this sweeping historical saga. Inspired by the famous 19th-century slogan, the song chronicles the exodus of pioneers who left behind the harsh comforts of Eastern cities to face the vast open frontier, guided by the promise of gold, land, and freedom.

2. Voices on the Wind
Carried by a soft, captivating female voice set to an acoustic folk-country melody, "Voices on the Wind" gives voice to the famous Shoshone guide Sacagawea. Guided by the stars and the whisper of the mountains, she moves along dark paths, carrying her people's memory and past into the heart of the expedition.

3. Come and Take It
Driven by an atmospheric banjo, a lively fiddle, and an infectious country/bluegrass tempo, this track makes direct reference to the 1835 Battle of Gonzales. It recounts the Texan settlers' flat refusal to surrender the six-pound cannon demanded by the Mexican army, cementing the famous challenge emblazoned on their flag: "Come and take it."

4. Tear Trail
Sitting at the intersection of Americana, alt-country, and Southern rock, "Tear Trail" stands out for its narrative power and the finesse of its rootsy arrangements, elevated by Billy Cardine’s dobro and Grant Maloy Smith’s B3 organ. Evoking the poignant depth of major artists like Tom Petty or Willie Nelson, the track delivers a stirring, captivating, and deeply moving historical portrait.

5. Wagon Train
Another excerpt from this major multimedia project, "Wagon Train" offers a cinematic dive into the heart of the 19th-century conquest of the American West. Driven by an epic, rousing chorus, the track features rich production blending guitars, keyboards, and contributions from exceptional musicians (notably dobro virtuoso Rob Ickes and banjo player Scott Vestal). This masterful composition pays a stirring tribute to the courage of the pioneers who set out to explore the unknown.

6. Good Lord, My God
Driven by a warm country-gospel rhythm and an infectious choral chorus, this track draws inspiration from Romans 12:2. It resonates as a vibrant hymn of faith, resilience, and redemption, celebrating the light regained after enduring hardships and traversing dark paths.

7. Elizabeth My Woman
An intimate, stripped-back, and deeply moving Americana-folk ballad led by acoustic guitar and fiddle. The song tells the poignant story of a pioneer mourning his late wife, Elizabeth – a woman whose memory lives on in the prairie landscape and the daily life of their home.

8. Pony Express
Propelled by the galloping rhythm of guitars and banjo at a dynamic folk-country tempo, this song is an epic tribute to the riders of the Pony Express. The lyrics evoke the dust, the spirit of pushing one's limits, and the courage of the 80 young messengers who rode across the Sierra and the plains to deliver precious mail before the advent of the telegraph.

9. If Wishes Were Horses
A melancholic, nostalgic country-folk ballad featuring acoustic guitar, fiddle, and pedal steel. Drawing on the traditional proverb "If wishes were horses, beggars would ride," the song expresses a man's regrets regarding the choices he made in the past. He dreams of a simpler time, regretting having let love and serenity slip away in favor of illusions and modernity.

10. The Golden Spike
An epic, driving Country/Bluegrass track – propelled by banjo and guitars – celebrating the 1869 completion of the first transcontinental railroad at Promontory Summit. The song pays heartfelt tribute to the thousands of workers – particularly Chinese and Irish – whose grueling labor and bloodshed united the Eastern and Western United States.

11. Gunslinger (The True Story of Bass Reeves)
A powerful, epic Country/Western track recounting the heroic life of Bass Reeves. Born into slavery, he rose to become the first African American Deputy U.S. Marshal west of the Mississippi. Featuring masterful arrangements that blend acoustic guitars, fiddle, and backing vocals inspired by gospel and traditional folk, the song honors his determination, his knowledge of Native American territories, and his reputation as an upstanding lawman who arrested over 3,000 criminals without ever being wounded.

12. Kill The Cowboys
A lively, dynamic Country & Western track driven by the galloping rhythm of infectious guitars and country fiddles. The song energetically captures the end of an era, when the advent of the railroad, the telegraph, and modernity threatened to wipe out the traditional cowboy lifestyle and the great cattle drives across the plains.

13. John Henry Holliday
An engaging Country/Americana waltz, written in the first person from the perspective of the famous "Doc" Holliday. The track traces his journey: his youth in Georgia, his dental training, his battle with tuberculosis (consumption) that drove him West, his friendship with Wyatt Earp, the O.K. Corral shootout in Tombstone, and the tragic end of his life, ravaged by illness rather than falling to gunfire. 

14. Teddy O Teddy
A warm, upbeat Folk/Americana track recounting the epic story of Theodore "Teddy" Roosevelt. The song evokes his love for the Great Plains and the Wild West (particularly his years as a rancher in North Dakota), his iconic role leading the Rough Riders during the war in Cuba, and his passion for preserving nature and America’s vast wilderness.

15. Ro-dee-o
This dynamic Country/Western track pays tribute to traveling Wild West shows and the cowboy lifestyle. The narrator recalls his travels across Arizona and California, memories shared with legendary figures like Buffalo Bill, and the trade's physical demands – from roping and bronc riding to the injuries sustained along the way.

16. El Paso Señorita
An upbeat Texas Swing track set on the Texas/Mexico border along the Rio Grande. The narrator is a Texas cowboy who falls under the spell of a beautiful Méxican señorita in a red dress. Amidst laughter, tequila, and captivating music, the song celebrates borderland love at first sight and romance.

17. Colorado
A majestic, introspective Americana ballad that pays homage to the mountains of Colorado. The narrator reflects on the wisdom passed down by his elders, the raw beauty of the open landscape, and the serenity nature offers in the face of life’s hardships and the need for redemption.

18. Westward Dreams
This track paints an epic historical portrait of the settling of the American West. Through vivid imagery of pioneers, wagon trains, and vast wilderness, the song captures hope for better days, determination in the face of natural obstacles, and the quest for a new future as they journey westward.

6 POPULAR SCAMS TO WATCH FOR
Scammers are constantly changing their tactics, but many of their tricks follow the same patterns. Here are six common scams to watch for:
Impersonation Scams Someone pretends to be with law enforcement, a government agency, utility company, bank, or other trusted organization. Tip: Hang up and contact the organization directly using a verified phone number.
Phishing Texts & Emails You receive a message about a package, toll, account problem, payment, or other urgent issue and are asked to click a link. Tip: Don’t click unexpected links. Go directly to the company’s official website or app.
Bank Fraud Alert Scams A caller or text claims there is suspicious activity on your account and asks for passwords, account information, or verification codes. Tip: Never give security codes or passwords to someone who contacts you unexpectedly.
Online Shopping Scams Fake websites, marketplace listings, or social media ads offer products at unusually low prices. Tip: Research the seller and be cautious of deals that seem too good to be true.
Romance Scams Someone develops an online relationship, gains your trust, and eventually asks for money, gift cards, or financial help. Tip: Be especially cautious if you have never met the person in real life.
Tech Support Scams Someone claims your phone, computer, or account has been compromised and asks for remote access or payment. Tip: Never allow unexpected callers remote access to your devices.
⚠️ Remember: Scammers often create a sense of urgency and pressure you to act immediately.
If someone demands payment by gift card, cryptocurrency, wire transfer, payment app, or Bitcoin ATM, stop and verify before sending anything.
STOP. VERIFY. PROTECT.
Please share this information with friends and family. A quick conversation could help prevent someone from becoming the next victim.
