text:
If I inherited a B2B company doing $5M a year with 4 reps & no outbound motion, here's exactly what I'd build in the first 90 days:

(We've run this build for 100+ B2B companies & it's the same sequence every time)

Step 1: Pull the last 20 sales calls before touching a tool

Nobody gets to buy a domain until this is done.

> the last 20 recorded sales calls
> the last 10 closed-won accounts
> the last 10 closed-lost, with the reason

Read the transcripts for the pain that repeats, in the prospect's own words.

Not "pipeline problems." The actual phrase they used.

Then look at what was observably true about the closed-won accounts before they bought.

> a role they were hiring for
> a tool they'd just added
> a complaint pattern in their reviews.

That becomes the scoring rubric for the entire market.

The output is a persona written as a situation.

"VP Sales" is everyone with the title. "VP who inherited 8 reps on a 2019 stack" is 400 people with the same problem this quarter.

Write the disqualifiers with the same care. Without them the model invents reasons a company qualifies.

Prompt I'd feed Claude with the transcripts attached:

"Read these 20 call transcripts & 10 closed-won account summaries. Return: the 3 pain points that appear most, quoted in the prospect's words. The observable signals that were true before each closed-won account bought. 3 personas written as situations rather than titles. A list of hard disqualifiers. Return none where nothing is found. Never invent a signal."

Step 2: Map the whole market, not a list

A list is 2,000 contacts someone hand-picked. A market is every account that could ever buy, scored.

Apollo's free account gives a rough count.

Plug in the filters, read the number, multiply by 0.7 for what survives verification.

Under 10,000 contacts, this is an ABM motion & everything below is manual.

10,000 to 100,000 is where the machine makes sense.

Past 100,000 you're leaving money on the table every month you don't run it.

Score every account on timing signals, weighted:

> hiring for the role you replace: 10 points
> raised in the last 12 months: 10 points
> new exec in the seat you sell to: 10 points
> complaint pattern in reviews: 10 points
> running paid ads: 6 points
> tech on the stack that pairs with yours: 5 points

An account carrying 3 of those is worth several times the effort of one carrying none.

Re-score every 90 days. A funding round from 14 months ago says nothing about this quarter's budget.

Step 3: Be honest about the offer

(This decides more than anything else below & it's the step everyone skips)

The offer decides which band you land in:

> blue ocean, nothing like it: 1 lead per 25 to 200 contacts
> real product market fit: 1 per 200 to 500
> crowded category: 1 per 500 to 1,000
> SEO, security, recruiting: 1 per 1,000 to 10,000

That's a 400x swing on one variable.

Then build the front-end offer.

What goes in the email is something a stranger can say yes to with nothing at stake.

3 kinds that work:

> a sales asset: a case study deck, a playbook, a demo video
> a front-end service: a free campaign, a $500 build, a 30 day pilot
> a free sample: 5 contacts already searching for them, handed over

3 kinds that don't work:

> a free 20 step audit from a stranger
> "we can replace your entire marketing team"
> "your current system is broken, let us rip it out"

The test is whether the prospect loses anything by saying yes.

If the answer is time, trust or a meeting, it's NOT a front-end offer.

Step 4: Buy the infrastructure on day one

Because it needs 3 weeks before a single cold email sends, & everything above happens in parallel while it warms.

> domains from Porkbun, .com only, no hyphens or numbers
> inboxes from ScaledMail, they set up DNS & swap burned accounts
> Google: 2 to 3 inboxes per domain, 15 cold sends each per day
> Microsoft Azure: 25 to 49 per domain, 2 to 3 sends each

Warmup runs 14 to 21 days. Start at 5 warm emails a day, add one a day until you're at 20. Leave it running forever.

Then a ramp.

Nobody goes from zero cold sends to 15. Start at 5, add one a day, watch the reply rate. If it dips when you step up, step back.

Campaign settings that are never negotiable:

> plain text, no HTML
> no open tracking pixel, it hurts placement
> no unsubscribe link, a spintax opt-out keyword instead
> 8am to 5pm EST, weekdays
> one follow-up, 3 days later, then a new campaign

And pull the MX record for every contact before sending.

Google & Microsoft filter differently enough that the two halves reply at rates that aren't close.

Run them as separate campaigns.

Step 5: Build the list while the inboxes warm

3 sources, in order of how much everyone else is using them:

> Google Maps, one zip code at a time, for anything local
> trade directories & certification bodies for niche verticals
> Apollo via a scraper, for the general B2B core

Google Maps is the one nobody runs properly.

There are 32,000 zip codes in the US & pulling one at a time means every query returns something.

Local businesses live there, not on LinkedIn.

Directories are where the odd data lives.

One client wanted architecture firms certified by a specific body.

The body publishes a member list. Instant Data Scraper pulled the whole thing in an afternoon.

Then qualify before you enrich.

Run every company's website through an AI column with the ICP & disqualifiers from step 1.

Raw scraping lands 50 to 60% ICP fit.

Qualifying first lands 90 to 95%, and you stop paying credits on companies you were always going to drop.

Then the waterfall:

> Icypeas first, cheapest
> Prospeo & LeadMagic for whatever's left
> LeadMagic to verify every result

Roughly 70% of a raw pull survives all of that.

For local markets, scrape the public addresses too.

On one build we ran for a client: the paid route found 3,621 contacts and their own websites found 4,553 more.

The paid ones took 94.94 contacts per positive reply. The public ones took 54.97.

Step 6: Write 15 variants, not one

The rules every script follows:

> under 65 words, ideally under 45
> subject line 1 to 3 words, lowercase, relevant
> written like you're messaging a coworker
> spintax on every sentence, or the filters fingerprint you
> a soft CTA, never "got 15 minutes?"
> social proof only from the same industry, or none

Then the frameworks. (These are the ones that have held across every vertical)

The one-liner free offer:

"Hey Sarah, interested in a free cold email campaign where we target 10,000 of your ICP prospects for Acme?"

One of the best performing emails we've ever sent. The whole thing rides on the offer being a no-brainer.

Lead magnet plus case study:

"Hey John, created a TikTok Shop playbook for Acme outlining what we used to take a client from $0 to $200k/month in 90 days. Mind if I send it over?"

Pain point plus solution:

"Hi Tyler, how are your crews handling roof inspections, phone in one hand & clipboard in the other? We built smart glasses that capture photos & checklists hands-free while they're on the roof. Mind if I share how they work?"

That roofing email did phenomenally, because nobody had ever named that specific pain to a roofer before.

Write 15 to 30 of these. Launch all of them at once.

Step 7: Launch & give every variant 1,000 sends

Nobody's allowed an opinion on a script before it's had 1,000 sends.

After 2 weeks, kill the bottom two thirds & put every send behind what's left.

We've had campaigns where one of four variants was producing every lead.

Removing the other three TRIPLED results overnight, and it was only visible because someone checked.

What the numbers mean in the first month:

> reply rate under 0.5%: deliverability problem, stop & diagnose
> reply rate dropped overnight: copy fatigue or a burned domain
> bounce rate over 3%: pull the list
> zero replies & zero bounces: the emails never left, copy's shadow-banned

Step 8: Add the phone in week 3

This is the layer that separates a campaign from a system.

> a parallel dialer, Salesfinity
> callers hired & trained for 2 weeks before a dial
> 500 dials a day per caller
> every positive email reply called the same day

On our recent build for a landscaping SaaS, 41,150 emails booked 20 meetings & 32,577 dials booked 33.

The phone produced 62% of the meetings off 44% of the touchpoints.

Every one of those dials was into a phone that hadn't rung with a real person in weeks, because everyone else moved to email years ago.

9.2% connect rate is the benchmark. Under that, the list is wrong.

Step 9: Score every reply the day it lands

This is where cost per meeting gets decided & it's the layer that never gets built.

The system:

> EmailBison fires a webhook on every reply
> n8n classifies intent: interested, more info, wrong person, cost, out of office
> the reply lands in Slack with full context & the prospect's number
> a rep responds inside 5 minutes

After 20 minutes, meeting conversion drops 50 to 80%. That's the whole reason for the automation.

Then tier them.

Score every reply against your own rubric as a percentage:

> 90 to 100: senior rep, account research attached
> 75 to 90: rep, personalised sequence
> 50 to 75: automated cadence
> under 50: flagged in Slack, never binned

Templates for the 5 replies you'll get. Never type them fresh.

Interested: "Thanks Sarah, here's a bit more context on what this looks like for Acme. Free Tuesday at 2pm EST?"

Cost: "Pricing varies but we typically run a monthly retainer. Can't give exact numbers since it depends on scope. Happy to talk for 7 minutes about it if you're open to it, if not no worries."

That second one pulls back more skeptical people than anything else we've written.

Step 10: Protect the meeting

Cold outbound meetings show at 30 to 50% with nothing in place. This gets them above 75%.

> confirmation email with a 60 second video of who they'll meet
> a longer video or one-pager to watch before
> reminders at 24 hours, 4 hours, 1 hour, 10 minutes
> a LinkedIn connection request the day they book
> a call from the rep before the meeting if there's a number

Book them inside 2 days. A meeting 2 weeks out is a meeting they'll forget.

Step 11: Optimise on the right number

Reply rate is a deliverability signal. It is not a performance metric.

The number that matters is contact-to-lead ratio. How many people do you contact to produce one interested reply.

> 300 to 1 is strong
> 500 to 1 is solid
> past 1,500 to 1, the offer or the market is the problem

Split it by segment every week.

One or two segments carry almost everything & the average hides which.

Re-enrich the whole list monthly. 30 to 50% of it has moved or changed inside 6 months.

Step 12: SCALE

The volume formula: total verified TAM, divided by 3 months, multiplied by emails per sequence. That's your monthly send.

The goal is every account in the market contacted once every 90 days across email, phone & LinkedIn.

Then the list re-scores, the winning angle rotates, and the next pass starts.

What 90 days looks like when it's done in this order:

> a foodservice manufacturer: 1,061 leads in 70 days at 100k emails a month
> a landscaping SaaS: 53 meetings in the first 50 days from zero
> a financial services firm: 31 interested replies, $4M in pipeline

None of those 3 companies changed their product, reps or pricing.

The order changed. That's the whole build.

P.S. If you'd rather have this built & run for you, DM me "GTM" & I'll walk you through what it looks like on your market.

text:
The hardest part is always to start.

The first cold call.
The first email.
The first piece of content.

Because once you make that first action, the next one is easier.

When I started out in business, I made 50 cold calls per day.

I would go onto Google Maps, search for local businesses, and scrape all the phone numbers directly from the page onto an excel sheet.

The process was simple: Call each business. 

For organization, I had color coded cells:

A pickup = green
A voicemail = yellow
A flat-out no = red

Every lead is called for 3 days.

3 yellows in a row = abandonment.

Greens can break the cycle, reds can end it instantly.

For meetings booked we had a separate column with similar color coding segments.

It can truly be that simple.

But this isn’t the best way… It’s the cheapest way.

No Ads.
No CRM.

Just a phone, a spreadsheet, and some elbow grease.

When you start out, you need to rely on outdated methods like cold calling to get clients because you don’t have the money to spend on ads, or hire outbound sales reps.

But there’s a surprising reality that presents itself even with some of the more experienced operators with many years of experience...

They personally are still stuck on word of mouth, networking events, & cold outreach.

These owners have never evolved past this stage for a particular reason.

It’s called risk.

In business, you have risk, and you have upside.

The more risk you take, the higher the upside can be (or the downside).

If you don’t take calculated risks in business, you will stay small.

The business owner who never adapts can grow, but never reach their full potential.

Growing could mean: 

Hiring a new sales rep.
Running your first ad campaign.
Moving upmarket.

What do all of these have in common? They cost money to experiment.

The good news: Growth is the best place to bet your money.

Hire the rep.
Run the ad.
Win the game.

And the reason I can say this is because I've personally made the transition, and helped 30+ other businesses (25 of them being advisory practices) do the same.

The cherry on top: It's much easier to compete in boring markets like financial services because people aren't tech savvy there.

You can set up a funnel with a basic offer and generate qualified leads TODAY (if you didn't have compliance :( )

And with AI? Everything is faster.

You just need the right context.

It takes 20 hours to learn this skill.

You could also hire somebody to implement it for you.

I have a free guide that teaches exactly how to start: https://t.co/omVM0tQI1d

text:
Hebrews 9 Bible Study - Please read

The Earthly Holy Place

1Now even the first covenant had regulations for worship and an earthly place of holiness. 2For a tenta was prepared, the first section, in which were the lampstand and the table and the bread of the Presence.b It is called the Holy Place. 3Behind the second curtain was a second sectionc called the Most Holy Place, 4having the golden altar of incense and the ark of the covenant covered on all sides with gold, in which was a golden urn holding the manna, and Aaron’s staff that budded, and the tablets of the covenant. 5Above it were the cherubim of glory overshadowing the mercy seat. Of these things we cannot now speak in detail.

6These preparations having thus been made, the priests go regularly into the first section, performing their ritual duties, 7but into the second only the high priest goes, and he but once a year, and not without taking blood, which he offers for himself and for the unintentional sins of the people. 8By this the Holy Spirit indicates that the way into the holy places is not yet opened as long as the first section is still standing 9(which is symbolic for the present age).d According to this arrangement, gifts and sacrifices are offered that cannot perfect the conscience of the worshiper, 10but deal only with food and drink and various washings, regulations for the body imposed until the time of reformation.

Redemption Through the Blood of Christ

11But when Christ appeared as a high priest of the good things that have come,e then through the greater and more perfect tent (not made with hands, that is, not of this creation) 12he entered once for all into the holy places, not by means of the blood of goats and calves but by means of his own blood, thus securing an eternal redemption. 13For if the blood of goats and bulls, and the sprinkling of defiled persons with the ashes of a heifer, sanctifyf for the purification of the flesh, 14how much more will the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without blemish to God, purify ourg conscience from dead works to serve the living God.

15Therefore he is the mediator of a new covenant, so that those who are called may receive the promised eternal inheritance, since a death has occurred that redeems them from the transgressions committed under the first covenant.h 16For where a will is involved, the death of the one who made it must be established. 17For a will takes effect only at death, since it is not in force as long as the one who made it is alive. 18Therefore not even the first covenant was inaugurated without blood. 19For when every commandment of the law had been declared by Moses to all the people, he took the blood of calves and goats, with water and scarlet wool and hyssop, and sprinkled both the book itself and all the people, 20saying, “This is the blood of the covenant that God commanded for you.” 21And in the same way he sprinkled with the blood both the tent and all the vessels used in worship. 22Indeed, under the law almost everything is purified with blood, and without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness of sins.

23Thus it was necessary for the copies of the heavenly things to be purified with these rites, but the heavenly things themselves with better sacrifices than these. 24For Christ has entered, not into holy places made with hands, which are copies of the true things, but into heaven itself, now to appear in the presence of God on our behalf. 25Nor was it to offer himself repeatedly, as the high priest enters the holy places every year with blood not his own, 26for then he would have had to suffer repeatedly since the foundation of the world. But as it is, he has appeared once for all at the end of the ages to put away sin by the sacrifice of himself. 27And just as it is appointed for man to die once, and after that comes judgment, 28so Christ, having been offered once to bear the sins of many, will appear a second time, not to deal with sin but to save those who are eagerly waiting for him.

Yes, here’s a comparison of everyday household staples across Carrefour, Naivas, Chandarana Foodplus, and Quickmart using 2026 Kenyan shilling (KES) prices.

Prices vary by branch, exact brand/pack size, promotions, and whether you shop in-store or online. The most complete side-by-side basket comes from a June 2026 Nairobi tracker of 10 common items. Later 2026 snapshots (July–September) show some movement, especially on sugar and promotional bread/flour. Always check current deals, as weekly offers can shift totals by 50–200 KES.

June 2026 10-item basket (Nairobi sample)
This used consistent pack sizes across the four chains:

| Item                  | Naivas | Quickmart | Carrefour | Chandarana | Lowest     |
|-----------------------|--------|-----------|-----------|------------|------------|
| Maize flour 2kg      | 139   | 154      | 124      | 149       | Carrefour |
| Rice 2kg             | 324   | 307      | 306      | 324       | Carrefour |
| Wheat flour 2kg      | 129   | 135      | 129      | 135       | Naivas/Carrefour |
| Sugar 2kg            | 298   | 309      | 300      | 324       | Naivas    |
| Cooking oil 1L       | 299   | 312      | 298      | 299       | Carrefour |
| Cooking fat 1kg      | 355   | 343      | 342      | 339       | Chandarana |
| Milk 500ml           | 42    | 43       | 42       | 45        | Naivas/Carrefour |
| Bread 400g           | 55    | 65       | 54       | 63        | Carrefour |
| Toilet paper (2 rolls)| 145  | 80       | 88       | 75        | Chandarana |
| Eggs (tray)          | 560   | 600      | 628      | 510       | Chandarana |

Basket totals (June 2026 sample):  
Chandarana Foodplus ~2,263 KES (lowest)  
Carrefour ~2,311 KES  
Naivas ~2,346 KES  
Quickmart ~2,348 KES  

The gap between cheapest and most expensive in this sample was only about 85 KES. Carrefour tended to win on maize flour, rice, oil and bread. Chandarana was strongest on eggs, cooking fat and toilet paper. Naivas and Quickmart were very close overall.

Later 2026 snapshots (July–September)
Prices moved with promotions and market conditions:

Sugar 2kg**: Dropped in July (Naivas 240–248, Carrefour from 240, Quickmart ~250–260). By late July some listings were around 304–305 for Mumias 2kg. Naivas online recently showed their own-brand 2kg at 289.
Maize flour 2kg**: Carrefour often cheapest on popular brands (Soko ~151 in one July check). Naivas online recently had Ndovu/Masterchef around 125–135.
Bread 400g**: Heavy promotions appear. Naivas recently advertised own-brand sweet bread at 39 (from 54).
Cooking oil**: 5L packs commonly 1,199–1,299 at Naivas (promos). 1L equivalents stay in the high 200s depending on brand.
Rice 2kg**: Own-brand or mid-tier often 399 at Naivas; premium Basmati/Pishori higher.
Eggs 30-pack**: Carrefour listings around 504 in August data; Chandarana was notably cheaper in the June sample.
Toilet paper**: Larger packs (10 rolls) at Naivas recently 279–439 depending on brand.

Carrefour’s online catalogue (checked around August 2026) showed examples such as 1L milk 120, 400g bread 56, 30 eggs 504, and 1kg sugar 152.

Quick takeaways
Cheapest overall basket in the detailed June sample**: Chandarana, followed closely by Carrefour.
Best on core staples (unga, rice, oil, bread)**: Often Carrefour.
Best on eggs and tissue in that sample**: Chandarana.
Naivas and Quickmart**: Very similar totals; Naivas frequently competitive on sugar and own-brand items, Quickmart strong on convenience and some promotions.
Differences are usually small on a full weekly shop. Promotions, loyalty programmes, and buying the right pack size matter more than the chain name.

text:
Study Notes - (Pulpit Version Explained) (PART B) I. PUTTING OUR HONOR ASIDE. "Not unto us … give glory." It is a universal experience that when God is really apprehended, self goes into the second place. It must be so. God can be in no place but the first. In the sphere of morals it is true that the most miserable of men is he who is anxious about his own dignity. He will turn everything into offence. In the sphere of religion it is true that the first sign of regeneration is the humility that claims nothing for self. "Not by works of righteousness which we had done;" "Not of works, lest any man should boast."
II. SEEKING GOD’S HONOR. "Unto thy Name give the praise." Dr. Chalmers spoke of "the expulsive power of a new affection." It is fully true of the soul’s affection for God. It expels self and everything else, and compels a man to set God’s honor first, to live for God (compare St. Paul’s exclamation, "To me to live is Christ"). God’s honor is sought by being good and by doing good; in relations, worship, and work. This aim glorifies all forms of life.
III. FINDING THAT WE GAIN OUR HONOR IN SEEKING GOD’S. In two ways.
1. The very effort to seek God’s honor cultures us in the character that wins for us honor.
2. And God makes the honor of men come to us as his benediction. on our loyalty.—R.T.
Psa_115:2
The taunt of the unbeliever.
"Where is now their God?" (comp. Psa_42:3). The expression is to be understood by the help of the associations of the psalm. It is always trying to be despised; always hard to work on faithfully under jeers and taunts. The neighbors of the restored exiles did not dare actually to interfere with them, because they were under the protection of the Persian authority; but they could taunt them and laugh at them. And it must be admitted that there was apparent occasion. The exiles were poor and few. They had been stopped in building their temple, and there were nothing but foundations to be seen. It might be said—If your God can do anything, he surely can get his own temple built. They dare not attempt to raise the walls and fix new gates and enclose the city; for every attempt would be checked. It might be said—If your God really cared for you, he would help you to defend yourselves. The pious souls were deeply hurt by this reproach cast on their God, and could only find rest in assuring themselves that if his will was a sovereign will, it was influenced by covenant promises. We can always turn from our doubtings as to what God does, and find our satisfaction in what God is.
I. THE STRAIN INVOLVED IN INCOMPLETENESS. We start out with a distinct life aim and purpose; but the years pass by, and all we have, as the result of labor and waiting, is an unfinished building, like some of the cathedrals. Then we are apt to lose hope, and to say—Not done now, it will never be done. So the years had passed for the exiles, and the new nation was still in a most incomplete state. No walls, no temple, no real freedom, no independent native government. It was a big strain on faith to see the nation’s hope ever realized.
II. THE INTENSIFYING OF THE STRAIN THROUGH MISCONCEPTIONS, It was hard to see and to feel the incompleteness; but it was harder still to be told about it, to have it pointed out, and to be taunted with it. Those enthusiastic Jews who came out from Babylon expecting at once to accomplish great things, could see well enough the mere foundations of the temple, and the heaps of the ruined walls; but it was bitter ness indeed to have some one come up as they were looking, and whisper in their ear, "Where is now thy God?"
III. THE RELIEF OF THE STRAIN BY CHERISHING TRUSTFUL THOUGHTS OF GOD. (Psa_115:3.) The check on our work God puts. Incompleteness is his permission. Failure is his discipline. If God is in them, and their state pleases him, then our incomplete things are blessings in disguise.—R.T.
Psa_115:4
The inefficiency of idolatry.
"The work of men’s hands." Denunciation of the idolatry of the heathen is characteristic of the psalms of the restoration. With this passage may be compared such passages as Isa_44:9-20. In treating of idols it should be borne in mind that they are differently regarded by their intelligent and unintelligent worshippers. The mystical Hindu will tell us that his idols are to him nothing more than are to us the pictures of absent or dead friends. They are helps to memory and imagination. But to the great mass of heathen the idol-figure is the actual god worshipped, the embodiment of the god, the shrine of the god. So Scripture is justified in its scorn of the idol-deities. The point presented here is the helplessness of idols, in that they have organs of sense, but no sensibility. There is an argument in the simple statement that they are "the work of men’s hands."
I. MAN’S HANDIWORK IS INFERIOR TO HIS BEST THOUGHT. No man ever yet reached with his hands what he had conceived in his mind. The artist’s idea is better than his picture. It is inferior to the artist himself. The sculptor’s figure is better than the model he produces. The literary man never writes as good a book as he intends to write. It is the universal fact that a man is always greater than anything he creates, or anything he accomplishes. And this must be true when a man attempts to mould with his hands the figure of his thought of God. He cannot imprison in gold, or silver, or clay, or wood, his whole thought. And he himself remains a nobler being than the god he creates; and so the god should worship him, and not he the god.
II. MAN’S BEST THOUGHT MUST BE INFERIOR TO DEITY. This is true of the best man’s best thought. But what guarantee can we have that the idol-maker is a best man, and that best man at his best? Grant that the primary creations of Baal or Vishnu were the best conceptions of best men, still we face the fact, that, necessarily, the conception was short of the reality. No man by searching can find out God; and no man by imagining can find him out so as to represent him. Then this follows: God himself must give to men the earth-pattern of himself. He has done it. But the earth-pattern is no thing, no likeness of any thing in heaven and earth and sea. It is the living Being, the "Man Christ Jesus," "express Image of his Person."—R.T.
Psa_115:6
Like god, like people.
"They that make them shall be like unto them." This suggests a topic in the line of the previous homily. It is a law which works in a twofold way. As is the god who is worshipped, so are the people who worship. As is the people who worship, so are the gods whom they create for worship. It is, indeed, the very essence of the idea of a God worthy to be worshipped, that he shall be revealed to man, not created by him; that he shall be in the sphere of man’s thoughts, and so apprehensible; but beyond the reach of man’s thoughts, and so a perpetual inspiration to him. The reproach which Jehovah makes to his people is that they have not kept him beyond them, but have reduced him to their level. "Thou thoughtest that I was altogether such an one as thyself." We have seen that what men attempt to embody when they make their own gods is themselves; the gods are like the people. The characteristics of any nation can be known by a study of its gods; and the characteristics of any particular age of a nation can be known by its relation to, and treatment of, the national gods. Therefore the history of the nations is so largely the history of the national religions.
I. Let men make their own gods like themselves, and THEY WILL NEVER MAKE THE GODS LIKE THEMSELVES AT THEIR REST. Whatever may be thought about the formulated doctrine of original sin, the fact of universal moral deterioration is bound to be generally accepted. And the sign of it is that man is not interested in his best; perhaps not even able to set before himself the image of himself at his best possible. So there never yet was an idol-god made that even represented its maker at his noblest.
II. Let men make their own gods like themselves, and THEY WILL BE SURE TO MAKE THE GODS LIKE THEMSELVES AT THEIR WORST. This can be effectually illustrated by the Kali, Sarasvati, Juggernaut, of India; the Baal and Ashtaroth of Phoenicians; the Moloch of Amorites; and even the refined and artistic creations of Grecian genius; for these represent man sensual, which really is man at his lowest. And this fact, that if man makes his own gods he makes them like himself at his worst, may be shown to be equally true of those immaterial, mental, figures of God which men now make as the idols of an intellectual age. They are no more worthy of God than the hideous figures of India, and this is the serious feature of the case. Let man make his god after the pattern of himself at his worst, and the god he makes and worships will inevitably debase him lower and lower.—R.T.
Psa_115:9
The call to trust implies imperiled trust.
This and the following verses were, apparently, sung as responses. This explains the repetition of the same idea. The scornful taunts of the surrounding peoples might have had a serious influence on Jehovah’s servants. It might have taken all heart out of them. Probably many of the weaker ones did flag under the discouragements, and so there was a real need of this pleading of the psalmist for full and even rejoicing trust in God. The confidence felt by one man will often inspire the confidence of others. When one man can see God plainly working as Helper and Defender, he, in a very wonderful way, opens the eyes of others to see the same signs of Divine presence and power. Our trust in God passes from one to another, even as does an epidemic disease. And it may also be shown how often psalm and song help us to fetch back imperiled trust. Treating the case of the restored exiles as illustrative, we may see how our trust in God may now be imperiled—
I. BY GOD’S UNFULFILLED PROMISES. Some of God’s promises really belong to our future, and we have no right to look for their present fulfillment; but such is the restlessness of man, that he persists in thinking he ought to have everything now. And as he cannot, he readily regards some of God’s promises as unfulfilled. So through long ages men expected the promised Messiah, and often lost their faith and dimmed their hope because he did not come. But God’s promises never are unfulfilled. It is only this—he has our whole lives to work in, he has all the ages to work in. Compare our Lord’s saying, "My time is not yet come, but your time is always ready." Trust should make a treasure of the promises.
II. BY GOD’S INCOMPLETELY FULFILLED PROMISES. It is harder to keep trust when a promise has begun to be fulfilled, and has been checked in the fulfillment, than when it is altogether delayed. It was harder for the exiles to look on the new foundations of the temple than on the old ruins. There is no feature of Divine discipline that so severely tries our power to keep on trusting, as this checking of blessings that have begun to be bestowed; this asking us to accept of incomplete fulfillments.
III. BY GOD’S MISUNDERSTOOD PROMISES. So often we take God to promise what we wish him to promise, rather than what he does promise. Then we raise unreason able expectations, and get unreasonably depressed when they are not fulfilled. God may test and try our trust, but he never puts it in peril; we do that when we cannot wait, and persist in misunderstanding.—R.T.
Psa_115:12
The certainty of the Divine benediction.
"He will bless us." The repetition of the word "bless" adds great effect to this passage. The Lord has many blessings, each one worthy to be remembered—he blesses, and blesses, and blesses again. Where he has once bestowed his favor, he continues it, his blessing delights to visit the same house very often, and abide where it has once lodged. Blessing does not impoverish the Lord; he has multiplied his mercies in the past, and he will pour them forth thick and threefold in the future. He will have a general blessing for all who fear him, a peculiar blessing for the whole house of Israel, and a double blessing for the sons of Aaron. It is his nature to bless, it is his prerogative to bless, it is his glory to bless, it is his delight to bless; he has promised to bless, and therefore be sure of this—he will bless, and bless without ceasing. The subject dealt with should be this—The past is the pledge of the future. A nation makes a fatal mistake when it separates itself from its past; though it misuses the past when it binds itself with precedents, and so destroys its own freedom and individuality. A man makes the gravest mistake when he separates himself from his past, but he makes as grave a mistake when he persists in forcing his present life and relations into the old moulds. What is always safe to do is, keep in mind what God has been to us in the past. Our selves in our past seldom teach us much. In regard to human experience, Froude’s word is a wise one, "Experience is like the stern-lights of a ship, which throw their rays on a way which has been taken." God in our past always teaches us much, seeing that we have no very definite aim in working for ourselves, and he has a very definite aim in working for us.
I. GOD HAS BLESSED US. How true this is seen to be in a review of the history of God’s people Israel! Especially if we take, as the chief idea of God’s blessing, over ruling for God. The more clearly we understand our own lives, the more fully we shall realize that as our best idea of God’s blessing. Certainly it is what would most come home to the restored exiles.
II. GOD IS BLESSING US. This is a fact of observation; a conviction of feeling; and an argument from the nature of God. We cannot conceive of him as beginning to do a good, and leaving it off; and the blessing we need is blessing that we continuously need.
III. GOD WILL BLESS US. Since we are well assured that our conditions, relations, and needs will remain much the same, and call still for his merciful overrulings and blessings.—R.T.
Psa_115:17
The responsibility of being alive.
"The dead praise not the Lord." Joy in life is the characteristic of every healthy, right-minded person. Pining for death is, altogether and always, a sign of a morbid condition of body or of mind. It is a delusion to imagine that religion requires of us an indifference to life, and a yearning for heaven. The psalmists and kings of the old Israelite times loved life and dreaded death. One says, "I shall not die, but live, and declare the works of the Lord. The Lord hath chastened me sore, but he hath not given me over unto death" (Psa_118:17). Hezekiah expresses but the universal sentiment of the good men of his day when he says, "The grave cannot praise thee; death cannot celebrate thee; they that go down into the pit cannot hope for thy truth. The living, the living, he shall praise thee, as I do this day; the father to the children shall make known thy truth" (Isa_38:18, Isa_38:19). But if we have life, we must take it with all its responsibilities, and the first of these is that we acknowledge the God who made us, on whom we are wholly dependent, and who lays his righteous claims upon us. One of those claims is indicated by the psalmist. God calls for praise. All his works praise him in their order and fitness, in the precise fulfillment of the end for which they were designed. But God seeks that higher praise which can be offered by intelligent and free-willed beings. And the time in which they can offer the praise is the time of their lives amid terrestrial things. It is the praise of the living that God wants. It is praise while living that man can alone render.
I. PRAISE-TIME IS THE PRESENT TIME. It is never a mere duty that has been done; a demand that has been met. The praise that is God’s due can never be paid, so that we can get a receipt in full for all our obligations. It is never a duty that can be put off to some by-and-by, something that we can promise to do some day. It is the duty of the hour. It is immediate response to God’s present blessings.
II. PRAISE-TIME IS A LIMITED TIME. It is limited to life, and life is always short and always uncertain, so that a man’s call to praise is a call of the moment. For praise "now is the accepted time." No man has any to-morrow until God gives it to him, and then he must call it today. Only by doing just the duty of the hour can any man meet his human obligations.
III. THE OCCASIONS OF PRAISE BELONG TO THE PRESENT TIME. It is true that there is call to praise for God’s past dealings with us; and call to praise in view of the promises on which we are permitted to hope; but we can always find, if we will, calls to praise in the things actually around us; God’s good hand is ever on us for good.—R.T.
HOMILIES BY C. SHORT
Psa_115:1-18
The honor due to God.
A call to the God of Israel, the living God, to rescue the honor of his Name from the reproach of the heathen.
I. GOD IS WORTHY OF THE HIGHEST HONOR. In contrast to heathen idols.
1. Because of his loving-kindness or mercy. (Psa_115:1.)
2. Because of his truth or faith fullness. (Psa_115:1.) Emphatically "truth and grace came by Jesus Christ."
3. Though invisible, he reigns and rules from the exalted heaven. (Psa_115:3.) The idols are earthly things, and have no power.
4. God is omnipotent, able to execute his own will. (Psa_115:3.) The idols are dead things, with no will; and their worshippers become as dead as they are.
II. GOD IS WORTHY OF TRUST. (Psa_115:9-14.)
1. Because he is the Helper and Defender of those who trust in him. (Psa_115:9-11.)
2. Because his past goodness is the pledge for future blessing. (Psa_115:12-14.) He will bless and multiply both the great and the small together.
III. GOD IS WORTHY OF PRAISE AND WORSHIP. (Psa_115:15-18.)
1. As the Creator of heaven and earth. (Psa_115:15.) And the heavens are for the dwelling-place of Jehovah.
2. Because he hath given the earth to men for their possession.
3. God must be praised now and forever—before we go down into the silence of Hades. (Psa_115:17, Psa_115:18.) "The Old Testament," says Delitzsch, "knows nothing of a heavenly exclusion that praises God without intermission, consisting not merely of angels, but also of the spirits of all men who die in the faith" (but see Psa_103:20-22).—S.

Lourmarin captivates with its picturesque profile. Imagine a beautiful town perched atop a hill, with striking bell towers dotting the landscape. Strolling through the village is a must; with its quaint alleyways, impressive fountains, and historic homes, Lourmarin offers a glimpse into centuries past.

Lourmarin boasts a rich historical, artistic, and cultural heritage. Nobel Prize-winning writer Albert Camus lived here and is buried in the local cemetery. The village hosts numerous art galleries, festivals, and events throughout the year, attracting many visitors—especially in the summer. Landmarks such as the bell tower, the Church of Saint-André-et-Sainte-Trophime, the Protestant temple, and the château date back to the 12th century and are well worth a visit for history enthusiasts.

Lourmarin is officially recognized by the association "The Most Beautiful Villages of France" (*Les Plus Beaux Villages de France*), established in 1982 to promote the tourism appeal of small rural communes with rich heritage. This prestigious designation highlights the village's exceptional charm and cultural significance.

text:
In 1985, an Alabama man was convicted of murdering his wife and sentenced to LIFE in prison.

The only physical evidence purportedly connecting Charles McCrory to the murder?

These two tiny marks on his wife’s upper arm.

No DNA tied him to the crime. No blood or tissue from his wife was found on his clothing or in his vehicle. Hair found clutched in her hand did not belong to him.

But a forensic dentist testified that these marks were human bite marks—and that Charles McCrory’s teeth made them.

Decades later, that same expert fully recanted his testimony, acknowledging that his identification lacked a scientific basis. Other forensic odontologists have concluded the injuries weren’t even human bite marks.

After spending decades behind bars, McCrory was offered a plea deal: plead guilty, accept responsibility for killing his wife, and walk out of prison with time served.

He refused.

Charles McCrory has consistently maintained his innocence.

Now, more than 40 YEARS after he was convicted, a federal judge has granted his habeas petition and ordered Alabama to either retry him or release him.

Charles McCrory is still in prison.

text:
What are three things legislators can do to increase housing supply?
Housing is expensive because we don't build enough of it, and local rules are a big reason why. Here are three things state lawmakers can do to increase housing supply:
📷 Preempt exclusionary local zoning. Rules like very large minimum lot sizes block starter homes from ever getting built.
📷 Make permitting faster and easier. Streamline state-level permits into a one-stop shop, set shot clocks for slow municipalities, and allow certified third-party inspections.
📷 Give builders real legal remedies. Arizona lets landowners seek compensation when a locality's rezoning cuts their land's value, which has curbed exclusionary zoning there. New Hampshire's Housing Appeals Board offers a quick, low-cost alternative to court for housing disputes.
For developers, time is money, and every delay shows up in what you pay for a home.
📷 Subscribe to AIER for more on economics, markets, and policy.
From - @JasonSorens

Eight days later he was on life support.

Matthew Mayich, 21, Stoney Creek kid, St. Louis Blues draft pick, transferred to ASU hockey.

First official team workout of the year. Outdoor grind at Sun Angel Stadium in August heat.

An uncertified guest trainer an ex-Green Beret running a military-style session with little water, little rest, and extra punishment for anyone who lagged.

He stumbled.

He fell.

ASU’s own heat policy required cooling tanks ready for immediate ice-water immersion.

Staff used wet towels and a hose instead.

The family’s attorney says the water was near-boiling faucet water. 

Matthew never recovered.

Exertional heat stroke starved his brain of oxygen.

Arizona is investigating.

ASU reviewed itself and named no one.

A 21-year-old who had barely set foot in the Valley was broken on the first official day.

Preventable catastrophes are not accidents.

text:
My agency grew from $200K to $700K a month.
Then I poured $1.7M into France in 9 months and hired a scammer to run it.
His friend, a cocaine trafficker, swindled me out of another $275,000.

Once we opened an office in Montreal, French speaking clients started showing up.
So I hired people who spoke French and we became a bilingual agency.

Then our SDR process took us from $200K a month to $700K a month, which was insane.
With that kind of extra money coming in I got overly ambitious and decided we're going to open an office in France, because we can work in French.

I started talking to the French government and they offered a bunch of support.
I flew over 3 times to meet w/ them and with people at the bank, and they wanted us in Strasbourg.
It was cheaper, it looked great, so I hired a very expensive CEO for the French side and handed it to him.

Over the next 9 months I poured about $1.7M into that office and we got nothing out of it.
Every client we landed there went horribly, while all our North American clients were doing great.

One of those clients was a company called Be In Meta.
This was when Facebook had renamed itself Meta and everybody thought the metaverse was the future.
They'd signed GIMS, a huge French artist, to play a concert inside a metaverse environment and sell tickets to it.

The founder kept telling me he had hundreds of people working for him, that he was talking to Warner Brothers and Disney, and that this was going to make so much money.
So when he said "I'll pay you once the tickets come in, we're keeping our money for the ads, it's going to sell out, don't worry" I said okay, fine.

The concert went live, the tickets didn't sell out, and he owed me $275K worth of work.

That's when I finally researched him.
There's a huge article in France about how this guy trafficked cocaine from Morocco into France with the chief of police in his pocket feeding him information.
He got caught, it was all over the news, he did 5 years in jail, and the police chief got fired and went to jail too.

This is who I'd been dealing with the whole time and I never checked.
I could have Googled his name.

When I confronted my CEO he started panicking and trying to get advances on his paycheck, so I fired him and shut the office down.

Then the trafficker sent me a message, and in it he complained about how I'd done wrong by my CEO.
And that's when it clicked for me that these two had been working together.
I found out my CEO had been pocketing some of the money.
The way I see it now, the plan all along was to funnel money from a Canadian business into France for 9 months, deliver nothing, and then create a bogus project they never intended to pay for.
If it worked, great, and if it didn't, they weren't paying us anyway.

A contact put me in touch w/ a commercial collection agency out of Arizona and I hired them.
Let's say they go above and beyond if the amount is large enough… showing up at his house, talking to his landlord, dropping by...

text:
have you ever watched your conversion rate swing all week with zero idea what caused it?

been getting a TON of questions lately around how to actually test landing pages without turning your Meta account into a complete mess lol

and the answer is actually quite simple

this is something i’ve been helping clients with a lot lately because the instinct is usually:

“should we test Collection vs PDP vs Presale vs Advertorial for every ad?”

and… no.

that gets messy FAST.

one ad suddenly becomes 3–4 destinations, spend gets diluted, tests take longer, and half the time you’re testing pages that don’t even make strategic sense for the traffic.

the way i think about it is much simpler:

start with the ad.

ask:

“what does this person still need before they’re ready to buy?”

if the ad is broad / product discovery-led → Collection may make sense

if it’s product-specific + high intent → PDP

if it’s problem-aware and the buyer still needs education / belief-building → Presale or Advertorial

then instead of testing:

Collection vs PDP vs Presale vs Advertorial

test:

your current best destination vs ONE challenger you have an actual hypothesis for.

for example:

say you’re selling a recovery supplement.

your winning ad is built around:

“why you still wake up sore even though you’re doing everything right”

sending that person straight to a generic PDP might be asking them to make too big of a leap.

so rather than randomly testing every page type…

i’d test:

existing PDP vs a problem-aware Presale page

same traffic.

same offer.

same creative.

different destination.

this way you’ve got a clear outcome you’re trying to test for, and you’re actually learning something.

and i’ve seen how big the upside can be when the destination finally matches what the ad started.

for one of my clients an 8-figure pet brand, we tested an Advertorial against the existing landing experience.

same product.

same traffic source.

the biggest difference was what happened AFTER the click.

over 90k visitors:

CVR 2x’d

RPV 2x’d

and this is where the testing gets more interesting over time.

you start building a routing playbook.

maybe after enough tests you learn:

problem-aware ads → usually prefer Presale

high-intent product ads → usually prefer PDP

broad discovery ads → usually prefer Collection

now you’re not wasting budget re-testing the same basic question every time.

you’re using previous experiments to decide what deserves to be tested next.

and if one destination clearly wins?

keep the creative.

kill the weaker landing page variants.

because at that point you’re not testing the ad.

you’re testing where that ad should send people.

small distinction.

huge difference in how clean your CRO programme becomes.

don’t test everything against everything.

use the ad to choose the most logical destination.

test it against the current control.

learn the pattern.

then reuse that learning across future funnels.

that’s how you stop “doing CRO” and start building a conversion system.

text:
American leaders and thinkers on freedom of speech:

"Men who injure and oppress the People under their Administration provoke them to cry out and complain; and then make that very Complaint the Foundation for new Oppressions and Prosecutions. . . . That, to which Nature and the Laws of our Country have given us a Right - The Liberty - both of exposing and opposing arbitrary power… by speaking and writing truth." - Andrew Hamilton

"Without Freedom of Thought, there can be no such Thing as Wisdom; and no such Thing as publick Liberty, without Freedom of Speech." - Benjamin Franklin

"If Men are to be precluded from offering their Sentiments on a matter, which may involve the most serious and alarming consequences… reason is of no use to us—the freedom of Speech may be taken away—and, dumb and silent we may be led, like sheep, to the Slaughter." - George Washington

"I have always strenuously supported the right of every man to his own opinion, however different that opinion might be to mine. He who denies to another this right, makes a slave of himself to his present opinion, because he precludes himself the right of changing it." - Thomas Paine

"I am… for freedom of the press, and against all violations of the Constitution to silence by force and not by reason the complaints or criticisms, just or unjust, of our citizens against the conduct of their agents." - Thomas Jefferson

"A power not delegated by the constitution, but on the contrary, expressly and positively forbidden by one of the amendments thereto; a power, which more than any other, ought to produce universal alarm; because it is levelled against that right of freely examining public characters and measures, and of free communication among the people thereon, which has ever been justly deemed the only effectual guardian of every other right." - James Madison

"Liberty is meaningless where the right to utter one's thoughts and opinions has ceased to exist. That, of all rights, is the dread of tyrants. It is the right which they first of all strike down." - Frederick Douglass

"To announce that there must be no criticism of the President, or that we are to stand by the President, right or wrong, is not only unpatriotic and servile, but is morally treasonable to the American public." - Theodore Roosevelt

"In a free country, we punish men for the crimes they commit, but never for the opinions they have." - Harry Truman

"Don't join the book burners. Don't think you are going to conceal faults by concealing evidence that they ever existed." - Dwight Eisenhower

"Without debate, without criticism, no Administration and no country can succeed—and no republic can survive." - John F. Kennedy

"Somewhere I read of the freedom of speech. Somewhere I read of the freedom of press. Somewhere I read that the greatness of America is the right to protest for right." - Martin Luther King Jr.

"Freedom is the recognition that no single person, no single authority or government has a monopoly on the truth, but that every individual life is infinitely precious, that every one of us put on this world has been put there for a reason and has something to offer." - Ronald Reagan

text:
Today’s Daily Brief covers the FDA’s Request for Information to reclassify deceased-donor islet cells as transplant organs rather than biological drugs, HRSA awarding $51 million to expand specialized dental care for children with neurodevelopmental disorders, an NIH-funded study showing a modified HIV drug reversed some multiple sclerosis related paralysis, and Florida Surgeon General Dr. Joseph Ladapo calling for a formal investigation into reports of an alleged coverup of Covid mRNA shot harms.

1. FDA Seeks Public Input on Easing Access to Deceased-Donor Islet Cell Treatments for Type 1 Diabetes

The FDA announced a formal Request for Information (RFI) on whether unmodified deceased-donor pancreatic islet cells used to treat type 1 diabetes should remain regulated as biological products or instead be treated as organs under the transplant system.

According to an official statement, “The RFI specifically seeks comment on whether ‘unmodified’ deceased donor islet cells should be classified as organs for transplantation rather than biological products. Under such an approach, oversight of procurement, allocation, and transplantation could move from FDA’s product-based framework to the Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA) and the Organ Procurement and Transplantation Network (OPTN). HRSA oversees the OPTN, the national system that sets transplantation policies, maintains the national waiting list, and matches donors with recipients.”

2. HRSA Announces Investment of $51 Million to Expand Dental Care for Children With Neurodevelopmental Disorders

HRSA announced $51 million in awards to 28 health centers to improve access to dental care for children with conditions such as autism, Down syndrome, cerebral palsy, and intellectual disabilities.

According to a statement from HHS, “The new Quality Improvement Fund – Improving Access to Dental Services for Children with Neurodevelopmental Disorders (QIF-DNDD) investment will help health centers build on evidence-based models and test innovative approaches to improve dental care for children with neurodevelopmental disorders. The funding will support expanded and tailored preventive and other dental services, strengthen the health center workforce, and identify promising approaches that can be replicated in other communities.”

Commenting on this, Secretary Kennedy stated, “Children with neurodevelopmental disorders should not struggle to get the dental care they need. We are investing $51 million in HRSA-funded health centers to remove barriers to care, equip providers to better serve these children, and give families more options close to home. We will identify the approaches that work, scale them across the country, and ensure more children can get the preventive care they need to live healthy lives.”

3. NIH Study Finds Modified HIV Drug May Assist Those With Multiple Sclerosis

An NIH-funded study found that Kamuvudine K-9, a modified derivative of approved HIV drugs called NRTIs, reversed paralysis and vision loss in a mouse model of multiple sclerosis rather than only slowing future attacks.

According to an NIH report on the study, “Further examination suggested that K-9 shielded axons and their insulating myelin sheaths, which are the primary conduit for signals in the central nervous system, from degeneration. Levels of a blood-based marker of nerve damage called neurofilament light chain (NfL) in these mice were also reduced, which the authors note is an indicator that the United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has previously used to approve certain medications for neurodegeneration.”

4. Florida Surgeon General Calls for Investigation of Potential Covid Shot Data Coverup

Making reference to recent reports about a federal coverup of flawed data related to mRNA Covid shot harms, Florida Surgeon General Dr. Joseph Ladapo called for a thorough investigation.

According to Dr. Ladapo, “Every American who cares about government accountability should want an investigation into whether health officials knowingly and intentionally used an inferior method to monitor COVID-19 vaccine adverse events. How many Americans have been injured or killed because of their decisions?”

As previously reported in the Daily Brief, 

“According to a new article published in BMJ, Covid era federal public health officials used a flawed FDA algorithm to scan VAERS for mRNA Covid vaccine harms. Because nearly all reports came from Pfizer and Moderna shots, the system compared the two mRNA shots against each other and failed to flag myocarditis, pericarditis, tinnitus, and other major harms signals. According to the article, officials erroneously cited the supposed lack of signals as proof of safety, while silencing the FDA doctor who warned them and offered a fix.

An FDA drug-safety officer, Ana Szarfman, and statistician William DuMouchel flagged the problem in early 2021 and offered an updated algorithm that did detect accurate signals. Top officials, including Peter Marks, the FDA’s top Covid vaccine regulator at the time, ignored the warnings.Szarfman was later told to stop sending analyses. Internal records and emails obtained by The BMJ show CDC and FDA leaders were aware of the limitation before and during the Covid era but continued to use the compromised system and other surveillance methods that also missed early signals.”

text:
One of the most dangerous things you can do on a cold call:

Ask boring questions.

If you’ve actually solved a problem 100 times…

You don’t ask:

“How are you currently handling this?”

“What’s your biggest challenge right now?”

“Can you walk me through your process?”

This tells the buyer one thing:

You’re figuring this out as you go.

And no one allocates serious money to someone figuring things out.

Confirm statements instead.

“Most companies at your stage are leaking money here…”

“From what I’ve seen, this usually comes down to [specific issue]…”

“Let me guess, you’re doing X, but it’s creating Y.”

You’ll still get an answer to your question.

And you’ve just delivered it in a way that demonstrates understanding rather than ignorance.

And when the buyer feels understood before they explain themselves…

They assume you’ve done this before.

Once you’ve seen a pattern enough times, you don’t need them to explain it to you.

You just need them to confirm it.

text:
Let’s let super intelligence do its thing for @_willcompton & @taylorlewan77 

SI: The arc of Bussin’ With the Boys is even better than the version you described, because it actually begins before COVID.

2019: Two teammates buy a shitty old bus

Taylor Lewan and Will Compton became teammates with the Tennessee Titans in 2018. Compton had already been thinking about doing a podcast; Lewan essentially told him, let’s actually do it.

So Lewan bought an old Budweiser promotional bus for $2,000, they converted it into a makeshift studio, parked it in Nashville and started recording. The first podcast was in May 2019. 

And this wasn’t two retired stars arriving with a production company and a media strategy. They were active NFL players. Lewan was a Pro Bowl offensive tackle; Compton was bouncing around the league trying to keep his playing career going.

The premise was almost absurdly simple:

What if you could sit on the couch with NFL players and hear them talk the way they actually talk to each other?

Beer. Football. Teammates. Stories. Stupid arguments. Serious football discussion that could suddenly become completely unserious.

Even the presentation mattered. The acoustic-guitar intro—the guy singing about drinking beer, gambling and hanging with the fellas—eventually became part of the identity. The roughness wasn’t something they needed to overcome. The roughness was the product.

Their July 2019 episode description literally called it a “shoot the shit conversation about anything and everything.” 

2020–24: Barstool teaches the Boys how to become a media business

Then came the transformational relationship with Barstool Sports⁠.

They brought the show into Barstool in early 2020. COVID arrived almost immediately afterward and even forced Lewan and Compton into solo episodes when NFL protocols kept them apart. 

But the Barstool years were enormously important.

Barstool didn’t invent their chemistry. It industrialized it.

Lewan later described the experience almost like going to school for the internet: Barstool taught them about engagement, downloads, audience behavior, promotion and how to turn a podcast into a recognizable brand. Both men have repeatedly credited Dave Portnoy, Erika Nardini, Big Cat and the broader Barstool ecosystem with accelerating their growth. 

And you can actually watch the sophistication increase.

The bus remains. The beers remain. The inside jokes remain. Twisted Tea becomes integrated into bits like the “Twisted Question.” 

But gradually the guest list gets better. The clips get bigger. The social operation gets smarter. They start doing college tours. They build recurring segments. Their relationships with players and coaches become an enormous competitive advantage.

Most importantly, Bussin’ becomes bigger than the novelty of two NFL players having a podcast.

Eventually they’re no longer NFL players who happen to make content.

They’re media personalities who used to play in the NFL.

January 2025: They bet on themselves

This is probably the most important business moment in the story.

After roughly five years with Barstool, Lewan and Compton announced on Jan. 21, 2025, that they were leaving.

And remarkably, they weren’t leaving because the relationship had gone bad.

They repeatedly said they wanted to stay.

Someone simply offered them so much money that the economics changed. Compton said one outside sponsor’s offer by itself exceeded what Barstool could assemble for the entire deal. They said they’d even have accepted a hometown discount to remain at Barstool, but the gap was simply too large. 

That sponsor turned out to be FanDuel⁠.

The reported number was extraordinary:

roughly $30 million over three years. 

And this is where the story becomes much bigger than “podcast success.”

They didn’t sell Bussin’ to FanDuel. They retained their independence and ownership while FanDuel became the presenting sponsor.

Suddenly the guys who once recorded inside a $2,000 discarded beer bus had become owners of a valuable independent sports-media company with about eight employees, interns, multiple shows and the ability to make their own distribution and partnership decisions. 

Then the establishment comes calling

And this is the part that makes the old acoustic intro so funny in retrospect.

In August 2025, ESPN⁠ announced that Lewan and Compton were coming aboard.

Not because ESPN acquired Bussin’.

Not because ESPN turned them into conventional analysts.

ESPN essentially said:

Bring Bussin’ here.

Beginning Sept. 4, they started appearing primarily on Get Up, alongside Mike Greenberg, while also contributing to SportsCenter and other ESPN programming. ESPN’s own president of content, Burke Magnus, specifically cited the audience connection, chemistry and energy they had created themselves. 

Their regular appearances were on Thursday mornings.

So now think about the visual.

The show that began with two football players sitting on couches inside an old Budweiser bus is now rolling that same brand into ESPN’s Manhattan operation and sitting beside Greenberg on one of the network’s signature morning programs.

They didn’t abandon the bus to get onto television.

The bus got invited onto television.

2026: Now it’s becoming a network of its own

That’s the latest evolution.

Bussin’ isn’t simply Lewan + Compton + one podcast anymore.

They’ve built additional football programming, worked with Josh Pate, expanded into NASCAR through a show produced with Omaha Productions, developed major commercial partnerships and continued working with ESPN. 

And in July 2026, it went another step: ESPN planned a new college-football show featuring Josh Pate, Will Compton and Taylor Lewan, airing from college campuses during the season. 

They’re also now involved in national campaigns with major Anheuser-Busch brands; in August 2026, NÜTRL announced a national integrated college-football campaign starring Lewan and Compton that runs across streaming, digital, social, radio, out-of-home and retail. 

So the progression looks almost ridiculous when compressed:

2019: Two teammates buy an old Budweiser bus for $2,000 and start talking football.

2020: Barstool brings them into its ecosystem.

2020–24: They learn how internet media actually works and turn their chemistry into a brand.

2025: They leave Barstool because FanDuel makes an offer Barstool can’t economically match.

2025: The independent company lands a reported $30 million/three-year presenting sponsorship.

2025: ESPN brings them onto Get Up and SportsCenter.

2026: Bussin’ expands into additional shows and partnerships, including NASCAR/Omaha, Josh Pate and further ESPN programming.

And that’s why the story works.

They didn’t climb the traditional sports-media ladder.

There was no journalism degree → local sports desk → regional network → ESPN progression.

They essentially built a clubhouse, invited the internet inside, and made the clubhouse valuable enough that eventually ESPN wanted access to it.

The acoustic guitar, the bus, the beers, “the boys,” the deliberately stupid arguments—those weren’t embarrassing early-stage artifacts that had to disappear once they became successful.

They became the intellectual property.

Seven years after Lewan spent $2,000 on an abandoned promotional bus, Will Compton and Taylor Lewan can sit behind an ESPN desk on Thursday morning precisely because they never tried very hard to look like people who belonged behind an ESPN desk. @elonmusk @katiemiller @kimbal @sawyermerritt @marionawfal @cb_doge @martysmithespn @espn @adamschefter @kirkherbstreit @ariemanuel
