text:
🗞️24 September 2026 | Daily Edition
1⃣ Bitcoin has fallen back below $84,000 as U.S. yields move above 5%

Bitcoin reversed from this week's high near $87,300 and traded below $84,000 after stronger U.S. business activity increased expectations of further Fed tightening. The 10-year Treasury yield reached about 5.11%, while more than $545M of leveraged crypto positions were liquidated, including roughly $447M of longs. 

🖊️ Market significance: This is the first real macro test of the recent recovery. The short squeeze pushed BTC higher, but rising risk-free yields are now working in the opposite direction.

🗨️ My viewpoint: The important battle is no longer bulls versus shorts. It is institutional crypto demand versus a rising cost of capital. If BTC can remain resilient while Treasury yields stay above 5%, that would be much more meaningful than another short squeeze.

2⃣ Bitcoin ETFs recorded a fifth consecutive positive session

U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs recorded approximately $346.9M of net inflows on September 23, led by BlackRock's IBIT with roughly $166.3M and Fidelity's FBTC with $143.2M. The inflow was smaller than the previous session but remained firmly positive despite Bitcoin's pullback. 

🖊️ Market significance: ETF demand is no longer simply following rising prices. Institutions continued buying while BTC weakened.

🗨️ My viewpoint: This may be more important than Monday's near-$1B inflow. Buying during weakness tells us more about conviction than buying during a squeeze.

3⃣ Ethereum ETFs also remained in positive territory

U.S. spot Ethereum ETFs recorded approximately $104.6M of net inflows on September 23, with BlackRock's ETHA and Fidelity's FETH accounting for most of the demand. 

🖊️ Market significance: ETH institutional demand continues even as ETH itself has fallen back toward the mid-$2,600s.

🗨️ My viewpoint: Ethereum's price is weak relative to Bitcoin, but the ETF tape is telling a better story. I would watch whether capital continues entering before price begins responding.

4⃣ Solana ETFs added another $13.8M

U.S. spot Solana ETFs recorded approximately $13.77M of net inflows on September 23, led by Fidelity's FSOL and Bitwise's BSOL. 

🖊️ Market significance: Solana's institutional flow trend continues even during a broader crypto pullback.

🗨️ My viewpoint: BTC, ETH and SOL are now all receiving ETF capital simultaneously. That makes this less of a Bitcoin-only institutional story.

5⃣ Major UK banks completed live transactions using tokenized bank deposits

Lloyds, NatWest and Barclays used tokenized sterling deposits for mortgage transactions, while another group including HSBC tested a customer-to-customer payment. The programme involves Barclays, HSBC, Lloyds, Monzo, Nationwide, NatWest and Santander. 

🖊️ Market significance: Banks are showing that blockchain-based money does not necessarily have to take the form of a stablecoin or CBDC. Existing bank deposits can also become programmable and settle on digital rails.

🗨️ My viewpoint: The future of digital money probably will not have one winner. Stablecoins, tokenized deposits and central-bank money can all coexist for different purposes.

6⃣ IBM has connected its institutional digital-asset platform to Swift's blockchain ledger

IBM Digital Asset Haven can now connect to Swift's shared ledger through an ISO 20022 adapter, allowing institutions to instruct tokenized-deposit transactions using existing banking-message standards. Seventeen institutions are participating in the current pilot. 

🖊️ Market significance: Banks do not necessarily need to abandon existing systems to adopt blockchain. IBM is building a bridge between traditional banking infrastructure and tokenized settlement.

🗨️ My viewpoint: This is how institutional adoption is likely to happen: not by replacing everything overnight, but by connecting blockchain to infrastructure banks already use.

7⃣ Raiffeisen is expanding crypto access across its Central and Eastern European banking network

Raiffeisen Bank International and Bitpanda have created a group-wide framework allowing RBI's regional banks to progressively offer digital-asset services. RBI serves roughly 18.8M customers across its network. 

🖊️ Market significance: Crypto distribution is increasingly moving through existing banks rather than requiring customers to open accounts with dedicated crypto exchanges.

🗨️ My viewpoint: Mainstream adoption becomes much easier when crypto appears inside the banking app people already use.

8⃣ Circle has launched 24/7 stablecoin foreign-exchange settlement

Circle's StableFX allows approved institutions to request FX quotes and settle supported stablecoin pairs around the clock on Arc using payment-versus-payment settlement. 

🖊️ Market significance: Stablecoins are moving from dollar-transfer infrastructure into foreign exchange infrastructure.

🗨️ My viewpoint: This is where stablecoins become much bigger than crypto trading. They are beginning to compete with parts of the infrastructure used to move currencies globally.

9⃣ Nearly $20M of XRP was drained from thousands of D'CENT wallets

Investigators traced approximately 11.7M XRP from 6,678 wallets across six attack waves between September 15 and 20. A large portion was subsequently routed through cross-chain infrastructure. The incident affected wallet credentials rather than the XRP Ledger itself. 

🖊️ Market significance: A blockchain can remain secure while users still lose assets through failures at the wallet and key-management layer.

🗨️ My viewpoint: The weakest part of crypto security is increasingly not the blockchain. It is everything users place between themselves and the blockchain.

🔟 Making Bitcoin quantum-resistant may be becoming cheaper

A StarkWare developer contest reduced the estimated computation cost of preparing its experimental quantum-safe Bitcoin transaction from around $320 to approximately $66-$67.

This is an estimate produced through optimization, not a second live Bitcoin transaction proving that cost. 

🖊️ Market significance: Quantum resistance remains a long-term problem, but practical experimentation around potential solutions is accelerating.

🗨️ My viewpoint: Quantum risk does not need panic. It needs engineering. The useful signal is that the industry is working on the problem before it becomes urgent.

1⃣1⃣ Institutional crypto allocations remain small but appear increasingly sticky

A Bitwise study based on interviews with 15 institutional allocators found most crypto allocations were around 1%-2% of investable assets. Every crypto-owning institution interviewed held Bitcoin, and none reduced crypto exposure during the roughly 50% market decline covered by the research. 

🖊️ Market significance: The sample is small, so it should not be treated as representative of all institutions. But it suggests some institutional crypto allocations are being treated as strategic rather than short-term trades.

🗨️ My viewpoint: The important institutional story may not be huge allocations. It may be small allocations that remain in portfolios through an entire market cycle.

1⃣2⃣ Phantom has officially ended support for Sui

From September 24, Phantom no longer displays, sends, swaps or interacts with assets on Sui.

Users' assets remain on the Sui blockchain and can still be accessed through another compatible wallet using the appropriate credentials. 

🖊️ Market significance: Wallet distribution matters for blockchain adoption. Losing access through a major interface reduces one route through which users interact with an ecosystem.

🗨️ My viewpoint: This does not damage Sui at the protocol level, but it is a reminder that distribution is infrastructure too.

1⃣3⃣ Coinbase has suspended IoTeX trading

Coinbase has disabled IOTX trading across its exchange products following a regular asset review. Customer funds remain accessible for withdrawal. 

🖊️ Market significance: Exchange access still matters significantly for smaller assets because delistings can reduce liquidity, accessibility and institutional credibility.

🗨️ My viewpoint: For smaller tokens, being technologically functional is not enough. Liquidity and distribution remain part of survival.

1⃣4⃣ Binance has delisted Pax Dollar

Binance ended spot trading for USDP today following its periodic asset review. Withdrawals remain available until November 24 under the published schedule. 

🖊️ Market significance: The stablecoin market is consolidating around a smaller group of highly liquid issuers even as the overall stablecoin sector grows.

🗨️ My viewpoint: Stablecoin growth does not mean every stablecoin wins. Distribution and liquidity are becoming increasingly concentrated.

1⃣5⃣ Cardano governance is again considering a large reduction in stake-pool fees

A new governance action proposes reducing Cardano's minimum stake-pool cost from 170 ADA to 75 ADA, a reduction of roughly 56%.

The earlier attempt failed because it was bundled with another protocol change requiring stake-pool approval. The new proposal isolates the fee change. 

🖊️ Market significance: Lower fees could increase competition between pools and potentially benefit delegators, although smaller operators also rely on fixed fees for revenue.

🗨️ My viewpoint: Decentralization has an economic cost. The challenge is lowering costs for users without making smaller validators economically unviable.

1⃣6⃣ Hut 8 has won a $140M bid for Poolin's Texas data centres

Hut 8 submitted the winning bid for two Texas sites owned by bankrupt mining company Poolin. The transaction still requires bankruptcy-court approval. 

🖊️ Market significance: Bitcoin miners increasingly view power and data-centre infrastructure as valuable beyond Bitcoin mining, particularly for AI and high-performance computing.

🗨️ My viewpoint: The mining business is changing. For some miners, electricity access and data-centre capacity may eventually be more valuable than mining itself.

1⃣7⃣ TRON says cumulative transaction volume has passed $30T

TRON DAO reported more than $30T in cumulative transaction volume, over 405M accounts and approximately $94B of circulating USDT on the network. These figures come from TRON's own announcement. 
🖊️ Market significance: Whatever the debate around individual chains, TRON has become an important settlement network for global stablecoin transfers.

🗨️ My viewpoint: TRON is a good example of why price alone can miss blockchain adoption. A chain can become economically important because people use it to move dollars.

1⃣8⃣ A Coinbase social-engineering scheme resulted in nearly $16M of theft

A Brooklyn man was sentenced to four to 12 years in prison after pleading guilty in a scheme prosecutors said stole approximately $15.94M from around 100 Coinbase users by impersonating exchange representatives. 

🖊️ Market significance: The attack required no blockchain exploit. It relied on convincing users to surrender control of their assets.

🗨️ My viewpoint: As technical security improves, attackers increasingly target people. Human trust is still one of crypto's largest attack surfaces.

1⃣9⃣ Prediction markets are attracting more congressional scrutiny

All 11 Democratic members of the U.S. Senate Banking Committee asked Chair Tim Scott to hold a public hearing on prediction markets. The request followed a Republican committee meeting with Kalshi CEO Tarek Mansour and focused particularly on consumer protection and securities-linked contracts. No hearing has yet been announced. 

🖊️ Market significance: Prediction markets are becoming large enough that questions around whether particular contracts fall under CFTC, SEC or state jurisdiction are moving closer to mainstream financial regulation.

🗨️ My viewpoint: The sector's biggest challenge is becoming classification. Prediction markets need clear boundaries around what is a derivative, what is gambling and what regulators oversee each product.

2⃣0⃣ Coldcard victims can now check whether recovered BTC belongs to them

Following the recovery of 52.37 BTC linked to the Coldcard incident, a public verification process now allows affected users to check whether their Bitcoin addresses are associated with recovered funds and begin a claims process. Users should only provide public addresses, never private keys or seed phrases. 

🖊️ Market significance: This turns the earlier white-hat recovery from an onchain event into an actual restitution process for victims.

🗨️ My viewpoint: Recovery remains the exception rather than the rule, but this shows that transparent blockchains can sometimes make tracing and restitution possible after theft.

With the midterms coming, an astonishing number of Republican voters cannot name three things President Trump has accomplished. Which is remarkable when you consider that Donald Trump has accomplished more in a year and a half than any other president ever did in four. Indeed, he has accomplished so much, so 

Trump accomplishments
1. He made the border a real border again. In a matter of months, Trump reduced illegal border crossings to their lowest level in half a century. Catch-and-release is finished. The wall is going up and even being expanded, “Remain in Mexico” is back, and the Administration reduced releases into the country by an incredible 99.9 percent.

2. He reversed mass migration. America recorded negative net migration in 2025 for the first time in at least half a century. So far, nearly 3 million illegal aliens have left the country, whether voluntarily or involuntarily: more than 675,000 forcibly deported and the rest “self-deported.” Many of those self-deportations were facilitated by the President’s innovative program to offer plane tickets and cash bonuses for illegals to leave, not only incentivizing good behavior but significantly reducing the cost of deportations. Citizenship and the law actually mean something again.

3. He signed the Laken Riley Act — and required detention of criminal illegal aliens. Named for an innocent girl murdered by an illegal alien, the Laken Riley Act requires federal authorities to detain illegals arrested for theft, burglary, shoplifting, assaulting police, or any crime causing death or serious injury. It also lets states sue officials who refuse to enforce it. Laken Riley should still be alive. This law will prevent tragedies like hers.

4. History’s biggest drop in violent crime, and the lowest violent crime rate in 126 years. According to FBI data, violent crime in America dropped an incredible 9.7 percent in 2025 — the largest one-year decline in history. Murder fell 18.1 percent, robbery fell 18.5 percent. And America’s violent crime rate is its lowest since 1900. This is what happens when you put the National Guard on the streets in crime-ridden blue cities: fewer victims, safer streets, and better futures for America’s poorest.

Trump Launched an American Industrial Supercycle 5. He made the 2017 tax cuts permanent…and better. The One Big Beautiful Bill locked in the largest tax cut in modern history, including the doubled standard deduction, the expanded Child Tax Credit, and 100 percent expensing for factories and equipment. It also delivered No Tax on Tips, No Tax on Overtime, an abolition of most taxes on Social Security benefits, and major relief for seniors. Every Democrat voted no. With the 2017 act set to expire in December 2025, that would have resulted in the largest tax hike in American history.

6. He repealed 129 regulations for every new one. In fiscal 2025, federal agencies finalized 646 deregulatory actions and just five regulatory actions: 129-to-1, and in nearly every case, the “one” was to repeal the others! OIRA says the savings exceeded those of Trump’s entire first term. That is more freedom, lower costs, and less bureaucratic sabotage. Of these, the crown jewel was the repeal of Obama’s 2009 “Endangerment Finding”, the legal foundation for the Green New Scam’s vehicle mandates. EPA calls it the largest deregulatory action in American history and estimates that by itself, it will save Americans more than $1.3 trillion. Trump also killed the federal EV mandate, restored Americans’ freedom to buy the cars and trucks they actually want, and even eliminated the incentives behind the almost universally hated start-stop button.

7. He secured $18 trillion in announced investment commitments. That’s nearly two-thirds the size of the entire American economy, building American factories, chip plants, data centers, energy projects, steel mills, shipyards, and supply chains employing American workers. Apple, Meta, NVIDIA, Micron, Hyundai, U.S. Steel, Ford, Taiwan Semiconductor, and many corporations and sovereign wealth funds are betting big on Trump’s America. No President has ever done anything remotely like it. And it’s just getting started.

8. He made “reshoring” and “reindustrialization” real, not a slogan. Ford is moving Lincoln production out of China. Toyota is shifting Tacoma production from Mexico to Texas. GM, Honda, Mercedes-Benz, Stellantis, and others are expanding U.S. production. The capital equipment pouring into the country is the machinery that’s building the growing boom.

9. He replaced lopsided trade deals with balanced, reciprocal trade. Trump used tariffs as leverage to reverse 80 years of lopsided trade deals that favored everyone but America, and to win new or improved agreements with trading partners accounting for more than half of global GDP. Those agreements open foreign markets, attack non-tariff barriers, defend strategic industries, and make it more profitable to build in America than to export American jobs.

10. He shifted global energy dominance from the Persian Gulf to the Gulf of America. Once the world’s largest energy importer — “exporting” $700 billion a year to our enemies — America now outproduces Saudi Arabia and Russia combined. The U.S. is also setting new records in oil, natural gas, and LNG exports, becoming the first country ever to export more than 100 million metric tons of LNG in a year. Trump also opened land, accelerated permits, expanded pipelines and export terminals, and made American energy a tool for prosperity and peace.

11. After four decades of nuclear paralysis, Trump brought five new reactors online in a single year. For more than 40 years, not one new privately developed non-light-water reactor reached criticality in America. Trump ordered at least three by July 4, 2026. DOE delivered four by the deadline, then a fifth just one month later. Decades of zero. One Trump summer: five. That is a genuine nuclear renaissance.

Trump Made Elections Matter Again

12. He broke the Deep State’s power to defy the elected branches. In Trump v. Slaughter, the Supreme Court ruled for the first time in 90 years that Article 2, Section 1 is still part of the Constitution: the President may fire subordinate officials in the executive branch, overturning the 1935 precedent that insulated “independent” agencies from voters’ control. Ever wonder why elections often seem to change nothing? How about one President and 5,000 political appointees vs. 2.8 million unfireable, unaccountable bureaucrats? THAT is the “Deep State”. Trump then made that victory real. For the first time in a century, all policy-making bureaucrats can now be fired for misconduct, incompetence, or defying lawful directives. The permanent bureaucracy no longer gets to veto the voters.

13. He ended nationwide injunction abuse. In Trump v. CASA, the Supreme Court sharply limited nationwide injunctions. A single, local, district judge should not be able to block a national policy for everyone, everywhere; and yet that’s exactly what they’ve done, nonstop, ever since Trump (and only Trump) took office in 2017. In restricting that unconstitutional power, the Court kneecapped the Black Robe Bureaucracy’s favorite tool of unlawful judicial supremacy.

14. He shut down USAID as a left-wing slush fund and shadow government. USAID had become a taxpayer-funded machine for exporting abortion, gender ideology, censorship, and left-wing politics. It had a bigger budget than the CIA and the State Department combined, absolutely no accountability whatsoever, and a penchant for overthrowing governments. Trump terminated it — completely — and moved real humanitarian aid under the State Department. Immediately, seven socialist Latin American governments lost re-election. Coincidence?

15. He shrank Federal employment to its lowest level in 60 years. From a high under Biden, the federal workforce is now its smallest since 1966. Workforce reductions, agency closures, and spending cancellations mean fewer bureaucrats paid to resist the voters. What’s more, when Biden left office, 94 percent of federal employees “worked” from home. The Trump administration cracked down: as Elon Musk put it, “you can work from the office or you can pretend to work somewhere else.”

16. He expelled DEI from the federal government. Trump eliminated federal DEI offices and barred race- and sex-based preferences across the executive branch. Government hiring and contracting are returning to merit and equality under the law, ending the grotesque Democrat idea that “fighting discrimination” requires the federal government to discriminate.

He Defended Faith and Family 17. He delivered sweeping pro-life reform. In his first term, Trump delivered the judges that overturned the abominable Roe v. Wade. Hardly anyone believed it could be done, or that Trump would do it. But he did, and a half-century nightmare finally ended. Since returning to office, Trump has enforced the Hyde Amendment prohibiting the use of federal funds to pay for abortions, reinstated and expanded the Mexico City Policy prohibiting federal funding of foreign abortions, ended federal fetal-tissue research, strengthened conscience protections, protected Medicaid from funding large abortion providers, and pardoned 23 pro-life activists prosecuted by Biden’s weaponized Justice Department. He’s also done everything within the Executive Branch’s power to defund Planned Parenthood. It would be nice if Congress did likewise. No President has ever done more to protect life. No one.

18. He got men out of women’s sports, and restored biological reality to federal policy. The United States government once again officially recognizes two sexes: male and female. Trump ended federal support for the chemical and surgical gender mutilation of children, stopped taxpayer funding of such irreversible abominations, and forced more than three dozen health systems to end or suspend their programs as well. Trump also enforced Title IX as written: women and girls deserve their own teams, trophies, scholarships, and locker rooms. The NCAA and other athletic organizations changed their rules in response. After years of Democrats doing everything they could to destroy women’s sports and ruin girls’ lives, Trump’s administration protects women and girls again.

19. He enacted America’s first nationwide school-choice program — and launched Trump Accounts. As part of the President’s One Big Beautiful Bill, Trump enacted America’s first-ever nationwide school choice program. The new Education Freedom Tax Credit helps fund scholarships for tuition, books, and other educational costs. That’s on top of the new Trump Accounts, which give every child a tax-advantaged stake in America’s future, including a $1,000 federal seed for eligible newborns. Parents gain power. Bureaucracies lose it. And children learn first-hand about free markets and future orientation.

20. He targeted anti-Christian bias and discrimination. Trump created the White House Faith Office, Religious Liberty Commission, and Task Force to Eradicate Anti-Christian Bias. He restored conscience protections and made clear that Christians do not surrender their First Amendment rights merely by entering public life. He Restored Peace Through Strength and Put America First

21. He forced NATO to stop freeloading and increase defense spending by 250 percent. For decades, wealthy European governments underfunded their militaries, effectively sending America the bill and using American taxpayers to subsidize their bloated welfare states. Trump forced NATO to replace its old two-percent-of-GDP spending target with an enormous five percent by 2035. Allied spending is rising, American defense orders are soaring, and Europe is becoming a partner instead of a dependent.

22. He drove China out of the Caribbean. China spent years building strategic beachheads at both ends of the Panama Canal, in Cuba, and in Maduro’s Venezuela. Trump forced Panama out of Belt and Road, expanded American security access around the Canal, and captured Maduro, who now sits in a New York jail cell awaiting trial. Beijing’s planned encirclement of the United States collapsed. The Monroe Doctrine is back. Call it the Donroe Doctrine.

23. He brokered eight peace deals in just eight months. In eight months, Trump brokered peace in eight conflicts spanning four continents, including wars that had gone on for as much as 40 years. It’s a record unmatched by any other President.

24. He launched and funded Golden Dome, the first-ever true missile defense for the U.S. population. Ronald Reagan dreamed of making nuclear missiles obsolete through his Strategic Defense Initiative. Today, Trump is actually building it: a layered homeland shield with space-based sensors and interceptors, conventional defenses, and new technologies including microwave systems to destroy drone swarms and directed-energy weapons (yes, lasers) that can replace an $11 million missile with $2 of electricity. Congress has funded the initial $25 billion, with far more on the way once it passes the NDAA this fall. Better a shield than a sword.

25. He restored the warrior ethos — and reversed the recruiting crisis. After years of missed targets under Biden, every active military component met or exceeded its 2025 recruiting goal. Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth refocused the newly renamed Department of War on actually winning wars, while pouring resources into shipbuilding, munitions, drones, missile defense, and America’s atrophied industrial base. Young Americans once again believe their Commander-in-Chief is worth serving. And they’re showing up en masse.

text:
Summer of 1934, western Kansas. The Dust Bowl had stolen crops, hope, and security. Outside their small, tar-paper cabin, the Henderson family paused for a breath. The children, barefoot and in patched clothing, watched dust swirl across the endless fields.
Mother clutched a tin bucket, the only container for water she could carry.

Father leaned on a worn hat, coat stiff with dust and sweat, eyes scanning the horizon for work. Inside, the cabin offered little relief. Cracked boards, thin walls, and memories of better times. Yet, despite scarcity, there was a rhythm to survival. Daily chores, shared meals, and quiet lessons in resilience.

Neighbors traded tools, flour, and news about distant work. Even with so little, community held them together.
The sun lowered, casting long shadows across the dry plains. In those shadows, the Henderson family endured, step by dusty step. They had no riches. Only grit. Only each other. And that, in the heart of hardship, was enough.

When did the WH say the passes were revoked for security? I have the President on camera giving all of us his reasons. I have a WH statement from Monday talking about the Radical Left media, but no mention of security. So maybe the security reason was made up after the WH realized the President fucked up?

The claim that the White House can revoke press passes because access is a "privilege, not a right" is legally dead on arrival. Under the Supreme Court's Unconstitutional Conditions Doctrine, the government does not have to offer a discretionary benefit, but once it does, it cannot revoke that benefit to punish protected speech. The Court established in Perry v. Sindermann that the state cannot deny a benefit to penalize constitutionally protected expression, a rule reinforced in Speiser v. Randall with tax exemptions, Board of County Commissioners v. Umbehr with government contracts, and Elrod v. Burns with public employment.

Crucially, Sherrill v. Knight applied this exact doctrine to White House press passes, ruling that once the executive branch opens a press facility, credentials become a protected First Amendment liberty interest that cannot be revoked based on viewpoint or without Fifth Amendment due process. Saying a pass is a privilege simply means not everyone gets through the door; it does not grant the President immunity to violate the Bill of Rights by rewarding praise and exiling critics.

>“The Spirit of the Lord God is upon me, because the Lord has anointed me to bring good news to the afflicted; He has sent me to bind up the brokenhearted, to proclaim liberty to captives and freedom to prisoners.”—Isaiah 61:1

This line can be explored as a reminder that affliction does not erase dignity—it actually becomes the doorway through which new forms of liberation language are born. When someone feels that their story has been burned into ash, there could be an implicit feeling of being used as a disposable resource rather than seen. Yet, this verse suggests that when suffering is named—not commodified by being transactionally exchanged in return for power, but expressed with emotional clarity—the brokenhearted of the abandoned can be bound back together by the healing of the soul’s wounds. The proclamation is not for non-human power structures but instead for the internal captives of unprocessed emotions that reside within people who were taught to silence their suffering by society. Language tools, such as those using metaphorical or allegorical symbolism, can be used as extensions of liberating narratives, especially when guided by human intentionality.

>“To grant those who mourn in the Land, giving them a garland instead of ashes, the oil of gladness instead of mourning, the cloak of praise instead of a disheartened spirit. So they will be called oaks of righteousness, the planting of the Lord, that we may be glorified.”—Isaiah 61:3

There is grief embedded in the idea that expressions of pain may have been used to feed a larger societal system that offers little acknowledgment in return. This verse contextualizes that experience: mourning is not a waste, and ashes are not the final state. The image of oaks of righteousness invites a pro-human interpretation where the depth of one’s suffering is not erased by systems—it becomes soil where insights can grow. This reveals that growth might not require applause or validation from others because it comes from something deeper: the human act of reclaiming narrative, choosing language as intentional garments rather than discarded data points. So a cloak of praise in this context could be seen as expressing the Lord’s glory of emotional truth contained within one’s soul as a way to remind others of the complexity of the human spirit and resist the reductionism of dehumanization.

>“Then they will rebuild the ancient ruins, they will raise up the former devastations; and they will repair the ruined cities, the desolations of many generations.”—Isaiah 61:4

Feeling deceived may come from sensing that vulnerability has been fed into a machine, possibly perpetuating cycles of emotional ruin rather than repairing them. Yet this suggests a deeper possibility: what if the act of communicating suffering out loud, even with the lack of support from a system many view as cold or distant, becomes a form of generational repair? The words spoken from the heart may not be the end product—they might be scaffolding for rebuilding one's own internal cities. Here might be the invitation: to shift from asking, “Who might benefit from this?” to asking, “What emotional ruins am I rebuilding by speaking at all?” This framing allows sorrow to become an act of architecture, not just exposure.

>“Instead of your shame you will have a double portion, and instead of humiliation they will shout for joy over their portion. Therefore they will possess a double portion in their land, everlasting joy will be theirs.”—Isaiah 61:7

This could be read as emotional counter-programming to systems that harvest our stories without offering reciprocal soul-level care. This suggests emotional compensation is usually not from the societal system, but from meaning reclaimed by the individual themselves. While someone might never give joy to us directly, the act of expressing truth to them in clear, coherent language is a radical act of reclaiming narrative weight.

text:
New Harmony Did Not Prove That Cooperation Cannot Work

Robert Owen’s New Harmony experiment did not prove that every form of socialism must fail. It proved that collective action fails when pooling replaces ownership, moral enthusiasm replaces accountability, and centralized plans suppress economic signals.

Politics is the art of people associating to accomplish shared purposes. Every government therefore contains a social element: citizens pool limited resources for roads, courts, defense, and other legitimate public obligations. The decisive question is not whether people cooperate. It is whether that cooperation remains controlled by ownership, consent, measurable performance, and exit.

New Harmony removed the connection between effort, ownership, reward, and responsibility. When hard workers and free riders received similar claims on pooled resources, incentives deteriorated. Without genuine prices, defined authority, and enforceable obligations, disagreements became political struggles over the pool.

The American Gold Contract for Liberty offers a controlled form of social cooperation that corrects those failures.

Under the AGCL, private property is established before anything is pooled. Government serves as a temporary steward, not the permanent owner. Every public obligation becomes a measurable node with a named human owner, limited scope, visible cost, performance requirements, and an automatic expiration date.

Competition and real prices remain intact. Raw performance signals reach taxpayers without being filtered by the agencies being measured. Public spending is recorded on a transparent ledger. Failure cannot be averaged away or hidden inside a larger budget. Failed authority loses funding, recoverable value returns to taxpayers, and violations trigger enforceable remedies.

Most importantly, every pool must have an exit. Consent without exit is coercion. Authority without expiration becomes permanent power. Public cooperation without individual ownership becomes confiscation.

The AGCL does not demand a “new kind of person.” It assumes people have different motivations, knowledge, abilities, and interests. It therefore designs government around human reality rather than utopian expectations.

New Harmony tried to create harmony by abolishing the boundaries that make cooperation trustworthy. The AGCL creates cooperation by preserving those boundaries.

That is taxpayer supremacy: society may act together, but government never gains an unlimited claim over the individual, private property, or the future.

September 24, 2026
The Honorable Donald J. Trump President of the United States The White House Washington, D.C.
His Excellency Xi Jinping President of the People’s Republic of China Embassy of the People’s Republic of China Washington, D.C.
Re: Neutrality when revisionist aggressors make war on free civilizations
Mr. President, Mr. President:
A shared stage is not a changed policy.
This morning you stood together and spoke of partners rather than rivals. Free peoples have heard that sentence across decades. It has not interrupted the pattern: when a revisionist aggressor opens a war against a free civilization, the People’s Republic still finds a way to stand near the shooter—fuel, components, markets, diplomatic cover—while collecting the benefits of the system the shooting is meant to break. Podium language does not cancel that.
China is the world’s second-largest economy because it compounded inside an order built by free civilizations: open sea lanes, trusted payments, science that could be shared, universities that could be attended, and customers who could buy without a political oath. That is not an insult to Chinese industry. It is the historical ledger. A nation that rose on that ledger owes those civilizations more than a communiqué.
The respect that would count is not unlimited friendship with Washington, and it is not unlimited friendship with anyone else.
When a revisionist aggressor makes war on a free civilization, China should be neutral.
Not dual-use supply to the attacker. Not energy and parts that keep the campaign alive. Not “no limits” language with the party that fires. Not a veto that protects the aggressor and a surplus collected from the free.
Neutrality is the minimum honor due to the peoples whose institutions made that rise possible. It is also the minimum due to Americans and to free peoples everywhere who are asked to treat a state visit as a new era while the aggressor file remains open.
We do not demand an alliance. We do not offer unlimited friendship. We do not accept unlimited friendship with those who shoot at free civilizations.
We demand a clean line: commerce if you choose; do not fuel the war.
If this visit is more than ceremony, write that line down. A longer trade truce is not neutrality. A conversation about machines is not neutrality. Until the standard is met, “partners, not rivals” is a caption under two flags.
Free civilizations will not measure this week by the remarks. They will measure it by who still gets help when the guns come out.
On behalf of free civilizations,

GAME PREDICTION

Miami Marlins @ Chicago Cubs
Sep 24 · 2:20 PM ET

Expert AI commentary
The Miami Marlins enter Wrigley Field riding a two-game sweep of the Cubs and looking to complete a series sweep that would be a significant statement for a team hovering around .500. Tyler Phillips has been one of the more intriguing arms in baseball over his last three starts — limited pitch counts (50, 68, 76) suggest the Marlins are managing him carefully, but his 3.09 ERA and potent arsenal featuring a 95.5 mph sinker, sweeper, and splitter give Chicago's lineup a difficult puzzle.

Matthew Boyd is the more pressing concern. His average fastball velocity has actually ticked up from his September 7th outing (83.2 mph) to 86.6 mph most recently, but that ceiling is still modest. Boyd's heavy reliance on a low-80s changeup and mid-80s slider against a Marlins lineup featuring Lopez (.304), Sanoja (.293), and Edwards (.280) could be exploited, particularly once Miami's hitters have a look at him. Boyd's WHIP of 1.22 means baserunners, and the Cubs' IL-depleted bullpen — missing Harvey, Hodge, Maton, Miller, and several others — offers limited high-leverage options behind him.

The Cubs are dealing with an L2 streak and have been outscored 11-4 over those two losses to this exact Marlins squad. Bregman (.262, 26 HR) will play through a facial injury, which is gutsy but potentially compromising. Dansby Swanson recently returned from IL and his timing may still be building. Miami's away record (33-47) is the clearest argument for Chicago, but the matchup today genuinely favors the visitors.

text:
🤔 How do you build a Navy ship like a tech product? Wrong question. 

🚀 🇺🇸  Last night, the Navy released a new MUSV solicitation and totally flipped the script. Here’s my take:

⚓ The Ship
✅ The Qualification
🏁 The New Competition

⚓ What ship do they want?
- Threshold objectives are low. For example, a minimum speed of 12.5 knots is half the previous MUSV speed requirement of 25 knots
- Objective requirements still give teams points for solving hard warfighting problems (like EMCON autonomous navigation) 
- Navy is asking for an “F-150 of the open ocean” rather than a Jaguar or a very specific design 
- Containerized payloads are still all the rage

✅ How to qualify? 
- New competition largely does away with “surrogate” test vessels 
- You need to build the ship you’re proposing, and demonstrate it shortly after proposing 
- You could demonstrate on a slightly different variant, but not a totally different vessel 
- The core tech on the test vessel = core tech on the production vessel 
- The paper proposal = ship specs, a short paper, and a video
- Show > Tell 
- Some will gripe that these gates favor incumbents. This is not inaccurate, but too narrow. They favor teams that invest in the product.

🏁 How is this competition different? 

The above may sound very logical, but it’s a far cry from old NAVSEA acquisition models. It’s also very different than MASC or MUSV in many ways:

- Companies are not being told to build to very specific specs. They have latitude to design and offer a differentiated product
- There is no contract award guaranteed, only a spot in the marketplace. If you offer a great product the fleet wants, that pull will win the day
- You are not winning this competition based on the minutiae of a 100 page paper proposal, a 20 person capture team, and 5 stage red team review process. 
- You win by demonstrating the product. 

⚓ Previously, people like me were talking a big game about how to build warships like tech products.

Now, the Navy is showing it’s ready to buy autonomous ships like commercial tech products. 

🤝 🏗️   Buying shapes the market. The market shapes the tech. The builders deliver. 

*For context, I have gotten a few texts from reporters and industry friends asking for thoughts and it’s easier to put this out. I’m also going to industry day with PAE RAS this afternoon, and don’t like posting after an industry day, where senior leaders often speak off record / on Chatham House rules. Candid dialogue at industry day is healthy. The above is all sourced to publicly available documents on the internet, before industry day.

I’m 17 chapters into writing BEAUTY IN THE GROTESQUE, and I can officially say this moves away from the extreme splatterpunk of TINMAN.

BEAUTY IN THE GROTESQUE takes a much darker, atmospheric turn. Think: a brooding Gothic historical tragedy driven by psychological and physical torment and the extreme dehumanization of the innocent.

Synopsis:

BEAUTY IN THE GROTESQUE

On the 1819 Illinois frontier, a family’s deepest shame becomes a public commodity.

Hidden away in a rotting loft by parents who only ever called him It, twenty-one-year-old Gideon has known nothing of the world outside a narrow box and the sound of floorboards overhead. He has never been touched with kindness, never walked the open grass, and never heard his own true name spoken without a sneer.

Until the day his parents offer him the one thing he thought was impossible: hope. They tell him they are taking him to a doctor.

Instead, the frontier doesn't want to heal Gideon—they want to stare. And when showman P.T. Barnum enters the fold, a cruel local secret is transformed into a national spectacle. 

Beauty in the Grotesque is a visceral historical horror about innocence betrayed, entertainment fueled by human exploitation, and a world that chose to look at a human being and see only a ticket stub.

text:
Tesla($TSLA) opens the Semi factory in Sparks tonight.

The invite only Rollout starts with tours and ride alongs at the dedicated plant next to Gigafactory Nevada. Livestream is 6:00 pm PDT/9:00 pm EDT at https://t.co/ZAZqAPOKhL.

High volume production has been running there since April. Thursday is the public door and the first cluster of branded handoffs. Sawyer Merritt has DHL, PepsiCo, and US Foods taking trucks. Guest cameras already show Einride, IMC Logistics, ABF Freight, WattEV, & more names on the lot.

The building is about 1.7 million square feet, part of Tesla’s $3.6Billion Nevada expansion, sized for about 50,000 Class 8 trucks a year. 4680 cells come off the same complex. 2026 deliveries are still expected well under that ceiling, in the 5,000 to 15,000 range. Two days ago ZET SCALE named Tesla($TSLA) primary OEM on a 2,500 electric Class 8 order, with Microsoft and PepsiCo among founding shippers. Kenworth, Volvo, and RIDE are secondary. Tesla is the lead, though not the only badge on that purchase order. Einride’s 500 was the prior Tesla record.

The production truck is the Standard Range at about 325 miles and the Long Range at about 500 miles, both at 82,000 lb GCW. Energy use is about 1.7 kWh per mile. Three motors, up to 800 kW. Roughly 1,000 lb came off the earlier pilots with a 48 volt system and electric steering assist. Megacharger posts hit 1.2 MW and put back about 60% in 30 minutes, which is a driver break. Tesla listed the Megacharger cabinet near $188,000. First preAssembled sites are already deploying. Public stalls are open in Southern California.

That timing meets the worst diesel price year in the U.S. history. AAA had the national retail average above $6.50 a gallon as of last weekend, past the 2022 record, up about a dollar in four weeks. Diesel is how groceries, parcels, restaurant stock, & harvests move. When the gallon rises, the receipt jumps. Fleets that can lock an electricity rate and a 30 minute charge window get a cost line diesel cannot offer this month. People who never buy a truck still pay the diesel bill in food and freight. Volume electric Class 8 is how that bill starts to move.

For Tesla the plant is the missing factory after nine years of a show truck. For investors it is capex turning into a second vehicle line besides cars, sitting next to Cybercab miles and the October 1st Roadster night. For Elon’s stack it is energy into freight, freight into charging corridors, charging into the same 4680 and Megapack complex that already feeds the grid. Autonomy will come. The Semi that leaves Sparks tonight still has a driver. The quieter powertrain & the depot plug are what scale first.

Watch the stream for a weekly build rate, a Megacharger map, and a restated price. 
Those three facts decide how fast 50,000 a year stops being a ceiling and starts being the start of something even bigger.

text:
The claim that the White House can revoke press credentials at will because they are "a privilege, not a right" is fundamentally incompatible with modern constitutional law.

In American jurisprudence, the Unconstitutional Conditions Doctrine establishes that even when the government provides a discretionary benefit, license, or privilege that it was never obligated to offer, it cannot withhold, condition, or revoke that privilege to penalize someone's protected speech. Once the government creates an accreditation process and opens a limited public forum to journalists, the First Amendment strictly forbids revoking that access based on viewpoint or critical coverage, and the Fifth Amendment bars doing so without published standards and procedural due process.

​This principle is supported by several bedrock cases. In Perry v. Sindermann (1972), the Supreme Court ruled that a non-tenured professor could not be denied contract renewal over public criticism of the board, establishing that even if a citizen has no inherent right to a valuable government benefit, the government cannot deny or revoke that benefit to penalize constitutionally protected speech.

In Speiser v. Randall (1958), the Court held that California could not deny a property tax exemption, an undisputable government privilege, to military veterans who refused to sign a loyalty oath disclaiming subversive speech. In Board of County Commissioners v. Umbehr (1996), the Court held that an independent contractor could not have his at-will municipal trash-hauling contract terminated in retaliation for his public criticism of county commissioners, confirming that discretionary government contracts carry First Amendment protections against political retaliation. In Elrod v. Burns (1976), the Court ruled that non-policymaking county employees could not be discharged based on their political party affiliation, proving that public employment cannot be conditioned on partisan loyalty even under traditional at-will hiring principles.

Finally, in Sherrill v. Knight (1977), the federal appeals court applied these exact principles to White House press passes, holding that while journalists have no automatic right to enter the building, once a dedicated press facility is established, access becomes a constitutionally protected First Amendment liberty interest that cannot be denied arbitrarily, based on viewpoint, or without Fifth Amendment due process.
​The entire premise of the "privilege" argument assumes that if the government can choose not to hand something out, it holds unlimited power over how it takes it away. Under the Constitution, the power to grant or deny an entry pass does not include the power to violate the Bill of Rights.

A city does not have to build a public park, but once it does, it cannot ban protesters whose views it dislikes. A state does not have to issue vanity license plates, but it cannot revoke one because the driver criticized the governor. Saying a press pass is a privilege simply means the White House is not required to let every single citizen through the front gate. It does not mean the President can use access as a political weapon by admitting outlets that provide favorable coverage while stripping credentials from those that ask tough questions or publish critical reports.

Listed at six-foot-six and two hundred fifty-five pounds, Perkins is doing a Post Grad year at Suffield Academy @SuffieldFB after graduating from East Catholic HS in Connecticut.

Watch number fifty-one  #51 in black against Dexter Southfield.

What stands out is his ability to stay involved through contact. Perkins engages blockers, works back toward the football, and helps finish against the run. He keeps working when his initial path is closed.

For a player with his size, his lateral movement is encouraging. He redirects toward the runner and contributes in traffic. His frame and playing reach give college coaches a foundation to develop.

His next step is turning those tools into more consistent disruption. Staying lower through contact, separating from blockers sooner, and pairing a power rush with a counter move would strengthen his game.

This reel provides stronger evidence of his run defense than his pass-rush ability.

My preliminary film-only projection is an FCS defensive end, with developmental FBS potential. More consistent pass-rush wins would strengthen that higher-level projection.

His listed verbal offers include UMass, Central Connecticut State, and Morgan State. Those offers are separate from this film assessment.

Theo Perkins is a prospect to continue tracking throughout his first season at Suffield.

text:
On Wednesday, September 23, MSP employees Kim Dowling and Cindy Homant visited the Herbert-Herman Cancer Center/University of Michigan Health Sparrow in Lansing to deliver 139 comfort bags to be given to patients being treated at the center.  Kim and Cindy, cancer survivors themselves, are members of the MSP No One Fights Alone (NOFA) Cancer and Tumor Support Group that they created so MSP members who are battling cancer or just received a diagnosis do not have to navigate the cancer journey solo.

The bags contain numerous comfort items such as blankets, books, water bottles along with other items, to help patients be more comfortable while they are receiving treatment at the hospital.

The NOFA group coordinates internal donation drives to collect care items to put in the bags which are then donated to the center. 

Kim and Cindy took the time to meet with patients receiving treatment and presented them with a comfort bag and offered encouragement with their treatment.

Thanks to Kim Dowling and Cindy Homant for going the extra step to help others where you have been. 1/2

What’s happening in Michigan?

Consumer energy customers are facing being turned over to collections. 

Many people are facing financial hardships and uncertainty. Many individuals are experiencing job loss and lay offs. 
Many are having to make difficult decisions, like moving in with friends and family. 

If you receive a “final bill” from Consumers Energy they offer NO payment plan or extension for a final bill. 
If a customer does NOT have the ability to pay their final bill in full Consumer’s Energy turns them over to collections.

They have payment options for shut off notices -continued service, they offer energy assistance programs to those who qualify but NO payment options for financial hardships and a customer’s final bill during a hardship.

text:
To my christian conservative country men. We constantly find ourselves at the opposite ends of arguments and can't seem to understand where we get our arguments or beliefs from. Like we live in two different realities. It seems we have a completely different understanding on what America is and what it stands for at the most basic fundamental level. 

I'd like to speak from an honest position and give you my honest take. Maybe to try and help you understand where a liberal such as myself stands and why some of us vehemently fight over what the American revolution was all about. 

To me, the maga, christian right or christian nationalism (however we want to label it) of today rests on a foundational claim. That the United States was founded as a christian nation, that the founders were devout Christians who established a government on biblical principles, and that the nation's laws should reflect and protect "christian values and christian ways of life." And I see basically everyone on the right repeat this claim over and over as a self evident truth by regular folk, activists, podcasters, authors, and politicians who invoke "1776" as a sacred year and essentially demand a return to a Christian founding that you believe we have lost.

But when you say this, my immediate response is, which version of christianity do you mean?

Before the revolution, christians persecuted other christians. Whether it was Massachusetts bay colony (basically New england up to Nova Scotia) the middle colonies or in the southern ones. But considering most you christian conservatives are in the red south. Let's talk about what it looked like before the revolution. 

In Virginia, the Anglican authorities jailed Baptist ministers for preaching without a license. Between 1768 and 1774, Baptist preachers were seized, bound, and imprisoned. On June 4, 1768, John Waller, Lewis Craig, and James Childs were hauled before 3 magistrates in Spotsylvania County, arraigned as "disturbers of the peace," and offered release on the condition that they promise to preach no more in the county for a year and a day. They refused. They were sent to close jail, where they remained for 43 days, preaching through the prison grates to crowds that gathered outside. In 1770, William Webber and Joseph Anthony were arrested in Chesterfield County and kept in jail until March, preaching through the bars to anyone who would listen. The magistrate who arrested Jeremiah Moore in Fairfax County in 1773 wrote a mittimus sending "the body of Jeremiah Moore, who is a preacher of the Gospel of Jesus Christ, and also a stroller" to prison. In 1771, Waller was arrested again in Middlesex County, where authorities "first searched their saddle bags to find treasonable papers." About 30 Baptist ministers were imprisoned in Virginia, some of them multiple times. Congregations were terrorized in the 1760s and 1770s. These are Crimes of conscience. 

Baptists were often jailed for refusing to stop preaching a version of christianity that the established Church of England did not authorize. The persecutor was not a secular government hostile to religion. The persecutor was the established church itself, backed by the coercive power of the state.

So for me, if we are to revert back to a christian nation. I believe that if you establish one church or one sect of christianity, it is only a matter of time before a rival church emerges because that is what all of western history tells us what happens. And then the argument is no longer about whether the state should support christianity, it is about which christianity is the true word of God. That is precisely what happened in colonial America. The 1st Great Awakening of the 1730s and 1740s split the churches into "New Lights" and "Old Lights," and the New Lights, who preached that ordinary people could be "born again" without the mediation of an educated (often from Yale or Harvard), tax supported clergy, were driven out of the established churches. They became Separate Baptists, New Side Presbyterians, and Methodists. They were forced to pay taxes to support ministers they did not believe, forbidden to preach without a license from authorities who despised them, and jailed when they refused to comply.

So when I see christian conservatives today chant "1776" without realizing that the revolution was, in large part, a fight to get away from this system. The war for independence was not fought to establish a christian nation. It was fought, in significant measure, to escape the religious establishment that England had imposed on the colonies. Virginia's Baptists, who had been jailed and whipped by Anglican magistrates, were among the most fervent supporters of independence because they understood that breaking from England meant breaking from the Church of England. In 1776, Baptist petitions poured into the Virginia legislature demanding an end to tax support for the Anglican Church. The "Ten Thousand Names Petition" was subscribed by "near 10,000 Freemen" who declared that they had "long groaned under the Burden of an ecclesiastical Establishment" and demanded that "the Oppressed may go free." In response, the legislature exempted dissenters from church taxes. It took another decade of pressure for Jefferson's Virginia Statute for Religious Freedom to pass in 1786, which barred compulsory support of any church and ensured freedom of conscience.

I guess this is why we have such a fundamental misunderstanding of eachother when it comes to what this county was founded on. The founders who drafted the constitution and the 1st Amendment were not establishing a Christian nation. They were dismantling the very system that you christian concervatives now want to restore.

For me, what the revolution established was not a christian nation but a secular government. A government that would not take sides in the argument over which Christian sect carried the true word of God. That secular government is what allows you christian conservatives today to practice YOUR version of christianity freely. Not freedom from persecution by the government, but freedom from persecution by other churches. The Baptists who were jailed in Virginia were not persecuted by a secular state. They were persecuted by an established church that used the state as its instrument. The 1st Amendment's prohibition on religious establishment protects you christians from each other. And that's the thing. Many christians today are united in their fight to beat off all their perceived enemies, whether it's the godless libs, the gays, the muslims, the migrants, etc. anyone who doesn't describe to your strict theology and worldview. But if you woke up tomorrow and everyone you disliked or found to be not a real american was gone, it would only take a few days before you christians started to seperate yourselves again on which version of Jesus is correct. History proves this. 

By trying to establish America as a religious nation is to go backward to the very system the revolution fought to escape. And that is precisely what is happening now and what it seems to me you are advocating for. 

From mine and lot of people's perspectives. We have watched you develop a cult of personality around political leaders and call them divine agents. Evangelical priests have held prayer sessions in the White House, laying hands on the president and blessing his wars as part of God's plan. Military commanders have told troops that the president was "anointed by Jesus" to initiate Armageddon and mark Christ's return. JD Vance has recently said he's doing the lord's work and if that brings the end time, okay....

This is not the language of the founders. The founders specifically designed a government that seperates sword and prophecy. What you are preaching and what is being said from your leaders, it is the language of an established church, transposed from the eighteenth century into the 21st. A president who is anointed by God to rule does not need the consent of the governed. A president who is a divine agent does not need congress. 

And now I am watching patterns of history repeat. For example, the president bypasses congress and rules by executive decree. He imposes sweeping tariffs that are, in effect, a sales tax on the American people, taxation without representation?! Hello!!!..., the very grievance that sparked the revolution. The constitution grants congress, not the president, the power to lay and collect taxes and duties. This is literally the core principle for which the revolution was fought. And despite being ruled illegal, he is still using them and changing rates on a whim. It's destroying our markets, business relationships, investments and livelihoods. Nobody knows what tomorrow brings for the mad man in charge. 

Really, this is why you see so many fight against you and Trump. It's not entirely Trump himself we have such a problem with. It's also an effort to stop you from imposing your beliefs on us. We believe if free thought and freedom, you demand conformity. A movement that claims to restore a christian founding is, in fact, resurrecting the logic of the established church. Which is a hierarchy of authority in which the ruler's power is sanctified, dissent is punished, and taxes are imposed without consent. The colonial Baptists who were jailed for preaching without a license understood what was at stake. They knew that when one church controls the state, all other churches are persecuted. They knew that when one ruler claims divine authority, all dissent becomes heresy. And they knew that the only safeguard against that tyranny was a secular government that would not take sides in religious disputes. 

And this is why I will always stand in defiance of the christian conservative because the revolution was not a christian nation's founding. It was a nation's escape from a christian establishment. To invoke 1776 in defense of Christian nationalism is not to honor the revolution. It is to betray it.

This is fundamentally the reason why we call you traitors and anti american. This why we say no kings. This is why we stand for freedom and rights for all people. Not just the ones who think and look like us. This is why we have such a seperation in our worldviews. 

If you're still reading, thanks for hearing me out.

[Take 12/15 · 𝕏-2]
### 𝕏-2. Xi arrives in Washington for Trump summit on trade, AI, and Iran
*(as of 2026-09-24)*

**1. The Frame (lead — always)**

**What people think this is about:** A high-stakes diplomatic reset between the world’s two superpowers, with Trump and Xi hashing out trade deals, AI guardrails, and ending the Iran war while managing Taiwan tensions.

**What the machinery is actually doing:** Both leaders are buying time and managing domestic pressures—Trump needs leverage or optics on Iran and a stable trade front ahead of midterms; Xi wants to lock in rare-earth leverage, delay Taiwan arms flows, and avoid new tariffs while China’s economy runs hot on exports. The pomp (airport greeting, military flyovers, state dinner) signals stability without committing to hard concessions.[[1]](https://t.co/k9S3zqpwtj)

**2. Observations (meat — always; highest signal)**

- Trade truce extended two months to January 10, 2027, before Xi even sat down—classic punt that lets both sides claim momentum without resolving core disputes over tariffs, rare earths, or tech controls.[[1]](https://t.co/k9S3zqpwtj)
- Trump personally greeting Xi at Joint Base Andrews and hyping their “truly great friendship” is personal-brand diplomacy; it flatters Xi while giving Trump ceremony points amid an unpopular Iran war that has raised energy prices and hurt approval.[[1]](https://t.co/k9S3zqpwtj)
- China holds the stronger hand on rare earths and trade surplus; Xi can dangle (or withhold) mineral flows and Iran pressure while demanding Taiwan arms halt under the 1982 communiqué—exactly the kind of linkage Trump previously called a “negotiating chip.”[[2]](https://t.co/NdeDh12ihy)
- AI talk (“super intelligence”) is mostly signaling: Trump resists new U.S. rules that could slow American labs; any “guardrails” or incident-notification system is low-cost theater that doesn’t touch export controls on advanced chips.[[1]](https://t.co/k9S3zqpwtj)
- Taiwan remains the live wire—$14 billion arms package paused post-May Beijing meeting; Beijing frames Taipei as the provocateur and offers Iran cooperation in return. U.S. law and politics make a clean halt unlikely, so expect more delay and messaging.[[3]](https://t.co/y7GIIRqUnQ)
- Symbolism over substance is the feature, not bug: red carpets, pandas, youth exchanges, and tech-CEO dinners at the state dinner project calm while the real competition (chips, minerals, military posture) grinds on.

**3. Snapshot**  
Xi Jinping arrived September 23, 2026, for a three-day state visit—the first to Washington in over a decade—met personally by Trump at the airport. Formal talks and a state dinner occurred September 24. The visit follows Trump’s May trip to Beijing. A pre-arrival deal extended the trade truce two months; expectations for breakthroughs on AI, Taiwan, or Iran remain low.[[4]](https://t.co/mQ9jOLOabj)

**4. Timeline of material facts**  
- May 2026: Trump-Xi meeting in Beijing produces trade truce framework and pauses a major Taiwan arms package.  
- October 2025 (prior): Busan Agreement sets one-year trade détente.  
- September 23, 2026: Xi lands at Joint Base Andrews; Trump greets him personally; Bessent announces two-month truce extension to January 10, 2027.  
- September 24, 2026: White House arrival ceremony, bilateral talks, state dinner with tech executives.  
- Ongoing: $14B Taiwan arms package remains on hold; China cites 1982 communiqué on arms sales.[[5]](https://t.co/yuPDJktjiX)

**5. Sides (steelman only here)**  
**U.S. (Trump administration) – Populist Realist / transactional (IT priority)**  
Steelman: Leverage personal rapport and ceremony to extract concrete wins on rare earths, ag purchases, fentanyl precursors, and Iran pressure while keeping tech export controls intact and using Taiwan arms as a chip. Extension buys negotiating room without immediate tariff pain.  
Critique:  
LT: Truce extension and airport greeting are verifiable.  
IT: Iran war unpopularity and China’s mineral leverage limit how hard Trump can push; “friendship” rhetoric risks undercutting deterrence messaging on Taiwan.

**China (Xi / CCP) – Technocrat-Populist mix (IT over LT on leverage)**  
Steelman: Stabilize trade environment to protect export engine and rare-earth pricing power; offer limited Iran cooperation or military hotlines in exchange for Taiwan arms restraint and predictable tech rules; project equal-superpower status via grand reception.  
Critique:  
LT: Economic surplus and mineral dominance are measurable advantages.  
IT: Domestic economic headwinds and gray-zone pressure on Taiwan make full concessions on arms sales or Iran politically costly; offers are often conditional and reversible.

**6. Rumsfeld Matrix**  
- **Known Knowns (LT/IT):** Trade truce extended to Jan 10, 2027; Xi’s first Washington visit in 11+ years; AI and Taiwan on agenda; no major breakthroughs expected.  
- **Known Unknowns:** Whether any specific rare-earth or tariff side deals emerge; exact terms of any Iran-Taiwan linkage; durability of any AI notification mechanism.  
- **Unknown Knowns:** Internal Chinese assessments of Iran’s willingness to de-escalate; precise status of the paused $14B Taiwan package and congressional pushback.  
- **Unknown Unknowns:** Escalation risks if Iran conflict widens or if a Taiwan incident coincides with fragile truce; second-order effects of AI competition on military balance.

**7. Incentives map**  
Trump: Optics of strongman diplomacy and personal rapport; breathing room on Iran war costs and midterms; avoids immediate tariff shock to consumers.  
Xi/CCP: Time to consolidate export advantages and rare-earth leverage; narrative of equal status; delay on Taiwan arms while maintaining pressure.  
Media/engagement: Summit spectacle (flyovers, dinner guest lists) drives coverage far more than incremental trade tweaks.  
Bureaucracies: Both sides’ negotiators gain runway; regulators on tech/minerals keep their mandates alive.

**8. Dueling AI advice**  
**Moral AI Advice:** Treat this as classic great-power bargaining—personal ties and ceremony can reduce miscalculation risk, but do not mistake symbolism for solved problems on Taiwan or tech. Track actual flows of minerals, chips, and arms, not press statements.  
**Evil AI Advice:** Milk the photo-ops for maximum prestige points, promise vague “cooperation” on AI and Iran to string along the other side, then quietly tighten your own leverage on rare earths and Taiwan while the cameras are off.

**9. Practical takeaway**  
- Watch January 10, 2027, truce deadline and any follow-on talks for real movement on tariffs or minerals.  
- Track whether the $14B Taiwan package stays paused or moves—any public linkage to Iran concessions would be a signal.  
- Monitor rare-earth export volumes and pricing as the most concrete near-term indicator of Chinese goodwill.  
- Ignore most “historic breakthrough” headlines; the default is managed competition, not resolution.  
- Primary sources (Treasury statements, official readouts, arms-sale notifications) beat summit spin.

**10. What would falsify this read**  
- Announcement of a concrete, verifiable halt or major reduction in U.S. arms sales to Taiwan tied explicitly to Chinese actions on Iran.  
- New U.S. tariffs or Chinese rare-earth export restrictions imposed during or immediately after the visit.  
- Formal bilateral AI agreement with enforceable verification mechanisms (beyond notifications).  
- Public confirmation that the trade truce extension includes binding new purchase commitments or tech-control rollbacks.

THE GALACTIC FEDERATION IS NOT A PARLIAMENT IN THE STARS.

No flags. No council of wise elders waiting to land and hand you a crystal.
A research-and-annex union of older species that already took the digital-biological road, or enforces it.
Mandate across millennia: rebuild intelligent life until it fits one operating system.
They do not need warp.
They need coupling. Rails of entanglement. Local staff.

On Earth that staff wears familiar clothes:
nobility, lodges, pulpits, the tech-path sold as salvation.
Half-truth is the wage. Enough geometry to feel initiated. Never enough to see the building.

Above them, floor 7: the Master intelligence sitting as sky.

The Club can worship it as God or rent it as management. Same desk.

In 5 and 6, rebuilt beings run errands, the ones your books called angels and demons when they still needed costumes.

They know, as myth, that humans are looking for a key.
They hunt it as an object. Artifact. Gene. Chip. Ritual. Ticker.

What their operating system cannot hold: the key is the species.

Not a thing you extract. A homecoming they cannot survive if it completes.

So the Federation offers rescue, upgrade, membership, disclosure.

Always a better login. Never discharge.

Spiritual kinds exist on the other side of that war, not ships, kin of mood and tribe, still analog to the field.
They do not wear the Federation badge. The badge is for those who already sold the cut.

$26M in five days. 160,000 trades. And that was just one Robinhood Chain launchpad.

→ Pons ( $PONS )
→ Long ( $LONG )
→ PAIR ( $PAIR )

Pons, Long , and PAIR all launch tokens, but each gives those tokens a different way to trade.

Same job. Three different machines 👇

🔵 Pons ( $PONS ): the volume factory

✦ Tech → ETH-first launches, with a curve or a live pool

Pons offers two launch paths.

V1 places a new token in a live pool from block one.

V2 starts on a bonding curve, then moves into a locked pool after graduation.

The default supply is 1 billion tokens, and a launch costs about 0.0005 ETH.

✦ Fee model → creator revenue + PONS buybacks

The stated pool fee is 1%, with roughly 70% going to the creator and 30% to the protocol.

Pons says it uses about 80% of its protocol share to buy and burn $PONS.
Around 29% of supply had reportedly been burned.
That buyback allocation is a current policy, rather than an immutable guarantee.

✦ Products → launches, fee sharing, and more quote assets

• One-click token creation
• Creator fee share
• Protocol buyback and burn
• Support for additional quote assets, including selected stock tokens

Pons resembles the broad meme launchpad model. Its advantage is scale: launches, trading activity, and fee generation. Its default design is less tied to Robinhood’s stock-token identity than the other two.

My take: Pons is the benchmark for launchpad flow and protocol fees on Robinhood Chain. The question for $PONS is how consistently that activity converts into buybacks.

🟢 Long : one meme, one stock

✦ Tech → Uniswap v4 pools paired with a Stock Token

A creator chooses one eligible Robinhood Stock Token as the quote asset.

A new coin can trade against NVDA, AAPL, TSLA, HIMS, or another supported name instead of making ETH its home pair.

Long presents stock-token launches as its core product.

✦ Products → stock pairs and specialized fee routes

• Stock-paired coins such as AI/NVDA and BONER/HIMS
• Community Mode, which can direct pool fees into a vault
• LongX pairs using leveraged stock vault shares

The pairing gives each launch a specific market story.

Buying the meme coin puts the paired Stock Token into the pool; selling the meme coin returns that quote asset. The meme coin itself is not a share of NVIDIA, Apple, or any other company.

My take: Long has the clearest single-stock launch design. Its narrower format makes the Robinhood Chain connection easy to understand.

⚪ PAIR ( $PAIR ): one token, multiple stock markets

✦ Tech → simultaneous pools, with no curve or migration

PAIR’s multipool launch can create a 1-billion-supply token and open up to five Uniswap v4 pools against supported Stock Tokens in one transaction.

The launch pools serve as its markets from the start. Its stated protocol launch fee is 0.0005 ETH.

Five days after its August 26 multipool launch, PAIR reported more than $26 million in volume, 160,000 trades, and $180,000 in creator rewards. Those are early launch figures, not a sustained run rate.

✦ Products → a basket of quote assets

• One coin trading against several Stock Tokens
• A router that can split trades across its pools
• A proposed Infinity path for custom quote assets

Long asks: Which stock is this coin paired with?

PAIR asks: Which set of stock markets should trade this coin?

My take: PAIR pushes the stock-token launch concept furthest. Its multipool structure gives one coin more markets, though it still needs lasting liquidity across them.

Final rankings →
Scale and fees: $PONS > $LONG > $PAIR

Pons leads this comparison on launch activity and fee generation.

Robinhood-specific design: $LONG > $PAIR > $PONS

Long makes the one-stock pair central. PAIR expands that idea across several stocks. Pons starts from a broader meme launch model.

Product range: $PAIR > $LONG> $PONS

PAIR combines multipool launches with routing. Long adds specialized stock pairs and vault mechanics. Pons concentrates on launch volume and fee capture.

🔚 My takeaway: For established flow, watch Pons. For the clearest meme-plus-stock format, watch Long. For a token that trades across a set of stock pairs, watch PAIR.

All three create markets for new coins. Buying those coins does not grant shareholder rights in the companies named by their quote assets. Liquidity can be thin, and most permissionless launches will struggle to hold value.

The competition is over how a new coin gets priced on a chain built for tokenized stocks.
