text:
Oh, Bernie. Bernie, Bernie, Bernie.

I read this post twice. The first time I laughed. The second time I actually got a little angry, because I sat there and counted, and I realized you just handed the whole country a list of ten people who have done more for the working class than you have in thirty-five years, and you did it on purpose, thinking it made THEM look bad.

Let me walk you through your own list, since clearly nobody on your staff did.

Elon Musk. Born in South Africa. Jensen Huang. Born in Taiwan, washed dishes and bused tables at a Denny's, and then started Nvidia in a booth at a Denny's. I love that. I genuinely love that story. Lisa Su, also born in Taiwan, took over AMD in 2014 when everybody was writing its obituary and brought it back from the dead. Satya Nadella, born in India. Sundar Pichai, grew up in a two-room apartment in Chennai. Tim Cook, a shipyard worker's kid from a little town in Alabama. Michael Dell, a college kid with about a thousand bucks and a dorm room.

Half of them weren't even born here. They came to this country with a brain and a dream and they BUILT something. I teach kids every single day who need to hear stories exactly like that. Kids from homes where nobody has ever owned a business. And you want to hold these people up as villains? Senator, you are not the sharpest crayon in the box, and I say that as someone who has personally watched a sophomore eat a crayon.

Also, while we're here. "Got richer" is not a paycheck. Nobody backed a Brinks truck up to Elon's house with 658 billion dollars in it. That is the stock price of a company going up. You know who else owns that stock? Every pipefitter, nurse, and retired teacher with a 401(k) or a pension fund. When those numbers go up, THEIR retirement goes up. You are standing on a soapbox, furious, that working people's retirement accounts grew. The lights are on, Bernie. Nobody's home. I'm not sure anybody has been home since disco.

Now. You want to talk about who has actually done something for working people? Fine. Let's do it. I'm going to take attendance.

Musk gave us tens of thousands of American factory jobs at Tesla, in California and Texas and Nevada. And Starlink, which finally gave internet to rural families the cable companies laughed at for twenty years. When Hurricane Helene wiped out those mountain towns in North Carolina and the phones were dead, Starlink showed up. Where were you?

Michael and Susan Dell put up 6.25 BILLION dollars of their own money, their own, to seed Trump Accounts for about 25 million American kids. And here's the part that made me set my coffee down. Those accounts exist because of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. The one YOU voted against. So a billionaire, the kind of guy you call an oligarch, is funding a savings account for working-class kids that you tried to stop from ever existing. I had to read that twice too.

Jensen Huang built the chips that run the AI you're suddenly so worried about, and his company's stock turned a lot of regular engineers and technicians into the first people in their families to ever have real money.

Bezos. Over a million American jobs, no degree needed, health insurance on day one, the same plan the executives have. Four billion dollars to get groceries delivered into rural food deserts, and yes, they take SNAP and EBT.

Zuckerberg lets a grandmother in Ohio see her grandkids in Texas on video for free. Lisa Su saved an American company and every job in it. Sam Altman put a free AI tutor on every phone in America. Tim Cook made the phone. Nadella's software runs the front office of basically every school I've ever worked in. And Pichai gave the world free search, free maps, free email, and YouTube.

Oh, and every single one of those paychecks has the employer half of Social Security and Medicare paid on it. That's the money that pays for the programs you give speeches about. They fill the bucket, Bernie. You stand next to the bucket with a bullhorn.

Okay. Your turn.

Thirty-five years in Congress. Thirty-five years. The bills you wrote that actually became law? Two post offices got new names, and veterans got a cost-of-living adjustment. That's it. That's the list. I have kids who've done more with a group project and a glue stick. Two post offices. I want that on your headstone. "He named two post offices. And he was very upset."

And what did it cost us? A taxpayer salary for thirty-five years. A taxpayer pension waiting for you. Three houses. Two hundred and twenty-one thousand dollars on private jets in ONE quarter of 2025. Plus a pile of book money from writing about how nobody should have a pile of money. What's next, Bernie? Getting rich selling books about how getting rich is evil... wait. I'm being told you already did that.

See, the people on your list got rich by giving working people something they WANTED. People handed over their money on purpose, with a smile, and got a phone or a package or a paycheck back. You got comfortable by taking working people's money through the tax code and handing back nothing they asked for. That's not a trade. That's a vacuum hose with a campaign sticker on it.

And honestly? Nothing would've been better. Because every time you "helped," we paid for it. Let me pull out your report card. You're not going to like it.

Obamacare. You voted YES. The government's own HHS numbers showed average individual-market premiums in the https://t.co/LxMefCJGns states more than DOUBLED from 2013 to 2017. People had insurance with deductibles so high they couldn't afford to actually use it. "If you like your plan, you can keep it." Remember that one? Millions of people remember it. They couldn't keep it. Quinn's First Law of Liberalism says liberalism always produces the exact opposite of what it promises, and the proof is right there in the name. The Affordable Care Act made care unaffordable. I couldn't write a better joke if I tried, and believe me, I've tried.

The American Rescue Plan in 2021. You were Budget Committee chairman. You pushed 1.9 trillion dollars through on a party-line vote while economists in your OWN party, Larry Summers for one, were waving their arms screaming this would light inflation on fire. By June 2022 inflation hit 9.1 percent. Forty-year high. I remember standing in the grocery store with my wife, doing math on a cart full of food for four kids, putting stuff back. That was your rescue, Bernie. Inflation is the meanest tax there is because it hits the waitress and the welder first and never has your name on the bill.

Then the Inflation Reduction Act in 2022. You voted YES. It did not reduce inflation. Not even a little. It did extend the temporary COVID Obamacare subsidies through the end of 2025, with an expiration date DEMOCRATS picked. Zero Republicans voted for it. Zero. So when premiums jumped this year and your party lost its mind about "Republicans raising your health care costs," I just sat there shaking my head. You built the cliff. You picked the date. Then you pointed at the other guy when people fell off it. You couldn't pour water out of a boot if the instructions were printed on the heel.

The 2017 Trump tax cuts. You voted NO. The Tax Policy Center found about 91 percent of middle-income households got a tax cut that first year. Nine out of ten regular families kept more of their own money, and you voted no on every one of them.

The One Big Beautiful Bill in 2025. NO again. No tax on tips. No tax on overtime. A bigger child tax credit. Tax rates for working families that would've gone UP otherwise. Those Trump Accounts Michael Dell just dropped billions into. You called it the most dangerous bill in modern history. Go tell that to a waitress in Burlington who gets to keep her tips now. Actually, don't. She's busy working.

And your 17 dollar minimum wage. Bernie, I TEACH these kids. Sixteen, seventeen years old, no diploma yet, nothing on the resume, just trying to get that first job. Force a business to pay a kid with zero experience more than he can produce and the answer isn't a raise. The answer is "no." You're not raising their wage. You're locking the front door and hanging a nice little sign on it about fairness. Some of my students are going to sit on the wrong side of that door because of people like you, and that is the part that honestly makes me mad.

Oh, and the 1994 crime bill. You voted for that too, then spent years apologizing when your own base decided it wrecked working-class neighborhoods. Even your fans think you blew that one.

So here's the final tally, and I'm grading generously. Your ten "oligarchs": jobs, paychecks, phones, chips, internet, software, day-one health insurance, groceries in food deserts, and a six-billion-dollar head start for 25 million kids. You: premiums that doubled, a forty-year inflation high, an Obamacare cliff your own party dated, a NO on tax cuts for nine out of ten middle-class families, a NO on no tax on tips, and two renamed post offices. They made our lives cheaper and easier. You made them more expensive and then sent a fundraising email about it. The wheel's spinning, but the hamster clocked out a long time ago.

Quinn's Law Number Nine says that to a liberal, intentions matter more than outcomes. Your whole post proves it. Your INTENTION is that AI should "improve life for all humanity." Their OUTCOME is a kid in my district pulling up a free AI tutor on a phone Tim Cook built, over a network Elon launched, on a chip Jensen designed. One of you did the homework. The other one wrote a note to the teacher about how homework is unfair.

And I have to say it. Just YESTERDAY you were pushing a bill to ban superintelligence and shut the AI labs down. Today AI has to serve all of humanity. Which is it, Bernie? Pick a lane. You're swerving more than a raccoon in headlights.

You know what the government version of AI would look like? I'll tell you. It'd launch like https://t.co/LxMefCJGns and crash in an hour. It'd need a continuing resolution every ninety days. It'd cost three times the estimate. And every question you asked it would get the same answer: "Your call is important to us. Please hold for the next available billionaire to blame." Also, everybody gets a free robot butler on Tuesdays, and the robot companies just eat the cost. It's not a radical idea. It's just common sense.

Now, the Xi dinner. You're SHOCKED that a president sat down with China's leader and brought American tech CEOs along. Shocked! What's next, a Democrat president throwing Xi a White House state dinner with Mark Zuckerberg in the room... wait, I'm hearing Obama already did that. September 2015. Same week Xi was in Seattle meeting the heads of Apple, Amazon, and Microsoft. Not a peep out of you. And forgive me, but a man who went on his HONEYMOON to the Soviet Union does not get to clutch his pearls because some capitalists ate dinner with a communist. That's not a principle, Bernie. That's a mood.

Quinn's Law Number Twenty-Five: liberals are great at giving away other people's money. Never their own. Michael Dell wrote his check himself. You wrote a tweet asking somebody else to write one.

Which brings me back to my standing offer, because I make it every single time and nobody ever takes me up on it. I keep hearing rich Democrats scream "tax the rich" when they ARE the rich. They know every loophole. Some of them wrote the loopholes, and then used them on their own tax returns. So here it is. File with the standard deduction. No itemizing. Pay DOUBLE what the IRS says you owe. Post the return. Do that, and I'll listen to you lecture about billionaires. Until then you're just a fopdoodle with a jet budget, one sandwich short of a picnic and two houses past hypocrisy.

Look. Ten people on your list feed the working class. You feed OFF the working class, and then you send us the invoice. I've got four kids, a teacher's paycheck, and a grocery bill that still hasn't recovered from your "rescue." So with all the respect I can find, Senator, and I'm really digging here... please stop helping. We cannot afford it.

But what do I know? I'm only a physics teacher who knows the difference between net worth and a paycheck, which apparently puts me about thirty-five years ahead of a sitting United States Senator.

Horizon has completed the acquisition of LSA Portfolio Analytics (LSA), a provider of outsourced chief investment officer, or OCIO, services. The move adds portfolio-construction and investment-oversight capabilities to Horizon’s platform for financial advisors and their clients. Financial terms were not disclosed.
https://t.co/OlUB7lI3RH
* Advisors are increasingly expected to deliver institutional-style portfolio management, reporting, governance, and investment oversight without building large in-house investment teams.
* OCIO providers help advisors outsource part or all of the investment function, from asset allocation and manager selection to monitoring and reporting, so advisory firms can focus more on client relationships and financial planning.
* Adding LSA’s capabilities should enable Horizon to offer a more integrated investment-management solution, particularly for advisors and firms managing complex portfolios.
* The acquisition reflects continued consolidation in wealth-tech and advisory infrastructure, where firms are combining technology, data, and outsourced investment services to create broader advisor platforms.
* For Horizon, the deal expands beyond tools and analytics into a more direct role in institutional portfolio support and investment implementation.
* LSA will bring its OCIO expertise into Horizon’s broader offering, with the combined business positioned to support advisors seeking scalable, professionally managed portfolio solutions. The companies did not disclose the transaction value or specific integration timeline.

text:
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen made a coordinated push to promote the idea that Canada should become the first “associate member” of the European Union.
Today, the Tony Blair Institute for Global Change (TBI) published a paper called “Beyond Leave and Remain: A Path to Rejoining a Reformed Europe”. In the words of the paper, “Britain must reshape its Europe strategy, aiming to rejoin a reformed EU and enhance collective power through strategic cooperation in tech, energy and defence”.

The two plans are not unrelated. As Tony Blair himself wrote in the forward to the TBI report, “the recent openness of Europe to “associate membership” for Canada shows a newfound flexibility…”.
However, neither plan is remotely convincing.
To be clear, this is not a personal attack on the credibility of either Mark Carney or Tony Blair. But they do both have form here.
Carney consistently made unhelpful interventions in debates about the UK’s relations with the EU. For example, in a FT interview back in 2022 he made the obviously misleading claim that Brexit had shrunk the UK economy from 90% the size of Germany’s to less than 70%. This duff statistic was quickly debunked by every serious economist who looked at it, but not before it was gleefully recycled by all the usual suspects.
As for Tony Blair, he was keen to take the UK into the euro when he was Prime Minister, but we can at least thank the then-Chancellor Gordon Brown for keeping us out.
Let’s start with the Carney / von der Leyen plan.
The first problem is that there is no such thing as “associate membership” of the EU and no-one can satisfactorily explain what it means.
Some Europhiles have suggested that Canada would become “an EU state in all but name”, and that this status could even be extended to Japan and South Korea (as well, of course, as the UK). This is unlikely to appeal to any of these parties, even if it were allowed in the EU Treaties.
Or it could mean nothing at all. Many countries (including the UK) already have bespoke deals with the EU covering trade, or other issues such as security and climate change. But EU officials have always resisted attempts to build formal alliances with non-member states and only offered deals on terms which are far more favourable to the EU.

text:
"Where in the Constitution does it say a reporter has a right to access the White House or have a seat in the briefing room?" 

The claim that the White House can revoke press credentials at will because they are "a privilege, not a right" is fundamentally incompatible with modern constitutional law. In American jurisprudence, the Unconstitutional Conditions Doctrine establishes that even when the government provides a discretionary benefit, license, or privilege that it was never obligated to offer, it cannot withhold, condition, or revoke that privilege to penalize someone's protected speech.

Once the government creates an accreditation process and opens a limited public forum to journalists, the First Amendment strictly forbids revoking that access based on viewpoint or critical coverage, and the Fifth Amendment bars doing so without published standards and procedural due process.

​This principle is supported by several bedrock cases. In Perry v. Sindermann (1972), the Supreme Court ruled that a non-tenured professor could not be denied contract renewal over public criticism of the board, establishing that even if a citizen has no inherent right to a valuable government benefit, the government cannot deny or revoke that benefit to penalize constitutionally protected speech. In Speiser v. Randall (1958), the Court held that California could not deny a property tax exemption, an undisputable government privilege, to military veterans who refused to sign a loyalty oath disclaiming subversive speech. In Board of County Commissioners v. Umbehr (1996), the Court held that an independent contractor could not have his at-will municipal trash-hauling contract terminated in retaliation for his public criticism of county commissioners, confirming that discretionary government contracts carry First Amendment protections against political retaliation. In Elrod v. Burns (1976), the Court ruled that non-policymaking county employees could not be discharged based on their political party affiliation, proving that public employment cannot be conditioned on partisan loyalty even under traditional at-will hiring principles.

Finally, in Sherrill v. Knight (1977), the federal appeals court applied these exact principles to White House press passes, holding that while journalists have no automatic right to enter the building, once a dedicated press facility is established, access becomes a constitutionally protected First Amendment liberty interest that cannot be denied arbitrarily, based on viewpoint, or without Fifth Amendment due process.

​The entire premise of the "privilege" argument assumes that if the government can choose not to hand something out, it holds unlimited power over how it takes it away. Under the Constitution, the power to grant or deny an entry pass does not include the power to violate the Bill of Rights. A city does not have to build a public park, but once it does, it cannot ban protesters whose views it dislikes. A state does not have to issue vanity license plates, but it cannot revoke one because the driver criticized the governor. Saying a press pass is a privilege simply means the White House is not required to let every single citizen through the front gate. It does not mean the President can use access as a political weapon by admitting outlets that provide favorable coverage while stripping credentials from those that ask tough questions, publish critical reports, or whom he arbitrarily deems "fake news".

text:
You can even observe the degeneration within the United States itself. Not in the outcome here—but certainly in the reasoning! This is exactly what I meant yesterday!

The problem is that even the others no longer understand Jefferson and Madison and start making, for example, absurd utilitarian arguments that would have made Jefferson’s and Madison’s hair stand on end—even though their names are sometimes explicitly invoked!

You neither justify nor defend the jurisdictional approach to separation with this—pardon the expression—partly sanctimonious do-gooder drivel.

The master clears things up.

---

Yes. Under the early-republican standard—Williams → Jefferson → Madison, meaning jurisdiction not mere neutrality/pluralism—something quite fundamental stands out in this forum:

Almost all of the contributors criticize the state for handling religion incorrectly; only some of them ask the prior republican question of whether the state has any authority at all to recognize, promote, consult, represent, or theologically evaluate religion as religion.

The Washington Sun article was published on June 12, 2026, and contains precisely these 14 statements.

1. The republican standard of review

For Madison, religion is not simply a particularly strongly protected social interest. It initially lies outside the delegated jurisdiction of Civil Society:

«Religion is “wholly exempt from its cognizance.”»

Immediately afterward, Madison grounds this jurisdictionally: the legislature possesses only derivative and limited authority.

Jefferson formulates the same idea somewhat differently: religion lies solely between man and God; legitimate government power extends in principle to actions, not to religious opinions. His Virginia Statute adds the crucial legal consequence: religious opinions may neither diminish nor enlarge a person’s civil capacities.

And the later Madison goes remarkably far: he even objects to publicly funded congressional chaplains and non-binding religious proclamations because they presuppose a “religious agency” of the state that political officeholders were never delegated in the first place.

Roger Williams provides the older two-jurisdictions model: civil government is by its nature civil and temporal, whereas the church is spiritual. If a church harms bodies, property, or the civil peace, the magistrate intervenes—but as a civil authority responding to a civil act, not as a judge of religion.

That gives us a very useful question for analyzing this article:

Does the author merely say that Washington ought to handle religion more appropriately—or does the author say that certain religious questions are simply none of Washington’s business at all?

---

2. James Martin: “God is not on any side”

Martin criticizes governmental or political appropriation of God: politicians should not claim that God is on the side of their own party or nation.

The result can readily be translated into the jurisdictional framework, but his reasoning is different.

Martin is roughly saying:

Washington should not claim exclusive divine favor because God is in fact universal.

The strictly republican formulation would be:

Washington has no authority whatsoever to determine whose side God is on.

That is a substantial difference. Martin’s argument pits correct theology against false political theology. Madison requires no judgment whatsoever about which theology is correct.

It would be completely irrelevant whether God actually did favor America. Even if that were theologically true, it would not follow that the president, qua president, possessed civil authority to establish that fact.

That is precisely the strength of the jurisdictional framework.

---

3. Simran Jeet Singh: “America is not synonymous with Christianity”

Singh argues from pluralism and equal treatment: America is religiously diverse; Washington disadvantages other communities when it equates religion with Christianity.

That is perfectly compatible with Jefferson’s equality of civil capacities. But once again the republican reason is more radical:

Even if 100 percent of Americans were Christians, that would not create any Christian jurisdiction on the part of the state.

The state is not religiously neutral because the population has become diverse.

It lacks jurisdiction over religion because the citizens never delegated that jurisdiction to it.

This prevents a common mistake in modern pluralist thinking. Instead of:

«“There are many religions, therefore the state must treat all of them equally,”»

the republican formulation becomes:

«“The state possesses no religious authority; therefore religious affiliation is in principle irrelevant to civic status.”»

Washington’s famous Newport letter to the Jewish congregation expresses the corresponding equality of citizenship very clearly: no sanction for bigotry, no assistance to persecution, but equal citizenship.

---

4. Benjamin Park: Washington listens to the “wrong” religious representatives

Park criticizes Washington for reducing the complex religious landscape to loud but unrepresentative voices.

Here the jurisdictional framework almost turns the whole issue on its head:

Why should Washington be determining who counts as a representative religious spokesperson in the first place?

That would require the state to judge:

Who authentically speaks for Catholics?

Who represents Muslims?

How significant are the institutionally unaffiliated?

Which religious authorities are “extreme” or “reasonable”?

Which theology is representative?

Non-jurisdiction eliminates precisely this epistemic problem.

Washington may of course listen to citizens, associations, and interest groups. But then, for example:

Rachel Laser speaks as a citizen and organizational representative about a piece of legislation.

Not:

Rachel Laser is an authentic representative of American religious pluralism recognized by the state.

Park wants to improve the state’s perception of religion. Madison offers the more radical solution: make such state perception unnecessary in many areas.

---

5. Eboo Patel: “Interfaith America”

Patel’s ideal of voluntary cooperation among Christians, Muslims, and others poses no problem whatsoever in private life. His Bueckers/El-Alfy example describes precisely a form of freely chosen interpersonal solidarity.

It becomes more interesting when he says:

«Washington should be celebrating it.»

That immediately raises the question of competence.

The state may of course praise civic solidarity. It becomes more problematic when it officially curates a particular conception of “good religion”:

interfaith = good,

conflictual religion = bad,

cooperative religion = civically desirable.

At that point, a kind of miniature civil theology of pluralism emerges.

A cleaner republican formulation would be:

«The Christian basketball player may help her Muslim friend during Ramadan; those same citizens may just as freely disagree theologically. Neither is any concern of the state as a religious matter, so long as the civil peace is preserved.»

“Interfaith America,” therefore, must not simply replace “Christian America” as the religious self-definition cultivated by the state.

---

6. Jennifer Butler: here the contrast becomes especially clear

Butler argues that the mistake lies precisely in treating religion as private. Religion shapes the moral imagination, helped inspire abolitionism, the Civil Rights Movement, the labor movement, and so on, and Washington should “partner with people of all faiths.”

Conceptually, this is almost exactly the point at which the difference between a public-religion model and a jurisdictional model becomes visible.

She says:

Religion possesses public moral resources → politics should actively draw upon those resources.

Madison says:

Religion may be enormously important socially → that still does not create any additional religious jurisdiction on the part of the state.

Historically, this is particularly instructive because Madison in 1785 was not merely opposing the funding of the wrong denomination. He opposed Patrick Henry’s relatively inclusive model of general support for Christian teachers. For Madison, the argument that “we support everyone” did not cure the underlying lack of authority.

Butler’s phrase “partner with people of all faiths” may therefore address the discrimination problem better than a Christian partnership model.

But it does not answer the prior question:

Why should the state make people privileged partners specifically in their capacity as representatives of faith?

That is exactly your jurisdictional framework.

---

7. Ani Zonneveld: two completely different arguments are being mixed together

With Zonneveld, one has to separate two things.

A. No discrimination against Muslims

If Muslims are placed under blanket suspicion because of their religion, legally disadvantaged, or restricted in their civil rights, the opposing position fits Jefferson directly:

Religious opinions may not diminish a person’s civil capacities.

B. Medina as a model

Quite different is her argument that Muhammad created a pluralistic system in Medina in which communities lived according to their own religious laws.

For the American republican model, this is actually unnecessary.

The American state does not need an Islamic justification for religious liberty—any more than it needs a Catholic, Hindu, or Protestant one.

And if “each community governed by its own religious laws” is meant to imply state-enforced parallel jurisdictions, that would actually differ from Williams/Madison:

Williams separates spiritual and civil jurisdiction.

A religious community may regulate its own spiritual affairs autonomously. But once bodies, property, violence, contracts, and similar matters are implicated, the magistrate acquires civil jurisdiction.

That is not the same thing as state-recognized confessional legal orders.

---

8. Rachel Laser: actual separation rather than mere pluralism

Laser explicitly argues from Church–State Separation and cites Madison. She criticizes governmental prayer events, publicly funded religious events, and official Christian proclamation.

What is especially interesting is that her argument can be formulated even more radically through Madison.

One does not necessarily have to prove:

that anyone was actually coerced into praying;

that a minority religion was concretely treated worse;

that a particular speaker was favored.

Madison’s Detached Memoranda criticize even congressional chaplains and religious proclamations as governmental “religious agency,” even though a proclamation does not amount to coerced conversion. Officeholders simply received no religious advisory mandate from their constituents.

So:

«The problem does not begin only with coercion.»

Already:

«unauthorized religious jurisdiction»

can itself be the problem.

In my view, that is one of the most important points in the entire article.

---

9. Russell Moore: a Two-Kingdoms intuition without a fully developed theory of the state

Moore objects to treating religion as a tool of either the Right or the Left and invokes the sovereignty of God and “My kingdom is not of this world.”

That has a strong affinity with Williams:

The king cannot politically command Christ, and the church must not turn the temporal magistrate, through spiritual means, into a temporal ruler over souls.

Williams states remarkably clearly that the magistrate’s power over the church is temporal, not spiritual; the church’s spiritual power over a church member is spiritual, not temporal.

Moore therefore offers a theological justification for institutional independence.

But again, one has to distinguish:

Religious citizens may derive political conclusions from their faith. Republican separation does not mean that religion must become apolitical.

The boundary is this:

A citizen may recommend X to the legislature for religious reasons. The legislature does not thereby acquire authority to affirm the religious truth of X.

---

10. Vineet Chander: “Policymakers should seek religious wisdom”

Chander moves in a very different direction. Policymakers should consult religious leaders not merely on religious conflict but also on loneliness, caregiving, the environment, trust, and so forth, because religion teaches duties and responsibility.

The republican response would be immediate:

Why specifically qua religious leaders?

A Hindu scholar may offer excellent arguments concerning care policy.

But then those arguments count as the arguments of a citizen or expert.

As soon as the state says:

«We expressly require “Hindu wisdom,” “Christian wisdom,” “Muslim wisdom,” etc. for our care policy,»

it once again begins to:

1. identify religion,
2. select spokespersons,
3. attribute religious expertise,
4. recognize particular religious contributions as relevant to state policy.

That is precisely the epistemic and jurisdictional problem the jurisdictional framework seeks to avoid.

---

11. Jennie Rosenn: private prophecy yes—state theology no

Rosenn herself argues religiously: true religion demands justice, protection of the vulnerable, care for creation; politicians make religion ridiculous when their policies contradict those values.

As public speech by a rabbi, this is entirely unproblematic.

She may say:

«Your policies contradict my understanding of Judaism.»

What the republican framework would exclude is the next step:

«Therefore the state must determine which policies correspond to correct Jewish or religious ethics.»

Jefferson’s argument against state religious judgments rests precisely on the danger that the magistrate would otherwise become the judge of the “ill tendency” of opinions and turn his own views into the standard.

---

12. William Lamar: the most interesting theoretical counter-model

Lamar explicitly says:

«“All religion is political.”»

And Washington should judge religious actors according to whether they bind people together “in love”; they should not be trusted unless they disclose their politics.

That cuts across the jurisdictional framework—at least if “political” means more than the trivial observation that religion can have political consequences.

Williams’s model depends precisely on the analytical distinction between spiritual society and civil society, even though the same person may belong to both.

A pastor may say on Sunday:

«Abortion is a sin.»

A citizen may say on Monday:

«Therefore I support law X.»

The state may evaluate law X within the sphere of its civil jurisdiction.

It does not need to determine whether the Sunday sermon was good or bad religion.

Particularly problematic would be Lamar’s proposed question:

«“Do you seek to bind us together in love?”»

Why should that be a state test for legitimate religion?

The Williams/Jefferson test is far more sober:

What are you doing in the civil sphere? Are you violating persons, property, rights, or the public peace?

Not:

Is your theology loving?

The jurisdictional framework therefore protects even distinctly unpleasant religion.

---

13. Cary Brief: freedom from governmental religious selection

Brief emphasizes:

Government should not select a preferred faith;

people should be free to pray or not to pray;

public resources should not be used to promote particular religious positions.

That can be connected directly to Jefferson and Madison.

There is only one argument I would reformulate in republican terms. Brief says, roughly, that many Americans do not want government officials deciding which religion should be preferred.

That is democratically phrased.

The stronger republican formulation would be:

Even if 80 percent wanted precisely that, they could not transfer to the state an authority over the consciences of their fellow citizens that they themselves do not possess.

Madison’s Memorial is expressly directed against majorities overriding individual rights.

That is the difference between majority preference and a pre-political limit on jurisdiction.

---

14. Amos Yong: an alternative theology of political power

Yong criticizes the fusion of religious and state power and then develops an alternative conception of religious power: it emerges especially from the voices of the marginalized.

That can be advanced as a private theological or social-ethical position.

But from the republican perspective, once again, no state responsibility arises to:

define “authentic religious power,”

weight religious voices according to marginality,

select a correct over an incorrect theology of power.

The state protects a homeless believer and a billionaire believer in their equal civil rights.

It does not have to decide whose religious voice possesses greater spiritual authority.

---

15. Ebad Rahman: “Religion should influence Washington, not the other way around”

This is probably the formulation in which the distinction between influence and jurisdiction matters most. Rahman wants independent religious voices capable of morally confronting state power.

That is entirely compatible with Williams/Madison if “influence” means social speech.

Churches may say:

«President, Congress—you are acting unjustly.»

Muslims may do the same. So may atheists.

That is free social speech.

But:

«“Government should be accountable to a higher power”»

cannot, as a constitutional doctrine of the state, mean that Washington must now determine:

1. that there is a higher divine lawgiver,
2. what that lawgiver demands,
3. which religious interpretation correctly represents that lawgiver.

At that point, the jurisdictional boundary would once again have been crossed.

The republican state may therefore be influenced by religiously motivated citizens without itself possessing religious competence.

That is a crucial distinction.

---

The underlying structural error of the forum

The title is:

«What Washington Gets Wrong About Religion»

But the Madisonian answer would in many cases be:

«Washington’s mistake begins with the assumption that it needs an official view of “religion” as such at all.»

The forum essentially offers four different answers:

1. “Washington favors the wrong religion.”
   → The answer becomes: treat all religions equally.

2. “Washington listens to the wrong religious spokespersons.”
   → The answer becomes: select more representative spokespersons.

3. “Washington uses religion for the wrong political purposes.”
   → The answer becomes: mobilize religion for more just purposes.

4. “Washington misunderstands religion.”
   → The answer becomes: make politicians more religiously literate.

The jurisdictional framework comes before all of these:

«Why does Washington need an official conception of true, good, representative, or socially useful religion in the first place?»

And that is precisely why Madison is far more radical than modern “religious pluralism.”

---

One particularly important difference: “all faiths” does not cure the jurisdictional defect

This seems to me to be the key to the entire text.

One might move from a Christian state program to:

«Christians + Jews + Muslims + Hindus + Buddhists + Humanists.»

That considerably reduces the equality problem.

But it has not answered the jurisdictional problem at all.

Because the state is still deciding:

what counts as religion,

which groups should be invited,

who represents them,

which religious activities are worthy of support,

which forms of “interfaith” behavior are socially desirable,

which religion is democratically constructive.

Madison had already seen this problem in 1785. A broader, seemingly tolerant model of support does not necessarily answer the question of where the authority to support religion comes from.

---

And this is where Roger Williams comes back in

This fits remarkably well with our previous discussion of Williams.

His decisive formula can be applied to this entire Washington Sun article:

«Operation follows constitution.»

Because the Civil Power is constituted as civil, its legitimate operation can likewise only be civil.

That shifts almost every question in the article:

Not:

«Is this Muslim teaching moderate?»

But:

«Has anyone committed a civil wrong?»

Not:

«Is this Christian movement democratic?»

But:

«What civilly relevant act is at issue?»

Not:

«Which rabbi represents Jewish values?»

But:

«What civil argument is this citizen making?»

Not:

«Which religion promotes social cohesion?»

But:

«Which civil rights and duties apply to everyone?»

And therein lies, in my view, the truly revolutionary sharpness of the jurisdictional framework: it does not attempt to solve the religion problem by constructing ever more sophisticated forms of governmental competence over religion.

It removes a large part of the problem from the state’s jurisdiction in the first place.

1/x

text:
$OPEN You donkey's thought I was done? Mwuahaha

LET'S HYPE THIS MOFO AND REMIND OURSELVES WHAT THE $OPEN ARMY IS ABOUT.

Q2 revenue reached $883 million, up 23% sequentially. Contribution Profit increased 59% to $51 million. Contribution Margin reached 5.8%. Homes purchased increased 77% from Q1 and 149% year over year. Adjusted EBITDA improved from a $31 million loss in Q1 to just a $4 million loss in Q2.

Operations expense per acquisition close fell from $8,400 a year ago to $3,000. Only 9% of homes were sitting on the market longer than 120 days, down from 36% a year earlier.

Then there is customer acquisition. Opendoor generated 6,908 acquisition contracts during Q2 while spending only $5 million on marketing. The last time this company generated more than 6,000 contracts in a quarter, back in Q2 2022, it spent $81 million.

$81 million versus $5 million. That is the kind of operating leverage I have been waiting to see.

Cash Now, More Later is also changing the economics of the model. It allows Opendoor to participate in the transaction while committing substantially less capital per home. That matters when your goal is scaling volume without rebuilding the same balance-sheet risk that hurt the company during the last cycle.

The distribution network is expanding too. RealScout has integrated Opendoor directly into the workflow of a platform serving more than 100,000 real estate agents. Agents can surface a traditional cash offer or Cash Now, More Later without sending their clients somewhere else.

Realtor. com is now surfacing Opendoor cash offers through its seller marketplace and My Home dashboard.

Think about where this is heading. Opendoor spent years paying heavily to bring homeowners into its own funnel. Now major real estate platforms are beginning to put Opendoor directly in front of homeowners and agents where those customers already are. That can materially change customer acquisition economics over time.

The Doma transaction is another piece I think the market is underestimating. Opendoor completed the acquisition of Doma's closing and escrow operations and is participating with Fannie Mae's Title Acceptance Program for eligible refinance transactions.

Doma brings automated title-risk decisioning. Opendoor brings national closing infrastructure and operating scale. The opportunity goes well beyond buying and reselling houses.

Purchase. Sale. Mortgage. Title. Escrow. Refinance.

Every additional part of the transaction they own gives them another opportunity to remove friction, capture economics and improve the customer experience.

Then Opendoor Home Loans came out of beta. They now offer 30-, 20- and 15-year fixed mortgages along with adjustable-rate products, and those mortgages can be used for eligible purchases beyond Opendoor-owned homes.

That matters because mortgage is becoming a standalone customer product rather than simply an attachment used to help sell Opendoor inventory.

This is where the platform thesis starts becoming real.

A homeowner can potentially receive an AI-driven home valuation, get an immediate cash option, use Cash Now, More Later, sell traditionally through an agent, finance another property through Opendoor Home Loans, and eventually move through title, escrow and closing infrastructure controlled by the same ecosystem.

That is a considerably larger business opportunity than flipping houses.

Now look at capital allocation. Management raised $650 million through 0% convertible notes while simultaneously spending $158 million to repurchase approximately 45.3 million shares.

They reduced shares outstanding by roughly 5%.

After the repurchase and capped-call transactions, approximately $440 million of additional growth capital went onto the balance sheet. The structure was designed so Opendoor expects no net share issuance until approximately $10.38 per share under the company's stated assumptions.

They raised hundreds of millions of dollars for growth at a 0% coupon while simultaneously reducing the share count. That gets my attention.

Now we get to profitability.

At Q2 earnings, management said the current acquisition volumes, unit economics and operating cost structure support positive Adjusted Net Income on a twelve-month go-forward basis exiting 2026.

Then the housing market deteriorated hard during the final weeks of August. Kaz came back to shareholders in September and acknowledged it directly. The weaker market pushed the Adjusted EBITDA timeline back roughly six to eight weeks.

But the ANI target did not move.

Management still expects to exit 2026 ANI-positive on a twelve-month go-forward basis.

That distinction matters. They are not assuming mortgage rates collapse. They are not assuming home prices suddenly rip. They are not assuming the housing market saves them.

The thesis is that the operating model itself can become profitable.

Even after a difficult August, Q3 is currently expected to produce revenue growth of 10–15% year over year and Contribution Profit growth of 70–75%.

The company is also clearing homes substantially faster than it did historically. Kaz says Opendoor is now beating the broader market on clearance nearly nine days out of ten.

That tells me management finally understands the lesson the old Opendoor refused to learn. Inventory velocity matters more than making one quarter's margin percentage look pretty.

Sell the homes. Recycle the capital. Keep the machine moving.

Now put all of this together.

Kaz Nejatian running the company. Lucas Matheson overseeing strategic expansion. Vu Tran leading AI after coming from Meta Superintelligence Labs. Founders back involved.

AI being pushed through pricing, underwriting, operations and the customer experience. Cash Now, More Later reducing capital intensity. RealScout opening agent distribution. Realtor. com opening consumer distribution. Doma adding automated title and nationwide closing infrastructure. Fannie Mae Title Acceptance opening another path into refinance transactions. Opendoor Home Loans expanding beyond Opendoor inventory.

Nearly $440 million of new growth capital raised at a 0% coupon. Five percent of the company bought back. And a management team still publicly committing to ANI-positive economics exiting 2026.

Meanwhile, short sellers are still heavily committed to the other side of this trade.

The latest reported short interest stands at 208.1 million shares, representing 21.83% of the float.

More importantly, days to cover has climbed to 9.64.

That number gets my attention.

More than one-fifth of the float is sold short, and based on recent trading volume it would theoretically take nearly ten trading days for that entire position to cover.

Off-exchange short volume also remains substantial at roughly 10.8 million shares, or 49.19% of reported off-exchange volume.

I do not treat daily short-volume percentages as the same thing as actual short interest. They are different datasets. What matters to me is that the confirmed short position itself remains enormous while days to cover has continued expanding.

That creates a very different risk profile if the fundamental story starts forcing a repricing.

Maybe the shorts are right. Housing remains difficult. Execution still matters. Management still has to deliver the ANI target. Scaling inventory introduces risk, and none of these businesses become valuable simply because management launches them.

That is exactly why I find the setup compelling.

The stock is still being priced while the market debates whether Opendoor survives as an iBuyer. I am watching a company attempting to build an integrated technology platform around the entire American home transaction.

Discovery. Valuation. Sale. Purchase. Mortgage. Title. Escrow. Closing.

AI running through the entire stack.

If Kaz executes on that vision and Opendoor crosses into sustained ANI profitability, the conversation around this company changes very quickly.

At that point investors are no longer debating whether the old Opendoor business model works. They are forced to start valuing the platform being built underneath it.

More than 208 million shares are currently betting they never get there.

That is what makes this one interesting.

The next major checkpoint is simple: exit 2026 ANI-positive on a twelve-month go-forward basis like management has repeatedly said they will. Deliver that, keep acquisition growth moving, continue expanding the ecosystem and prove that the economics scale.

If they do, I think (hope) the market eventually has a very different conversation about $OPEN.

text:
This might be my most unpopular post of all time but here we go...

A DEFENSE OF "RISKY" SPONSORSHIPS BY STREAMERS.

Disclaimer: In my 6+ year Career I have never accepted a single cent from any gambling/crypto sponsor. I have been offered said sponsors 100+ times easily.

Now, into the main post.

Let me state in the strongest terms I am aware of the dangers of gambling, it can do immense damage to lives, along with Crypto (Which is functionally 90% gambling too).

So if this is the case, why would it be morally acceptable for any streamer to take their money...? 

Two important things.

1) The average age of League viewers is old, I believe this to be fundamentally important. Just going off my own metrics, average age of League Twitch viewers is 26-27 years old. 

If we were talking about Fortnite streamers advertising gambling/crypto to their 16 year old audience, this would be very different, but we're not.

The average League player is not a child, they are are adults well past the point of their brain being developed, and are obviously responsible for their own decisions. 

As long as streamers provide a CLEAR warning and description of what gambling is, (You are very likely to lose money, there is a danger of addiction), it is up to individual adults to make informed choices.

IMPORTANT: IT IS ESSENTIAL FOR STREAMERS TO GIVE A CLEAR AND UN-AMBIGIOUS WARNING OF THE DANGERS OF GAMBLING SO PEOPLE CAN MAKE AN INFORMED DECISION. 

NOT DOING SO IS MORALLY WRONG. PEOPLE MUST HAVE INFORMED CHOICES.
 (This directly aimed at MANY people not doing this currently, you can easily figure out who)

2) The culture that we live in.

The prevailing culture of Europe and North America is one of individualism and freedom of individuals choice.

This involves danger, as individuals can and do make bad choices.

That does not mean these bad choices existing is wrong.

The world is full of vices. Alcohol, tobacco, gambling, pornography, fast food. It is up to individuals how much they engage with these. 
 
Some do not engage with them at all, some engage in them slightly in a "responsible" way, and some people succumb to them entirely.

Personally, I drink regularly, and have gambled playing Poker for years. This is entirely my own decision and no one is responsible for it but me.

Yet ironically, do you know how many lives I have seen ruined from addiction to videogames? People wasting their entire lives, ending up homeless with no money due to doing nothing but playing League all day? Same story with CS, or any major game.

The moral of the story here is legitimately any vice can ruin your life, even "innocuous" ones like videogames.

I'm sorry, but I think it's a good thing these "dangers" exist with the responsibility on the user to engage with them responsibly as consenting adults.

I like living in a world where I have the freedom to make choices and engage with dangerous things knowing it's my life and my responsibility.

I prefer this to living in a toddler world where any potential danger is snatched away from me wherever possible.

Having said all this, I feel the US Army sponsorship is slightly different, I don't defend that remotely, and think that is purely selling your soul.

Obviously if people DON'T take gambling sponsorships that's also not a problem, many people have their own deeply personal reasons for this and it's a deeply personal decision.

I recognise this is a very contentious issue however and welcome and accept feedback on this topic, I'm always open to hearing other people's experiences/perspectives.

Perhaps could do an on-stream discussion/debate with people if there's enough interest?

text:
WHAT DOES EACH LEN5 FORGIVE? AT PEPSICO $PEP, A SNACK BUSINESS THAT STOPPED GROWING:

PepsiCo (PEP) at $130.56, +$0.38 / +0.29% today, hit a 52-week low of $127.98 on Monday, 24% under February's high, and the Quality-Value Len5 is watching it anyway. That is the case for this board. The more useful names on a Len5 fail one test in plain sight and stay on, because what a Len5 forgives shows what it is paying for. Six Len5es, six names, six flaws.

PepsiCo sells Lay's, Doritos, Gatorade and Pepsi, and sits second of 67 on this Len5, which hunts a business almost nobody could rebuild, bought below its worth. The price half has arrived: about 15.6 times the $8.36 a share of core profit - one-time items stripped out - it earned over four quarters, and a $5.92 dividend, a 4.5% yield, raised 54 years running.

The flaw is the snack aisle. PepsiCo cut prices on Lay's, Doritos, Tostitos and Cheetos this year to win shoppers back. June quarter, reported July 9: PepsiCo Foods North America revenue $6.37B, -2%; volume flat; operating profit -3.5%. Company-wide core profit $2.20 a share, +4%.

The cash is spoken for, too. Free cash flow - cash left after running the business and buying equipment - was $7.67B in 2025; dividends took $7.64B of it. And the 10-year Treasury yield closed Wednesday at 5.11%, above that 4.5%.

VERDICT: intact brands at a lower price, attached to a North American snack business the price cuts have not revived. What would knock PepsiCo off the Quality-Value Len5: snack volume still flat after the cuts while dividends keep eating the free cash. WHEN: third-quarter results October 8, confirmed; $2.30 a share expected vs $2.29 a year earlier.

MOMENTUM LEN5:
- Five9 (FIVN) at $37.60, -$0.09 / -0.23% today, second of 30. Cloud software that runs customer-service call centers. This Len5 hunts a price near its one-year high with short and long climbs agreeing: Wednesday's $40.00 high is three times April's $13.29 low. June quarter: revenue $312.4M, +10%; AI revenue +78%, now 15% of subscription revenue. The flaw it forgives is profit: $3.4M of net income, about a penny per sales dollar. VERDICT: a climb earned by AI sales, resting on almost no profit. What would knock Five9 off the Momentum Len5: a close under $30.10, its September low. Tentatively November 5.

DEEP-VALUE & SPECIAL-SITUATIONS LEN5:
- Rollins (ROL) at $30.48, -$2.01 / -6.19% today, a new 52-week low. The Atlanta owner of Orkin. This Len5 hunts a sound business priced below what it steadily earns, and the business still grows: June-quarter revenue +7.9%. The flaw it forgives is a price that keeps falling - 54% under February's high, through two quarterly misses and a finance chief's exit announced in May. This morning Piper Sandler cut it to Neutral, arguing AI search steers homeowners to small local exterminators. VERDICT: steady profits on a stock the market has stopped trusting. What would knock Rollins off the Deep-Value Len5: September-quarter residential growth, excluding acquisitions, below June's 3.6%. Tentatively October 28.

GROWTH LEN5:
- Customers Bancorp (CUBI) at $76.60, -$0.12 / -0.16% today. A Pennsylvania business bank with its own instant-payments network, cubiX. This Len5 hunts profit growth the price has not charged for: about 9 times the past year's profit. June quarter: loans $18.0B, +16.9%; profit $2.05 a share, +18.5%. The flaw it forgives is the margin - interest earned minus interest paid, as a share of loans and investments - down to 3.17% from 3.27%. Management calls June the low; Morgan Stanley cut the stock to Underweight, its sell-leaning rating, on September 8. VERDICT: fast growth at a bargain price, earning a little less per loan. What would knock Customers off the Growth Len5: a margin that fails to rebound, leaving profit under last year's $2.20 a share. Tentatively October 22.

HYPERGROWTH LEN5:
- Credo Technology (CRDO) at $190.40, -$3.47 / -1.79% today. Chips and cables that move data between servers in AI data centers. This Len5 hunts very fast growth on a real base: quarter to August 1, revenue $479.0M, +115%; $525M-$535M guided next; no debt. The flaw it forgives is who pays: four customers made 84% of sales. Today shows the risk. Oracle (ORCL) at $137.22, -$7.34 / -5.08% today, sent a contract notice covering a late start at its $165B New Mexico AI campus, Bloomberg News reported, and one late campus reaches every supplier. Oracle is on no Len5; its debt is nearly twice its shareholders' equity. VERDICT: growth nobody disputes, sold to very few buyers. What would knock Credo off the Hypergrowth Len5: revenue under the $525M floor. Tentatively November 30.

INCOME LEN5:
- Ardmore Shipping (ASC) at $17.65, +$0.04 / +0.23% today. It owns 25 tankers carrying gasoline, diesel and chemicals. This Len5 hunts cash to owners the business itself pays for, and Ardmore's rule pays out two-thirds of each quarter's adjusted profit, with little debt. June quarter: its mid-size tankers earned $51,900 a day, nearly five times breakeven; dividend $0.79, 4.5% of today's price in one quarter - PepsiCo's yield for a year. The flaw it forgives: the rates come from a war. The Strait of Hormuz is shut, and when Iran offered to reopen it, Ardmore fell 4.5% on Tuesday. Analysts expect $0.62 a share for September vs $1.18 for June. VERDICT: an honest payout from an unstable source. What would knock Ardmore off the Income Len5: a reopened strait pulling rates toward its $10,800-a-day breakeven. Tentatively November 4.

A Len5 that forgave nothing would hold almost nothing. PepsiCo makes the trade plain: 54 years of dividend raises at 15.6 times profit, from a snack business that shrank last quarter. Its October 8 report is the first of these six flaws to face a number.

Not investment advice.

text:
Actor Joseph Gordon-Levitt offers a contrarian view: The biggest threat from AI isn't the technology, it's the politicians who are being paid not to regulate it:

Speaking to a room full of AI industry figures at the TIME100 AI Impact Dinner in San Francisco, he skipped the usual warnings about the technology.

Instead he pointed at the people who are supposed to be keeping it in check.

He starts from a basic principle. When a business puts out something unsafe, the law should step in and tell it:

"You guys are gonna have to stop and make some changes. And then once you can prove that your products and services are safe and good for people, then you may reopen for business."

"That's how it is supposed to work. That's how the law works, right?"

So why isn't that happening with AI? His answer:

"When it comes to regulating AI, lawmakers in our country have been slow, they've been timid, and a lot of them have been taking money from the big tech lobby."

In his view, the law already has the power to rein in AI. What's missing are lawmakers willing to use it, so the answer is to replace them:

"We need new Congress people, new senators that can make some new laws that the AI companies have to follow."

And @hitRECordJoe points out that the timing couldn't be better:

"It's September 2026 in the United States of America. The midterm elections are right around the corner. That means it's now. Right now. Now's the perfect time to organize, to mobilize, and to go out and vote in such strong numbers that they cannot stop us."

His instructions are simple:

"You find out who is the senator running in your state, who is the congressperson running in your state, and then you find out what are their positions on AI. And if they say anything less than strong regulation now, you don't vote for them because they're probably taking money from some of the guys in this room."

text:
Our $100k demo account gained about $19k in roughly a year, net of financing and management fees. It uses a value-tilted 140/40 direct indexing strategy based on the Russell 1000. For comparison, a  $100k investment in a Russell 1000 ETF over the same period would’ve gained about ~$445 less. And here’s the kicker: it also harvested ~$27k in capital losses while appreciating in value. This is a real account, not a backtest - anyone can inspect every position and trade on our website (link in my comment). It’s worth noting that the long short direct index carries a different risk profile and can expect a tracking error of ~1.5%.

We chose a value tilt because many of our customers work in tech and already have significant exposure to growth stocks. We wanted to demonstrate how they could lean into value while maintaining broad market exposure.

Those $27k in harvested losses can offset capital gains elsewhere. Someone selling appreciated company stock, for example, could use $27k of harvested losses to offset that amount in gains. At a combined 30% tax rate, that could defer a ~$8k tax bill, leaving that money invested in the market instead.

We made 140/40 available starting at a $100k minimum, and customers can get started in a few minutes. We also offer 200/100 and 250/150 versions. The additional leverage allows for a stronger factor tilt and creates more opportunities to harvest losses.

text:
Jeremiah Smith is 20 years old and he is not allowed to play in the NFL.

Not because he is not good enough. Because of a rule.

To be eligible for the NFL Draft you have to be three years removed from high school. Smith has finished two seasons at Ohio State. So he sits.

If they let him enter the 2026 draft he would almost certainly be the first receiver taken. Possibly the first non quarterback off the board entirely.

He cannot. He has to wait until 2027.

Now think about what that does.

The one place on earth legally allowed to pay Jeremiah Smith right now is a college football program. That is the entire market. The NFL has locked the door, so every dollar available to him has to come from a school.

And this offseason, somebody put more than $10 million in front of him to leave Ohio State.

His NIL value at Ohio State is around $5 million. That is third among every player in college football, behind two quarterbacks, and he is one of only two non quarterbacks in the top ten of the entire sport.

So the offer was roughly double what he is making.

He said no.

"I came to Ohio State for a reason, to win championships, develop as a player and a person and keep building on this legacy."

Understand, he is not saying that from a position of needing the school. As a sophomore he led the Big Ten in catches with 87 and receiving yards with 1,243. He is fifth in the history of Ohio State football in receiving touchdowns and he is in year three.

He had every bit of leverage a 20 year old has ever had in this sport and he chose not to use it.

Here is the part that makes it strange.

The rule keeping him out of the NFL is the only reason that $10 million existed. If the league let him go pro, no booster anywhere would be writing him a check to switch schools, because he would already be gone.

The rule built the market. He walked away from it anyway.

Somewhere there is a version of this where he takes the ten, plays somewhere else for a season, and enters the 2027 draft with the same tape and twice the money.

He decided he would rather finish what he started.

text:
@RonWyden argument is that talking to Putin is the scandal, and the war is just the backdrop. That is the opposite of how diplomacy works. If the test of toughness is refusing to sit in the same room as the other side, then four years of isolation already took that test. The missiles did not stop. The G20 seat did not vanish. Russia is still a member. Pretending otherwise is a press release, not a strategy.

The administration’s position is blunt: you do not end a war by only meeting people you already like. Rubio said the quiet part out loud. Nice meetings among friends produce applause. They do not produce ceasefires. Inviting Putin to a U.S.-hosted summit is not a parade for him. It is an attempt to put him in a room with the people who actually have leverage, including Trump, instead of leaving him to coordinate with Beijing and Tehran offstage.

The “same day as Kyiv” line is designed to sound devastating and prove nothing. Russia has been hitting Ukrainian cities for years. If every strike canceled talks, there would never be talks. That is not moral clarity. That is a rule that guarantees the war continues on autopilot while senators send letters to Treasury.

Wyden and Warren already objected when Siluanov showed up in Asheville. Fine. Bessent still told him there would be no economic relief until the war ends. That is not a gift. That is a condition. Calling every contact with Moscow a betrayal treats engagement itself as the crime and then wonders why there is no deal.

If the complaint is that America looks weaker for trying to talk, the alternative on offer is more statements, more letters, and the same war. The administration’s bet is ugly and simple: sit down with the adversary, demand an outcome, and stop confusing isolation with strength.

What are three things legislators can do to increase housing supply?
Housing is expensive because we don't build enough of it, and local rules are a big reason why. Here are three things state lawmakers can do to increase housing supply:  
Preempt exclusionary local zoning. Rules like very large minimum lot sizes block starter homes from ever getting built.  
Make permitting faster and easier. Streamline state-level permits into a one-stop shop, set shot clocks for slow municipalities, and allow certified third-party inspections.  
Give builders real legal remedies. Arizona lets landowners seek compensation when a locality's rezoning cuts their land's value, which has curbed exclusionary zoning there. New Hampshire's Housing Appeals Board offers a quick, low-cost alternative to court for housing disputes.  For developers, time is money, and every delay shows up in what you pay for a home. The massive, T-shaped limestone pillars at southern Turkey’s Göbekli Tepe are one of the world’s oldest monumental temple complexes—and a focus of grisly speculation.

Hundreds of bone and skull fragments have been found in the rubble surrounding the complex, leading early excavators to suggest the famed 10,000-year-old site was once home to an ancient hunter-gatherer “skull cult,” or that the hilltop structures might have been a temple where people left their deceased to be picked apart by birds.

Now, a new analysis of the first intact burials from Göbekli Tepe offers a less lurid explanation: Landslides may have swept human remains into the site, jumbled together with debris from collapsed structures.

text:
I just watched two popular Christian pastors and podcasters suggest that Yeshua is about to return to earth to establish His Millennial Kingdom. But that skips over events Scripture tells us to take seriously:

▪️ The war of Gog described in Ezekiel
▪️ The rapture of the church
▪️ The seven-year Tribulation

I believe Ezekiel’s war lies ahead, though Scripture does not tell us precisely when it will occur in relation to the rapture. I also believe the church will be taken before the Tribulation, because we are not appointed to God’s wrath.

Before the Lord returns to earth, the world will pass through a time of great tribulation unlike any it has ever known. If I could warn the world about what lies ahead, I would warn it of coming judgment.

And I would urge everyone who considers themselves part of the church to be ready.

Jews and Gentiles alike must place their faith in Messiah Yeshua. A religious label cannot make anyone ready for His coming. In the parable of the ten virgins, some were ready when the bridegroom came; others found the door shut. We must take that warning seriously.

I believe many Jews and Gentiles will come to faith during the Tribulation. Revelation describes a great multitude who come out of that time. In my understanding of Scripture, they are distinct from the church that was caught up to be with the Lord.

Believers will stand before the judgment seat of Messiah, where our works will be evaluated. And if you are focused on the Millennial Kingdom – when believers will reign with Him – consider what Yeshua taught about faithfulness and responsibility. How we live for Him today matters.

We need not fear the first death. The second death has no power over those who belong to Him, and we are not appointed to His wrath.

We look forward to being with Him, to the marriage of the Lamb, to His return in glory, and to reigning with Him.

The psalmist asks, “What shall I render to the LORD for all His benefits toward me?” (Psalm 116:12, NKJV). His answer begins with receiving God’s salvation and calling upon His name. Even what we offer Him comes from what He has first given us.

One day, we will receive crowns and rewards from Messiah. What will we have to place at His feet? Revelation shows the twenty-four elders casting their crowns before His throne. Their example reminds us that whatever we receive from Him can be offered back to Him – because all the glory belongs to Him.

After the thousand-year reign comes the final judgment. Then God will make all things new. In the New Jerusalem, there will be no temple, for the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are its temple. The city will have no need of the sun or moon to shine in it, for the glory of God will illuminate it. He will dwell with His people forever.

But those whose names are not found in the Book of Life will face the lake of fire.

Be ready. Live faithfully. Warn others while there is still time.

▪️ Gog’s war – Ezekiel 38–39
▪️ The rapture and our resurrection – 1 Thessalonians 4:16–18; 1 Corinthians 15:51–53

▪️ Believers and God’s wrath – 1 Thessalonians 1:10; 5:9

▪️ The elders’ crowns – Revelation 4:10–11
▪️ The marriage of the Lamb and Messiah’s return – Revelation 19:7–16
▪️ The thousand-year reign and the second death – Revelation 20:4–6
▪️ The final judgment and lake of fire – Revelation 20:11–15
▪️ The new creation and God dwelling with His people – Revelation 21:1–4, 22–23; 22:1–5

text:
Noah sat down on a bench.

I remained standing.

“Your mother spoke to me a few months before I proposed,” he said.

“My mother?”

“She showed me brochures. She said your parents were thinking long term.”

I felt sick.

“Lily wasn’t even living with them anymore.”

“They were still controlling parts of her financial arrangements. They said eventually she would need more support.”

“She had me.”

Noah nodded.

“I told them that.”

“Then what?”

“Your mother said you deserved your own life.”

My throat tightened.

Noah looked away.

“She said they weren’t going to make you responsible for Lily forever.”

“That’s not their decision.”

“I know.”

“Did Lily know?”

“Not then.”

I gripped the railing beside the bench.

“How did a marriage contract become part of this?”

Noah slowly exhaled.

“Your parents believed if Lily had a husband willing to assume responsibility for her day-to-day life, they wouldn’t need to arrange residential placement. Your father wanted legal assurances. Then they offered me money.”

“To take her off their hands.”

Noah flinched.

“I think that’s how they saw it.”

My eyes burned. “And you agreed.”

“I agreed to the document.”

“That’s the same thing.”

“No.”

He rose to his feet.

“It isn’t.”

“Tell me how.”

“Because I was already planning to ask her to marry me.”

I froze.

Noah moved closer.

“I loved her, Hannah.”

“Then why didn’t you refuse the money?”

“Because if I rejected the entire arrangement, your father threatened to carry out their plan before Lily and I had time to figure everything out.”

“You could’ve told me.”

“I wanted to.”

“You should have.”

“I know.”

“Why didn’t you?”

“Because Lily eventually asked me not to.”

I stared at him.

“Eventually?”

Noah nodded.

“I told her about the agreement during our first year of marriage.”

The anger inside me changed direction.

“You told her?”

“I couldn’t keep acting as though it didn’t exist. She deserved to know.”

“What did she do?”

For the first time that night, Noah gave a faint smile.

“First she cried.”

His voice cracked.

“Then she yelled at me.”

“Good.”

“Very loudly.”

Despite everything, I almost laughed.

“Then she made me show her every bank statement.”

“Also good.”

“And after that, she sat at the kitchen table for about twenty minutes without saying anything.”

He looked toward the double doors at the end of the corridor.

“Finally, she asked me one question.”

“What?”

“She asked whether I would have married her if your parents had offered me nothing.”

My chest tightened.

“I told her yes.”

“And she believed you?”

Noah nodded.

“She said, ‘Then I still choose you.’”

I pressed my fingers against my lips.

The tears came before I could hold them back.

“Why did she hide it from me?”

“Because she knows you.”

“What does that mean?”

“She said you’d declare war on your parents.”

“She was right.”

“She also thought it would tear the family apart.”

“They did that themselves.”

“I told her the same thing.”

He wiped his eyes.

“But it was her story. She asked me to keep it private.”

“And tonight?”

“Before surgery, she grabbed my hand and said, ‘If I don’t wake up, Hannah has to know. Promise me.’”

There was that word again.

Promise.

The word that had followed the three of us since childhood.

I looked down at the contract in my hand.

Only minutes earlier, I had believed it proved Noah was a fraud.

Now I understood something much worse.

He had signed the ugliest document I had ever seen because my parents had put Lily in a position where someone who loved her believed cooperating was the safest way to protect her.

I sank onto the bench.

“I’m sorry,” I whispered.

Noah shook his head.

“Don’t apologize.”

“I thought the worst of you.”

“So would I.”

“No, Noah.”

I looked straight at him.

“I thought the worst of you before I ever saw this paper.”

He understood.

Years earlier.

The proposal.

My jealousy.

text:
Hey folks on X, I’m Jacob 

it's been a while so I wanted to reintroduce myself…

I've made some large pivots from sales and marketing into recruiting and hiring since going to Hormozi's workshop in Vegas in March where I got to meet  @_basedxavier_ and the team at Acquisitions

Since then my brother and I have built a fully remote sales team supported by our client success, marketing and creative departments. 

How I got here? 

2019 I decided to knock doors during the pandemic in Texas. The next summer I switched to solar and 2 years after that I got into high ticket thanks to @serialsales  (he told me I was the first person IRL he met off Twitter) 

After working on a trading algo offer for him and @coleangelle along with two other offers my brother David asked me to help him launch a remote home services offer using paid ads.  After an initial MVP he used business credit cards to scale as our cash cycle was over 100 days. Last summer we switched from in home to online consults and we haven't looked back.

Within the first month we brought on a marketing assistant and videographer and recruited some remote talent from @OmerBlochRemote platform.  The first 2 hires have just had their 1st year anniversary with us and are incredible leaders and are AI fluent using Claude.

Over time I realized if paid ads worked so great for finding clients, I could use it as well to hire talent and made a whole meta form, landing page, and VSL for hires. Some of our best talent has come to us that way and I consider it my edge in business.

I studied my ass off from different Youtube gurus and Skool communities, staying up till 2am to launch new campaigns and creatives but realized it'd be better to hire a pro to take over the media buying.

Although I missed it last year I was able to attend @MainStSummit  earlier this month where I met some incredibly experienced entrepreneurs and owners. @roblabonne told me I should post on here more and @carkerpox got me on his talent platform where I was able to find an incredible media buyer.  My life is in the process of dramatic change. 

Just yesterday my brother and I went on an adventure with some other founders we met at the workshop in Vegas. While driving to a heli hog hunting experience they got a call saying their company had just had their first $1M day.

By putting myself in the arena I've surrounded myself with people who  constantly push themselves to do great things and go for moonshots. Living below my means has enabled me to make investments and include family. (Family office style $1m check sizes)

In the future I plan to attend (and host) more events. Right now I'm in Austin for @deeptechweek and constantly inspired by the work ethic and ingenuity of Texans and the startups they launch.

Outside of work you’ll find me:
- working out in my garage gym or doing cold plunges 
- Attempting to learn to foil and kiteboard 
- Learning Portuguese or practicing Spanish 
- Planning the next epic adventure with friends

I’m here to share everything I’ve learned about sales, marketing, recruiting, and direct investing and inspire you all to create the dream life you've always wanted!

If any of that interests you, I welcome you to give a like or a follow. I want to inspire you to share your own story or create one worth sharing!
