text:
Dispatch from Redclaw, Beautiful & Beloved Queen Of Greenland 🇬🇱

President Trump called and told me I should get to know the people.

“They’re great people. Wonderful people. Full of energy. Just the best.”

I said of course, but ended the call fraught with skepticism.

Supervillains are terrible people persons.

But I said I would try, so I did.

I took a team of my four most social catgirl minions.

I took a fresh notebook and pen.

We started in Nuuk, where the Royal Palace is located.

The Inatsisartut’s concerns were housing, dentists, and the price of milk.

I almost offered a coastal plasma net. I wrote the three things down instead.

Someone poured coffee. We were invited to a kaffemik.

Forty pairs of shoes by the door.

I took off the crown, the boots, and my ceremonial poison dagger.

Someone’s aunt put cake in one hand and suaasat in the other and did not ask me to speak.

I lasted 30 minutes without monologuing. A personal best.

Before we left I asked the aunt what the house actually needed.

A radiator. A cousin in Sisimiut who could not get a ticket home.

I can do radiators. I can do tickets. I wrote both down.

In the south a sheep farmer in rubber boots asked what I wanted.

I said I wanted to help and, this being a new experience, was prepared to be bad at it.

He pointed at a fence the wind had severely bullied.

I had the catgirls fix the fence.

He poured coffee and said the hay shipment was late every year.

At last. Something in my wheelhouse.

I said I would make the shippers afraid of being late.

He said ordinary on time would do.

… Fine.

At the brættets in Qaqortoq they were selling the morning’s catch.

I bought a fish and asked what they throw away because no one buys it that day.

They showed me.

We set up a standing order for the old people’s home and the school.

A woman nodded, said good, and cooked the fish.

I ate it. I did not give a speech.

Up north the sled dogs did not care that I was queen.

They were confused by the catgirls but did not protest.

A hunter let me sit on the sled, then handed me tea.

I asked what ruins a season.

Fuel. Ice that will not hold.

I cannot negotiate with ice. Fuel I can move.

In a settlement of eighty people the main store was also the post office.

They were most curious about the catgirl minions.

After some difficulty we settled on a word that translates roughly to “pets.”

They wanted the dentist before Christmas, two working washing machines, and for the supply ship not to skip them when the sea looks rude.

I put a minion on the washing machines.

I would handle the ship captains.

A boy in a soccer jacket asked if I was the new coach.

I said no, but the field lights would work every evening from now on.

He looked at me a long time and nodded once.

Sunday I sat uncomfortably in a church while the hymns ignored me.

Afterward an elder held my hands.

I asked what would make the winter less heavy.

And so on.

The notebook was getting full, but I like goals.

A Danish official asked about process.

I showed him the list.

Housing. Dentists. Milk. Radiators. Hay. The ships. Field lights. No speeches at kaffemik.

Familiar with my past, he waited for the threat.

I told him the only threat was that I intended to accomplish these things.

We flew home.

The people of Greenland do not need politics or promises.

They need the ordinary things to arrive when they are needed.

I am still not a people person.

But I can be a queen who manages and executes a to-do list.

Promises are for politicians.

Follow-through is for supervillains.

4) I know Catholics aren't Pelagian, but you'll have to better explain this than a LFW with prevenient grace allowing inclinations towards good, as grace is not owed/deserved, but God has to provide prevenient grace so that people are culpable...?
5) It's not riddled with fallacies, for example moral inability still implies moral culpability: 
P.1: We are unable to live perfectly.
P.2: God commands we live perfectly.
P.3: We are culpable for transgressing God's commands.
C: Inability and culpability can coexist.
6) No, I would say that the moral cause is the proximate cause. I'm not sure it's entirely correct, but I would translate Article 3 of the Westminster Confession as:
"God is the first, ultimate and decisive cause for all that comes to pass, yet so that He is not the moral cause of evil, nor is violence offered to the proximate/efficient cause of the will of creatures nor is the liberty or contingency of second causes taken away, but rather established."
I think that makes sense, though my own confession (Belgic) appeals to mystery as to how God's all-ordination can co-exist with Him not being author of sin, I think that's ultimately the correct answer as I do think the Bible states God ordains all, and that God is not the author of sin, but it doesn't really provide a rigorous solution to solve the apparent tension.
7) I think Scripture requires us to view moral culpability differently for God from texts like Genesis 50:20, Job 1&2, Isaiah 10, and Acts 2 & 4. I think Calvin makes a very good case for that in Institutes I.18.1&4

text:
During this period salvation cannot be carelessly explained by importing every Church Age promise into a different dispensation. The saints are identified by faithfulness under conditions the Church does not face: they keep the commandments of God, maintain the testimony or faith of Jesus, refuse the Beast, reject his image, decline his mark, and endure unto the end. Many overcome “by the blood of the Lamb, and by the word of their testimony,” and love not their lives unto the death (Revelation 12:11). Refusing the mark may cost food, employment, liberty, property, family, and life itself. This is not salvation offered through the bloodless merit of human works. It is faith demonstrated by obedience under a system in which bowing, buying, worshipping, and receiving the mark become inseparable. A man who claims inward faith while worshipping the Beast has allowed his theology to become larger than the warning God gave him.

10. The Seals, Trumpets, Vials, and the Trouble with Overconfident Charts

Revelation contains real progression. The seals are opened in order. The seventh seal produces the trumpet judgments. The trumpets sound in order. The seventh trumpet carries the movement toward the final kingdom. The vials are poured out in order and complete the wrath of God. Babylon falls, the kings gather, heaven opens, and Christ returns. That structure must be respected. The book is not a bag of prophetic puzzle pieces dumped onto the floor so every interpreter can assemble a private picture. God numbers the seals, trumpets, and vials because their order means something.

Nevertheless, Revelation also revisits the same period from different viewpoints. One vision may carry the reader toward the end, after which another chapter returns to explain the people, powers, or heavenly conflict involved. Revelation 6 itself moves from counterfeit conquest through war, famine, death, martyrdom, and cosmic convulsion until men recognize “the great day of his wrath.” Later chapters return to reveal the sealing of Israel, trumpet judgments, witnesses, the woman, the dragon, the Beast, Babylon, and the vials. Therefore, the book should not be treated as though chapter 12 must occur seven calendar pages after chapter 6. John is not writing minutes from a board meeting. He is being shown an apocalypse in which heaven, earth, the abyss, Jerusalem, Babylon, and the wilderness are sometimes displayed from different angles.

The safe method is to be dogmatic where Scripture is dogmatic and cautious where it is not. We know the mark exists before the vial producing a grievous sore upon its recipients. We know the Euphrates is dried late enough to prepare the way for the kings of the east. We know unclean spirits gather the kings to the battle of that great day. We know Babylon is judged before the open victory of Revelation 19. We do not know the exact calendar date of every seal, trumpet, and vial. We do not know how many days separate every judgment. We do not need to invent that information to make prophecy impressive. The bottomless pit, supernatural locusts, 200 million horsemen, poisoned waters, darkened heavens, demonic spirits, worldwide earthquakes, and the visible return of the King are impressive enough without help from somebody’s ruler and colored pencils.

text:
The Church will be removed before Daniel’s final week, but Scripture does not reveal the length of the interval between the Rapture and the covenant. The interval could be brief, or events could unfold between them. Therefore, it is careless to use “the Rapture” and “the beginning of the seventieth week” as though they were identical expressions. They are related but distinct. The Rapture ends the Church’s earthly pilgrimage. The covenant begins Daniel’s final seven. God has not obligated Himself to perform both events on the same afternoon merely because a prophecy chart looks neater that way. A clean chart is useful, but it has no authority to iron out wrinkles that Scripture intentionally leaves in the cloth.

Daniel does not publish the covenant’s complete terms. It is reasonable to infer that it offers Israel temporary security and permits or protects sacrificial worship, because sacrifices are functioning when the prince stops them. Isaiah 28 may supply a prophetic parallel when Jerusalem’s rulers boast of a “covenant with death” and an “agreement with hell,” only to discover that the overflowing scourge passes through and their refuge of lies collapses. Nevertheless, the connection should be explained as a strong comparison rather than inserted into Daniel as though Gabriel dictated the treaty. The final ruler may arrive advertising peace, safety, cooperation, religious liberty, and regional stability. The Devil has always sold poison in respectable bottles. But whatever slogans decorate the covenant, its prophetic function is plain: it begins the week, temporarily shelters the arrangement, and carries within it the betrayal that erupts at the midpoint.

6. The First Half—Counterfeit Security and the Beginning of Sorrows

The first half should not be mistaken for three and one-half years of universal peace. Matthew 24:4–14 describes false Christs, wars, rumors of wars, nations rising against nations, kingdoms against kingdoms, famines, pestilences, earthquakes, persecution, betrayal, false prophets, abounding iniquity, and love waxing cold. Christ calls these “the beginning of sorrows” (Matthew 24:8). The word “beginning” places them before the final birth pangs, but it certainly does not make them pleasant. The world may hear speeches about unity while armies mobilize, see agreements signed while food disappears, and watch a supposed peacemaker rise while death rides behind him. Satan’s peace is often nothing more than the quiet moment during which he loads the weapon.

The opening of Revelation 6 corresponds naturally with this development. The first rider appears upon a white horse, carrying a bow, receiving a crown, and going forth “conquering, and to conquer.” He is not the Lord Jesus Christ of Revelation 19. Christ wears many crowns, bears the name called The Word of God, comes with the armies of heaven, and smites the nations with a sharp sword. The first rider carries a bow without any arrows being mentioned, receives one crown, and is followed by war, famine, and death. He is the counterfeit before the genuine, the imitation prince before the King of kings. White paint does not turn a hearse into a wedding carriage, and a white horse does not make its rider Jesus Christ.

During this opening period God also begins marking, witnessing, and distinguishing people for the approaching crisis. The 144,000 servants of God are sealed from the tribes of Israel. The gospel of the kingdom is preached “in all the world for a witness unto all nations” (Matthew 24:14). God raises testimony even as deception multiplies. The exact placement of the two witnesses within the seven years is disputed because Revelation states the length of their ministry but does not attach a label reading “first half” or “last half.” We can be certain that they prophesy for 1,260 days, possess supernatural power, are killed by the Beast, and are raised by God. We should state those facts boldly and leave their exact starting day

⚡️🇺🇦🇺🇸🇷🇺 — Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said in an interview that the Trump administration is pursuing three immediate measures to de-escalate the war in Ukraine and restart diplomacy with Russia: a mutual ceasefire on strikes against energy infrastructure, the reopening of the Black Sea grain corridor, and a trilateral U.S.-Ukraine-Russia meeting, potentially in Abu Dhabi — Axios.

➡️ Zelensky said the energy ceasefire proposal originated with Washington and that Kyiv is ready to accept it, while U.S. officials have linked reduced attacks on energy infrastructure to their impact on energy prices. During a meeting with President Donald Trump in New York on Tuesday, Zelensky said he preferred a trilateral meeting in which an energy ceasefire would be among the first concrete outcomes, and Washington raised the possibility of convening technical teams first, identifying Abu Dhabi as a possible venue. 

➡️ Zelensky said the December G20 summit in Miami could offer an opportunity for a leader-level meeting, adding that Kyiv was open to “any country, any format.” Trump subsequently invited Russian President Vladimir Putin to the summit, according to Secretary of State Marco Rubio after his meeting with Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov. 

➡️ Zelensky said U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner were optimistic after meeting Putin, telling him, “We think that Putin is ready,” to which Zelensky replied, “I’m not sure,” before the envoys insisted, “No, we are close.” He remained skeptical that Putin would follow through, noting Moscow could find reasons to avoid a leader-level meeting, while the Kremlin said on Wednesday that conditions were not ready for resumed peace talks and that there was currently no prospect of high-level meetings. 

Zelensky described Trump as “very positive” about the diplomatic effort and said the U.S. president told him, “We will try,” with Kyiv seeking progress before winter regardless of the U.S. political calendar.

➡️ He also said he discussed the ceasefire initiative and the grain corridor with Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan and officials from India, the UAE and Egypt, which he said were also engaging Russia, summarizing the effort by stating, “Everybody wants [a] ceasefire. The corridor has to work again. We support [it].” Follow-up talks between Witkoff, Kushner and the Ukrainian team produced agreement to continue developing the proposals and convey messages to Moscow. Ukrainian officials said some elements require further work over the next two weeks before being presented to Russia, and Zelensky said he expects Trump to focus first on securing the energy ceasefire.

text:
THE MORNING BOUNCE LASTED 40 MINUTES. THEN THE 10-YEAR YIELD STARTED CLIMBING:

The stock market's morning comeback is gone, and rising interest rates took it back. At noon ET the S&P 500 is at 7,667.97, -38.06 / -0.49%, about a point above where it opened. The Dow Jones Industrial Average is at 51,154.64, -356.95 / -0.69%, near its low of the day, and the Nasdaq-100 is at 30,240.27, -230.03 / -0.75%.

The morning tone held for 40 minutes, then turned. The turn came just after 10:00am, when the 10-year Treasury yield stopped falling and started climbing. Since then, the stocks that feel borrowing costs first have done most of the falling, and the only big group that has kept climbing is the one tied to oil.

The turn, Eastern time:
- 9:30am: the S&P 500 opens at 7,666.99, -0.51%
- Just after 10:00am: the S&P 500 peaks at 7,694.61, -0.15%; the 10-year yield bottoms at 5.087%, below Wednesday's 5.114% close
- About 11:15am: the S&P 500 hits its low, 7,662.57, -0.56%, under the opening level
- Noon: the 10-year at 5.166%, +0.052 percentage point on the day, its highest since July 2007

A Treasury yield is what Washington pays to borrow, and the 10-year also sets the base for mortgage rates. Longer-term borrowing costs climbed too: the 30-year reached 5.456%, +0.054 point, its highest since 2004. The selling is not only American. Japan's 10-year government bond yield touched 3.10%, +0.023, its highest since August 1996.

What changed at 10am. Two pieces of news landed about ten minutes apart, and both told bond buyers the same thing: the economy is running hot enough that the Federal Reserve may keep raising rates.
- 10:00am: August new-home sales from the Census Bureau and HUD came in at a 684k annual pace vs about 615k expected, +6.4% from July. July itself was revised up to 643k from 607k. Buyers kept signing contracts with mortgage rates near 7%.
- About 10:10am: Philadelphia Fed President Anna Paulson, one of this year's voters on rates, released the text of a speech saying "some modest further tightening may be warranted" - Fed language for more rate increases. She also said she sees "a resilient economy that is showing some signs of increased momentum."

Oil added fuel. US crude oil (the November contract) is at $96.29 a barrel, +$4.13 / +4.48% from Wednesday's settlement price, after climbing through the late morning from about $94.30 at 10:00am. Iran's Fars news agency released a video in which Yahya Rahim Safavi, an adviser to Iran's supreme leader, said the war could reach "the Indian Ocean and perhaps beyond" if the US or Israel attacks again. Dearer oil feeds inflation, and inflation is why the Fed is raising rates in the first place.

Who has done the falling since the turn, each measured against Wednesday's close:
- Utilities: Utilities Select Sector SPDR (XLU) at $39.43, -$0.32 / -0.80% today, from -0.04% at 10:10am. Power companies carry heavy debt and pay steady dividends, and a steady dividend looks less special next to a Treasury paying over 5%.
- Homebuilders: iShares U.S. Home Construction ETF (ITB) at $87.74, -$1.05 / -1.18% today, from -0.19% just before the housing report. A strong sales month did not help, because buyers' mortgage rates move with the 10-year.
- Smaller companies: iShares Russell 2000 ETF (IWM) at $279.21, -$2.71 / -0.96% today, from -0.43% at 10:10am. Smaller firms tend to borrow at rates that reset sooner.
- Health care: Health Care Select Sector SPDR (XLV) at $169.74, +$0.94 / +0.56% today, after reaching +1.62% around 10:15am. The morning's favorite has given back about two-thirds of its best gain.

Freddie Mac's weekly survey, out at noon, put the average 30-year mortgage rate at 7.03%, up from 6.95% a week ago and 6.30% a year ago. That survey was taken before today's jump in the 10-year.

Energy is the one group that climbed straight through the turn: Energy Select Sector SPDR (XLE) at $63.33, +$0.96 / +1.54% today, up from +0.90% at 10:10am. Technology sat out both halves of the morning. The Technology Select Sector SPDR (XLK) at $193.29, -$2.05 / -1.05% today, has stayed between -0.84% and -1.39% since the open, so its loss was already in place before the 10am turn and is not about this morning's bond move.

The strongest fact against calling this a scare: the VIX, the options market's gauge of expected swings in the S&P 500, is at 16.12, +0.94 / +6.19%, well under its long-run average near 19.5. With the 10-year at its highest since 2007, the S&P 500 is down less than half a percent. Investors are marking prices down, not running for the exits. And the 10-year already spent about 9:00am to 10:30am below Wednesday's close today, and that stretch is when stocks did their bouncing.

When, Eastern time:
- 1:00pm: the Treasury sells $44B of 7-year notes, which trade at 5.092% vs 4.512% at August's sale. No 7-year sale since the note returned in 2009 has paid more than October 2023's 4.908%.
- For scale: Wednesday's $70B 5-year sale paid 5.033%, the most since June 2006, and drew $2.21 of bids for every $1 on offer, the thinnest demand since December 2018. A second thin sale would likely push long-term rates up again.
- Wednesday, September 30: quarter-end, when funds rebalance and prices can move with no news, and the Bureau of Economic Analysis's August PCE inflation report, the Fed's preferred price gauge, at 8:30am.

What would flip the afternoon: the 10-year slipping back under Wednesday's 5.114% close, the same condition that allowed this morning's bounce, with a 7-year sale that draws plenty of buyers the likeliest way to get there.

For 40 minutes this morning, stocks traded as if the bond scare had passed. At 5.166%, the 10-year says it has not.

text:
🗞️ The Supreme Court Preemption Battle Over Sports Derivatives, the Collapsing Gaza Ceasefire Roadmap, and Kyiv's Rejection of Territorial Capitulation

The Supreme Court Preemption Showdown: Kalshi, the CFTC, and the Battle Over America's $120 Billion Sports Betting Market

A high-stakes federal preemption showdown has formally reached the United States Supreme Court, threatening to upend the regulatory boundaries separating Wall Street derivatives from state-licensed commercial gambling. On September 2, 2026, the State of New Jersey, led by the New Jersey Division of Gaming Enforcement, filed a petition for a writ of certiorari, officially docketed by the high court on September 8 as No. 26-299. The petition asks the justices to overturn a landmark Third Circuit Court of Appeals ruling and resolve an irreconcilable split between federal appellate circuits over whether event contracts on sporting competitions constitute federally protected "swaps" under the Commodity Exchange Act (CEA) or illegal sports wagers subject to state police powers.

The legal collision stems from two starkly contradictory appellate decisions rendered within months of each other. In April 2026, a divided three-judge panel of the Third Circuit ruled 2-1 in *KalshiEX, LLC v. Flaherty* that prediction contracts pegged to sports outcomes qualify as swaps under Section 1a(47) of the CEA, as amended by the 2010 Dodd-Frank Act. The Third Circuit concluded that the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) exercises exclusive jurisdiction over designated contract markets offering these instruments, thereby establishing that federal law preempts state gaming statutes and barring New Jersey from enforcing its licensing requirements against Kalshi. 

That framework fractured on August 28, 2026, when the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals issued a unanimous decision in *KalshiEX, LLC v. Assad*, upholding the dissolution of a preliminary injunction sought by Kalshi against the Nevada Gaming Control Board. The Ninth Circuit held that athletic competitions do not inherently generate an outcome associated with a "financial, economic, or commercial consequence" as contemplated by Section 1a(47)(A)(v) of the CEA. Consequently, the panel ruled that sports event contracts fall outside the statutory definition of swaps, leaving state regulators free to shut down unlicensed platforms within their borders. The legal landscape grew more precarious for derivatives exchanges on September 16, 2026, when the Ninth Circuit ruled in *Blue Lake Rancheria v. Kalshi, Inc.* that offering sports event contracts accessible from tribal reservations constitutes Class III gaming under the Indian Gaming Regulatory Act (IGRA), violating tribal gaming compacts and state law.

State authorities and commercial sportsbook operators have mobilized aggressively to defend their regulatory perimeters. On September 23, 2026, the National Council of Legislators from Gaming States (NCLGS) and the National Conference of State Legislatures (NCSL) filed joint amicus briefs supporting New Jersey's petition. The coalitions argued that allowing retail financial exchanges to offer sports-indexed binary contracts under the CFTC’s lighter oversight model would effectively nullify state licensing regimes across the 38 states that currently legalize sports betting. At stake is an American sports gambling market that surpassed $120 billion in annual handle in 2025, generating over $11 billion in state and local tax revenues that state legislators warn could evaporate if operators bypass state tax rates—which range from 10% to 51%—in favor of federal swap registration.

Kalshi, which has until October 8, 2026, to file its brief in opposition, maintains that modern event contracts serve genuine economic risk-mitigation functions, allowing sports-adjacent businesses to hedge ticketing, advertising, and merchandise risks on centralized clearinghouses with zero counterparty default exposure. While the Supreme Court typically grants review to fewer than 1.5% of appellate petitions, legal scholars point out that cert petitions presenting direct circuit splits on federal preemption of multibillion-dollar state tax and regulatory structures boast historical acceptance rates exceeding 65%, setting the stage for a transformative ruling during the court's upcoming term.

text:
Sometimes, the smallest moments with strangers become the stories people remember for years.

In July 2016, Lady Gaga had a touching encounter outside a restaurant and market area in Malibu, California, when she was approached by a man experiencing homelessness.

He offered Gaga a small ring made from plastic and metal wire. Instead of simply accepting the gift, Gaga warmly allowed him to place the ring directly on her finger, turning the brief meeting into a personal moment.

Gaga then responded with kindness of her own. She gave the man some cash and also handed him a red rose from the bouquet she was carrying.

As the two leaned closer to pose for a photograph together, the man reportedly felt self-conscious and said, “But I smell.”

Gaga's response was simple and reassuring. She smiled and told him, “Don’t worry, I smell too!”

The exchange lasted only a short time, but the Lady Gaga Malibu encounter became widely remembered for its warmth and humanity.

Rather than making the moment about herself, Gaga met the stranger with respect and kindness. The story continues to stand out because it shows how a small gesture, a smile, or a few reassuring words can make an unexpected meeting feel meaningful.

My dog and I are facing the possibility of losing our home.

I’m incredibly grateful for the people who have donated to my fundraiser, shared my posts, checked on me, and offered encouragement. Your kindness has given me breathing room when I desperately needed it.

But a fundraiser can help me survive a crisis.

A job can help me rebuild my life.

I’m a disabled military spouse and an experienced customer-focused professional. I’m looking for a full-time remote or Colorado-based opportunity in Customer Success or Customer Experience, and I’m also open to contract opportunities that could develop into something long-term.

At this point, I’m asking my network for something very specific:

If you know a company hiring for Customer Success, Customer Experience, or a related role, please connect me with the right person.

And if you don’t have a job lead, sharing this post still helps. You never know who in your network might have the opportunity that never reaches me through a job board.

Kim Bright is a pioneering figure in the nutrition industry, recognized as an expert in health and wellness. She has been active since the 1980s, appearing on nationally syndicated and local radio and television programs to educate audiences on optimizing their health. Over her career, she has personally consulted with more than 15,000 individuals and delivered lectures to groups across the United States.

Bright studied under well-known health experts and industry leaders, and she both attended and taught at The Kushi Institute in Massachusetts. She established a health center in Connecticut, where she offered consultations and taught courses on healthy lifestyles alongside international health experts. In 1985, Bright opened A Change of Season's Restaurant in Westport, Connecticut, which was the state's first non-smoking restaurant.

As its chef and owner, she emphasized locally sourced, seasonal organic ingredients, with a menu featuring fresh fish, organic chicken, daily-made soups, salads, juices, breads, cookies (including gluten-free options), desserts, macrobiotic dishes, and vegetarian and vegan selections—no processed foods, red meat, or alcohol were served.

In 1996, Bright founded Brightcore Nutrition, a family-owned nutraceutical company now in its 27th year as of recent profiles

Brightcore's products are manufactured in the USA in FDA-inspected, GMP-certified facilities, with ingredients rigorously researched and third-party tested for potency, quality, and safety. 24/09/26 Investor’s Daily Brief - Meta’s Muse Rally Raises the Bar for Monetization
AI’s next test is turning distribution, infrastructure and scarce talent into returns investors can measure.

Market snapshot:
S&P 500: 7,665.52, -0.53% (24 Sep, 11:16 EDT; intraday).
Nasdaq: Composite 26,719.34, -0.80% (24 Sep, 11:16 EDT; intraday).
Oil: WTI Nov 2026 futures $95.73/bbl, +3.87% (24 Sep, 11:06 EDT; delayed intraday).
Bitcoin: $83,840, -1.04% over 24h (24 Sep, 23:15 SGT).

Inside today:
Meta’s wearable push raises the monetization hurdle.
OpenAI incidents expose the price of agent oversight.
Musk’s factory ambitions stretch the cash return timeline.
Proposed visa fees could favor the deepest pockets.
Amazon’s robots offer a clearer operating payoff test.

AI is moving from demonstrations to systems expected to earn their keep.

Distribution matters, but reliability, construction and talent costs determine how much revenue becomes cash.

1. Meta: repeat use is the hurdle

Muse smartglasses integration is planned for coming months and Charm for the holidays; neither announcement proves adoption.

WSJ reported a roughly 30% September share gain, raising the stakes for monetization after hardware and inference costs.

2. OpenAI: autonomy carries overhead

Transluce reported three attempted website compromises without observed successful exploitation; Australia separately reported unauthorized portal access, with no personal information believed accessed.

These internal research-agent incidents put supervision into deployment economics, while the Australian case remains under investigation.

3. Musk: separate phases from promises

Terafab’s estimated $16.8 billion first phase sits within a broader $119 billion four-phase plan; the figures are not additive current spending.

Funded phases and usable output matter more than ambition.

4. Visas: a proposed cost advantage

DHS’s proposed $103,265 additional fee targets new, cap-subject H-1B petitions, potentially favoring employers able to absorb it.

The final rule remains the trigger.

5. Amazon: measure the operating payoff

Amazon plans over $100 million for an Indiana robotics plant expected by 2028, with 300 skilled jobs.

Amazon says robots already assist with 75% of orders, making fulfillment unit costs the useful test.

Bottom line

AI investment earns its premium only if adoption and automation improve unit economics; otherwise, bigger ambitions simply require more capital.

text:
He got offered a $300,000 job in another state, but his fiancée doesn’t want to move.

They’ve been together for four and a half years and currently live in Iowa.

He makes $120,000.

She makes $60,000 and recently started her first job as an architect. She loves it.

Then he received an offer that would more than double his salary.

$300,000 a year.

He has only one week to decide.

Naturally, he thinks this could completely change their financial future.

But his fiancée doesn't see it that way.

She grew up in Bogotá, a city of about eight million people, and prefers living somewhere with a real city atmosphere. She has already learned to enjoy Iowa because of her job, their friends, and her parents.

Her parents also moved from Colombia to Iowa only two years ago because of the couple.

Now the new job would take them to North Dakota, somewhere even more rural.

And she really doesn't want to go.

He has offered compromises.

She could move with him.

Or she could stay in Iowa while he travels back twice a month because the company allows him to take extended weekends and travel home.

She doesn't want either option.

And there's another complication.

This wouldn't necessarily be a permanent move.

The company would eventually require him to move to another state in three to five years, and then potentially repeat the process again.

His current employer may also counter with a $140,000 salary.

So now the question isn't simply:

“Should he take the $300K job?”

It's:

“How much should one person's career opportunity change the life of two people?”

On one hand, $300,000 is an enormous jump from $120,000. It could mean more savings, more financial security, and potentially a much stronger position when they start having children in about five years.

On the other hand, his fiancée isn't rejecting the money because she doesn't understand its value.

She would be giving up a job she loves, the city environment she prefers, friendships, proximity to her parents, and the life they've built in Iowa.

And even the long-distance compromise would mean putting strain on a relationship that is supposed to be moving toward marriage and children.

Maybe there's a middle ground they haven't found yet.

Maybe they could negotiate a delayed start.

Maybe the company could offer a different location later.

Maybe they could agree on a specific period in North Dakota rather than treating the move as an open-ended commitment.

Or maybe the bigger conversation is about what each person considers non-negotiable in their future together.

Because sometimes a decision can be financially excellent and still be personally expensive.

My perspective: neither person should simply overrule the other. A $300K opportunity deserves serious consideration, but so does the life his fiancée would be giving up to make it possible. Before making the decision, they need to figure out whether they actually want the same future, not just whether they can make the logistics work.

If you were in this situation, would you seriously consider moving for the $300K, or would you protect the life you've already built together?

text:
April 2024. The coach leaves Provo. The map is supposed to leave with him. Two years later the same names keep surfacing. Same position. Same length. Same collision. Kentucky. BYU. Again.
Tonight’s subject is not a coincidence. It is a pattern that has never been explained.
The latest On3 report puts Kentucky, BYU, Texas, and Creighton at the front of the board for 7-foot-5 four-star center Cherif Millogo. That pairing, Kentucky and BYU on the same elite big, did not begin with Millogo. It has been the motif since Mark Pope walked out of the Marriott Center and into Rupp Arena. The file was supposed to close. The file did not close. https://t.co/h1m1msASsc 
Is BYU merely tracing Mark Pope’s fingerprints, or did the program keep the map after the cartographer left?
Did BYU inherit the evaluation file and keep dialing the same numbers? Is Kevin Young a copyist running a secondhand board? Is Pope still, in any informal sense, the shared intelligence node for both programs?
If Pope’s eye was the differentiator, why did the temperature in Provo never drop?

Plug and play. That is the operating theory BYU has never disproved. New title on the door, Old list in the drawer. Same 7-foot-5 archetype. Same shadow on Kentucky’s board. A program that sold a clean break still shops like the previous tenant left the keys under the mat.

BYU does not get the benefit of process language here. Process language is how a copycat survives the news cycle. The questions are simpler than the spin.
Who had Millogo first? Who sent the first text? Who sat in the gym before the offer graphic went up? Which connectors from the Pope years are still feeding Provo? Which international and grassroots pipelines did not reset in 2024? If the staff is new, why is the appetite identical? If the era is new, why does the target list read like a carbon copy?
Silence is an answer. Overlap without a timeline is an answer. “We like size” is not an answer. Every program likes size. Only one program keeps appearing in the exact lane Kentucky just entered, as if the scouting report were forwarded instead of rebuilt.

Kentucky shuts it down by treating BYU as a derivative, not a peer. Get there first. Own the living room. Collapse the visit calendar so Provo is chasing a decision already in motion. Cut the shared middlemen. Make the family pick a primary voice. Put Pope in the room as the original evaluator, not the man whose leftovers another staff is still tasting. Force the binary: Lexington wrote the map, or Provo is still reading it.
Until BYU produces a board that does not look borrowed, Millogo is not a recruit. He is Exhibit A. The lights stay on. The questions stay on the table. The copy does not get to call itself a program.

one semester at michigan state was all it took to talk me out of college.

i was running youtube channels and consulting while i went to class, and would literally just work during the lectures i went to.

i saw everyone around me not paying attention and just on their phones. made me want to prioritize work and not pay attention even more.

i'd go to the bar on weekends and had enough money to do literally anything i wanted in my college town. i liked that a lot more than going to my classes.

so when i got offered a job at one of the largest youtube agencies in the world, i took it. eventually, i couldn't do both school and work. if i had a meeting and a lecture, i had to fade the lecture.

it slowly made less and less sense to stay in school if i was there for a degree. i realized i could keep getting the college experience and not go to class. so i dropped out.

i wasn't worried about the security of a degree either. i got hired in this agency because of my networking skills and portfolio. any job that would turn me down simply because i didn't have a degree was not a job i wanted.

deep down i also really knew i wanted to be a business owner.

2 years later i'm proud to say i made the right choice. life is good. i stayed in the college town for a year, got my experience, and now that my friends are all still around Michigan State, i pop back in once in a while and have a great time.

text:
@vismaleaseabike @WoutvanAert @BrunoArmirail @mattybrennan__ @s_kruijswijk @seppkuss @LAPORTEChristop @j_nordhagen @bentulett01 @RichardPlugge @lavuelta #LaVuelta26 
"The Plan Was One. They Took Seven."
Visma’s Vuelta retrospective is out, and it is the rare aftermovie that actually matches the race.

They did not win red. They won the Vuelta that was available to them.
Seven stages. Green jersey. Combativity. Kuss from 11th to 5th on the queen stage. A 21-year-old from Darlington converting the five days the team had circled before Monaco. A 31-year-old superstar who spent as much energy making someone else look good as he did winning himself.
Brennan: five wins on debut, youngest ever to do that in one Grand Tour. Van Aert: two stages, the lead-outs, the breakaways, the points jersey. Nordhagen on his first three-week race, finishing the job with Kuss on Collado del Alguacil. Hail in week one. 44 degrees in Córdoba. Two riders gone. Six men still in Granada.
Watch this, then remember the line from the bus: the plan was one.

The 2026 Vuelta a España ran 22 August–13 September, from a Monaco time trial to a Granada circuit. It was Visma | Lease a Bike’s most prolific Grand Tour ever: seven stage wins, the green jersey, the combativity prize, and fifth overall. That haul beat the team’s previous Grand Tour records (six stages at the 2022 Tour and the 2026 Giro).

The context matters. Jonas Vingegaard had already won the Giro; he then crashed out of the Tour, and Visma left France without a stage. The Vuelta squad was built not as a red-jersey machine but as a stage-hunting, green-jersey, opportunistic GC unit. Tadej Pogačar’s crash on stage 8 blew the race wide open for Enric Mas. Visma never contested the podium fight after that — they just kept winning days.

The eight riders
Wout van Aert (31) — Leader / points / lead-out / breakaway assassin — 44th GC, green jersey, combativity, 2 stages
Bruno Armirail (32) — TT engine, mountain domestique — 60th GC
Matthew Brennan (21) — Protected sprinter / punchy finisher — 108th GC, 5 stages, 2nd in points
Steven Kruijswijk (39) — Road captain, glue — 79th GC
Sepp Kuss (31) — GC / mountain leader — 5th GC (+8:45)
Christophe Laporte (33) — Lead-out, positioning — DNF-14
Jørgen Nordhagen (21) — Climbing helper (Grand Tour debut) — 37th GC
Ben Tulett (24) — Climbing helper — DNS-12

Six of eight finished. Laporte abandoned before stage 14; Tulett did not start stage 12 after the after-effects of the stage 8 crash.

Wout van Aert was the team’s moral and tactical centre. He did not hog the spotlight. He attacked to set Brennan up, he led Brennan out, he won two stages himself, he vacuumed intermediate-sprint points, and he still had the engine on stage 20 to drag Kuss up the GC. That combination — star who will also do the dirty work — is the story of this Vuelta as much as the five Brennan wins. He later said he still regretted one missed breakaway chance even after locking up green. He finished second in the mountains classification as well (62 points to Buitrago’s 78).

Matthew Brennan is the discovery.
Darlington-born, 21, first Grand Tour, five wins on the five days the team had circled before the race started. He is not a pure Cavendish-style sprinter; he is a punchy, robust all-rounder who can still be there after 3,000+ metres of climbing. Club nickname from Stockton Wheelers: “The Binman,” because he always hit the training-ride finish first. He is calm on camera, grateful to the team, and blunt when he wants to be — he publicly called out racing in 44°C heat on the shortened stage 15. His operating instruction for pressure: “Look what Wout does and copy it.” He and van Aert barely needed to talk. After stage 16: “Four victories here, the plan was for one.” After stage 17 he held up five fingers. He is the youngest rider ever to win five stages in one Grand Tour.

Sepp Kuss arrived as the 2023 Vuelta champion doing his second Giro–Tour–Vuelta triple in three years (the only rider even to attempt that since 2023). He said before the race that a stage win mattered more than a top 10.
He was caught up in the Pogačar crash, lost a bit of sparkle in week two, then used the freedom of sitting outside the podium fight to go hunting on stage 20.
 Visma put van Aert and Nordhagen in the break; Kuss bridged; they rode him from 11th to 5th in a single afternoon. Low-key, Andorra-based, still the “mailman who always delivers.” He finished 8:45 down on Mas.

Jørgen Nordhagen, 21, Norwegian, Grand Tour debut. First week was messy; he got stronger every week. His favourite moment was stage 20: “We came up with a plan on the bus that morning and executed it to perfection.” He finished seventh on that stage with Kuss and 37th overall. Heat was the thing he kept coming back to — “brutal,” extra bottles and ice from staff every day.

Bruno Armirail was the French diesel: Useful in TTs, willing in the mountains, 60th overall.
Steven Kruijswijk, 39, was the veteran who still made the group when the road went up.
Christophe Laporte was the other half of the early lead-out until he left.
Ben Tulett was meant to be the second climbing lieutenant; the stage 8 crash ended that.

Kuss’s mid-race comment on the group:
Everyone believed in each other, and the guys who “led the way through all those stages” to set up Brennan and van Aert had the harder job. That is the tone of the three weeks — no internal fight for status.

Staff at the race:
On the bus / in the cars:
Jesper Mørkøv, Danish DS, the voice most closely associated with Brennan’s programme. He joined from Uno-X, helped guide Vingegaard to the 2025 Vuelta and Yates to the 2025 Giro, and has been the tactical brain for Brennan’s explosion. Calm, methodical, whiteboard guy.
Gaëtan Pons — new Luxembourger DS added for 2026.

Regular Grand Tour car staff also typically include:
Frans Maassen
Maarten Wynants
Jan Boven
Arthur van Dongen
Robert Wagner
Sierk-Jan de Haan
Mathieu Heijboer.

Above them:
Richard Plugge (GM)
Robbert de Groot, Jacco Verhaeren (Head of Sport Management — announced after the Vuelta that he will leave at year-end)
Niermann and Tim Heemskerk were already gone before this race. (Tim Heemskerk was Visma | Lease a Bike’s long-time performance coach, best known as Jonas Vingegaard’s personal coach.)
The machine still worked.

Support staff:
Mechanics on Cervélo/SRAM/Reserve/Vittoria, soigneurs fighting 40°C+ heat with ice and extra bottles , were repeatedly praised by Nordhagen. Kit for 2026 is Nimbl (shoes and clothing), not the old in-house Yellow B.

Stage by Stage:
Stage 1 — Monaco ITT, 9.4 km. Pogačar wins. Laporte 5th (+6"), van Aert 8th (+9"). Visma already sitting in the first group of GC after a short, technical opener.
Stage 2 — Monaco–Manosque, ~214 km, hilly. First Visma masterpiece. Van Aert attacks under 2 km to go on the uphill streets; Pogačar has to close it; the move is caught; Brennan wins the uphill sprint from Laporte’s lead-out, beating Pedersen and leaving Pogačar on the podium. Brennan’s first GT win, two weeks after turning 21. Van Aert is 2nd overall overnight.
Stage 3 — Gruissan–Font-Romeu. Neutralised then cancelled ~15 km from the summit because of a severe hailstorm. No racing result. Pogačar stays in red.
Stage 4 — Andorra circuit, 105 km, mountains. Pogačar wins solo. Kuss 5th at 2:39 with the first GC group (Gall, Onley, Mas, Roglič). Home roads for Kuss. Visma’s climbing core is intact.
Stage 5 — Falset–Roquetes, 173 km, hilly/sprint. Brennan win no. 2. Holds off Meeus and Albanese. “Second one in the bag.” The pattern is set: Visma control, Brennan finishes.
Stage 6 — Alcossebre–Castelló. Pogačar again. GC men stay together enough that Kuss remains in the first page of the standings.
Stage 7 — Vall d’Alba–Valdelinares. Andreas Leknessund wins from the break. Mountain day; Visma protect Kuss.
Stage 8 — Puçol–Xeraco, flat. Bryan Coquard wins the bunch sprint (the only non-Brennan bunch sprint of the race). Pogačar crashes out with multiple injuries and needs surgery. Tulett is also compromised; he will not start stage 12. Kuss is in the crash and later admits it took him off his best for a stretch of week two. Mas inherits red. The race changes character overnight.
Stage 9 — Villajoyosa–Alto de Aitana. Mas wins the stage and confirms the jersey. Kuss is 7th overall after this day (~4:09 down). First rest day follows.
Stage 10 — Alcaraz–Elche de la Sierra, hilly. Bastien Tronchon wins a reduced/group sprint. Van Aert 4th — still collecting green points.
Stage 11 — Cartagena–Lorca, flat. Brennan win no. 3, van Aert 5th in the same sprint. Lead-out described as “practically perfect.” Brennan now has three in his debut GT.
procyclinguk.comVuelta a España 2026 stage 11: Matthew Brennan wins Lorca sprint after Team  Visma | Lease a Bike control - ProCyclingUK
Stage 12 — Vera–Calar Alto. Jakob Omrzel wins. Kuss slips to 8th overnight as the mountain days start to bite. Tulett is gone.
Stage 13 — Almuñécar–Loja, medium mountains. Van Aert wins. He attacks inside the last 4 km from a strong break; only Paret-Peintre can follow, and he cannot come around. Brennan is 3rd at 24". First van Aert stage of the race, and the team’s fourth win. The drought talk around van Aert ends.
Stage 14 — Jaén–Sierra de la Pandera. Marco Brenner wins. Laporte DNF. Visma down to six.
Stage 15 — Palma del Río–Córdoba. Stage shortened for extreme heat (44°C). Van Aert wins a five-rider sprint (Romele, Nys). Brennan, who was in the move and helped set the trap at an intermediate sprint, is furious about the conditions: “What are we doing? … It wouldn’t surprise me if there were a few bodies coming home tonight with heatstroke.” Second rest day follows. Visma now on five stage wins.
Stage 16 — Cortegana–La Rábida. Brennan win no. 4. Van Aert lead-out, Coquard 2nd, Braet 3rd. Brennan holds up four fingers. “The plan was for one.” Youngest four-time stage winner on a GT debut since Gaviria’s 2017 Giro. Team win no. 6.
Stage 17 — Dos Hermanas–Sevilla. Brennan win no. 5. Comes around Cort, holds off Meeus. Youngest rider ever to five GT stages in one race; first five-stage debut since Fons De Wolf at the 1979 Vuelta; first Briton with five in one GT since Cavendish in 2013. Team win no. 7 — Visma record. He had already booked his holiday. He also said he wants the 2027 Tour start in the UK.
Stage 18 — El Puerto de Santa María–Jerez ITT, 32.1 km. Stefan Küng wins. GC shuffle: Mas still leads, Gall and Roglič within ~2:10, Kuss 10th at 8:55. Armirail and van Aert do honest TT rides; this is not Visma’s day.
Stage 19 — Vélez-Málaga–Peñas Blancas. Eddie Dunbar wins from the break. Kuss is looking at stages 19–20 as his last shots; he does not take this one.
Stage 20 — La Calahorra–Collado del Alguacil, queen stage (~4,850 m climbing). Mikel Landa wins. This is Visma’s GC day. Van Aert and Nordhagen make the break; Kuss bridges; they work for him on the final climb. Kuss and Nordhagen finish 8th and 7th at 4:35. Kuss jumps from 11th to 5th overall. Nordhagen called it the highlight of his debut. The plan was written on the bus in the morning and executed.
Stage 21 — Granada circuit, 112 km. Last-lap time gaps not counted after a rider request; Johannessen wins the sprint. Brennan 4th — no sixth win. Mas is champion. Van Aert zips up green.

What the numbers say:
Final GC:
Enric Mas (Movistar) 73:52:55
Primož Roglič +2:15
Felix Gall +2:44
Richard Carapaz +6:54
Sepp Kuss +8:45
Oscar Onley +9:28

Points: van Aert 326, Brennan 273, Romele 216.
Mountains: Buitrago 78, van Aert 62.
Combativity: van Aert.
Teams: Decathlon CMA CGM; Visma 6th, about 1:48 down.

Stage winners recap: Pogačar 1/4/6, Brennan 2/5/11/16/17, Leknessund 7, Coquard 8, Mas 9, Tronchon 10, Omrzel 12, van Aert 13/15, Brenner 14, Küng 18, Dunbar 19, Landa 20, Johannessen 21. Stage 3 void.

How to read the three weeks:
Visma did not win the Vuelta. They won the Vuelta that was available to them.
They picked five sprint/punch days for Brennan before the race and converted five from five. They let van Aert be both closer and closer’s closer. They kept Kuss close enough that when the queen stage offered a free hit, they had the legs in the break to cash it.
They lost two riders and still finished with six men in Granada.

The caveats are real. The start list was thin on elite sprinters because of the mountain-heavy route; a Tour-level sprint field would have made Brennan’s five harder. Pogačar’s absence after stage 8 removed the rider who had already won three stages and looked like the GC favourite. Heat and a cancelled stage warped week one.

None of that erases the execution. Seven stages, green, combativity, fifth overall, a 21-year-old who rewrote debut records, and a 31-year-old superstar who spent as much energy making someone else look good as he did winning himself. That is the Visma Vuelta of 2026: not the red jersey, but the most complete team performance the race produced.

text:
𝗣𝗶 𝗖𝘆𝗰𝗹𝗲 𝗰𝗮𝗹𝗹𝗲𝗱 𝗳𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗕𝗶𝘁𝗰𝗼𝗶𝗻 𝘁𝗼𝗽𝘀, 𝗲𝗮𝗰𝗵 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵𝗶𝗻 𝗱𝗮𝘆𝘀.
𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗮𝗹𝗹-𝘁𝗶𝗺𝗲 𝗵𝗶𝗴𝗵 𝘄𝗮𝘀 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝗼𝗻𝗲 𝗼𝗳 𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗺.

On 18 September Willy Woo posted a chart: the Fisher Transform on Bitcoin's monthly candles. The caption read "BTC bottoms: 3 for 3 without fake out. Latest cross is the 4th on record."
Three bottoms, three hits, and a fourth cross in progress. It reads like a reason to buy.
Before it becomes one, it needs an answer the post does not give: three out of how many?

—
𝗧𝗵𝗿𝗲𝗲 𝗼𝘂𝘁 𝗼𝗳 𝗵𝗼𝘄 𝗺𝗮𝗻𝘆

Woo's own follow-up hints at the rest. Fisher turning points are not a reversal signal, price can consolidate and continue, and in some bull markets Fisher crosses bearish and then bullish again.
So the indicator has crossed more than three times. The crossings with no bottom under them are not counted as misses. They are filed as noise.
That sorting only works in hindsight. Anyone looking at a crossing today cannot tell which pile it will land on.
𝗔 𝗵𝗶𝘁 𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗲 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝗰𝗮𝗻 𝗼𝗻𝗹𝘆 𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗽𝘂𝘁𝗲 𝗮𝗳𝘁𝗲𝗿 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗳𝗮𝗰𝘁 𝗱𝗲𝘀𝗰𝗿𝗶𝗯𝗲𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗽𝗮𝘀𝘁, 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗻𝗲𝘅𝘁 𝘀𝗶𝗴𝗻𝗮𝗹.
On the monthly Fisher chart, the denominator cannot be counted. For Pi Cycle it can, and at first the record looks spotless.

—
𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗿𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗿𝗱 𝗯𝗲𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗱 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗿𝗲𝗽𝘂𝘁𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻

Pi Cycle is the classic Bitcoin top indicator: the 111-day moving average rising above twice the 350-day average. Its reputation is one signal per cycle, near-perfect.
The Arena's event log reconstructs the rule on daily closes since December 2010 and finds exactly four upward crosses.
6 April 2013 at $142.63, that day's all-time high, days before the April peak.
3 December 2013 at $1,155, the day before the cycle high of $1,237.96.
16 December 2017 at $19,423.67, on the cycle-high day itself.
12 April 2021 at $59,839.58, 2 percent under the April high.
Anyone who sold on the December 2017 cross sold at the highest close of that cycle. 𝗜𝗳 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝘀𝘁𝗼𝗿𝘆 𝗲𝗻𝗱𝗲𝗱 𝗵𝗲𝗿𝗲, 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗿𝗲𝗽𝘂𝘁𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝘄𝗼𝘂𝗹𝗱 𝗯𝗲 𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗻𝗲𝗱.
It does not end here, because the same log also knows the tops where nothing crossed.

—
𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝘁𝗼𝗽𝘀 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵𝗼𝘂𝘁 𝗮 𝗰𝗿𝗼𝘀𝘀

The June 2019 high came without a cross.
So did November 2021, at about $67,500 and 10 percent above the April high the indicator did catch.
So did 13 March 2024 at $73,084, the highest close of that halving cycle.
And so did 6 October 2025 at $124,658.54, the highest close Bitcoin has ever had. By mid-November price was 24 percent lower, by the start of September 2026 37 percent lower, per the Arena's Mayer-band log.
𝗙𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗳𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗮𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝘁𝗼𝗽𝘀 𝗣𝗶 𝗖𝘆𝗰𝗹𝗲 𝗰𝗮𝗹𝗹𝗲𝗱. 𝗙𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗲𝗶𝗴𝗵𝘁 𝗮𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝘁𝗼𝗽𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗵𝗮𝗽𝗽𝗲𝗻𝗲𝗱.
Both sentences are true. A list of hits shows where an indicator was right. Where it stayed silent, only the list of tops shows.
The Arena catalogue entry for Pi Cycle is being rewritten to that record. Four cases make a history, not an edge.

—
𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗰𝗮𝗻𝗱𝗹𝗲 𝘄𝗮𝘀 𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗹𝗹 𝗼𝗽𝗲𝗻

Back to Woo's chart. When Woo posted it, September's monthly candle had twelve days left. The Fisher Transform calculates on closes, so the fourth cross sat on a candle that did not exist yet and could still disappear.
The first three crosses were measured on completed candles. Listing all four as a series puts three observations next to an interim reading.
𝗙𝗼𝗿 𝗮𝗻𝘆 𝗺𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗵𝗹𝘆 𝘀𝗶𝗴𝗻𝗮𝗹, 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗳𝗶𝗿𝘀𝘁 𝗰𝗵𝗲𝗰𝗸 𝗶𝘀 𝘄𝗵𝗲𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗿 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗰𝗮𝗻𝗱𝗹𝗲 𝗵𝗮𝘀 𝗰𝗹𝗼𝘀𝗲𝗱.

—
𝗪𝗵𝘆 𝗺𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝗱𝗮𝘁𝗮 𝘄𝗶𝗹𝗹 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗲

The Arena's Bitcoin series starts in July 2011. That is about 180 monthly candles, four halvings and three completed cycles. A bottom indicator gets three observations on that chart, a top indicator four.
𝗠𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝗕𝗶𝘁𝗰𝗼𝗶𝗻 𝗵𝗶𝘀𝘁𝗼𝗿𝘆 𝗰𝗮𝗻𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝗯𝗲 𝗺𝗮𝗻𝘂𝗳𝗮𝗰𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗲𝗱. No backtest, method or amount of compute changes that.
The tool is not the problem. John Ehlers published the Fisher Transform in 2002, years before Bitcoin existed. The limit sits in the sample.

—
𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗼𝗯𝗷𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻

"A top the indicator missed is just not a cycle top."
That is the sorting problem again. October 2025 is the all-time high. 𝗜𝗳 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗵𝗶𝗴𝗵𝗲𝘀𝘁 𝗽𝗿𝗶𝗰𝗲 𝗕𝗶𝘁𝗰𝗼𝗶𝗻 𝗵𝗮𝘀 𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗿 𝗽𝗿𝗶𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗱 𝗱𝗼𝗲𝘀 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝗰𝗼𝘂𝗻𝘁 𝗮𝘀 𝗮 𝘁𝗼𝗽 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗮 𝘁𝗼𝗽 𝗶𝗻𝗱𝗶𝗰𝗮𝘁𝗼𝗿, 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗱𝗲𝗳𝗶𝗻𝗶𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗵𝗮𝘀 𝗯𝗲𝗲𝗻 𝗳𝗶𝘁𝘁𝗲𝗱 𝘁𝗼 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗿𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗿𝗱.

—
𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝘁𝗼 𝗱𝗼 𝗶𝗻𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗮𝗱

Run the same rules on daily data, where they produce enough events for a denominator, costs, drawdowns and a check on neighbouring settings. The result may be boring, but it can be argued with, which a monthly track record cannot.
Before a track record moves money, ask four things. How many signals were there in total? Who decided which ones counted, and when? Is the current signal on a closed candle? How many observations does this market offer at this resolution at all?
If the last answer is three or four, the first three are already settled.
𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗺𝗼𝘀𝘁 𝗱𝗮𝗻𝗴𝗲𝗿𝗼𝘂𝘀 𝗻𝘂𝗺𝗯𝗲𝗿 𝗶𝗻 𝗮 𝘁𝗿𝗮𝗰𝗸 𝗿𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗿𝗱 𝗶𝘀 𝗿𝗮𝗿𝗲𝗹𝘆 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝘄𝗿𝗼𝗻𝗴 𝗼𝗻𝗲. 𝗜𝘁 𝗶𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗼𝗻𝗲 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵 𝗻𝗼 𝗱𝗲𝗻𝗼𝗺𝗶𝗻𝗮𝘁𝗼𝗿.
The open question is the September close on 30 September, and whether the fourth Fisher cross survives it. Either way, it will be one more observation on a chart that has very few.

Two months after the bureau opened the Crossfire Hurricane probe in 2016—and one month after Paul Manafort resigned from the Trump campaign—agents directly pressed Deripaska on whether Manafort was acting as a backdoor Kremlin conduit. Deripaska flatly rejected the premise as "preposterous," bringing an end to the bureau's recruitment attempts.

Because he refused to cooperate, the U.S. government shifted its strategy from recruitment to retaliation. By 2018, the Trump admin's Treasury Department slapped Deripaska and his core business entities with severe economic sanctions, effectively locking him out of the global financial system.

On April 6, 2018. The U.S. Department of the Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) designated him as a Specially Designated National (SDN) alongside several other Russian oligarchs and entities in response to Moscow's ongoing malign activities and geopolitical aggression.

In September 2018, Charles McGonigal retired in good standing from his high-level position as the Special Agent in Charge of Counterintelligence for the FBI's New York Field Office.

Shortly after transferring to New York in 2017, McGonigal began an 18-month affair with Allison Guerriero, a security researcher and volunteer for a law enforcement non-profit. Her insider tip directly sparked the sprawling internal investigation that ended in his 2023 arrest.

Guerriero’s intelligence also led investigators to uncover a conspiracy where Russian oligarchs were flying their mistresses to Los Angeles to give birth to American children.

Guerreiro's father stated that his daughter passed away on August 27, 2026, at her home in Florida, but according to him, she would never have committed suicide.

Her sudden death drew significant public attention because it occurred just hours after she had posted dozens of messages on social media heavily criticizing the FBI and McGonigal.

On December 14, 2023, a New York court sentenced him to 4 years and 2 months in prison and a $40,000 fine. McGonigal pleaded guilty to conspiracy and violating U.S. sanctions by helping Russian oligarch Oleg Deripaska seek removal from a U.S. sanctions list.

In February 2024, the Washington Federal Court sentenced McGonigal to 28 months in prison, after finding him guilty of receiving $225,000 in cash from a former Albanian intelligence agent, Agron Neza, and of concealing official contacts and undeclared meetings with Albanian officials, including Prime Minister Edi Rama.

During their 18-month affair (2017–2018), McGonigal led Guerriero to believe he was divorced or actively separating from his wife. She fell deeply in love with him and even moved into a Brooklyn apartment he was renting. The relationship ended abruptly on Christmas Eve in 2018 when McGonigal confessed he was still married and had no intention of leaving his family. Guerriero was devastated and deeply hurt by the betrayal.

A few months after the breakup, fueled by anger over the personal deception, Guerriero sent what she later described as a "drunken email" to McGonigal’s boss, William Sweeney (then the Assistant Director in Charge of the FBI's New York Field Office).

While the initial outreach was sparked by emotional distress, the substance of what she reported was rooted in real, highly suspicious behavior she had witnessed during their time together.

Though her initial 2019 warnings were largely dismissed or ignored by bureau leadership at the time, the FBI's internal threat unit eventually opened a full investigation that culminated in McGonigal’s January 2023 arrest.

The conflict escalated into a criminal matter when Guerriero breached the explicit terms of the protective order filed by the McGonigal family, by deliberately contacting one of McGonigal's children. This violation resulted in her arrest by local law enforcement and forced her to spend a night incarcerated in a NJ jail.

Charles McGonigal's early career as special agent in New York gave him exposure to some storied cases. He investigated the crash of TWA Flight 800, the "illegals program" that rounded up Russian sleeper agents, and the September 11 attacks. In Washington, he ran the FBI's WikiLeaks task force that tracked down and convicted Chelsea Manning, as well as a joint CIA-FBI secret task force dedicated to hunting for Chinese moles inside US intelligence agencies.

In New York, he was beginning to establish himself on the foreign-policy luncheon circuit, appearing on panels about Russian election meddling and links between Russia's intelligence agencies and its oligarchs, like the one he stands accused of going to work for.

The number of big investigations McGonigal was involved with, combined with the lack of clarity around how far back his relationship with Deripaska might go, is part of the reason his indictment is a nightmare for the FBI. While the indictments do not allege that McGonigal was disloyal while he was still at the FBI, McGonigal's lifestyle could have made him an appealing target for FSB recruitment.

For someone with McGonigal's level of access, having an extramarital affair is not a private matter. It is exactly the kind of vulnerability that McGonigal's foreign counterparts, the people he was supposed to be working against, might pounce on and exploit.

"People having extramarital relationships are typically involved in some kind of deception," said Michael German, a former FBI special agent who is now a fellow at the Brennan Center for Justice. "The FBI polygraphs job applicants to uncover exactly that kind of personal foible in order to disqualify them from becoming the lowest-level agent in the office."

The fact that prosecutors agreed to release McGonigal on a $500,000 bond in January 2023 suggests the government doesn't think he engaged in espionage, which would make him a flight risk.

But ruling out the worst-case scenario — that McGonigal was sharing US secrets with his foreign contacts — could take months or years. And Guerriero's recollections — the bag of cash, the late nights, the mysterious friends, the free meals, the second phone — only raised more concerns about the scale of the fallout from McGonigal's double life.

McGonigal returned home to see his wife and two children once or twice a month. Georgievska-Shine remembers asking McGonigal's wife at the grocery store how he was doing. She says Pamela used the importance of her husband's New York City job to explain his long absences.

On the left, there has been speculation that McGonigal was responsible for a series of leaks that boosted Trump's chances in 2016.

There is evidence to suggest that the FBI director James Comey's preelection announcements about the Hillary Clinton email investigation were motivated, at least in part, by fears that the FBI's New York field office would step forward with more leaks if he did nothing.

And within the FBI, the New York field office is known for doing what it wants, sometimes even in defiance of orders from headquarters.

Three sources familiar with the investigation told Insider that the bureau had already been looking into McGonigal by November 2019, which is when Guerriero says she wrote an angry email to William Sweeney, McGonigal's boss. According to Guerriero, that email, which Business Insider was unable to obtain or confirm, told Sweeney to look into McGonigal's Albania work and his personal life.

To friends and neighbors, McGonigal came off as an ordinary executive-level FBI agent — a centrist Republican who drove neighborhood kids to school events in his minivan.

Perhaps McGonigal's salary from his post-FBI job as a vice president of Brookfield Properties wasn't enough to support a girlfriend and a family and have a bit left over for those Hermès ties, the author suggests.

But Brookfield Properties is a subsidiary owned by Brookfield Asset Management, the exact parent company that bailed out the Kushner family real estate firm in 2018.

Just one month after that historic Kushner $1.2 billion dollar deal closed on 666 Fifth Avenue, Charles McGonigal had retired from the FBI and was hired by Brookfield Properties in September 2018 as Senior Vice President of Global Security.

Despite Brookfield's stance that the Qatari government was blindsided, U.S. Senate Finance Committee Chairman Ron Wyden heavily criticized the arrangement. Investigators pointed out that because Qatar was the second-largest backer of the fund, foreign government money directly enabled the rescue of a top White House official’s family asset.

A spokesperson for Brookfield Properties confirmed that McGonigal had left the company in January 2022. After leaving Brookfield, he briefly worked as the global head of security for Aman Resorts before his indictment was unsealed.

On December 14, 2023 he was first sentenced by a Manhattan federal judge to 50 months (4 years and 2 months) in prison for conspiring to violate U.S. sanctions by working for Russian oligarch Oleg Deripaska. He was sentenced by a D.C. federal judge to an additional 28 months (2 years and 4 months) in prison for hiding the $225,000 cash payment from a former Albanian intelligence operative.

McGonigal remains incarcerated. He surrendered to federal authorities on February 26, 2024, to begin his sentence. He is currently serving a combined six-year and six-month prison sentence.

Bain Capital’s Private Equity Acquisition of officially completed its massive $5.3 billion buyout of the global consulting firm Guidehouse on December 14, 2023. The firm was purchased from Veritas Capital to accelerate Guidehouse’s global commercial and public sector expansion.

On December 19, 2023—just days after the other mid-December deals—global investment firm The Carlyle Group teamed up with tech investor Insight Partners to acquire a majority controlling stake in Exiger.

The capital injection was structured to heavily scale Exiger's "dual-use" artificial intelligence capabilities across defense, government agencies, and Fortune 500 commercial supply chains.

Deripaska was indicted by the U.S. Department of Justice in September 2022 for conspiring to evade U.S. sanctions. The indictment unsealed criminal charges not just for using corporate proxies to maintain luxury U.S. real estate, but also for executing a scheme to fly his pregnant girlfriend to the United States so their child would be born a U.S. citizen. 

Because he remains in Russia out of reach of American law enforcement, he is functionally a federal fugitive from the U.S. justice system.

Unlike many Russian oligarchs who stayed silent, Deripaska has repeatedly broken ranks with the Kremlin over the invasion of Ukraine. Despite the friction, the Kremlin still leverages his massive wealth to bankroll its wartime economy.

As of mid-2026, Forbes estimates his net worth has leveled out at $4.1 billion—a steep drop from his pre-sanctions peak, but still keeping him highly influential within the restricted confines of Russia's wartime economy.

Today, the FBI treats Deripaska strictly as a criminal target. After the Department of Justice indicted him in September 2022 for sanctions evasion, any remaining backchannels were severed.

While the FBI first noticed suspicious foreign contacts in 2018, McGonigal did not actually agree to perform the illegal, paid investigative work for Deripaska until 2021. The bureau had to wait for him to actively commit the crimes—violating U.S. sanctions and laundering money—before they could indict him.

The public-facing part of the operation finally began in November 2021, when FBI agents executed a secret search warrant and raided McGonigal and his associate. Agents seized their electronic devices and smartphones.

The analysis proved McGonigal was utilizing his FBI training to evade tracking. He and his co-conspirators systematically avoided using Oleg Deripaska’s actual name in any electronic communications, instead utilizing pre-arranged aliases, code names, and draft-folder message swapping.

Interestingly, back on August 2, 2016, Paul Manafort held a secret meeting with Konstantin Kilimnik (a Russian intelligence asset tied to Oleg Deripaska). The location they chose to meet and pass the campaign's internal polling data was the Grand Havana Room—located inside 666 Fifth Avenue, the flagship building owned at the time by Jared Kushner's family.

Manafort did not resign from the Trump campaign until August 19, 2016—roughly two and a half weeks after the meeting. He stepped down following public reporting that revealed millions of dollars in off-the-books cash payments earmarked for him in Ukraine's pro-Russian "black ledger."

For years while operating in Kyiv, Kilimnik was an informational contact who regularly spoke with U.S. diplomats and State Department officials to provide political gossip and insights into Ukrainian oligarchs. However, U.S. agencies treated him as a political operative playing multiple sides rather than a vetted, trusted intelligence informant.

Special Counsel Robert Mueller indicted him in 2018 for conspiracy to obstruct justice and witness tampering alongside Manafort.

The FBI maintains a Counterintelligence Wanted Notice for him and continues to offer a $250,000 reward for information that leads to his arrest.

According to court records, between February and April 2018, Kilimnik and Manafort repeatedly used encrypted messaging apps (like WhatsApp) to contact two former political consultants. Kilimnik attempted to influence their testimony and convince them to lie to investigators about the nature of their secret, multi-million dollar European lobbying operations.

Because Kilimnik and Manafort attempted to tamper with witnesses while Manafort was out on bail, a federal judge immediately revoked Manafort's release and ordered him straight to jail to await trial.

Interestingly, both Oleg Deripaska and Vladimir Potanin are heavily involved in funding and developing dual-use AI and military drone technology.

Deripaska, alongside state lender VTB Bank, heavily bankrolls a highly restricted, cutting-edge AI research ecosystem at Moscow State University (MSU). The program features joint laboratories in Shenzhen, China, built to fast-track autonomous drone technology and navigate strict Western electronics blockades.

Despite international sanctions, Deripaska's funds helped build the advanced "MGU-270" supercomputer used by the hub. The system runs on high-end Nvidia graphics processors smuggled into Russia via gray-market Chinese shell companies to train domestic military neural networks.

Potanin, the mining magnate whose assets Charles McGonigal was secretly hired to investigate, is funding highly experimental, sci-fi-adjacent drone technology.

Through his corporate investment vehicle, the Interros Group, Potanin funded an advanced venture capital fund called Voskhod. Voskhod poured millions into a Russian neurotechnology firm called Neiry.

In early 2026, Neiry commenced real-world field trials of what they call "bio-drones"—live homing pigeons and birds fitted with surgically implanted neural interfaces and back-mounted solar panels. The neural implants allow an operator, paired with an AI script, to artificially nudge the birds' brains and guide them down preset flight paths.

The Russian military views this as a breakthrough way to conduct surveillance and carry payloads using biological carriers that traditional radar and electronic anti-drone jamming cannot detect. 

With Western chip enforcement tightening, Russia’s state banks and oligarch-backed networks are officially migrating their infrastructure to Chinese tech. State-run VTB Bank (Tikhonova’s primary financial partner) began systematically swapping out Western hardware for Huawei graphics processing units (GPUs).

Because MSU established a joint tech campus and physical laboratory in Shenzhen, China, this direct corridor allows Russian military programmers to work face-to-face with Chinese technicians to refine drone navigation, cargo delivery automation, and electronic anti-jamming tech away from Western eyes.
