# PROJECT: "UNFINISHED" (未完) — The Unfinished Ronin
A 90-second, fast-paced, cinematic sumi-e ink film rendered in code, third-person camera

## MISSION
Build a 90-second film in which every frame looks like a living Japanese ink painting,
painted as we watch, following one character, the Ronin, through a violent cold open,
a desperate chase, a duel with his perfect opposite, and a profound ending.

The film must succeed on four levels at once:
1. ACTION: fights as thrilling, readable and brutal as the best animated sword duels ever
   made. Fast, rhythmic, no wasted seconds.
2. ANIMATION: character motion at the level of a top feature animation studio. Weight,
   arcs, timing, anticipation, follow-through. Not one foot slides, not one frame jitters.
3. ART: every paused frame must look like a genuine sumi-e painting on real washi, with
   vermilion accents, not a shader or filter.
4. MEANING: a viewer with no words or explanation must understand the story and feel its
   theme by the final frame.

Judge every decision against one question: "Would a master sumi-e painter, a lead
animator at a top studio, and a great action director all pause the frame and nod?"

This is incredibly ambitious on purpose. You will work autonomously across many
iterations and sessions. You will not stop when it "looks decent." You stop only when
the exit criteria at the bottom are met and proven with captured frames.

## THEME (every shot must serve this)
To be unfinished is to be alive. Completion is stillness; stillness is death. No one
finishes you. You pick up the brush yourself.
- Mujō (impermanence): the painted world fades behind the Ronin. Nothing lasts, and that
  is what makes it beautiful.
- Ma (meaningful emptiness): blank paper is possibility, not nothing. The final image is
  mostly empty paper, and it must feel hopeful.
- Perfection vs. life: the Finished One's flawless strokes are beautiful but dead. The
  Ronin's rough, splattering strokes are imperfect but alive.

## HARD RULES
1. 100% original characters, story and designs. Nothing recognizable from existing films,
   games or anime.
2. All geometry, textures and animation are authored or generated in code. No downloaded
   models, textures or motion capture.
3. No dialogue, no voice. At most three pieces of on-screen calligraphy.
4. Palette: ink blacks and greys on washi, plus VERMILION (shu-iro, about #C8322B) used
   only as specified in the RED INK section. Every red mark must mean something.
5. No gore. Enemies are made of ink. Wounds on the Ronin reveal blank paper.
6. Never claim something looks or moves well without captured frames proving it.
7. Never delete or simplify a working system to "fix" a bug. Fix the cause.
8. Fully deterministic: fixed timestep, seeded randomness, so every frame renders
   identically every time. Review depends on this.
9. Maintain PROGRESS.md, STORY.md and ANIMATION.md at all times. A fresh session must be
   able to resume cold from them.

## THE CHARACTERS

### The Ronin (protagonist)
Lean, tired, deadly. Moves like a real swordsman: economical, grounded, explosive.
- Wide straw kasa hat, cracked along one edge, with frayed ties that react to every
  movement and gust.
- Tattered haori over kimono, loose hakama that flare and snap in motion, straw sandals,
  one katana with a worn wrapped hilt.
- A single faded RED THREAD tied around the hat cord: the only color the painter gave him.
  A hint that he was loved, never explained.
- His FACE IS BLANK PAPER. Under the hat, only the faint suggestion of a jaw line.
- His LEFT ARM IS UNFINISHED: faint grey underdrawing, loose sketch lines, construction
  circles. It works like a real arm but is visibly incomplete.
- His sword is always the darkest mark in the frame: scorched ink, glossy near-black.
- Brushwork: wild, fast, expressive. His strokes splatter, break into dry brush and bleed.

### The Finished One — Kanzen (完全, "perfect / complete")
The painter's masterpiece. Not a villain: a tragic figure who believes completion is
peace.
- Ornate samurai armor, every lacing and plate painted with flawless precision.
- A fully painted, serene face. His eyes never blink.
- A vermilion seal stamped on his chest plate. He carries a vermilion seal stone.
- Brushwork: perfect, even, controlled strokes with crisp edges. No splatter, no dry brush.
- Motion: absolute stillness, then instant perfect movement, then stillness again. Like a
  statue that only moves to strike. Rain does not touch him.

### The Blots
The painter's rejected drafts: splattered mistakes, crossed-out half-warriors with
strike-through lines across their bodies, smudged limbs. They crawl out of blank paper.
Their motion is deliberately wrong: jerky, scribbled, on uneven frame timing. When cut
they burst into splatter that bleeds into the paper.

### The Brush (the unseen painter)
A giant brush tip descending from above the frame, painting the world just ahead of the
Ronin. We never see the hand or the painter. Its strokes are confident early, then grow
thin and shaky as the film goes on: the painter is failing.

## RED INK — the color has its own story arc
Vermilion begins as the color of stillness and ends as the color of life. Keep it rare:
no more than about 8% of any frame, except the climax burst.
1. COLD OPEN: a pale red sun disc behind the bridge, softly bleeding into wet paper.
   Beautiful, and quietly ominous.
2. THROUGHOUT: the faded red thread on the Ronin's hat cord, catching the eye in motion.
3. THE VILLAGE: every frozen villager bears a small vermilion seal. Red = finished = still.
4. KANZEN: his chest seal and seal stone, the most saturated red so far.
5. THE DUEL: the seal stone grazes the Ronin's sleeve, leaving a vermilion smear on him.
   Completion is trying to claim him.
6. THE FINAL STROKE: as the Ronin swings the fallen brush, it drags through the smear on
   his sleeve and loads with vermilion. The final stroke is black ink with a living red
   core: the only stroke in the film that is both.
7. THE RELEASE: when the seals crack, they burst into vermilion ink that falls across the
   village as red PLUM BLOSSOMS (a classic sumi-e subject, painted with single red dots
   and fine black stamens). Red transforms from seals into blossoms: from stillness to life.
8. THE ENDING: one red blossom drifts onto the Ronin's hat, beside the red thread. The seal
   corner of the scroll stays empty.

Red ink behaves differently from black: cinnabar is more opaque, slightly granular, sits
on top of black ink rather than mixing, and bleeds less. Simulate that difference.

## STORY AND SHOT LIST — 90 seconds, fast-paced
Pacing target: average shot length about 2 seconds during action, with deliberate longer
holds (3–5s) for the three emotional beats. The contrast is what makes both work.
Build a rhythm map: tension rises in waves, each wave ending in a bigger hit.

### COLD OPEN — "The Stroke" (0–15s) — must hook in the first 1.5 seconds
0.0–1.5s: Pure white washi. The sound of a brush dipping into ink. Then a single violent
  horizontal black stroke rips across the frame with a sharp swish. It is a sword cut.
1.5–3.5s: Whip-pull back into third-person over the Ronin's shoulder. He's mid-battle in
  heavy rain on a narrow wooden bridge over a void of blank paper. A pale red sun bleeds
  behind him. Twelve Blots swarm from both ends.
3.5–11.0s: One continuous third-person combat take (hidden cuts allowed on whip pans):
  - He ducks a lunging Blot, cuts it in half on the way up. Splatter.
  - Spins, two-cut combination through two more. Hakama snaps with the spin.
  - A Blot grabs his sketched left arm; he kicks it off the bridge into blank paper.
  - Slides under a leaping pair, cuts both mid-air. Slow-motion splatter for 12 frames,
    then back to full speed.
  - The bridge behind him is fading into blank paper, and the Blots keep crawling out of
    that blankness. He is fighting AND running out of world.
11.0–13.0s: The last Blot leaps at him. He draws low and cuts upward in a single iai
  stroke. Hit-stop, then one inverted "negative" impact frame (white ink on black), then
  back. The splatter hangs in the air.
13.0–15.0s: The hanging splatter drifts, bleeds and resolves into 未完, with "UNFINISHED"
  in small grey type beneath. He flicks the ink off his blade (chiburi) and sheathes it
  slowly (nōtō). Click. One beat of silence.

### ACT I — "The Chase" (15–35s)
15–22s: The bridge fades out from under him and he runs. Third-person trailing shot, low
  and fast. Ahead, the Brush paints a bamboo forest in rapid strokes just before he
  reaches it; behind him, the world fades, and the Blots pour out of the blankness in
  pursuit. He is racing the brush.
22–25s: Two Blots burst out of the mist ahead. Two cuts, 1.5 seconds, without breaking
  stride. The camera whips around him in a half orbit and back to trailing.
25–29s: EMOTIONAL BEAT 1 (hold). He skids to a stop at a still pool. The pursuit sound
  drops away. His reflection shows only the hat and blank paper where a face should be.
  He lifts his sketched left hand and looks at it. Rain drops ripple the reflection.
29–35s: A village in mist. Its people are fully painted and frozen mid-motion: a child
  mid-laugh, a woman pouring tea with the stream suspended in the air, a merchant mid-bow.
  Each bears a vermilion seal. He walks between them. Only rain. The camera weaves slowly
  through the frozen figures. Hard cut to:

### ACT II — "The Finished One" (35–65s)
35–39s: EMOTIONAL BEAT 2 (hold). A courtyard. Kanzen stands perfectly still, rain
  not touching him. Kanzen raises the seal stone and holds it out: an offer. "Let me
  finish you, and you will never fade." The Ronin looks at his sketched hand. Then he
  slowly draws his sword. Refusal.

THE DUEL (39–65s). Two brushwork styles colliding. Real kenjutsu throughout: distance,
timing, feints, blade binds, sliding footwork. Choreograph every move in ANIMATION.md.
39–43s: EXCHANGE 1. Kanzen strikes first: an instant perfect stroke appears in the air.
  The Ronin barely parries. Black ink flecks fly from the blade contact like sparks. He is
  driven back, sandals skidding across wet stone.
43–49s: EXCHANGE 2. The Ronin attacks: a five-cut flurry, wild, splattering, dry-brush
  trails across the frame. Kanzen deflects each one with minimal movement and returns to
  stillness between blocks. The fifth deflection spins the Ronin around.
49–53s: EXCHANGE 3. Kanzen's counter: one horizontal cut across the Ronin's chest.
  Hit-stop, negative frame. The wound reveals blank paper, and its edges begin to creep
  outward. He is being erased.
53–58s: EXCHANGE 4. Kanzen lunges with the seal stone at his heart. The Ronin deflects it
  with his sketched arm; the stone grazes his sleeve and leaves a vermilion smear. The
  force throws him across the courtyard into a pool of ink. He rises to one knee.
58–65s: Above, the Brush falters. Its strokes go thin and shaky, then stop. The world
  begins to fade everywhere at once: the walls, the village, even Kanzen's edges. Kanzen
  raises the seal for the final strike. Above them, the Brush slips.

### ACT III — "The Brush" (65–80s)
65–68s: The Brush falls in slow motion, spinning, flinging droplets. It lands and rolls
  to the Ronin's sketched left hand.
68–71s: EMOTIONAL BEAT 3 (hold). He grips it. As his fingers close, the underdrawing of
  his hand darkens into real ink for the first time, from fingertips up to the shoulder.
71–75s: Kanzen strikes with the seal. The Ronin rises and swings the brush; it drags
  through the vermilion smear on his sleeve and loads with red. He paints one enormous
  stroke across the whole frame: an ensō-like arc of black ink with a living red core. It
  meets the seal. The seal cracks.
75–80s: Kanzen does not die. His perfect strokes soften and bleed. For the first time,
  his painted eyes blink. His face shows relief. He dissolves into a soft grey wash, free.
  Across the village, every seal cracks and bursts into vermilion ink that falls as red
  plum blossoms. The tea finally pours. The child finishes laughing.

### EPILOGUE — "Ma" (80–90s)
80–85s: Third-person trailing shot, the reverse of Act I: the Ronin walks into blank
  paper, and HE paints the world ahead with the brush, trailing ink. His face is still
  blank. A single red blossom drifts down and settles on his hat beside the red thread.
85–88s: The camera rises and pulls back, higher and higher, revealing the whole film as
  one long painted scroll, the Ronin a tiny figure at its unfinished edge.
88–90s: The seal corner of the scroll stays empty. A faint grey 未完 appears there. Fade
  to white paper. Rain, then silence.

## THIRD-PERSON CAMERA LANGUAGE
Shot like the most cinematic third-person action games, reinterpreted as painting:
- DEFAULT: follow cam 3–4 m behind, slightly above, over the right shoulder, 35mm.
  Spring-damped lag so it feels operated, never locked. Subtle procedural handheld drift.
- COMBAT: widens to 24–28mm, orbits to keep the Ronin and the current threat both framed,
  and drifts toward incoming attacks a beat early so the viewer reads them.
- WHIP PANS: used to cut between attackers, painted as streaks of dry-brush motion blur.
- IMPACT: 2–4 frame hit-stop, camera kick along the strike direction, and on the four
  biggest hits only, a single inverted negative frame.
- SLOW MOTION: ramped smoothly, never abrupt, used only for splatter, the falling brush,
  and the final stroke.
- EMOTIONAL BEATS: the camera stops following and holds. Lens lengthens to 85–135mm.
  Stillness in the camera means something is important.
- Composition follows sumi-e: asymmetry, generous empty space, the Ronin often small in a
  large field of paper. Action must read even as a tiny thumbnail.

## ANIMATION STANDARD
Every frame of character motion must meet feature-animation quality:
- The 12 principles, applied with discipline: anticipation before every strike, follow-
  through and overlap after, slow-in and slow-out, clean arcs, strong staging, weight.
- Real swordwork: correct stances (chūdan, hassō, waki-gamae), sliding footwork
  (suri-ashi), cuts driven from the hips, the draw cut, chiburi and nōtō.
- Weight: every step transfers weight through the hips; landings compress the knees;
  heavy hits push the body back.
- Secondary motion: hakama, haori sleeves, hat ties and the red thread lag and settle
  with convincing cloth dynamics.
- Breathing whenever the Ronin is still: a subtle rise and fall of the shoulders.
- Contrast of motion styles is storytelling: the Ronin is fluid and alive; Kanzen is
  stillness broken by instant perfect motion; the Blots move on uneven, scribbled timing.
- Key poses must read as pure black silhouettes. If a pose doesn't read as a silhouette,
  it doesn't work.

## INK REALISM — real ink on real paper
The target is not photorealism. It is ink that a master would believe was painted by
hand. Every effect below is simulated, not faked with a filter.

### Paper
- Procedural washi: long visible kozo fibers, subtle thickness variation, a warm
  off-white tone, faint tooth visible under thin washes.
- The paper is the canvas, fixed to the screen like a real sheet. Intentional.
- Ink diffuses along fiber direction (anisotropic).

### Ink behavior
- Five tones of black: scorched (glossy near-black), dark, heavy, light, clear. Tone
  expresses depth: foreground dark and sharp, background pale and soft.
- Nijimi: wet ink bleeding into paper with feathered edges that keep spreading briefly
  after a stroke lands (GPU diffusion on a wetness field).
- Edge darkening as washes dry: pigment migrates to the rim.
- Kasure (dry brush): bristles separate when ink runs low or the stroke is fast.
- Bokashi: smooth graded washes for mist, sky and distance.
- Granulation: fine pigment speckle in pale washes.
- Pooling where strokes start or pause, tapered lift where they end.
- Splatter with main drops and satellite droplets, each bleeding where it lands.
- Drying: fresh ink has a faint wet sheen that dulls over a few seconds.
- Vermilion behaves as described in the RED INK section.

### Brush strokes
- Every line is a real brush stroke: pressure along its length, bristle texture, ink
  load that decreases along the stroke (long strokes end in dry brush), speed affecting
  width and dryness.
- Stroke anatomy: pressed entry, confident body, tapered exit.
- Linework is derived from 3D geometry (silhouettes, creases, contours) chained into
  brush strokes anchored to the objects so they never swim. Controlled "boil" on
  linework at 12 fps for a hand-painted feel; everything else at full frame rate.
- Interior form uses washes, not outlines: lighting is converted to ink tones.

### Painting-in and fading
- The Brush paints the world in a real painter's order: main structural strokes first,
  then secondary strokes, then detail touches and dots.
- Fading is not a crossfade: ink lightens, loses its edges, sinks into the paper fibers
  until only a faint ghost remains, then nothing.

### Weather and atmosphere
- Rain as fine, fast, pale dry strokes, denser in front, with some drops bleeding where
  they hit painted surfaces.
- Mist as layered pale washes with parallax.
- Wind moves bamboo, hat ties, sleeves, hakama and the red thread.

## SOUND
Procedural Web Audio, fast and punchy in action, with silence used as an instrument.
- Brush: dipping, dragging on paper, bristles lifting. Every painted stroke has a sound.
- Sword: cut swishes, sharp metallic rings on contact, the sheath click. Every blade
  contact must land on the exact frame of contact.
- Blots: wet, smeary, scratchy sounds.
- Rain, wind through bamboo, distant thunder.
- Music: taiko-like drums driving the cold open, chase and duel; a breathy flute tone for
  the three emotional beats; one low sustained tone when the brush falls; drums drop out
  completely at the final stroke, leaving only the sound of the brush.
- First sound of the film: a brush dipping into ink. Last sound: rain fading to silence.

## TECH STACK
- Three.js (latest), WebGPU renderer with WebGL2 fallback. Vite dev server.
- Custom sumi-e NPR pipeline:
  1. G-buffer: depth, normals, object IDs, lighting, surface-direction field.
  2. Line pass: silhouettes, creases and contours chained into polylines and rendered with
     the stroke model.
  3. Wash pass: lighting converted into the five ink tones, painted as wet washes.
  4. Ink simulation: GPU wetness and pigment diffusion on the paper (nijimi, edge
     darkening, granulation, drying), with separate behavior for vermilion.
  5. Paint-in and fade system driven by the Brush and time.
  6. Composite on procedural washi.
- Characters built procedurally in code on skinned skeletons, animated with hand-authored
  keyframes, procedural IK for foot planting, and cloth simulation.
- Two render modes:
  - REAL-TIME: 30+ fps at 1080p for interactive playback and scrubbing.
  - FILM MODE: renders frame by frame at maximum quality (more simulation steps,
    supersampling, full-resolution diffusion) at 1080p or 4K, 24 fps, then encodes to MP4
    with ffmpeg. This is the final deliverable.
- Headless, deterministic capture via Playwright.
- lil-gui debug panel with toggles for every pass, and a timeline scrubber.

## FILE STRUCTURE
/src/characters/  ronin, kanzen, blots, brush
/src/anim/        skeleton, IK, cloth, choreography, timeline
/src/world/       bridge, bamboo, pool, village, courtyard, scroll
/src/ink/         stroke model, line extraction, washes, diffusion, vermilion, paint-in, fade
/src/paper/       washi generation
/src/camera/      follow cam, combat cam, whip pans, hit-stop, impact frames, shot list
/src/audio/
/tools/capture.ts      frames, sequences, contact sheets, onion skins, silhouettes
/tools/anim-checks.ts  automated animation quality checks
/tools/checks.ts       performance, console errors, determinism, timeline integrity
/tools/render-film.ts  film mode export to MP4
/review/               captured material per iteration
PROGRESS.md
STORY.md       every beat: what the viewer sees, hears and should feel
ANIMATION.md   move-by-move choreography, key poses, timing charts per shot

## PRODUCTION PIPELINE (in order; do not skip ahead)
(A) INK LAB: stroke model, washes, diffusion, vermilion, paper. Paint test sheets (a
    bamboo stalk, a stone, a splatter, a plum branch with red blossoms) until single
    frames look genuinely hand-painted. Everything depends on this.
(B) ANIMATIC: the entire 90 seconds with grey block characters, final cameras, final
    timing and temp sound. Lock pacing here. It must already be exciting as grey boxes.
(C) BLOCKING: key poses for every shot, stepped (no interpolation), checked as
    silhouettes.
(D) SPLINE: interpolated motion, arcs cleaned, timing refined.
(E) POLISH: overlap, cloth, breathing, micro-motion, contact frames, hit-stops.
(F) INK RENDER: full sumi-e pipeline applied to the finished animation, shot by shot,
    starting with the cold open.
(G) RED, SOUND AND FINISHING: vermilion arc, full sound design, final pacing.
(H) FILM MODE EXPORT: final MP4.

## THE PERFECTION LOOP
Every iteration, without exception:

1. BUILD: implement the next highest-priority item from PROGRESS.md.

2. CAPTURE (deterministic): for every shot you touched, render
   - a frame-by-frame sequence of the shot,
   - a contact sheet (every 3rd frame),
   - onion skins: 8 consecutive frames overlaid, to judge spacing and arcs,
   - arc traces: the paths of the sword tip, both wrists, hips and head drawn over the
     shot, to check they are clean curves,
   - silhouette renders of every key pose (solid black on white),
   - one full-resolution "gallery still."
   Also, every iteration, render one middle frame of every shot in the film, in order,
   as a storyboard strip. Save everything to /review/iter_NNN/.

3. AUTOMATED CHECKS (tools/anim-checks.ts): report and fail the iteration on
   - foot sliding: a planted foot moving more than 2 mm per frame,
   - joint limits exceeded,
   - interpenetration: blade through body, limbs through limbs, cloth through body,
   - jitter: acceleration spikes in any joint or camera between consecutive frames,
   - popping: sudden pose changes not motivated by a cut or hit-stop,
   - sync: every blade contact aligned with its sound and hit-stop to the exact frame,
   - pacing: shot lengths vs. the targets in STORY.md.

4. CRITIQUE: actually look at every captured image. Score 1–10:
   a. Animation (weighted double): weight, arcs, timing, anticipation, follow-through,
      silhouette clarity, real swordwork.
   b. Ink authenticity (weighted double): would a sumi-e master believe a human painted
      it? Bleeding, dry brush, tone, stroke anatomy, paper.
   c. Action and pacing: clarity, impact, rhythm, no wasted seconds, holds that land.
   d. Third-person camera: operated, cinematic, purposeful, action always readable.
   e. Composition: asymmetry, empty space, focal clarity, thumbnail readability.
   f. Red ink: every red mark meaningful, the arc from stillness to life clear.
   g. Story clarity: could someone with no explanation describe what just happened?
   h. Emotional impact: does the moment make you feel what STORY.md says it should?
   i. Gut check: "Painting or shader?" and "Animated by a master or by a program?"
      Write one sentence each on the single biggest tell.

5. LOG: append to PROGRESS.md the iteration number, all scores, check results, the two
   biggest tells, the weakest moment in the film so far (timestamp and why), what
   changed, performance, and a ranked list of the next 3 fixes.

6. FIX: failed automated checks first. Then the lowest-scoring category, at its root
   cause. Then go back to step 1.

Self-critique rules:
- Common tells of fake ink: uniform line width, untapered lines, edges too clean, flat
  washes, no paper showing through thin ink, splatter without satellites, strokes
  swimming, everything the same darkness, red that looks like a digital overlay.
- Common tells of weak animation: floaty motion with no weight, even spacing (no easing),
  broken arcs, poses that don't read as silhouettes, everything moving at once with no
  overlap, sword hits without impact, idle characters frozen instead of breathing.
- Every 5 iterations, do a FRESH EYES pass: view the storyboard strip in order as if
  seeing it for the first time, and write what the story seems to be about and where
  attention drifts. If it doesn't match the THEME, fix the story before the visuals.
- Every 5 iterations, do a PACING pass: list every shot with its length and energy level
  (1–10), and check the rhythm map rises in waves with contrast between action and holds.
- If a score stalls for 3 iterations, change the approach, not the parameters.
- Every moment must earn its place. Cut or rework anything that doesn't serve the action,
  the art or the meaning.

text:
I had my first interview in nine years last week, and it went exactly how you would expect: pretty shit (my words not theirs) 😅

Being in the interview is a whole different type of experience and pressure compared to being in front of clients and pitching.

Over the last nine years of being a solo founder, I've done the hiring.

I was in charge of creating the talent pipeline, hiring systems and processes, the questions, and how the team structured hiring at @EconsDesign when I was Head of Remote.

To be on the other side of the table, having to be interviewed, was a whole different experience.

There's a quote by @naval: “A taste of freedom can make you unemployable.” That's sat with me for many years.

I would only interview or consider working with a business because I see the potential of the team and the business.

Being a solo founder is a lonely experience. You can learn a huge amount in a short period of time. I’ve worn ALL the hats you can possibly imagine, but being surrounded by a team and working in a team is something that I have missed for some time - and I don’t just mean me and my 7 Claude agents…

So I'm exploring opportunities around:

- AI engineering
- Forward-deployed engineering
- Forward-deployed strategy
- AI consulting

I'm looking at positions in businesses and teams that are working at the forefront of the AI space.

It's been three months now since I came back to London after spending five years in Thailand. What I’ve seen is a huge amount of energy, forward motion, and incredible, smart, talented people.

I would love to be surrounded by more of them to learn more, and also to offer my skills, expertise and experience. Working at the forefront of AI, making sure businesses can get the most out of AI, making sure humans are cared for, thought about, and taken on the journey as well.

I also bring the rich, diverse experience of being an emerging tech founder for the last nine years.

I bring systems thinking, an understanding of humans, and hands-on AI engineering experience, with the ability to be thrown in front of clients and sit with c-suites to simplify complex technology and turn messy business problems into systems people can actually use.

Before that, 12 years in wealth management, asset management and fintech, so I understand enterprise, startups and everything in between.

So yeah, as much as the interview was a slightly scary experience, and my expectations of my own performance are very high, I'm proud of myself for putting myself out there, sans the perceived founder ego.

If you’re hiring for AI engineering, forward-deployed engineering, forward-deployed strategy, or AI consulting roles - remote, London, SF or New York, I’d love to hear from you.

AND if your business is looking for someone to help with your messy workflows, turn them into AI-enabled systems and upgrade your humans, drop a comment or DM me.

Oh and a like or comment goes a long way for reach 🫶🏽

One of the things I built that I didn't cover in my last OpenClaw video was a support chatbot for my website. I provide it with my content posting history, posted tech tips, and info on the products I offer. People can ask it questions and get instant responses with links.

I have 15+ DM inboxes between all socials, plus email, plus Discord, plus Slack. Impossible to manage them all. Sometimes people have quick questions or need to find something. If I posted about it, the bot can find it. And if it can't, you can opt to send me an email.

It's not meant to replace me. It's meant to fill a gap I'm incapable of filling and helping people get to what they're looking for, faster.

Pro-Ukraine narrative says Ukraine needs advanced AI to find and fix vulnerabilities as Russian cyberattacks hammer hospitals, energy systems and telecommunications. Defending civilian infrastructure keeps essential services running and gives the entirety of the continent a stronger cyber shield through technology already offered to numerous European nations.

Pro-Russia narrative says more Western AI support for Ukraine is reckless escalation, turning the conflict into a live testing ground for integrated cyberwarfare and autonomous combat. Expanding Kyiv's high-tech arsenal raises the danger to civilian infrastructure and transport, leaving Moscow no choice but to attack the Ukrainian data centers that enable such a threat.

text:
CompuServe Was the Future Once. I Had an Account.

I used CompuServe, so I've been at this a while. Its consumer service launched on September 24, 1979. Getting online took a modem, a phone line and patience, and hourly charges

The company started in 1969 as the computing arm of Golden United Life Insurance in Ohio. It rented time on shared computers so expensive machines could serve many customers instead of sitting idle.

Connecting those customers took real engineering. CompuServe linked its central computers to remote users over phone lines and built its own network hardware and software along the way. Multiplexers let several users share one line, which carried the service well beyond Ohio.

Engineers including Sandy Trevor, Doug Chinnock and John Goltz designed a network that routed data between nodes without a central computer handling every decision. That let the service add users and spread the load

The hardware was cramped and homegrown. One employee remembered computers packed so tightly that cabinet doors had to come off for repairs. Jim Ward called Goltz's network plans dreaming, then joined the company three years later.

Home users dialed in at 300 baud for email, forums and file downloads. People gathered around shared interests and built reputations by helping each other.

A loyal community couldn't save CompuServe from changing expectations. AOL offered an easier interface, heavy marketing and unlimited use for a flat monthly fee. CompuServe was late to flat-rate pricing, and the open web gave customers more places to go. Its consumer business went to AOL in 1998. The name survived, the influence faded. A few years later broadband arrived and AOL went through the same thing.

Customers can value what you built and still leave when someone offers something easier or cheaper.

AI assistants may do this to consumer services next. If people use them to research purchases or book travel, they visit fewer websites. Publishers, search companies and retailers have a lot at stake when someone else controls the recommendation.

I'll still want access to people with firsthand experience. Useful tools and trusted communities can earn my time, especially if they respect my data and keep their charges clear.

CompuServe helped build an online world that outgrew it.

Having used it myself, I get wary whenever someone calls a tech company's lead permanent.

Illusion of Partnership — Why Mahmoud Abbas Cannot Be Trusted and Why a Sovereign “Palestinian” State Threatens Middle Eastern Security

Saturday, September 26, 2026
Dr. Joel P. Rutkowski
Policy Analysis

Executive Summary

In his September 24, 2026 address (https://t.co/cyW3QLaDzu) to the 81st  United Nations General Assembly, “Palestinian” Authority (PA) President Mahmoud Abbas presented a polished narrative of reform, moderation, and a commitment to a "non-militarized Palestinian state." However, a rigorous examination of historical precedents, structural institutional failures, and ongoing incitement reveals a profound disconnect between PA rhetoric and operational reality.

Under a framework of conservative principles—emphasizing realism, verifiable security guarantees, sovereign self-defense, and strict accountability—this policy paper argues that Mahmoud Abbas is fundamentally untrustworthy as a peace partner. Furthermore, the hasty creation of an independent “Palestinian” state under current conditions is directly contrary to the vital national security interests of Israel, the United States, and European allies.

Extensive Literature Review: The Evolution of the PA Paradox (1980–2026)

Scholarship and diplomatic record regarding the Israeli- “Palestinian” conflict over the past four decades divide into three critical periods:

1980–1993 (From Armed Struggle to the Oslo Framework): Literature from this era documents the Palestine Liberation Organization-PLO’s transition from recognized transnational terrorism to diplomatic engagement. However, historical declassifications and internal “Palestinian” documents confirm that the Oslo Accords were viewed by the leadership not as an end to conflict, but as a tactical step—the "phased strategy"—toward Israel's eventual dismantling.

1993–2010 (The Second Intifada and Institutional Duplicity): The collapse of the Camp David Summit in 2000 and the ensuing bloody violence of the Second Intifada demonstrated that the PA leadership, including Arafat and subsequently Abbas, retained militant networks (such as the Tanzim and Al-Aqsa Martyrs' Brigades) while paying lip service to counter-terrorism. Academic reviews highlight the failure of institution-building, characterized by rampant corruption and a failure to cultivate genuine democratic governance.

2010–2026 (The "Pay-to-Slay" Era and International Delusion): Modern policy literature heavily scrutinizes the PA's legal frameworks, notably the continued operation of the Martyrs' Fund (paying stipends to terrorists and their families), systemic antisemitism in state-sanctioned educational curricula, and the indefinite postponement of democratic elections. Scholarship post-2020 emphasizes that the PA has devolved into a sclerotic, autocratic entity that survives solely on international aid and security coordination with Israel—coordination it weaponizes politically.

Why Mahmoud Abbas Cannot Be Trusted

Mahmoud Abbas has spent over two decades leading the “Palestinian” Authority while maintaining a posture of diplomatic moderation abroad and radical incitement at home. Trust must be built on verifiable actions, yet Abbas's tenure is defined by systemic contradictions:

The "Pay-to-Slay" Institutionalized Incentive Structure: Despite claiming adherence to human rights and anti-corruption standards, the PA continues to allocate hundreds of millions of dollars annually to reward individuals who commit acts of terror against Israelis. This structural contradiction proves that the state apparatus remains tethered to a culture of violence.

Educational Curriculum and Radicalization: PA textbooks continue to glorify "martyrdom," erase Israel from maps, and promote blatant antisemitism. An educational system designed to foster hatred cannot simultaneously produce a populace ready for peaceful coexistence.

The Democratic Deficit: Abbas is currently serving in the 21st  year of a four-year presidential term, having repeatedly canceled scheduled elections whenever internal polling suggested a loss to Hamas or radical Islamist factions. His hollow promises of upcoming elections are transparent maneuvers to appease Western donors rather than genuine democratic reforms.

Diplomatic Warfare and Lawfare: While Abbas spoke of peace at the UNGA, the PA simultaneously pursues aggressive diplomatic warfare against Israel in the International Criminal Court and the International Court of Justice, seeking to criminalize Israel's sovereign right to self-defense while escaping its own obligations under the Oslo Accords.

Why a “Palestinian” State is Against U.S., Israeli, and European Interests

The international push for an immediate, unconditioned two-state solution—championed by various European states and external actors—ignores the catastrophic security vacuum such a state would create:

The Gaza-West Bank Convergence Threat: As demonstrated by the horrific events of October 7, 2023, and subsequent regional conflicts, premature statehood in the Judea and Samaria (“West Bank”) would likely replicate the Gaza scenario. Without robust, verified demilitarization and absolute Israeli security control over external borders, a Judea and Samaria  state would quickly fall under the sway of Iranian-backed proxies (Hamas and “Palestinian” Islamic Jihad), placing Israeli population centers, Ben Gurion Airport, and critical infrastructure within point-blank range of rocket fire.

Destabilization of Regional Security Architecture: A radicalized, unstable “Palestinian” entity would act as an immediate destabilizing force for neighboring Jordan, threatening the Hashemite Kingdom's stability and expanding Iran's "Ring of Fire" strategy directly into the heart of the Levant.

Compromising Western Counter-Terrorism: For Europe and the United States, a poorly conceived “Palestinian” state would become a safe haven for global jihadist networks, increasing the terror threat exported to Western capitals through radicalized diaspora networks and cyber-radicalization.

Conservative Principles for a Strategic Reset

A realistic, conservative approach to Middle Eastern stability rejects utopian state-building exercises in favor of hard security guarantees and regional integration:
Sovereign Deterrence over Diplomatic Appeasement: Peace is achieved through overwhelming strength and the unyielding security dominance of free-market democracies, not through paper agreements signed by corrupt and illegitimate autocrats.

Conditionality and Financial Accountability: Not a single dollar of Western aid or withheld tax revenue should flow to the PA until the "Pay-to-Slay" policy is permanently dismantled, textbooks are scrubbed of antisemitism, and verifiable governance reforms are enacted.

Regional Normalization over Bilateral Impasse: The Abraham Accords proved that the path to regional stability bypasses stagnant “Palestinian” vetoes. Economic integration, technological partnership, and security alliances between Israel and Arab states offer a far superior architecture for Middle Eastern prosperity.

Strategic Policy Recommendations

To protect Western and Israeli security interests while managing the “Palestinian” file realistically, the incoming U.S. administration and allied governments must adopt the following roadmap:

1. Condition All Financial Transfers on Zero-Tolerance for Terror: Establish an international verification mechanism to immediately freeze all budgetary support to the PA if a single dinar is traced to terrorist stipends or anti-Israel incitement.

2. Oppose Unilateral Statehood Recognition: Issue a joint U.S.-European veto and diplomatic blockade against any UN Security Council resolutions or unilateral international declarations recognizing a “Palestinian” state outside of a finalized, negotiated, and fully verified final-status agreement.

3. Maintain Israeli Security Control (Israel Defense Forces-IDF Freedom of Operation): Formally recognize that any viable interim or long-term arrangement must guarantee the Israel Defense Forces permanent operational freedom of movement throughout the Jordan Valley and Judea and Samaria airspace to prevent terrorist safe havens.

4. Pivot to Municipal and Regional Governance Models: Abandon the insistence on top-down, centralized PA state-building. Instead, encourage localized, clan-based municipal administration and economic partnerships that bypass corrupt central authorities and focus on civic improvement rather than political warfare.

The Imperative of Strategic Realism: Synthesis of the Geopolitical Dilemma

The address delivered by “Palestinian” Authority President Mahmoud Abbas to the 81st  United Nations General Assembly on September 24, 2026, encapsulates the core pathology of modern Middle Eastern diplomacy: a stark, irreconcilable divergence between performative international moderation and domestic operational reality. For decades, international bodies have accepted the premise that statehood is a standalone panacea, assuming that formal diplomatic recognition will magically induce institutional reform, curb terrorism, and foster a culture of peaceful coexistence.

As demonstrated throughout this policy analysis, this assumption is historically bankrupt and strategically perilous. Under a framework of conservative principles—prioritizing sovereign self-defense, absolute accountability, and strict conditionality—it is evident that Mahmoud Abbas’s regime is fundamentally incapable of acting as a trustworthy peace partner. The international community’s ongoing willingness to indulge the fiction of PA governance serves only to prolong the conflict, subsidize corruption, and endanger Western and Israeli security.

Discussion: The Core Imperatives for Washington and Western Allies

A sober evaluation of the post-UNGA 2026 landscape highlights three critical takeaways for policymakers navigating the Israeli- “Palestinian” file:

The Fallacy of the Moderate Facade

Diplomacy cannot succeed when built on a foundation of systemic deceit. While Abbas utilizes international forums to speak the language of human rights, non-militarization, and democracy, the structural machinery of the “Palestinian” Authority remains tethered to radical incitement. Financial reward systems for terrorists ("Pay-to-Slay") and state-sanctioned educational curricula that cultivate antisemitism completely invalidate any verbal commitments to peace. Western policymakers must stop grading the PA on its rhetoric and begin judging it strictly by its institutional behavior.

The Dangers of Premature Statehood

In the wake of regional conflicts and the enduring fallout of the October 7, 2023 massacres, the push for an unconditioned, rushed two-state solution is not a peace initiative—it is a security hazard. Without verified demilitarization, comprehensive counter-terrorism infrastructure, and independent institutional oversight, any nascent “Palestinian” state in the Judea and Samaria risks mirroring the trajectory of Hamas-controlled Gaza. Such an entity would quickly become an Iranian-backed launching pad, threatening vital Israeli population centers, critical civil aviation corridors, and regional stability across the Hashemite Kingdom of Jordan.

The Triumph of Regional Integration over Bilateral Stagnation

The paradigm of traditional land-for-peace negotiations centered on a recalcitrant Palestinian leadership has exhausted its utility. The historic success of the Abraham Accords demonstrated that true regional stability is achieved when nations bypass the stagnant “Palestinian” veto and focus instead on mutual economic, technological, and security partnerships. Pragmatic Arab states and Israel share a common interest in neutralizing radical proxies; U.S. and European foreign policy must align fully with this reality rather than trying to resurrect a failed two-state orthodoxy.

Final Thoughts: The Path Forward

Rejecting Diplomatic Illusion

The United States and its European allies must decisively transition away from the comforting illusions of the Oslo era. Continuing to press for unilateral statehood recognitions or injecting financial aid into a corrupt, autocratic authority without stringent oversight only delays genuine resolution. International engagement must be entirely conditional upon total systemic dismantling of terror-incentivizing frameworks.

Anchoring Policy in Conservative Principles

By adhering to conservative principles of strategic realism, security dominance, and financial accountability, Washington can establish a stable deterrence architecture in the Middle East. Peace is never secured through appeasement or by rewarding governance models that celebrate violence; it is preserved through overwhelming strength, unwavering support for democratic allies, and the insistence on verifiable accountability.

Preserving Western and Sovereign Security

Ultimately, the security architecture of Israel, the United States, and Europe is indivisible. Granting statehood to an un-reformed, hostile entity sitting on the strategic ridges overlooking Israel's coastal plain would introduce an unmitigated vulnerability into the global fight against violent extremism. Rejecting the illusion of Abbas’s partnership is not an abandonment of diplomacy—it is a mandatory defense of sovereignty, security, and long-term regional prosperity.

 (b) Table of Contents.--The table of contents for this Act
is as follows:

 Sec. 1. Short title; table of contents.
 TITLE I--PROTECTIONS OF STUDENT ATHLETES AND FAIR COMPETITION

 Sec. 100. Definitions.
 Sec. 101. Name, image, and likeness protections.

 sports.

 Sec. 207. Media rights utilization requirement for college
 sports other than football and basketball.

 TITLE I--PROTECTIONS OF STUDENT ATHLETES AND FAIR
 COMPETITION

 SEC. 100. DEFINITIONS.

 In this title:
 (1) Antitrust laws.--The term ``antitrust laws''
 has the meaning given that term in the 1st section of the
 Clayton Act (15 U.S.C. 12) and includes--
 (A) section 5 of the Federal Trade
 Commission Act (15 U.S.C. 45) to the extent that such
 section 5 applies to unfair methods of competition;
 and
 (B) any similar State antitrust law,
 including a State law provision that applies to
 covering unfair methods of competition having the force
 and effect of law.
 (2) Associated entity.--The term ``associated
 entity'' means any individual or entity, including a
 collective, that is--
 (A) known, or should have been known, to
 exist for or act for the benefit of, in coordination
 with, or at the direction of an institution to promote
 or support an institution's athletics program or
 student athletes, including by creating or identifying
 name, image, and likeness compensation opportunities
 for an institution's student athletes;
 (B) an individual or entity that is or was
 a member, employee, director, officer, owner, or agent
 of an individual or entity described in subparagraph
 (A);
 (C) an individual or entity that directly
 or indirectly (including contributions by an affiliated
 entity, individual, or family member) has contributed
 more than $50,000 over their lifetime to a particular
 institution or to an individual or entity described in
 subparagraph (A);
 (D) an individual or entity that has
 directly or indirectly been directed or requested by an
 institution or third party acting on behalf of, for the
 benefit of, in coordination with, or at the direction
 of an institution to assist in the recruitment or
 retention of student athletes or prospective student
 athletes, or otherwise has assisted in the recruitment
 or retention of student athletes or prospective student
 athletes; or
 (E) an individual or entity owned,
 controlled, or operated by, or otherwise affiliated
 with the individuals or entities described in
 subparagraph (A).
 (3) Athlete agent.--The term ``athlete agent'' has
 the meaning given that term in section 2 of the Sports Agent
 Responsibility and Trust Act (15 U.S.C. 7801).
 (4) Collective.--The term ``collective''--

 (A) means a person, corporation, booster
 organization, tax-exempt organization, or other entity
 that provides donations or other support directly or
 indirectly to or for the benefit or support of--

 (i) a student athlete who is
 enrolled, or who may enroll, at an institution;
 or
 (ii) the intercollegiate athletics
 program or any booster organization of an
 institution; and
 (B) does not include--
 (i) an immediate family member of
 a student athlete; or
 (ii) an individual or entity
 that--
 (I) licenses trademark
 rights of an institution; and
 (II) does not--
 (aa) license name,
 image, and likeness rights of
 student athletes; or
 (bb) make payments
 earmarked or designated to fund
 name, image, or likeness
 licenses or other payments to
 student athletes.
 (5) Compensation.--The term ``compensation''--

 (A) means any payment, remuneration, or
 benefit provided to a student athlete or a prospective
 student athlete; and
 (B) does not include--
 (i) grants-in-aid;
 (ii) Federal Pell Grants provided
 under section 401 of the Higher Education Act
 of 1965 (20 U.S.C. 1070a) or any other Federal
 or State grants unrelated to and not awarded
 with regard to participation in intercollegiate
 sports;
 (iii) health insurance and the
 costs of health care funded by an institution,
 intercollegiate athletic association, or
 conference;
 (iv) disability and loss-of-value
 insurance, including disability and loss-of-
 value insurance funded by an institution,
 intercollegiate athletic association, or
 conference;
 (v) career counseling, job
 placement services, or other guidance available
 to all students at an institution;
 (vi) hourly wages and benefits for
 work performed outside of participating in
 intercollegiate sports at a rate commensurate
 with the prevailing rate in the relevant State
 or locality for similar work;
 (vii) enhanced education benefits,
 including academic awards;
 (viii) financial literacy or tax
 education resources; or
 (ix) any program to connect
 student athletes with employers and facilitate
 employment opportunities, if--
 (I) the financial terms of
 such employment opportunities are
 consistent with the terms offered to
 similarly situated employees who are
 not student athletes; and
 (II) such program is not
 used to induce a student athlete to
 attend a particular
 institution.
 (6) Conference.--The term ``conference'' means any
 organization that is not an intercollegiate athletic
 association and that--
 (A) has 2 or more institutions as members;
 and
 (B) arranges championships for
 intercollegiate athletic competitions or sets rules for
 intercollegiate athletic competition.
 (7) Cost of attendance.--The term ``cost of
 attendance''--
 (A) has the meaning given that term in
 section 472 of the Higher Education Act of 1965 (20
 U.S.C. 1087ll); and
 (B) shall be calculated by the financial
 aid office of an institution applying the same
 standards, policies, and procedures for all
 students.
 (8) Grant-in-aid.--The term ``grant-in-aid''
 means--
 (A) a scholarship, grant, stipend, or
 other form of financial assistance, including the
 provision of tuition, room, board, books, or funds for
 fees or personal expenses, that--
 (i) is paid or provided by an
 institution to a student for the undergraduate
 or graduate education of the student;
 and
 (ii) is in an amount that does not
 exceed the cost of attendance for such student
 at the institution; and
 (B) does not include compensation paid to
 a student athlete.
 (9) Image.--With respect to a student athlete, the
 term ``image'' means a picture, video, computer-generated
 representation, or other depiction that identifies, is linked
 to, or is reasonably linked to the student athlete.
 (10) Institution.--Except as otherwise explicitly
 provided, the term ``institution'' has the meaning given the
 term ``institution of higher education'' under section 101 of
 the Higher Education Act of 1965 (20 U.S.C. 1001).
 (11) Intercollegiate athletic association.--The
 term ``intercollegiate athletic association''--
 (A) means any organization, not-for-profit
 corporation, association, or any other group organized
 in the United States that--
 (i) sponsors or arranges
 intercollegiate athletic competition between
 institutions;
 (ii) sets common rules, standards,
 procedures, or guidelines for the
 administration of intercollegiate athletic
 competition;
 (iii) is composed of 2 or more
 institutions or conferences that are located in
 different States or participate in
 intercollegiate athletic competition in more
 than 1 State; and
 (iv) is not a
 conference;
 (B) includes--
 (i) the National Collegiate
 Athletic Association; and
 (ii) any other national
 intercollegiate athletic association;
 and
 (C) does not include a corporation,
 association, or other group affiliated with
 professional athletic competition.
 (12) Intercollegiate athletic competition.--The
 term ``intercollegiate athletic competition'' means any
 intercollegiate sport contest, game, meet, match, tournament,
 regatta, or other intercollegiate sport event in which student
 athletes or varsity sports teams compete.
 (13) Intercollegiate sport.--The term
 ``intercollegiate sport''--
 (A) means a sport played between
 institutions for which eligibility requirements for
 participation by a student athlete are established by
 an interstate intercollegiate athletic association;
 and
 (B) does not include a recreational,
 intramural, or club sport.
 (14) Likeness.--With respect to a student athlete,
 the term ``likeness'' means a physical or digital depiction or
 representation that identifies, is linked to, or is reasonably
 linked to the student athlete, including--
 (A) the uniquely identifiable body,
 physical characteristics, or voice of the student
 athlete;
 (B) any other mark that identifies or
 distinguishes the student athlete; or
 (C) the jersey number associated with the
 student athlete during the period of athletic
 participation by the student athlete at an institution
 if the jersey number is accompanied by--
 (i) a logo or color scheme that is
 clearly associated with the institution;
 or
 (ii) some other means by which the
 jersey number is associated with the student
 athlete.
 (15) Name.--With respect to a student athlete, the
 term ``name'' means the first or last name that identifies the
 student athlete, a nickname or assumed name of the student
 athlete, or a username associated with the student athlete on
 any public-facing internet platform when used in a context that
 identifies, is linked to, or is reasonably linked to the
 student athlete.
 (16) Name, image, and likeness agreement.--The
 term ``name, image, and likeness agreement'' means a contract
 or similar agreement between a student athlete (or group of
 student athletes) and a conference, institution,
 intercollegiate athletic association, associated entity,
 collective, or third party regarding the commercial use of the
 name, image, and likeness rights of the student athlete (or
 group of student athletes).
 (17) Name, image, and likeness rights.--The term
 ``name, image, and likeness rights'' means the ability of a
 student athlete to market and profit from the commercial use of
 his or her name, image, or likeness.
 (18) Prospective student athlete.--The term
 ``prospective student athlete'' means an individual who is
 recruited, actively being recruited, or has been contacted for
 the purposes of recruitment to attend an institution as a
 student athlete, but has not yet enrolled at the
 institution.
 (19) Revenue share cap.--The term ``revenue share
 cap'' means the Benefits Pool Limit set forth in the Injunctive
 Relief Settlement Agreement approved by the court in ``In Re
 College Athlete NIL Legislation'', No. 20-cv-03919 (N.D. Cal.
 June 6, 2025), or as modified pursuant to the amendment
 provision specified in paragraph 55 of that
 settlement.
 (20) Student athlete.--The term ``student
 athlete'' means an individual who is enrolled as a full-time
 student at an institution and who--
 (A) makes satisfactory progress towards
 completing a degree; and
 (B) participates in intercollegiate
 athletic competition or competes for a varsity sports
 team as part of the institution's educational,
 developmental, or extracurricular programs.
 (21) Third party.--The term ``third party'' means
 an individual or entity that is not an institution, associated
 entity, collective, conference, or intercollegiate athletic
 association.
 (22) Valid business purpose.--The term ``valid
 business purpose'' means a purpose genuinely related to the
 promotion of goods or services provided to the general public
 for profit.
 (23) Varsity sports team.--The term ``varsity
 sports team'' means a sports team composed of student athletes
 that is organized by an institution for the purpose of
 intercollegiate athletic competition.

 SEC. 101. NAME, IMAGE, AND LIKENESS PROTECTIONS.

 (a) Student Athlete Name, Image, and Likeness
Compensation.--
 (1) In general.--Except as provided in this title,
 an institution, conference, intercollegiate athletic
 association, or any representative of such an entity may not--

 (A) restrict the ability of a student
 athlete, group of student athletes, or prospective
 student athlete--
 (i) to market or earn compensation
 for the value of their name, image, or likeness
 rights; or
 (ii) to enter into a name, image,
 and likeness agreement;
 (B) restrict the eligibility for
 intercollegiate athletic competition for a student
 athlete or prospective student athlete on the basis of
 the student athlete or prospective student athlete
 entering into a name, image, and likeness agreement or
 marketing or earning compensation for the value of
 their name, image, or likeness;
 (C) unless otherwise required by law,
 limit the eligibility or opportunity of a student
 athlete or prospective student athlete to apply for or
 receive a grant-in-aid, including the amount, duration,
 or renewal of such grant-in-aid, on the basis of the
 student athlete or prospective student athlete entering
 into a name, image, and likeness agreement, or
 marketing or earning compensation for the value of
 their name, image, or likeness; or
 (D) unless otherwise required by law,
 revoke, reduce, or decline to renew a grant-in-aid for
 a student athlete or prospective student athlete based
 on the student athlete or prospective student athlete
 entering into a name, image, and likeness agreement or
 marketing or earning compensation for the value of
 their name, image, or likeness.
 (2) Consent and compensation for group use.--An
 institution, conference, intercollegiate athletic association,
 collective, third party, or any representative thereof, may not
 use the name, image, or likeness of any group of student
 athletes to sell or promote any product or service unless the
 institution, conference, athletic association, collective, or
 third party, as the case may be, obtains an agreement from each
 member of the group for that purpose.
 (3) Exceptions.--
 (A) Certain agreements.--An institution
 may restrict the eligibility for intercollegiate
 athletic competition of a student athlete or
 prospective student athlete who enters into a name,
 image, and likeness agreement that violates the code of
 student conduct of the institution that applies to all
 students enrolled at the institution.
 (B) Certain uses.--An institution may
 restrict the eligibility for intercollegiate athletic
 competition of a student athlete or prospective student
 athlete if, in connection with a name, image, and
 likeness agreement, the student athlete or prospective
 student athlete uses a facility, uniform, equipment,
 registered or unregistered trademark, copyright-
 protected product, or the official logo, mark, or other
 indicia of the institution without the express consent
 of the institution.
 (b) Mandatory Disclosures by Student Athletes.--
 (1) In general.--All student athletes shall report
 to their institution--
 (A) not later than 30 days after entering
 into a name, image, and likeness agreement, the terms
 of any such agreement that exceeds $600 in value,
 including multiple payments, remunerations, or benefits
 from the same entity that exceeds a total of $600 over
 a 12-month period; and
 (B) to the extent not reported under
 subparagraph (A), not later than 30 days after
 receiving compensation for the name, image, or likeness
 of the student athlete, the amount and source of any
 such compensation that exceeds $600, including multiple
 payments, remunerations, or benefits from the same
 entity that exceeds a total of $600 over a 12-month
 period.
 (2) Mandatory disclosures by recruited athletes.--
 With respect to a student athlete or prospective student
 athlete who is recruited to attend, but is not yet enrolled in,
 an institution, the student athlete or prospective student
 athlete shall report to the institution--
 (A) the terms of any current or ongoing
 name, image, and likeness agreement that exceeds $600
 in value, including multiple payments, remunerations,
 or benefits from the same entity that exceeds a total
 of $600 over a 12-month period; and
 (B) to the extent not reported under
 subparagraph (A), the amount and source of any current
 or ongoing name, image, and likeness compensation that
 exceeds $600, including multiple payments,
 remunerations, or benefits from the same person that
 exceeds a total of $600 over a 12-month
 period.
 (3) Exception.--
 (A) In general.--Paragraphs (1) and (2)
 shall not apply to either marketing or earning
 compensation for the value of the name, image, and
 likeness rights of a student athlete or to the
 compensation within a name, image, and likeness
 agreement in which a student athlete receives less than
 $600, including multiple payments, remunerations, or
 benefits from the same person that totals less than
 $600 over a 12-month period.
 (B) Adjustment for inflation.--An
 intercollegiate athletic association shall adjust the
 amount described in clause (i) for inflation by the
 percent increase, if any, in the Consumer Price Index
 for All Urban Consumers published by the Bureau of
 Labor Statistics of the Department of Labor for the
 most recent 12-month period for which applicable data
 is available.
 (4) Release of information.--Except as provided in
 section 104, an institution may not release any information
 provided by a student athlete or prospective student athlete in
 a disclosure under paragraph (1) or (2) without the express
 written consent of the student athlete, prospective student
 athlete, athlete agent of the student athlete or prospective
 student athlete, or, in case of a minor, the parent or legal
 guardian of the minor.
 (5) Limitation.--This subsection shall apply only
 to Division I institutions as defined by bylaw 20.9 of the
 National Collegiate Athletic Association, or a successor bylaw,
 and student athletes or prospective student athletes of such
 institutions.
 (c) Name, Image, or Likeness Compensation by
Institutions.--Subject to the requirements of this title, an
institution, intercollegiate athletic association, conference,
collective, associated entity, or third party, may pay, provide, or
facilitate compensation to a student athlete for the use of the name,
image, or likeness of the student athlete.
 (d) Right to Representation.--An institution,
intercollegiate athletic association, or conference may not restrict
the eligibility for intercollegiate athletic competition, or any other
event or activity relating to intercollegiate athletic competition, of
a prospective student athlete or student athlete based on the
prospective student athlete or student athlete having obtained an
athlete agent or legal representative.
 (e) Educational Resources Regarding This Title.--An
intercollegiate athletic association shall provide student athletes and
prospective student athletes and the parents or guardians of student
athletes or prospective student athletes with educational materials
relating to this title.

 TRUST ACT.

The Full Table: 500 Years, One Machine, Zero Masterminds — Everything We Found, Told Straight
We've covered a lot of ground. Five hundred years of it. Kings, preachers, bankers, generals, statues, flags, maps, and highways. If you just found this table, welcome. Grab a seat. If you've been here since the start, thank you. Either way, this is the catch-up. No big words. No homework. Just the story, start to finish, the way you'd tell it to a friend on the porch.
Let's go.
Part One: Before America Was America
Picture Europe about six hundred years ago. One church. One story. Everybody was told the same thing about God, money, and who was in charge. Kings ruled because God said so. Poor people stayed poor because God said so. The story was simple and it worked for the people telling it. Then the story cracked. New continents, new money, new questions. The old answers started to fray. That is the soil everything later grew in. The machine did not begin in America. It just found better tools once it got here.
Part Two: The Go-Between Who Got Used Up
Albert Pike starts as a self-made lawyer who actually knew the Native nations he later recruited. The Confederacy needed him because five nations had already survived a death march less than twenty-five years earlier and had every reason to distrust the United States. Pike offered treaties that promised they would only defend their own land. They took the bet. The promise broke the first time his superiors needed extra men outside Indian Territory. At Pea Ridge the alliance frayed, scalping stories exploded, and Pike’s own command turned on him with charges that later fell apart. He resigned from hiding. The system used him, then discarded him. After he died, two fake stories grew around his name—one claiming he secretly ran the Klan, another a forged letter about three world wars. Neither holds up. What does hold up is the pattern: the machine does not need a mastermind. It runs on people reaching for the story that already fits what they want to believe.
Part Three: The Pedestal That Kept Lying
In 1898 Congress let the Scottish Rite put a statue of Pike in Washington—the only outdoor Confederate officer ever given that honor—on one condition: show him as a civilian. The plaque listed seven polite words. None of them said Confederate. The statue stood for more than a century. In 2020 protesters pulled it down and burned it. In 2025 an executive order put it back. Both sides reached for versions that fit their prior beliefs. One side repeated charges against Pike that the record never settled. The other side treated the missing word on the plaque as proof the statue was innocent. The pedestal itself is the machine: whoever stands closest decides what goes back on it.
Part Four: Written by Everyone
Reconstruction actually promised something. The 13th, 14th, and 15th Amendments, backed by federal troops, made citizenship and voting real for a decade. Black men held office. Communities built schools and businesses. Then the 1876 election produced a backroom deal. Southern Democrats accepted Hayes; Republicans pulled the last troops. Nobody voted for the Compromise of 1877. It simply ended the protection. What replaced it was convict leasing, debt peonage, and laws written carefully without the word “race.” The myth that made all of that feel like order instead of theft was built by four separate groups who never coordinated: the United Daughters of the Confederacy raising monuments and rewriting textbooks, a Columbia professor whose “Dunning School” dominated classrooms for half a century, a novelist and filmmaker whose Birth of a Nation gave the second Klan its origin story, and a sitting president whose own scholarship supplied the title cards. Four machines, same story, no single author.
Part Five: The Flag That Went Quiet, Then Woke Up
For eighty years after the war the Confederate battle flag mostly stayed folded. It was a grief object at reunions. Then 1948: the Dixiecrats needed a symbol of resistance to federal civil-rights pressure. The flag reappeared on the convention floor. After Brown v. Board, Georgia redesigned its state flag around it in 1956. South Carolina raised it over the capitol in 1961–62. Alabama raised it the day Robert Kennedy arrived to talk desegregation with George Wallace. Local councils and Klan chapters flew the same flag while they carried out the violence. Nobody coordinated the timing. Four different places reached for the same eighty-year-old symbol the moment the same federal pressure arrived. The first wave of myth-building had already left the flag lying around for the second wave to pick up.
Part Six: Still Born
Gold appeared on Cherokee land in Georgia. The state extended its laws into Cherokee territory. A missionary refused the license and was convicted. The Supreme Court ruled 5–1 that Georgia had no authority. Chief Justice Marshall called the Cherokee a distinct political community. Georgia ignored the ruling. President Andrew Jackson did nothing. The famous quote—“John Marshall has made his decision, now let him enforce it”—is almost certainly invented decades later. What Jackson actually wrote was colder: the decision was “still born.” Removal itself ran through a treaty signed by a minority Cherokee faction and ratified by one Senate vote. Jackson was already out of office when the army marched sixteen thousand people west and roughly four thousand died. Five nations went through versions of the same removal. The machine did not need one defiant one-liner. It needed convenience to line up, and it did.
Part Seven: Land, and Till It By Our Own Labor
January 1865. Secretary of War Stanton and General Sherman sat down with twenty Black leaders in Savannah and asked what freedom required. Garrison Frazier, a minister who had bought his own freedom, answered first: land, and the chance to till it by their own labor. Nearly all the others agreed. Four days later Sherman issued Special Field Order No. 15. Roughly four hundred thousand acres of coastal land were set aside in forty-acre plots. Forty thousand people were already farming it within months. Lincoln was killed. Andrew Johnson became president and began restoring the land to the former owners. By the end of 1865 the order was reversed. Union soldiers who had once protected the new owners now enforced the eviction. One man closed the door. The rest of the machine—laws, compromises, myths—kept it closed for a century.
Part Eight: Same Slavery, New Name
The moment the land went back, Southern legislatures wrote the Black Codes. Mississippi’s version made it a crime for a Black resident to be without a labor contract. Anyone could arrest a worker who left early and collect a bounty from the worker’s own wages. Unpaid fines meant the sheriff auctioned the person off. The word “slavery” never appeared. Congress fought back for a short window: Civil Rights Act of 1866, 14th and 15th Amendments, and the Ku Klux Klan Act of 1871. Grant suspended habeas corpus in nine South Carolina counties. Federal cavalry and U.S. marshals broke the first Klan. Attorney General Amos Akerman, a former Confederate, pushed the prosecutions. It lasted about a year. Then the will faded. Convictions were light. Federal appetite disappeared. By the mid-1870s the state governments were back under white Democratic control and the machine no longer needed federal troops standing in its way. Three chances in twelve years—land, law, and a real year of force—all closed.
Part Nine: The Loophole and the One Vote
The 13th Amendment ended slavery “except as a punishment for crime.” Those four words became the industrial loophole. States leased convicts to private companies. Alabama’s system put men in coal mines for thirteen to sixteen hours a day; ninety percent were Black, many arrested on trivial charges. By 1912 the practice generated nearly a third of the state’s revenue. It lasted until 1928. At the same time a deliberate test case was built in Louisiana. Homer Plessy, seven-eighths white, boarded a whites-only car on purpose, with a private detective hired to make sure he was arrested. The Supreme Court ruled 7–1 that “separate but equal” was constitutional. Justice Harlan, a former slaveholder, was the lone dissent. The decision stood for fifty-eight years. Both halves of this piece were on purpose: a legislature that left the loophole open and a state that built a budget around it, and a carefully engineered challenge that still lost the vote that mattered.
Part Ten: The Map Nobody Saw and the Manual Everybody Read
The viral story is the HOLC color-coded maps of the 1930s—red for “hazardous,” mostly Black neighborhoods. The maps were real. They were also almost certainly not the weapon. They were filed away; scholars have not found a single loan denied because of them. The real tool was the Federal Housing Administration’s Underwriting Manual. It told underwriters to treat the arrival of Black residents as a risk to property values. It recommended racial covenants in deeds. After the war the FHA and the G.I. Bill financed the biggest wave of homeownership in history—on the condition that the new suburbs met those standards. Levittown’s lease forbade occupancy “by any person other than members of the Caucasian race.” Black veterans who had fought the same war could not buy. The Supreme Court ended court enforcement of covenants in 1948. The Fair Housing Act came in 1968. By then the houses had already appreciated out of reach. The machine learned to talk like math: risk, value, economically sound. Nobody on the sales floor had to hate anyone. They just had to follow the paperwork. Equity is harder to topple than a statue.
Part Eleven: Right Through the Middle
The Interstate Highway System was a good idea—forty-one thousand miles, federal money covering ninety percent. But a highway has to go somewhere. In city after city the line ran through the Black part of town. Rondo in St. Paul: six hundred fifty families gone for I-94; the state and the mayor apologized sixty years later. Claiborne Avenue in New Orleans: the original plan ran by the French Quarter; the people with power moved it, the oaks came down, five hundred homes vanished under an elevated highway. Overtown in Miami: the Harlem of the South sliced by I-95 and I-395; eighty-five hundred households displaced. The FHA rulebook had already made those neighborhoods “risky” and the land cheap. Planners wrote “blight,” “slum clearance,” “progress.” Nobody had to say the ugly word out loud. The cheap land and the quiet voices had already been lined up. In 2021 Congress finally set aside money to reconnect some of those neighborhoods. Fixing what the bulldozer did will take longer than breaking it.
That is the table so far. Kings who ruled by divine right. A self-made go-between who got used and discarded. A statue that hid the inconvenient word and kept coming back. A myth written by four groups who never compared notes. A flag that slept for eighty years and woke when segregation needed a symbol. A Supreme Court ruling declared stillborn. Forty acres briefly real and then taken back. Black Codes that rebuilt forced labor without saying the word. A four-word loophole and a 7–1 decision that lasted fifty-eight years. A federal manual that turned risk into policy and equity into compound interest. Highways that found the cheapest land and the quietest voices.
The pattern this table keeps finding is the same in every century: the machine does not need a driver who hates out loud. It needs people who believe their own story, a policy that sounds neutral, a number that looks objective, and enough time for the results to look natural. Sometimes the people coordinate. Sometimes they never speak. Either way the line on the map, the clause in the deed, the word left off the plaque, and the road through the middle of town all point the same direction.
We’re close to today now. Close enough that some of you drive over one of these neighborhoods on the way to work. Next time you’re on the interstate, look down.
Still building. Still listening.

The Inspector-General of Police and the Commandant-General of the NSCDC are public servants and heads of statutory security institutions. They are not elected political office-holders, and their presence in a state in the course of their official security responsibilities is not the same thing as a political delegation from the Federal Government visiting victims and their families.

text:
Could the Islamic Mahdi and the biblical Antichrist be connected? Great question. 

I think there are some fascinating parallels worth considering, but we should also be careful not to say more than Scripture says.

From a pre-tribulational, dispensational perspective, I believe Scripture teaches that after the Church is caught up to be with Christ, a powerful world leader will emerge during Daniel’s seventieth week. Scripture describes him as the “man of sin” or “man of lawlessness,” the “little horn,” and the beast of Revelation (Daniel 7; 2 Thessalonians 2; Revelation 13).

He will initially appear to offer solutions in a world desperately looking for answers. Daniel 9:27 indicates that he will confirm a covenant involving Israel, but halfway through that seven-year period he will break it. Eventually, he will exalt himself, demand worship, persecute those who refuse his authority, and stand in opposition to the true Messiah.

That raises an interesting question when we look at Islamic eschatology.

In Islamic tradition, the Mahdi is an expected end-times leader who will emerge before the final judgment, bring justice, unite the Muslim community, and particularly in some traditions; rule alongside the returning Jesus.

Does that mean the Mahdi is the biblical Antichrist? I wouldn’t go that far.

The Bible never mentions the Mahdi, and Islamic traditions concerning the Mahdi developed centuries after the New Testament. So identifying the two as the same individual goes beyond what Scripture actually tells us.

But could Islamic expectations surrounding the Mahdi someday play a role in how people interpret or receive an end-times political or religious leader? I think that is a legitimate question to consider.

There are certainly intriguing similarities between various end-times expectations: a powerful leader arising during global turmoil, promises of peace and justice, worldwide religious significance, events centered around Israel and Jerusalem, and a climactic confrontation before the establishment of God’s Kingdom. But similarities are not the same thing as identification.

Our confidence shouldn’t rest on trying to match every current religion, government, leader, or geopolitical event to a character in Revelation. Jesus warned repeatedly about deception in the last days (Matthew 24:4–5, 23–27).

The better question is not simply, “Who is the Antichrist?” It is, “Do I know the true Christ?”

The Antichrist will ultimately be defeated, not by an election, an army, or a human movement, but by Jesus Christ Himself.

Paul says the Lord Jesus will destroy the lawless one “with the breath of His mouth” and bring him to nothing by the appearance of His coming (2 Thessalonians 2:8).

Revelation 19 gives us the same conclusion.

So yes, I think the parallels between Islamic end-times expectations and biblical prophecy are interesting and worth studying. But I would hold the Mahdi/Antichrist connection as a possibility, not a biblical certainty.

What Scripture makes certain is far more important:
-Christ will gather His Church.
-A time of unprecedented tribulation is coming.
-A counterfeit ruler will arise.
-Jesus Christ will return in glory.

And the counterfeit kingdom of this world will ultimately give way to the Kingdom of the true King.

Our hope isn’t in identifying the Antichrist before everyone else. Our hope is in knowing Jesus Christ and being ready for His return.

“Even so, come, Lord Jesus!” — Revelation 22:20
