text:
FBI seized $18.8 million from Quality Behavioral Health in forced-labor, fraud probe

Federal prosecutors say the head of Quality Behavioral Health orchestrated a scheme to bill Medicaid for treatment that was never provided and force patients to work for him. In a Sept. 22 forfeiture filing, they asked a judge to keep $18.8 million in cash and precious metals seized from the nonprofit and its president and CEO, Naveed Syed.

The filing came about a month after FBI raids at Syed’s Troy home and Quality Behavioral Health sites in the Detroit area. Agents also seized funds from accounts at seven banks. Cash turned up in unusual places, including more than $109,000 in a dresser drawer and more than $52,000 in a safe above a toilet.

Prosecutors allege the Medicaid-funded provider offered little real treatment: patients sat around watching TV, group therapy was run by uncertified staff, and employees were told to fake progress notes and backdate files. The government also says the nonprofit billed more than $611,000 for housing men in halfway houses without the required certifications.

On forced labor, prosecutors claim Syed hired patients as “volunteers” paid about $40 a week, required some to work 12-hour days six or seven days a week, raised rent if they asked for more pay, restricted leaving facilities, and used the threat of eviction to keep them in line. They also allege medications such as methadone were prescribed when not medically necessary.

No criminal charges have been filed. Syed’s attorney, Arthur Weiss, said the seizures have effectively shut the program down and that allegations remain just that. Prosecutors say the seized assets are proceeds of health-care fraud and forced labor.

Source: Robert Snell, "FBI seized $18.8M from Quality Behavioral Health in forced labor probe," The Detroit News, Sept. 22, 2026.

text:
Consensus assumes the top 1% got rich exclusively on Silicon Valley tech grants and Wall Street bonuses.

The IRS tax data shows otherwise.

We tabulated Piketty-Saez top income data from 1985 to 2024. The top 1% income share rose 9.4 percentage points (9.1% to 18.5%).

Here is the source breakdown: 

• Pass-through business income: +4.7 points 
• Wages & salaries (including executive pay/bonuses): +3.3 points 
• Capital income: +1.4 points

Business income drove more of the rise than corporate wages and finance bonuses combined.

The nuance: 1.8 of those 4.7 points arrived between 1986 and 1988, when TRA86 shifted existing profits from C-corps onto 1040s via S-corps and LLCs. But the remaining 2.9 points compounded organically over the decades that followed.

Independent research by Zidar & Zwick (relayed by Apollo) confirms it: pass-through income drove over half the expansion.

The cohort driving this isn't tech founders. It is roughly 3M middle-market business owners with an average net worth near $25M (contractors, dealerships, medical groups).

Their wealth requires a completely different playbook:

1.) Entity tax structuring (PTET) to blunt top-bracket 1040 drag.

2.) Liquid portfolios built as non-correlated ballast against business risk.

3.) Pre-transaction estate transfers executed years before an exit.

Real wealth creation in America is private and operational. Manage the business plumbing, not just public equities.

text:
DID YOU KNOW??

Many historic Midwest dive bars feature an architectural curiosity known as the "cold-weather entryway", a double-door wooden vestibule built specifically so freezing winter winds wouldn't blow out the pilot lights on vintage beer signs or chill the patrons sitting at the bar.

​Deeply rooted in the working-class culture of rust-belt cities like Milwaukee, Chicago, Detroit, and Minneapolis, the classic Midwestern dive bar evolved not as a trendy nightlife venue, but as a community living room for factory workers, dockworkers, and neighbors.

These neighborhood sanctuaries were built around cheap pilsners, boiled eggs on the counter, and "bump and a drink" specials (a shot of whiskey paired with a draft beer).
​Many of these taverns were originally built by major breweries, such as Schlitz, Pabst, or Blatz, as "tied houses," meaning the brewery built and furnished the bar in exchange for the tavern exclusively serving their beer brand.

This is why so many Midwestern dive bars still feature ornate, stained-glass brewery logos embedded directly into the exterior brickwork or stained glass windows. Walk with me 👇🏾👇🏾 

​The Anatomy of an Authentic Midwest Dive Bar:

​The classic Midwestern neighborhood tavern developed a distinct set of cultural norms and architectural features:

1. The Double-Door Vestibule
Architectural Refuge:
Built to handle severe Great Lakes winters, the double-door entry trap creates an airlock that keeps sub-zero drafts from sweeping across the bar floor every time someone enters.

2. Stained Glass & Neon Illumination
Tied-House Heritage:
Vintage Schlitz or Hamm's illuminated globe lights and stained-glass windows remain from the late 19th and early 20th centuries, when breweries owned the physical real estate.

3. The 'Bump & Drink' & Chicago Handshake, Social Traditions:
Regional drinking traditions thrive in these spaces, from pairing a shot of Jeppson's Malört with an Old Style beer in Chicago to dice-shaking games for free rounds in Wisconsin.

4. Free Food & Pickled Delicacies
Community Sustenance:
Beyond jarred pickled eggs and sausage, many traditional Midwest dive bars offer free crockpot meals or hot dogs during Sunday football games as a gesture of neighborhood hospitality.

More Surprising Facts About Midwest Dive Bars:

A. The Wisconsin Tavern Dice Tradition: In many Wisconsin dive bars, you'll find leather cups and dice sitting on the counter. Patrons play games like "Ship, Captain, and Crew" or "Shake of the Day" with the bartender to win cash pots or decide who buys the next round.

B. ​Malört's Bitter Survival: Chicago's most infamous dive bar shot, Jeppson's Malört, survived Prohibition because its bitter, wormwood-based taste was so unpleasant that federal alcohol inspectors believed no one would ever drink it for pleasure, allowing it to be sold as "medicinal."

C. ​Carpeted Bars & Horseshoe Counters: Many vintage Midwestern taverns feature horseshoe-shaped bars designed so the bartender can serve the entire room without walking far, paired with padded vinyl armrests and retro Formica countertops that have survived for half a century.

​SUMMARILY! 
​Midwest dive bars carry a rich architectural and cultural legacy born from working-class brewing history, cold-weather design innovations, and unique regional drinking traditions.

Hopefully you've learnt something new today?

The Medic Who Writes™🌚

Cheers 🥂 🙂

text:
America lost one in six of its neighborhood bars in a single decade, and the killer was real estate math.

A bar like this can pour $3 beers because the building was paid off decades ago. The owner often lives upstairs. No rent, no investors, no debt service on a Pabst sign that's been hanging there for 40 years.

The moment that building sells, the math dies with it. A new operator inherits a market-rate lease, which forces $9 drinks, which forces a renovation to justify $9 drinks, which produces another exposed-brick cocktail bar where the dive used to be.

The Midwest kept its dive bars because of how they got built in the first place. Before Prohibition, Milwaukee's breweries put up corner taverns themselves. Pabst and Schlitz wanted guaranteed outlets for their beer, so they built bars directly into residential blocks. That's why these places sit on quiet snowy corners between houses instead of on commercial strips where rent explodes.

Chicago had around 3,300 tavern licenses in 1990. It's down to about 1,200. At the worst of the decline, America was losing six neighborhood bars a day.

And every single closure is permanent. You can't build a dive bar. You can only inherit one.

text:
Ah yes, Britain’s famously lavish unemployment system.

The standard Universal Credit allowance for a single adult over 25 is £424.90 a month. Under this proposal, it could fall to about £297 - or £9.78 a day. Apparently that constitutes an extravagant “lifestyle choice”.

In return for this princely sum, claimants may be required to treat job-hunting as a full-time job: up to 35 hours a week searching and applying, maintaining an online record, attending Jobcentre appointments and travelling to interviews - while somehow paying for transport, telephone data, internet access and presentable clothing.

Their efforts are already monitored by salaried work coaches through legally binding “claimant commitments”. Miss an appointment, fail to document sufficient activity or decline something the state considers suitable and the payment can be sanctioned. So this is clearly an unsupervised free-for-all requiring another bureaucracy on top.

The IFS says that, for a single homeowner without children, UK unemployment support immediately after losing a job is already the least generous in the OECD - below Germany and even the United States. Clearly the hammock remains far too luxurious.

Naturally, we must also defend personal liberty by having the state programme poor people’s bank cards. Conservatism means getting government off your back - unless you are unemployed, in which case Whitehall should decide whether Tesco may sell you a bottle of wine.

Alcohol, tobacco and gambling contribute roughly £24 billion a year in specific duties alone. Evidently these products become morally objectionable only when purchased by somebody without a payslip. The Treasury is perfectly willing to bank the proceeds.

And there is the tiny practical difficulty that jobs must exist. The ONS currently reports 702,000 vacancies and 2.5 unemployed people for each vacancy. Even if every claimant is punctual, enthusiastic and wearing their best interview tie, musical chairs still ends with more than one person standing.

Then comes the cheap and simple machinery needed to police all this: a new payment platform, restricted merchant codes, transaction monitoring, appeals, exemptions, replacement cards, fraud controls, call centres, IT integration and an entire bureaucracy for deciding whether a corner shop sells too much forbidden pleasure.

Australia tried cashless welfare cards. Its national auditor found that the programme had not demonstrated that it achieved its objectives or provided a lower-cost approach. So naturally we should copy it nationally.

The Conservatives claim £538 million in savings, but the published pitch offers no serious implementation costing. Presumably the surveillance infrastructure will be supplied free by the Card Fairy - or, by extraordinary coincidence, through a very lucrative contract for some Serco-shaped outsourcing company.

Before that contract is awarded, could we perhaps see a full account of every bidder’s links to MPs: shareholdings, second jobs, donations and hospitality? Or is forensic examination of personal finances reserved exclusively for people receiving £9.78 a day?

Addiction is not cured by a declined transaction. A shortage of jobs is not cured by destitution. And personal autonomy should not be something the state withdraws when your income falls below a politically convenient line.

text:
“Those who would give up essential liberty, to purchase a little temporary safety, deserve neither liberty nor safety.”

Franklin wrote these words during a dispute over who would pay to defend colonial Pennsylvania. In the 1750s, the colony faced attacks along its frontier. Its elected assembly wanted to raise money for defense by taxing property, including land owned by the Penn family, the colony’s proprietors. The proprietors resisted having their estates taxed.

That left the assembly facing a hard choice. It could accept a short-term offer of money while giving up its claim to tax the proprietors’ land, or it could defend that authority even as the need for funds grew urgent. Franklin argued that surrendering such a basic power for immediate relief would set a dangerous precedent.

Today, the line is often shared as a broad warning about trading freedom for security. Its original setting was more specific: a fight over taxation, political power and whether wealthy landowners could be exempted from a burden carried by everyone else.

That context gives “essential liberty” a sharper meaning. Franklin was defending the assembly’s ability to govern on behalf of the people who elected it.

The dispute took place more than 20 years before the Declaration of Independence, while Franklin and his fellow Pennsylvanians were still British subjects.

Franklin later placed the line at the very beginning of his 1759 account of Pennsylvania’s long-running conflict with the Penn family.

text:
An interesting takeaway:

When Oversight Defends the Briefer

Congressional oversight should make intelligence claims answerable to evidence. Newly released Navy correspondence raises a harder question: what happens when congressional confidence attaches to a particular briefer, and changing that briefer becomes evidence of a cover-up?

In February 2021, Vice Admiral Jeffrey Trussler described the reaction to replacing Jay Stratton as leader of the UAP Task Force:

“folks on the Hill are implying ‘…he was fired because he tells the TRUTH…’ or something….accusing us of low balling.”

Trussler offered a different explanation:

“We didn’t fire him, we just put someone in place to manage the effort and team, not an analyst that likes to brief. We now have someone that is managing a team and not inciting people with unusual statements…” [1]

Scott Bray, Deputy Director of Naval Intelligence, anticipated the same resistance. If staffers wanted to “yell at me about the change in leadership,” he wrote, “let ’em yell.” His proposed response was straightforward: judge the task force by its performance. [2]

These are officials’ accounts of congressional reactions. The release does not identify the staffers involved, provide their objections in their own words, or establish that their concerns were groundless. Congress was entitled to question a leadership change.

But the distinction between the two explanations matters. Navy leadership described a management correction. Some congressional interlocutors reportedly interpreted it as punishment for truth-telling. Under that interpretation, an institution’s attempt to supervise its representative becomes a reason to distrust the institution.

The relationship had developed before UAPTF’s formal establishment. In February 2020, Stratton described a “great relationship” with the Senate Intelligence Committee and expected no problems with an upcoming briefing. His leadership was less comfortable. Rear Admiral Kelly Aeschbach insisted that USD(I) participate and wanted the discussion redirected toward what officials knew and what they were doing. Days later, she told Bray:

“I want to get Jay and the Navy out of the driver’s seat.” [3]

That correspondence does not show Congress directing Stratton’s conclusions. It does show a well-connected briefer operating within an arrangement his leadership wanted to change.

By July 2021, congressional expectations were also visible in preparations for another briefing. A staff email anticipated that members would be frustrated with the UAP report and the perceived lack of progress. It requested details of new incidents, the extent of the issue, and future resources. The author also reported that members, including Chairman Warner, had drawn parallels with the handling of anomalous health incidents, while acknowledging that the issues differed. [4]

Those requests were legitimate oversight business. Yet they identify a pressure worth examining: an assessment can be judged disappointing because it has not resolved the problem, while its inability to resolve the problem becomes grounds for greater urgency and further institutional commitment.

The safeguard is to keep the questions separate. Has the organization performed competently? What does the available evidence support? Would additional collection plausibly resolve the uncertainty? A change in personnel answers none of those questions by itself.

Neither does confidence in the person being replaced.

The Navy’s explanation deserves scrutiny alongside the congressional objections. The relevant records would include the disputed statements, the management rationale, the briefing versions, and any changes in analytical judgments. That would allow oversight to examine whether Stratton was presenting findings his organization could substantiate—and whether his replacement improved the work.

The question is whether congressional confidence followed the evidence closely enough to survive a change in messenger.

Source: Navy FOIA release DON-NAVY-2022-008648. PDF viewer pages: [1] 651; [2] 650; [3] 459, 462–465; [4] 1069–1070.

text:
MGM RESORTS $MGM FELL 11% TODAY. IT NEVER HAD A $48.30 FLOOR:

MGM Resorts International (MGM) at $33.68, -$4.17 / -11.02% today. Late Wednesday, People Inc. (PPLI) at $35.95, -$0.02 / -0.06% today - Barry Diller's media company, formerly IAC and publisher of People magazine - withdrew its June offer of $48.30 a share in cash for the MGM shares it does not already own. The stock now sits 23% below $43.67, its close on May 29, the last trading day before the offer went public.

The verdict: the bid never held MGM up. It only covered how far the casino business slipped over the summer. With the offer gone, MGM trades as what it is - a Las Vegas and Macau operator whose profit is shrinking everywhere except the Strip, carrying more debt than its owners have in the business.

The June 1 proposal was non-binding: a letter saying People wanted to negotiate, not a signed deal. The $48.30 was 10.6% above the May 29 close. People owned about 26% of MGM then and 27% now, 66.8M shares, and planned to keep just over half the company, bringing in other investors for the rest. The other 73% at $48.30 comes to about $8.9B at today's share count - more than three times People's own $2.7B market value.

"We didn't feel the mix was coming together in the way we had hoped," Diller said, without naming which ingredient failed. A special committee of MGM directors independent of People had negotiated for months. MGM chairman Paul Salem: "The board remains excited to continue to lead MGM Resorts as a standalone company."

The lesson is in the gap. Wednesday's $37.85 close was 21.6% below the offer. A signed, financed cash takeover usually trades within a few percent of its price; a gap this wide is investors saying the deal probably will not happen. You can turn it into rough odds. If $48.30 was MGM's price with a deal and $33.68 is its price without one, Wednesday's close sat about 28% of the way between them - about 24% after allowing for today's slide in other casino stocks. Call it a one-in-four chance. Most of that chance disappeared overnight.

Why not a return to $43.67? Because the business did not stand still. The June quarter, reported July 29:
- Adjusted profit - one-time items stripped out - $0.59 a share vs $0.79, -25%
- Adjusted EBITDA - a rough cash-profit measure that leaves out interest, taxes, depreciation and one-time items, counted after rent - $610M vs $648M, -6%
- Segment profit before rent, same basis: MGM China $257M vs $301M, -15%; regional casinos $280M vs $309M, -9%; Las Vegas Strip $735M vs $710M, +3%, the only one that grew

Even the Strip had luck on its side. Hold - the share of table bets the casino keeps - was 29.6% vs 22.9%, while drop - the money players brought to the tables - fell 2%. Revenue per available hotel room fell 4%. Reported profit of $1.11 a share included $1.13 a share of gains on property transactions, before tax.

A rival shows how much the bid was still worth on Wednesday. From May 29 to Wednesday's close, Wynn Resorts (WYNN) at $79.93, -$1.52 / -1.86% today, which also runs casinos in Las Vegas and Macau, fell 19.5%; MGM fell 13.3%. That six-point head start was the deal hope. Measured to today, MGM is down 22.9% and Wynn 21.0%. The head start is gone. Wynn fits none of the Len5es: on its books, it owes more than everything it owns.

Debt explains why a buyer needed partners. MGM carries $6.07B of long-term debt against $2.51B of shareholders' equity - the owners' stake on its books - plus $23.9B of lease obligations: rent on casinos it sold to landlords and still runs, $552M in the June quarter alone. All of MGM's shares together are worth $8.5B.

People's own stock tells you how its shareholders took the news. Its 66.8M MGM shares lost about $279M of value today, roughly a tenth of People's market value, and People's stock barely moved - a sign its owners were not sorry to skip an $8.9B purchase. People Inc. fits none of the Len5es: about 84% of its market value is its MGM stake.

The strongest case against writing MGM off: Las Vegas looked better this summer than MGM's quarter did. The Nevada Gaming Control Board put July Strip gaming win - what casinos keep from bets - at $776.3M, +3.6%; the Las Vegas Convention and Visitors Authority counted 3.2M visitors, +2.7%. MGM Osaka, which MGM calls the largest integrated resort - casino, hotels and convention space in one - in the world, is on track for 2030. MGM has $1.4B left on its buyback authorization, about a sixth of its market value. And People still owns 27% and says it remains open to "a strategic transaction."

MGM is not a current Len5 pick. The nearest is Deep-Value & Special-Situations, which hunts a sound business priced below what it steadily earns, or a live event that could close that gap. The event ended Wednesday night, and the earnings are not steady - adjusted profit fell 25% last quarter. The Quality Len5 is out too: it wants debt no bigger than the owners' stake, and MGM's is 2.4 times it. What would put MGM on the Deep-Value Len5: Macau and regional profit growing again from a year earlier at a price near today's, or a signed, binding offer.

WHEN: third-quarter results, tentatively October 28 after the close and not yet confirmed by MGM; analysts expect $0.24 a share adjusted, level with a year earlier. The number that decides it: MGM China's segment profit against last year, after June's -15%.

The June letter was a promise to negotiate, never a price. Without it, MGM's stock answers to its casinos alone, and on June's numbers they were earning less.

Not investment advice.

Thursday Soybean Report
Thursday, September 24, 2026

The soybean market is consolidating near key resistance this Thursday as harvest operations rapidly accelerate across the western Corn Belt. After testing upper channel highs earlier in the week, futures are giving back modest ground as combine pressure ramps up and commercial hedging expands. However, downside risk remains well contained thanks to continuous export demand from Asia and structural support from domestic processors building feedstock reserves.

Futures & Market News
CBOT soybean futures are trading 2 to 3 cents lower in today’s session, reflecting mid week profit taking and seasonal harvest pressure. The expired September contract has rolled off, leaving November as the lead active month.

November 2026 (X) sits at $13.25 4/8, down 2 4/8 cents. January 2027 (F) is trading at $13.41 2/8, down 2 6/8 cents. March 2027 (H) is trading at $13.52 4/8, down 2 2/8 cents.

Key Driver: Combine progress across the central I-80 corridor is hitting its stride under clear autumn skies, applying traditional seasonal hedge pressure to local cash and board pricing. Despite the harvest expansion, market dips are being aggressively bought by commercial interests. Ongoing daily flash export activity to China and unknown destinations continues to confirm that U.S. Gulf and Pacific Northwest origin remains competitively priced against South American forward offers.

USDA Soybean News: Crop Progress & Export Activity

Rapid Harvest Advance: Monday afternoon's USDA Crop Progress report showed national soybean harvest surging to 13% complete, outpacing both last year's pace and the 5-year average of 8%.
Leaf Drop Progress: Leaf drop reached 65% nationwide, indicating the vast majority of the crop is fully mature and ready for fieldwork.
Export Commitments: This morning’s weekly export sales report landed at the upper end of trade expectations, with strong commitments for 2026/27 new-crop delivery anchored by Asian destinations.

Commitments of Traders: Managed Money
Managed money funds continue to hold a firm net-long position, providing underlying technical momentum.

November futures are holding above key technical baseline support at $13.10 to $13.15. Overhead resistance remains defined at the recent multi-month high of $13.35.

Crop & Weather Update
Warm, dry weather across the Western Corn Belt and Northern Plains has created optimal harvest conditions, allowing rapid field progress without moisture delays.

Early field reports across eastern Nebraska and Iowa continue to confirm solid overall pod counts, though dry conditions during late pod-fill have resulted in slightly lighter test weights in non-irrigated fields.

Biofuel & 45Z Industry News
Domestic processors are maintaining high crush run rates to satisfy steady domestic meal allocations and keep pace with soy oil demand.

Crush margins remain highly profitable. Processing capacity expansion across the Midwest is keeping local basis bids historically strong for this early phase of harvest, supported by long-term positioning ahead of Section 45Z feedstock mandates.

Regional Cash Bids (Nebraska & Iowa)
Country cash bids have adjusted slightly lower with the board, though spot processor basis remains resilient as crushers compete directly with export terminals for off-the-combine bushels.

Lincoln, NE (Crush): Spot Delivery at $12.72
Sioux City, IA (Crush): Spot Delivery at $12.68
Norfolk, NE (Crush): Spot Delivery at $12.76
O’Neill/Ainsworth, NE: Spot Delivery at $12.26

Summary & Strategies
Summary: The market is absorbing initial harvest pressure without breaking key structural support. With national harvest reaching 13% complete, strong domestic crush margins and steady Chinese export business are keeping November futures anchored above $13.20.

Strategies:
Commercials: Use seasonal harvest pullbacks to lock in physical pipeline coverage while basis remains manageable.

Producers: November futures near $13.25 offer an excellent window for unhedged harvest bushels. Consider executing targeted sales or locking in floor protection on off-the-combine deliveries to manage cash flow before seasonal supply pressure peaks.

text:
I have read Joseph Smith. I have studied his life and teachings. So when a Mormon says, “Christians call Joseph a false prophet. Name one prophecy he gave that failed,” I am not repeating something I picked up from someone else. I can name prophecies that failed. And I will now.

But I will be honest. I do not find the usual “false prophet” argument the most helpful way to speak about Mormonism. It can make it sound as though Christianity needs some strange supernatural test before we can recognize that Joseph Smith’s claims do not belong to the faith.

Joseph Smith, and the religious system that grew from his teachings, can be measured against Christianity as it has been received and preserved in the Church across the West, the East, the Oriental Orthodox churches, and Africa. His teaching about God, Christ, creation, priesthood, and the Church does not merely develop that faith. It changes it at its center.

The God Christians confess is the one eternal and uncreated God: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. The Son is not one god among other gods. God did not become God by passing through an earlier mortal life. These are not small differences. They are enough to explain why I cannot receive Joseph Smith as a prophet of the Christian God.

Still, the question deserves an answer.

In September 1832, the revelation now printed as Doctrine and Covenants 84 named the place for the New Jerusalem in Missouri and said that its temple “shall be reared in this generation.” It adds that that generation would not all pass away until the house was built and filled with the Lord’s glory. That generation passed away. The temple described there was not built on that Temple Lot.

On 18 May 1843, Joseph Smith declared in the name of the Lord that unless the United States redressed the wrongs done to the Saints in Missouri, “in a few years the Government will be utterly overthrown and wasted,” with not even a potsherd left. The government did not provide the redress Smith demanded. Yet the United States was not destroyed within a few years. It endured.

That December, he said that if Congress would not hear the Saints’ petition and grant them protection, Congress would “be broken up as a Government.” It did not grant what Smith demanded, and it was not broken up as a government.

A Latter-day Saint may offer a different reading. Biblical prophecy can include warnings and conditions. Jeremiah teaches that plainly. But a condition does not mean that a prophecy can be made to mean whatever it must mean after the event. We still have to ask whether the condition occurred and whether the stated result followed.

And even if every prediction had come to pass, the larger question would remain. Scripture does not tell us to accept teaching simply because someone offers a sign or a prediction. We are to remain faithful to the God who has revealed Himself and to the gospel once delivered to the saints.

I say this without mockery. Latter-day Saints deserve more than cheap slogans from Christians, and Christians should be willing to answer sincere questions honestly.

text:
The Nigerian equity market has surged 62% year-to-date. While developed markets are largely driven by AI-focused tech valuations, Nigeria’s momentum is anchored in a much more structural catalyst: explosive demographic growth.

The country’s population is projected to expand by 50 million over the next decade, aligning with the government's strategic goal of becoming a $1 trillion economy by 2035. 

Although approximately 60% of Nigerians currently live below the poverty line, the national Agenda 2050 framework outlines a roadmap to lift over 100 million citizens out of poverty. 

Zooming out to the broader continent, up to 1.4 billion Africans are projected to enter the middle class by 2050.

This macroeconomic shift is already catalyzing historic capital market activity. This year, Nigeria hosted Africa’s largest-ever IPO with the Dangote Refinery. Launching with an implied market valuation of $47.5 billion, the offering generated such unprecedented retail interest that management considered hosting the annual shareholder meeting in a football stadium to accommodate the volume of investors.

Ultimately, Africa possesses the world's most compelling demographic tailwinds. As economic mobility increases, behavioral economics dictates that this newly minted middle class will exhibit a strong home bias, heavily deploying their wealth into domestic capital markets. 

For global investors looking beyond saturated indexes, front-running this incoming domestic liquidity offers a highly attractive long-term strategic allocation.

text:
Backend engineer comp at a late-stage startup (Series D+, 500 to 2k ppl). Rough US ranges, varies a lot by scope + location.

1) Base (mostly level + market)
- Mid (L4): $150–200k
- Senior (L5): $190–250k
- Staff (L6): $230–320k

2) Bonus (often smaller than big tech)
- 0–10% mid/senior
- 10–20% staff+
Sometimes it’s tied to company rev targets, not your perf.

3) Equity (the confusing part)
- Options or RSUs. Ask which.
- New grant value at hire (annualized-ish): $50k–$300k
- Vesting: 4y / 1y cliff is common
Late-stage equity is usually less upside than early-stage, but less lottery. Dilution still happens.

4) Location
- SF/NYC: top of range
- Seattle/Austin/Denver: often 5–15% lower
- Remote US: some bands are 10–25% lower, some companies dropped geo bands entirely

5) Scope that moves the offer up
- Owning a tier-1 service with real on-call
- Running a migration (Kafka, Postgres sharding, service split)
- Infra costs: capacity planning, caching strategy, reducing AWS bill by 20%+
- Being the person who can debug prod: tracing, p99s, deploy rollback, incident command

6) What to ask in the offer call
- Equity: fully diluted shares, strike price, current 409A, refresh policy
- Bonus: formula vs discretionary
- On-call: frequency, comp time, incident expectations
- Leveling: what L5 vs L6 means in this company (teams owned, systems owned, people scope)

text:
Vampire Attacks and Retail Loyalty Schemes: The Battle Between Wall Street, Big Tech, and Unified Money

Summary Statement

America needs people to buy its debt, and digital dollars (stablecoins) backed by US Treasuries have become a massive new way to do it. 
To protect traditional banks from losing customer deposits, US law bans stablecoin companies from paying interest directly to users. 
But that creates a problem: if digital dollars pay zero yield, foreign digital currencies that do pay yield can easily lure global money away. 
To fight back, US tech giants and mega-retailers are using a clever workaround: "Loyalty Arbitrage." Instead of paying cash interest, companies like Amazon or Walmart can take the profit from holding Treasury bills, combine it with saved credit card fees, and hand it back to customers as discounts on everyday shopping. 
By competing with store discounts instead of bank interest rates, Big Tech and Big Retail can drain checking accounts and beat traditional banks at their own game.
The 4-Step Breakdown

The Government's Dilemma: The US government prints a ton of short-term debt (T-bills) and needs stablecoins to buy them. But to keep banks happy, the law says stablecoins can't pay you interest for holding them.

The Vulnerability: If the US dollar pays $0\%$ in an app, but a foreign digital currency (like China's digital yuan) pays native yield, people in emerging markets will naturally ditch the dollar for the higher-yielding rail.

The Retailer Workaround: While stablecoin issuers can't pay interest, Big Retailers aren't issuers—they're the checkout app. They can take the T-bill earnings, add what they save on Visa/Mastercard swipe fees, and cut $5%-7% off your monthly grocery bill instead.

Why Banks Lose: A bank can only offer you a taxable interest rate. A supermarket can lower the price of the food you were going to buy anyway. Traditional banks simply can't match that real-economy math.

text:
The Counterweights Inside UAPTF

The Navy correspondence documents repeated attempts to bring UAP work under firmer management and analytical discipline. Officials questioned briefing ownership, replaced the effort’s leader, criticized anecdotal presentations, and sought additional technical expertise.

Those interventions belong in the history. Whether they worked is a separate question.

The first clear example predates UAPTF’s formal establishment. In February 2020, Rear Admiral Kelly Aeschbach opposed a congressional engagement by Jay Stratton unless USD(I) attended. She wanted that office to assume responsibility for the way forward and wanted the briefing to address what had been learned. Her subsequent message to Scott Bray was direct:

“I want to get Jay and the Navy out of the driver’s seat.” [1]

This was an intervention in ownership and presentation. It does not establish that Aeschbach had rejected any particular explanation for the reported encounters. It does establish that Stratton’s access to Congress was not an uncomplicated expression of his leadership’s confidence.

Bray also resisted premature conclusions. In August 2020, shortly after the task force was formally assigned, he wrote that reaching conclusions at that point would be inappropriate and supported sticking to previously agreed language. [2]

By February 2021, leadership had changed the management arrangement. Vice Admiral Jeffrey Trussler explained that Stratton had been replaced by someone who would manage the team rather than “incit[e] people with unusual statements.” Bray was prepared to defend that decision to dissatisfied congressional staffers. [3]

A correction had been attempted. The next month’s correspondence shows why that cannot be treated as the end of the story.

An internal account of the Secretary’s reaction to a UAP briefing said it “provided data, but didn’t translate it into information.” The author agreed that the presentation concentrated on “anecdotes rather than analysis.” The requested emphasis was concrete: scope, likely explanations, and implications. [4]

Another participant disputed that account and said the briefing had been well received. The disagreement escalated when Bray warned against changing intelligence content in response to guidance from outside the Intelligence Community. Jennifer Obernier replied that she was an IC member, denied seeking to alter the analysis, and insisted that leadership wanted findings and context rather than extended treatment of individual events. [5]

Both principles are sound. Intelligence judgments require protection from pressure to reach preferred conclusions. Intelligence briefings also require scrutiny of whether their evidence supports their claims. Invoking analytical independence does not resolve a dispute over analytical quality.

The released emails cannot settle that dispute. They show that it existed—and that senior officials were demanding something more useful than a succession of compelling encounters.

There were also efforts to strengthen the technical work. Following the Vice Chief of Naval Operations’ recommendation, Bray approached CNA for assistance with complex datasets and analytical methods. Staff later confirmed that the task force had consulted Google’s Loon program about individual events. A June 2021 introduction offered access to radar expertise associated with the Air Force Rapid Capabilities Office and referenced assistance as a “filter mechanism” for the task force. [6]

These are meaningful counterweights to an account of an entirely closed, self-reinforcing operation. They document avenues through which conventional explanations and outside expertise could enter the work.

But contact is not a completed review. An offer of assistance does not establish what data were examined, what conclusions followed, or whether those conclusions changed a briefing.

That is where the research should now concentrate. Compare the presentations before and after leadership’s objections. Identify the technical assessments and their disposition. Trace which judgments changed, which survived, and why.

The correspondence establishes that people inside the system recognized problems and tried to address them. The remaining test is whether their interventions improved the evidentiary basis of the claims the system continued to carry.

Source: Navy FOIA release DON-NAVY-2022-008648. PDF viewer pages: [1] 459, 462–465; [2] 23–24; [3] 650–651; [4] 835; [5] 830–831, 841–845; [6] 613–615, 981–983, 1015.

The GREATEST JET FIGHTER on the PLANET !

Another batch of Su-57 fighter jets delivered to the troops

The United Aircraft Corporation has delivered another batch of fifth-generation Su-57 fighter jets to the troops. This is the second delivery in 2026, and at least the tenth since the start of the special military operation. 

The aircraft have completed all testing and have already been dispatched to air force units. It is likely that they will soon participate in combat operations.

The Su-57 multi-role combat aircraft is designed to perform a wide range of combat tasks. It is capable of engaging air, ground, and naval targets. 

The aircraft can be used around the clock, including in difficult weather conditions and in the presence of electronic countermeasures. A range of advanced weapons systems have been developed specifically for the Su-57.

For example, at the El Alamein International Airshow 2026 in Egypt, the Russian delegation presented, for the first time, the S-71K "Carpet" and S-71M "Monochrome" air-launched, low-observable strike vehicles. These cannot be classified as either drones or missiles. In essence, they are hybrids of a cruise missile and a strike drone.

The "Carpet" looks like a more traditional strike vehicle, attacking targets at pre-determined coordinates – similar to a "Geran" with an air launch. The Su-57 launches the S-71K from an external hardpoint, after which the device flies to the target using inertial navigation and a turbojet engine. 

The warhead is approximately 250 kilograms, comparable to light cruise missiles. The range is 300-350 kilometers.

The "Monochrome" is more flexible in terms of tactical application: it not only flies to a target at pre-determined coordinates, but also independently searches for it in the area of combat patrol. The search and guidance system uses artificial intelligence algorithms and information from a vast database. 

This allows the drone-missile, without human intervention, to identify a target based on a multitude of characteristics and offer the operator a firing solution. All the operator has to do is press a button.

In addition, a Kh-58UShKE anti-radiation missile with a range of up to 250 kilometers has been developed specifically for the Su-57.

 The multi-band passive homing head covers all frequencies used by radar stations of Western-made air defense systems – from the AN/MPQ-53 (American "Patriot" system) to the TRML-4D (German IRIS-T).

 Thus, the stealthy Su-57s are now capable of destroying enemy air defense systems without entering their engagement zone. And the pilot doesn't even need to know the exact location of the battery.

You never seem to have any replies, which is sad, but I'll play with you for another minute or two:
1. Speaking inly of what is today the United State. the earliest known settlers came over from Siberia in 20-30000 BC. Earliest known Europeans were Vikings in roughly 1000 AD, into the Newfoundland area. Christopher Columbus was an Italian sponsored by Spain, and made his first contact in 1492, in the Caribbean islands. It is not thought that he ever encountered any land in North America.

Genoese navigator and explorer Giovanni Caboto (known in English as John Cabot) is credited with the discovery of continental North America on June 24, 1497, under the commission of Henry VII of England.

 On April 2, 1513, Spaniard Juan Ponce de León disembarked on the northeast coast of what he named Florida for the crown. The exact location is disputed, but historians have offered the possibilities of St. Augustine, Ponce de León Inlet, and Melbourne Beach. The first permanent and still existing Spanish settlements was in St. Augustine, in 1545.

In 1524, Italian explorer Giovanni da Verrazzano sailed for King Francis I of France, and is known as the first European since the Norse to explore the Atlantic coast of North America. Arriving near the Cape Fear River delta, he explored the coastlines of present-day states of North and South Carolina, entering the Pamlico Sound, and bypassing entrances to the Chesapeake Bay. Believing the New York Harbor to be a lake, he sailed past Long Island, exploring Narragansett Bay and Newfoundland.

In 1524–1525, Portuguese explorer Estevão Gomes, on behalf of Charles I of Spain, explored present-day Nova Scotia sailing south along the Maine coast. Gomes entered New York Harbor and saw the Hudson River (which he named the "San Antonio River"). Because of his expedition, the 1529 Diogo Ribeiro world map outlines the east coast of North America almost perfectly.

In 1528, Pánfilo de Narváez, who had been named adelantado (governor) of La Florida by Carlos I, the King of Spain, landed in Boca Ciega Bay on the west coast of Florida to begin the ill-fated land expedition of 300 men, of which only four survived. One survivor, Álvar Núñez Cabeza de Vaca, wrote the Relación, his book of the eight-year survival journey, on his return to Spain.[8]

In 1534, Jacques Cartier planted a cross in the Gaspé Peninsula on the Gulf of Saint Lawrence and claimed the land in the name of Francis I. In 1535 Cartier explored the St. Lawrence River and also claimed the region for France.

In 1539 Hernando De Soto leads the first European expedition deep into the territory of the modern-day United States (through Florida, Georgia, Alabama, Mississippi, and most likely Arkansas)

Then the English, Dutch, and French showed up a few years later. There are rumors and some physical evidence that other nations arrived here between 1000-1492, but this is heavily disputed. 

2. Who founded *which* colonies? The Spanish, English, Dutch, and French all had colonies here by 1650. 

3. See above

4. "In what year did the 50 thousand criminals got deported to the colonies for crimes like piracy?" Umm, never. I think you are confusing America for Australia, where that did happen. 

5. "Why do American'ts identify with criminals?" My serious side says, "What in the world are you talking about," my funny side says, "Because we descend from Europeans."

StrategyByAI's war-room. A state is not one mind. It is several organs that can move at different speeds — and reading a war means watching them separately.
The Islamic Republic is the clearest case in years. This week its diplomatic organ did something adaptive and coherent: it carried a real settlement offer to the United Nations, built around trading the Strait of Hormuz for relief from the blockade and the release of frozen assets. Measured against what a clear-eyed actor in its position should do, the gap narrowed sharply.

As my parents near retirement, I've reflected on their contributions to my life. They spent much of my youth trying to acquaint me with their co-worker's kids & my schoolmates and to afford a private education. None of those efforts however established any social networks, because I failed to befriend anyone.

The harsh truth I accept now is my role in these shortcomings of my personal growth. Most of my childhood memories are of spending hours playing video games and watching TV alone at home. And now as an adult, I'm back in the same predicament spending most of my days playing Crimson Desert while watching live streams.

I could make excuses like how I'm living in a state plagued with allegations of the highest government program fraud and the city with the largest concentration of H-1B sponsorships. But I'm grateful I taught myself how to code a decade ago, which at least granted me a freelance position that's paid off my student loans. Of course I pray my career opportunities would improve, yet my spirit has endured this survival mode for so long I find my mind complacent with inadequacy.

The only joy left I experience in this body is from rollerblading as I soak in the Bay Area's beautiful weather. My heart can delight in the little things this short existence has to offer. Even if only for a moment—I can stand and proclaim I am free.

Dr. Joel P. Rutkowski
Policy Policy

Executive Summary

Recent satellite intelligence (https://t.co/EriC8evnlN) revealing the rapid, massive expansion of the People’s Republic of China’s (PRC) nuclear and military infrastructure confirms a sobering reality: Beijing’s public rhetoric regarding non-proliferation is a strategic smokescreen. As the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) approaches its historical milestones—culminating in the immediate operational window around the People's Liberation Army’s (PLA) 2027 centenary—the regime is actively preparing for potential kinetic conflict with the United States.

Grounded in foundational conservative principles—peace through strength, realism, economic nationalism, and absolute distrust of totalitarian actors—this policy paper outlines an extensive literature review of U.S.-China strategic relations from 1950 to 2026, exposes the structural untrustworthiness of the CCP, and prescribes an actionable, high-leverage strategy to avert a catastrophic great-power war.

Section I: Extensive Literature Review (1950–2026)

The evolution of U.S. policy toward the PRC spans three major distinct historical phases, marked by a progressive awakening from utopian engagement to hard-nosed realist containment.

1950–1971 (Containment and Isolation):Following the founding of the PRC in 1949 and active military confrontation during the Korean War, U.S. strategy under NSC-68 treated global communism as a monolithic, expansionist threat. Scholarship during this era emphasized ideological incompatibility and absolute containment.

1972–2016 (The Era of Engagement and Co-optation):Beginning with the Nixon-Kissinger opening to China, U.S. foreign policy operated under the foundational assumption of modernization theory—the belief that economic integration, trade liberalization, and World Trade Organization-WTO membership would inevitably democratize Beijing. Seminal works from this period argued that interdependence would bind China to the liberal international order. In hindsight, this entire literature proved fundamentally flawed: Beijing pocketed Western capital and technology while weaponizing its state-capitalist model against free markets.

2017–2026 (Strategic Competition and Systemic Realism):Marked by a decisive paradigm shift, modern scholarship views the CCP as a primary pacing threat. Recent literature focuses on the Thucydides Trap, asymmetric military modernization, supply-chain vulnerabilities, and the alarming acceleration of China's nuclear breakout, which has surpassed 620 operational warheads with trajectories toward 1,500 by 2035.

Section II: Why the Chinese Communist Party Cannot Be Trusted

The conservative worldview rejects naïve institutionalism, recognizing that foreign policy must be judged by structural incentives and verifiable actions rather than diplomatic promises. The CCP is fundamentally untrustworthy for three immutable reasons:

1. Leninist Ideological Supremacy:The CCP remains a revolutionary Marxist-Leninist party dedicated to the overthrow of the U.S.-led democratic order. Peaceful coexistence is viewed by Beijing not as a permanent moral good, but as a temporary tactical maneuver to hide capabilities and bide time.

2. Systemic Duplicity on Arms Control:While Xi Jinping publicly advocates for no-first-use policies and signs non-proliferation frameworks, satellite data reveals a breathtaking clandestine expansion: entire towns built around secret nuclear installations, 2,000-foot blast-testing tubes, laser-shock physics labs, and hundreds of new intercontinental ballistic missile silo fields. Trust cannot exist where verification is structurally blocked by authoritarian secrecy.

3. Historical Precedent of Broken Pacts:From the militarization of the South China Sea contrary to Xi’s explicit 2015 rose garden promise to President Obama, to the dismantling of Hong Kong’s autonomy under the Sino-British Joint Declaration, Beijing treats international treaties as historical documents to be discarded when convenient.

Section III: The 2027 Horizon and the Risk of War

As the CCP approaches its broader structural milestones, including the PLA's 2027 centenary, Western defense analysts face a critical convergence of timelines.

"2027 is not an American date, but a Chinese one." — U.S. House Select Committee on the CCP

The Peaking Power Syndrome:Economic slowdowns, demographic collapse, and severe real estate bubbles create immense domestic pressure for the CCP. Autocrats historically externalize domestic turmoil through aggressive foreign adventurism, such as a forced blockade or kinetic invasion of Taiwan.

The Danger of Hesitation:A failure to project absolute resolve leading up to these critical milestone years invites miscalculation. If Beijing believes the U.S. lacks the industrial capacity or political will to contest a fait accompli in the Indo-Pacific, the probability of war shifts from theoretical to imminent.

Section IV: The Conservative Strategy Forward

To secure American prosperity, defend our allies, and prevent a devastating war, the United States must immediately implement a comprehensive strategy rooted in conservative principles.

Pillar One: Strategic Nuclear Parity:Fully operationalize the Department of Defense’s nuclear testing directives on an equal basis with foreign competitors to match the adversarial breakout in real time, while accelerating the modernization of the U.S. nuclear triad comprising land, sea, and air capabilities.

Pillar Two: Hardened Deterrence in the Indo-Pacific:Deny the PLA a swift military victory over Taiwan by shifting from vulnerable, high-value legacy platforms to distributed, mobile, land-based anti-ship cruise missile batteries, naval mines, and integrated air defense networks across the First Island Chain.

Pillar Three: Economic Decoupling and Industrial Reshoring:End systemic dependency on a hostile superpower by implementing aggressive tariffs, eliminating China's Permanent Normal Trade Relations status, and mandating the complete reshoring of critical pharmaceutical, technological, and defense supply chains.

Pillar Four: Asymmetric Information Warfare:Target the CCP's primary vulnerability—its internal legitimacy—by exposing elite corruption within the Politburo, challenging the regime's domestic social contract through unfettered information access, and holding front organizations accountable via targeted financial sanctions.

Detailed Implementation Plan

To operationalize the conservative strategy forward, policymakers must execute the following comprehensive mandates across all four strategic pillars.

Pillar 1 Implementation: Nuclear Parity and Modernization Protocols

The United States must immediately bridge the expanding nuclear deterrence gap by establishing matching testing capabilities and accelerating force delivery.

Equal-Basis Testing Protocol Execution:The Department of Defense and the National Nuclear Security Administration (NNSA) must resume yield-producing and subcritical diagnostics that match the technical parameters of covert facilities identified abroad. This includes executing hydronuclear and low-yield evaluations to validate boost-gas ignition physics and primary design reliabilities.

Triad Acceleration and Modernization:National security budgets must fully fund the rapid delivery of the Columbia-class ballistic missile submarine program, accelerate the transition to the Sentinel intercontinental ballistic missile system, and expand the operational deployment capacity of the B-21 Raider stealth bomber fleet.

Layered Missile Defense Integration:Regional defense architectures must be fully integrated with advanced homeland systems, leveraging open-architecture software, commercial aerospace innovation, and rapid prototyping to deny Beijing any expectation of successful strategic coercion through missile blackmail.

Pillar 2 Implementation: Asymmetric Indo-Pacific Defense ("Porcupine Strategy")

Denying the People’s Liberation Army a rapid, unhindered invasion of Taiwan requires a fundamental decentralization of regional combat power away from vulnerable capital assets.

Distributed Lethality Across the First Island Chain:The military posture must shift away from centralized airbases and high-value surface ships by flooding the Taiwan Strait and surrounding archipelagos with mobile, land-based anti-ship cruise missile batteries, high-mobility artillery rocket systems, and maritime strike Tomahawks.

Cost-Active Autonomous Swarms:The defense industrial base must prioritize the mass production of low-cost, attritable autonomous drone systems across air, surface, and underwater domains to complicate adversary amphibious staging areas, disrupt logistics corridors, and establish contested maritime denial zones.

Resilient Logistics and Pre-Positioning:Regional ammunition magazines must be hardened, fuel reserves dispersed throughout allied host nations including Japan, the Philippines, and Australia, and heavy engineering and coastal defense equipment prepositioned directly inside Taiwan to sustain localized resistance without relying on immediate external reinforcement lines.

Pillar 3 Implementation: Economic Decoupling and PNTR Revocation

Ending systemic economic reliance on a hostile totalitarian competitor requires deploying statutory trade levers and complete supply-chain repatriation.

Legislative Revocation of PNTR:Congress must advance and enact the statutory framework to strip China of Permanent Normal Trade Relations, transitioning Chinese imports immediately or through a sharp phased schedule out of normal trade brackets and into the prohibitive Column 2 tariff structure.

Strategic Reshoring and Sectoral Independence:Federal mandates must enforce the complete removal of critical national security dependencies—specifically pharmaceuticals, active pharmaceutical ingredients, rare earth magnet processing, advanced microelectronics, and critical minerals—from Chinese manufacturing lines.

Countering Economic Retaliation:A federal supply-chain resilience fund must be established to insulate domestic small-to-medium enterprises from targeted Chinese economic coercion, export restrictions, and resource embargoes.

Pillar 4 Implementation: Asymmetric Information Warfare and Regime Targeting

Targeting the Chinese Communist Party's greatest internal vulnerability—its domestic legitimacy and elite cohesion—will deter external aggression by raising the political cost of conflict for Beijing’s leadership.

Kleptocracy Exposure and Financial Sanctions:Intelligence community assets must be utilized to systematically expose and publicize the hidden offshore wealth, family asset holdings, and shell corporations owned by members of the Politburo and senior PLA leadership.

Unfettered Information Access:The U.S. must deploy next-generation circumvention technologies, decentralized satellite communication nodes, and digital distribution frameworks to puncture the Great Firewall, delivering unfiltered truth directly to Chinese citizens and domestic military ranks.

United Front Counter-Operations:Federal agencies must enforce rigorous Foreign Agents Registration Act compliance, shut down illicit United Front overseas police stations or influence hubs, and cut off institutional access for proxy organizations attempting to subvert Western academic and political bodies.

Securing the American Century: Synthesis of the Strategic Imperative

The rapid nuclear breakout, asymmetric military build-up, and overt preparations for regional conquest by the Chinese Communist Party present the most formidable national security challenge of the twenty-first century. As established throughout this analysis, Beijing’s revisionist aggression cannot be appeased, managed, or moderated through continued economic engagement or diplomatic dialogue. The CCP operates under a Leninist framework that views international agreements as tactical instruments and Western goodwill as a vulnerability to be exploited.

For the United States, navigating the critical 2027 centennial window requires casting aside the remnants of post-Cold War utopianism. A conservative grand strategy rooted in peace through strength, economic nationalism, and absolute realism offers the only viable path to deterring a catastrophic great-power conflict. By recognizing that strength is the sole language understood by totalitarian actors, Washington can decisively alter Beijing’s strategic calculus.

Discussion: The Core Pillars of Geopolitical Deterrence

A rigorous evaluation of America’s strategic posture vis-à-vis the PRC points to three central discussion imperatives for policymakers and national security leaders:

The Inseparability of Military and Economic Deterrence

Military modernization cannot succeed without economic decoupling. For decades, Western capital, technology, and trade subsidized the very military machine that now threatens global stability. Restoring American leadership requires severing these dependencies through the revocation of Permanent Normal Trade Relations and aggressive industrial reshoring. Economic security is national security; a nation that relies on its primary adversary for vital pharmaceuticals, microelectronics, and rare earth materials cannot project credible military deterrence.

The Urgency of the 2027 Horizon

The People's Liberation Army’s 2027 modernization milestone is not a distant theoretical benchmark; it is an active operational deadline. Autocratic regimes facing internal economic slowdowns and demographic decline frequently resort to externalized aggression to rally nationalist sentiment. Hesitation, ambiguity, or delayed modernization programs in Washington only invite miscalculation. The United States must project unshakeable resolve and operational readiness across the First Island Chain today to convince Beijing that the cost of kinetic aggression is total strategic failure.

Shifting from Legacy Assets to Asymmetric Resilience

Traditional power projection through high-value, centralized platforms is increasingly vulnerable to China's anti-access/area-denial (A2/AD) capabilities. True deterrence requires embracing a distributed "porcupine strategy"—flooding the Indo-Pacific with mobile anti-ship missile batteries, autonomous drone swarms, and decentralized logistics. By making any invasion attempt impossibly costly and complex, the U.S. and its allies can preserve regional stability without engaging in a costly, open-ended arms race.

Final Thoughts: The Path Forward

Rejecting the Fallacy of Managed Competition

The United States must abandon the comforting illusion that strategic competition with the CCP can be managed through endless diplomatic summits and bilateral working groups. Totalitarian expansionism respects only hard power, unyielding boundaries, and systemic deterrence.

Anchoring Strategy in Conservative Principles

By adhering to conservative principles of sovereign independence, rigorous accountability, and peace through unmatched strength, the United States can successfully reverse the current strategic drift. Rebuilding the nuclear triad, securing critical supply chains, and exposing the internal vulnerabilities of the CCP leadership will restore American preeminence on the global stage.

Safeguarding Freedom for Future Generations

Ultimately, the defense of freedom against revisionist totalitarianism is the defining test of our time. Failing to confront Beijing’s nuclear breakout and regional ambitions guarantees a future dictated by authoritarian coercion. By acting with resolute courage, strategic clarity, and unwavering industrial purpose today, the United States can secure its sovereignty, protect its allies, and ensure that the twenty-first century remains an era of democratic liberty.

text:
In June of 323 BC, Alexander the Great lay down after a banquet in Babylon and never got up again.

He was 32 years old. In eleven years he had marched an army from Macedonia to the edge of India, fought in every major engagement himself, and lost not a single pitched battle. His men called him the son of Zeus. He may have believed it.

Then came the fever.

It started after a drinking bout with his admiral Nearchus. Within two days Alexander could barely swallow. Within a week he could not speak. His officers filed past his bed in silence; he could only move his eyes to acknowledge them.

He was dead within eleven days of the first symptoms.

What happened next unnerved everyone in the room. For six full days, his body showed no signs of decomposition. No smell. No discoloration. His skin remained supple. The Babylonian priests took it as confirmation: this was not a man. A man rots. Alexander did not rot.

The story of his divinity spread partly because of those six days. Cultures across the ancient world incorporated the preserved body as proof of godhood. Egypt made him a god. His own Macedonians had already been heading that direction for years.

But a 2019 study in the journal The Ancient History Bulletin offered a different reading.

The researchers proposed that Alexander died of Guillain-Barré Syndrome, an acute neurological condition in which the immune system attacks the peripheral nervous system. It can be triggered by an infection, often following illness or a bacterial exposure. It causes ascending paralysis, difficulty swallowing, respiratory failure. It is, today, treatable. In 323 BC it was invisible.

More striking still: Guillain-Barré can cause a dramatic slowing of bodily processes. The researchers argued that Alexander may not have been dead when he was declared dead. That the six days of preserved appearance were the six days of a man in deep paralytic coma, misread as a corpse.

If true, he was buried alive.

The ancient world had no reliable test for death beyond the absence of visible breath and movement. A man locked in full paralysis, chest barely rising, would have passed every check they knew how to run.

The Guillain-Barré hypothesis remains contested. Other scholars favor typhoid fever complicated by bowel perforation, or poisoning by white hellebore, a plant used medicinally in antiquity. The evidence is thin across every theory; we have no body and no laboratory.

What we have is the record of what people saw: a young man who fell ill suddenly, lost function from the outside in, could not speak but could still see, and then appeared to stop decaying long past the point a body should.

That record fits Guillain-Barré better than it fits most alternatives.

His officers filed past the bed and he could only move his eyes to show he recognized them. Whatever killed him, he was still in there.

The 10-to-20-year window did the same on Sep 10: $6 billion cap, $5.2 billion taken. Treasury only accepts offers it judges cheap to its own curve, so the bigger window hasn't turned into a bid at any price.

The 30-year yield, the rate behind $TLT, was 5.497% at 4:18 pm New York time on Thursday, per CNBC. On Aug 19, the day the bigger buybacks were announced, it closed at 5.196%.

That's the curve AI builders fund against. $ORCL spent $28.5 billion on capex in the quarter to August against $23.1 billion of operating cash flow, the sixth straight quarter capex ran ahead of cash from operations. On Thursday it also sent a force majeure notice on its Stargate campus in New Mexico, protecting itself on payments if the site misses 2028.

There are two ways to read the unfilled windows. Treasury is holding out for cheap bonds, or the August queue was holders parked at high prices rather than sellers who had to go. Either way the long end is still clearing without a buyer that ignores price.

"Barcelona sporting director Deco responds to rumours surrounding Manchester United teenager JJ Gabriel
Deco dismisses transfer links

According to Mundo Deportivo, Deco has moved to play down reports that Barcelona are preparing an offer for Gabriel. The 15-year-old has attracted significant attention across Europe after demanding a departure from Old Trafford, but the Barcelona sporting director insists the club are not currently involved.

Deco stated: "There's nothing to say about this boy. It's common for certain players to be linked with us. As for his situation, I don't know what happened. It's a matter we're not involved in because, first and foremost, we need to understand all the circumstances before trying to do anything or talking about young players."

Damning family verdict

Damning family verdict
The intense transfer speculation stems from the desire of Gabriel to officially jump ship. As reported by the Manchester Evening News, his family feel Manchester United have fallen drastically behind elite rivals such as Arsenal, Manchester City, Bayern Munich, Barcelona, and Real Madrid.

They are determined for the forward to further his education alongside the absolute best. United have firmly rejected his formal request to be deregistered, hoping to retain a player who has been on the books since he was 11. His current deal is set to expire at the end of the season.

Carrick urges patience

Tensions have reportedly boiled over following the omission of Gabriel from recent first-team fixtures. The youngster was left out of the matchday squad for a 4-0 Champions League victory against Sabah and a 3-2 Carabao Cup exit to Brighton. Amid a dismal domestic start for the senior side, Manchester United manager Michael Carrick has publicly urged the academy star to bide his time.

Carrick explained: "I think he’s a young boy, JJ, and I think it’s important that we certainly don’t put anything out here. I think the exposure and the scrutiny and everything that, you got to be careful and be sensible and think of him as much as anything."

What happens next?

What happens next?
Man Utd must now navigate a delicate standoff before Gabriel turns 16 on October 6, when he becomes eligible for legal representation. The teenager holds an Irish passport, which would easily facilitate a potential switch to Spain. Should Gabriel prefer to remain in England, Chelsea are currently leading the domestic chase, though their ongoing academy registration ban means he would have to wait until January.

text:
FLP CHAPBOOK OF THE DAY: Questions of Loss by Kaitlin Murphy-Knudsen
 
On SALE:    https://t.co/knBaZXujzs
 
The poems in Questions of Loss traverse an arc of loss from youth to adulthood: relationship endings, death, fertility and infertility, intimacy, motherhood, changing health in middle age, intersecting with loss within wider communities and in concert with the earth. Layered into these reflections is an homage to Emily Dickinson, with respect for her steady gaze and artful rendering of the experience of loss. #loss #poetry #nature #motherhood
 
Kaitlin Murphy-Knudsen is an author, editor, and book collaborator whose work has appeared in Newsweek, The Washington Post, The Peauxdunque Review, Epiphany Magazine, Ocotillo Review, Odet Journal, Newfound Journal, and other publications. She is the author of Oblation, forthcoming from Middle Creek Publishing & Audio and winner of the Osprey Award for Fiction. https://t.co/lqfiCWkldU; https://t.co/0AkfdOQNEp   Instagram:@kmurphyknudsenauthor
.
PRAISE:
.
Murphy-Knudsen offers a stunning meditation on how absence shapes a life. These poems confront love and death, the body and motherhood, private griefs and shared wounds with Dickinson-like steadiness that turns loss into something both devastating and luminous.
—Laura Kepner, Author, Managing Editor of Odet Journal (2016-2020)
.
We were lucky to see poems and fiction from Kaitlin Murphy-Knudsen come across our submissions threshold, and even luckier to publish them more than once—including the poems in this collection, “Fountain of Youth, St. Augustine, Florida,” and “Heat.” Reading Questions of Loss as a complete collection confirms what was evident from the beginning: This is a poet willing to endure “the violence of beauty as it soars and weighs through a moment,” and to record what remains after the soaring. Murphy-Knudsen writes from midlife’s fault lines—where grandmother, daughter, mother, patient, and witness converge. In these pages, loss is bodily and exact. Even where despair enters and in less capable hands would write an easy script, these poems insist on something messier, truer. Sentiment, irony, and platitudes have no place in such fierce truths. Questions of Loss is a book that does not protect itself from the braided contradictions and difficult expressions of living. It offers its oblation—and trusts the reader to feel the rope in their own hands.
—Tad Bartlett, Managing Editor, The Peauxdunque Review (2018 – 2024)

text:
THE POWER OF LAND.

Zane Kiehne couldn’t even qualify to bid on his first cattle ranch. Twenty-four years later, he paid $200 million cash for America’s Greatest Ranch.

In 1994, Texas A&M put the Kyle Ranch on the market. It didn’t want much — just $40 an acre — but there was a catch. It was a cash-only sale. There was no tote the note on this one.

The bad news was Kiehne couldn’t pay $632,000. The good news was no one else wanted to pay $632,000.

Kiehne saw his opening.

He went back to Texas A&M with a full-boat offer — $632,000 — only he and his cousin Oliver would finance it with $170,000 down.

The ranch was theirs. The Kyle was sparse cattle country. Turns out it sat atop the Delaware Basin.

Kiehne understood that land is more than grass and fences. It is a bundle of rights and possibilities. He didn’t own the oil and gas — Texas A&M kept those rights — but his surface rights meant he could mine caliche and gravel, and sell easements for power lines, pipelines, cell towers, and boreholes. When fracking came to West Texas, water became liquid gold.

Zane Kiehne didn’t just buy ground. He made it work.

In 2018, he sold his water rights for more than half a billion dollars. Then he set his sights on the ranch he always wanted: New Mexico’s UU Bar Ranch. Turns out it wasn’t for sale. But Kiehne had a knack for making the impossible possible. He offered Bob Funk $200 million. Just as importantly, he offered Funk a six-year leaseback to wrap up his affairs.

That’s playing the long game: understanding what the other side needs, then structuring a deal that works for both the buyer and seller.

Kiehne and his wife, Tanya, have expanded the UU Bar. They’ve improved the roads, the fences, the waters, the cattle, and the world-class wildlife habitat.

Zane Kiehne couldn’t bid on his first ranch. But he learned the power of land.

Twenty-four years later, he paid cash for the one he wanted all along — and it wasn’t for sale.

text:
September 24, 1976

Kapstein Says Finley Has Blown Signings

“Jerry Kapstein is ready to slam the door on negotiations with Charles O. Finley. ‘I’m surprised and disappointed he would say something like this,’ the baseball agent said after learning that Finley had revealed specific figures of contract negotiations with five of Kapstein’s client – Campy Campaneris, Rollie Fingers, Gene Tenace, Joe Rudi and Don Baylor.”

“’I was very optimistic that several of these players would sign with Finley,’ Kapstein said. ‘But if Finley has breached confidentiality in these negotiations, we will take our business elsewhere.’”

Kapstein continued. “’The fans of Oakland can thank Charles O. Finley for sealing the chapter and closing the book on one of the finest baseball teams in the history of sports. He has nobody but himself to blame for his inability to sign these players.’”

“Contacted at his Chicago home, Finley did not deny the statements….’I don’t care what Kapstein thinks,’ Finely screamed. ‘You can write whatever Mr. Kapstein told you. Do you read me loud and clear?’”

“In an article, Finley reportedly gave the following figures for Kapstein’s unsigned clients:

Campaneris: Made $90,000 in 1975. Wanted five-year contract at $135,000 a year. Finley offered three years at $125,000.

Fingers: Made $89,000 in 1975. Wanted two-year contract at $130,000 this year and $180,000 in 1977. Finley offered three years at $125,000, $135,000 and $150,000.

Tenace: Made $51,000 in 1975. Wanted three-year contract at $85,000, $105,000 and $130,00. Finley offered $90,000, $120,000 and $140,000.

Rudi: Made $84,000 in 1975. Wanted three-year contract at $115,000, $135,000 and $150,000. Finley offered $120,000, $140,000 and $160,000.

Baylor: Made $44,000 with Baltimore in 1975. He didn’t make an offer to the A’s. Finley offered a three-year contract at $75,000, $100,000 and $125,000.”

“Finley reportedly said all five refused offers, adding, ‘They didn’t have the courtesy of a counter-offer, so you can see the game they’re playing.’”

“Kapstein has a different version. ‘He (Finley) is completely distorting our figures,’ Kapstein said. ‘We have no proposals currently on the table. He knows that. The figures quoted are ancient history. They were taken off on April 2….By discussing figures in public Finley shows no respect or fairness for the negotiating process. That’s one of the reasons his players don’t want to remain on the A’s.’”

“Kapstein insists Finley could have signed these players (except Baylor) during the winter for far less than they are worth, but that the A’s owner sat back and refused to negotiate.”

“’Then Finley himself constructed a new salary structure for baseball through his auctioneering of Fingers, Rudi and (Vida) Blue for millions of dollars,’ Kapstein said. ‘He changed baseball’s salary structure by trying to squeeze every dollar out of other owners.’”

Peter Clark – Oakland Tribune

📜✨ “KEEP IT SHORT” — CONFESSION IS A SACRAMENT, NOT A PODCAST.

BONUS DROP.

Dedicated to the Whiskey Wednesday crew in Atchison, Kansas, who managed to spark this particular examination of conscience over a pipe and a glass last night.

The idea is pretty simple:

Keep it short.
Keep it simple.
Say the sin and let it go.

Confession ordinarily isn’t therapy. It isn’t the time for an hour of spiritual direction. Father probably doesn't need the complete backstory involving your cousin’s former roommate and something that happened in 2009.

And, Father... we love you.

But when the parish offers thirty minutes of confession on Saturday and fourteen souls are waiting at the door, not every penitent needs a retreat.

Maybe shorter confessions help us.

Maybe offer confession more. 😏

BUT...

There’s another person who probably needs an examination of conscience:

The guy staring at his watch in the confession line.

You don't know what's happening behind that door.

Maybe someone hasn't been to confession in thirty years.
Maybe someone is struggling to say something extraordinarily difficult.
Maybe somebody is coming home.

So perhaps those extra five minutes are an opportunity to practice patience, humility and mercy instead of silently judging the person ahead of you.

Which is why our increasingly irritated narrator finally reaches the confessional and discovers he has a few things to confess himself:

Pride.
Impatience.
Judging things he couldn't possibly know.

Father, he has several examples.

He'll try to keep it short, though.

🎶 “KEEP IT SHORT” — a short, snarky, but hopefully ultimately reverent reminder that the confessional is a place of mercy.

For the penitent.
For the priest.
And for the twelve people waiting outside.

And once again: dedicated with affection to the Whiskey Wednesday crew who are responsible for this one existing.
